title: Would you eat the moon if it were made of ribs - another curious riff from Harry Caray
excerpt: "Insanity is going the same thing over and over again and expecting different results" - welcome to ecommerce. For years we not just expect the status quo but live for it. Our expectations have been tempered by a well trodden funnel where the path to
_body:
"Insanity is going the same thing over and over again and expecting different results" - welcome to ecommerce. For years we not just expect the status quo but live for it. Our expectations have been tempered by a well trodden funnel where the path to success or failure could be predictable to a large degree. As we have learned, this path may not actually be the best path for us all to be on. What of profitability? - "let them eat cake", I say.
In getting my Einstein quote right, I thought it right to research was it accurately represented. Apparently not. He never even sait it. Misattributions like this happen often. Love the crossover of misattribution, ecomm pun. It is not the only misrepped quote. There are many and interestingly many of them lend themselves well to feelings of a career in ecommerce.
1. "Let them eat cake." —
not
Marie Antoinette.
Most people assume "great princess" refers to Marie Antoinette. Jean Jacques Rousseau wrote those words in 1767 — when Marie Antoinette was 12 years old. She also didn't marry Louis XVI until 1770.
2. "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it." —
Hang on Voltaire
In her well-known biography of the French philosopher,
"Friends of Voltaire,"
Evelyn Beatrice Hall writes,
"'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it,' was his attitude now." The author was paraphrasing how she thought Voltaire felt about a certain topic. Everyone just decided the quote was real.
3. "Standing on the shoulders of giants" —
not
Sir Isaac Newton
But Newton didn't coin the phrase himself. He was alluding to a simile said much earlier by Bernard of Chartres, a 12th-century man.
In ecommerce language
That's just how it is - cos that's how it is - Spending ad $ on Meta
Tone of voice. The discussion between agency and brand owner. Leads to poor results.
Listing on Amazon. Advertising on Amazon. Using FBA. Brand Registry. A+ Content. Customer service. Waiting to fall from said perch.
Even by my standards this is one heck of a digression. Let's get back in line. "As far back as I remember, conversion rates have always been between 2 and 4%."
Henry Hill, Goodfellas.
We have a two tier system and it cannot be sustained
This has become the standard and one many of us in the SMB sector cannot get to. Having gone through multichannel, DTC and Omnichannel we e at a point in time where anecdotal and empirical evidence suggest that this way of working does not work.
Anecdotal -
Boohoo - the rise and fall
DTC cautionary tale
More empirical -
FatFace - Omnichannel retailer
- Hybrid strategy delivered well
2 swallows don't make a summer but there are many, many stories like these. Just open any newspaper or online publication. Adminstrations are rife and profits are non existant. We need to start having hard conversations as to why this is so - as in goodfellas, we need to follow the money. Before I jump in let me qualify this a bit more.
Folks, my I present the most advanced markets in the Western World. This is coming out of pandemic spikes. Since 2022 there has been a marked dropped to sub 3.5% in the UK and US has stopped around 2%.
https://www.statista.com/statistics/960419/online-shopper-conversion-rate-gb/
https://www.statista.com/statistics/439558/us-online-shopper-conversion-rate/
Strategies - SMB
Struggle on tech, hiring, spend and channels to maybe achieve these rates for 3 months of the year, most likely discounting only to do it all again the following year and hopelessly planning for growth.
Profile:
Commoditised products | Ubiquitous in availability | travels well for postage
Strategy success:
Dependent on volume sales and low marketing costs despite the number competitors.
Strategy Constraints:
Lack of distribution | requirement to build brand | data overload leads to lack of decision making | data gets ignored and replaced by cashflow needs
Mindset:
Let's start with DTC and go from there. Be in channels where our customers are " google and meta". Amazon is too expensive, no point.
(Amazon is where 65% of search begins in the US) or #tiktokmademebuyit
Strategies - MultiNationals/Enterprise
Struggle on tech and legacy systems. Don't care. Vehicle for entry to market can by DTC brand acquisition - access to tech, talent, funnel and low risk. Established revenues and proven sales channels.
Profile:
Commoditised products | Ubiquitous in availability | travels well
Strategy Success: Dependent on volume sales but distribution footprint is greated. Volume is lots of sales but margin protection above all is key. Most groups determine commercial viability before anything else.
Mindset: We know retail. We know its dependencies. We are commercial. We will try do Amazon first because as ol' blue eyes said,
"If we can make it there, we can make it.... anywhere. It's up to you... "
In the above scenarios the sunk costs are really only ever recoverable by the MN business.
Why? We are doomed before we start
Like bad airports, without a decent runway, we can get nowhere. Most small to growing businesses have to invest so much in brand whilst concurrently building a business, buying your 3% conversion and being happy to let 97% walk away year after year after year.
As we start 2023, we can look to the data to see how economics and social and political forces are placing even more pressure and force on businesses, already squeezed to the max.
All data courtesy of
IRP Commerce
ce - thanks
Daniel Loughlin
UK and IE focus but similar on other data sets for EU and US.
So to recap these images, what is in our control does not lend itself well to us all drinking from the cup and being satisfied. We are increasinly fighting for a tiny share. This in a world where retention is better than loyalty but retention is hard to foster without significant investment in this part of your business.
Are we focusing our marketing spend in the right areas? I'm dubious.
Evidence would suggest we are spending to get the 97% and ignoring the 3%. What if we were to invest in getting the 3% to 10% over 3 years. What would it take? Smaller funnels?
A point I made early on was that we need to follow the money. Over the last 20 years, ecommerce has been supported by an agency ecosystem that was devoted to this way of traffic sourcing and delivery. There is nothing wrong with whatthey did or how they did it. But investment in the education of ecommerce was either in development or in "digital advertising" - sub sections of skills needed to understand the levers of ecommerce, up until the last few years.
Education was needed in so many other areas - trading, retail, sourcing - actually this is already there. We should have been upskilling buying assistants and merchandisers.
It is October 2023, 1 week after the Shopify Enterprise Love in. Shopify has maneged to take technology and make it usable by the non technical user. Website management is easy and if you cannot do it, a quick trip on Youtube lane will solve most of your problems. Developers beware. This tech evolutiuon has also resulted in different technical skills that are emergent as key - analytical and more important, infrastructure design. This is difficult given the 45,000 different tech providers shopify have.
So all the money of the last 20 years has gone into digital ads and tech. PMAX google set ups and other self serve ad platforms make it feasible to imagine a world where agencies are not neede because, well, Google knows best. This is the world the SMB will/should live in. Google is a transient network for small catalogue retailers.
Emerging ad platforms such as
MNTN.TV
and #RMN are becoming self service - with good reason. They are targeted at retailers, designed for retailers. Margin rules and business rules determins success, not speculation and attribution.
Org Structures
Yesterday, I facetiously posted about the role of the ecommerce manager. Specs are ridiculous and uncover a few truths about the role: It is not 1 role. We do not empathise with the volume of skills you need to do this as a single entity. It shows that anyone with those "all in one" specs are crying out for a lutitude of skills without knowing the priority of each, largely because all plates need to be spinning all at once, all of the time - let's not forget, to get to 3% (on a good day)
Outcomes
Annual poor planning and excitement will be starting now for 2024 and the hope we can land a good influencer, for cheap, along the way. Luck does not bestow itself on those who do not practice hard work. But increasingly, success stories of the profitable ecommerce companies re harder and harder to find.
Hat tip to Aimee connolly and her team - Over $6M in accumulated profits in a business 6 years old. Omni channel. Great retail and brand background - but strategy is clear.
We continually invest in the wrong areas. If there were no adland, what would we do? How would we invest time - we would rearrange our store? Give it a lick of paint in the winter? Determine sales cycles and manage ageing inventory well.
On the vendor side - all 45,000 of you, i have a bone to pick with
you.You
spend 6 months of the year on the road selling your product and then you spend the other 6 trying to convince people not to churn.
Reason 1 - they don't see value
Reason 2- too expensive
Reason 3 - too big for what we need
Most of your clients do not have the traffic or sales to make your software outcomes meaningful. That is a fact - you know this to be true. How about this peak season try something different - unlock your top tier plan for free for 3 months and show what full value looks like. Demonstrate impact. Particularly where conversion is delivered. Show us what the world looks like when customers are on site. Help us spend more on yoru service than on traffic acquisition. Make life easier for yourselves. After all it is almost Christmas, you've earned it.
Make your own version of ecommerce - 2024 Mantra
What do I mean by this.
Choose complexity,
Choose multiple platform requirements
Choose Channels
Choose marketing budgets
Choose multi touch attribution
Choose first party data gathering
Choose 3% ...
Ireland go into a World Cup Rugby Quarter final this weekend against the All Blacks. Us Irish have read the column inches from wall to wall absorbing everything written about this game and will do so until kick off and hopeful the post game post mortem will make our hangovers on Sunday seem worth it. But what is written frequently is that they "play the game in front of them better than anyeone". This is down, in large part, to the knowledge of structure and freedom to be themselves.
So let's say you design a new product tomorrow and want to sell to the world and build a bit of a brand, what do you do? Do you " do ecommerce as we know it? Get 3 years down the line and realise the grind or do you play the game in front of you"
Enter smooth stick - Irish SME brand.
Aine Kennedy designed a great product and decided conventional marketing lining the pockets of Palo Alto was not for her. Her investmentt was in organic marketing on TikTok connected to Shopify - because at the time TikTok shop was not available in Ireland. But I am guessing she would have gone native were this possible. Marketing in one place, customer comms in one place, sales in one place - 75M views later she is running a 7 figure business with her sister delivering profitability. because her complexity is simple, she has been able to use profits to move manufacturing from the far east to Portugal - shorter lead times and better MOQs - control.
Were I starting today, I would do the same. Control your controllables. I will elaborate on this in the months ahead but if you want to talk why conversion rate optimisation and customer centicity should be your core invesmtent areas let me know. I will be hosting a dinner in London and Dublin on these topics and more. If you have read this far, god help you
but you can register here for London on November 2nd.
#retail #strategy #usretail #ukretail #marketingstrategy

title: 2023 A year in Christmas Songs
pullQuotes: "Slip inside the eye of your mind, and you know you might find a better place to play"
"When the kids start singing and the band begins to playOh, I wish it could be Christmas every dayLet the bells ring out for Christmas"
excerpt: In 2005 I completed my college dissertation titled, "MTV: The cultivation of a generation. How they transcended brand to become a lifestyle". Each chapter was described through the thoughtfully crafted lyrics of songs I loved that we linked to this mish mash of research, plagiarism
_body:
In 2005 I completed my college dissertation titled, "MTV: The cultivation of a generation. How they transcended brand to become a lifestyle". Each chapter was described through the thoughtfully crafted lyrics of songs I loved that we linked to this mish mash of research, plagiarism and surrealism. Chapter 4, I remember, used lyrics from the Oasis song, "Don't look back in anger" - the lyrics read (and still do to this day)
"Slip inside the eye of your mind, and you know you might find a better place to play"
In my head, this was a careful tip of the cap to unscrupulous marketers at MTV who somehow knew how to programme our brains and get us to say things like "dude", which in midlands Ireland at the time, was tantamount to using another language altogether. Imagine how I felt when Justin Timberlake brought out his first solo album and it debuted on MTV's the Lick, by Trevor Nelson - a predominantly, Hip Hop show - mind blown.
It set a tone for how I now write a lot of content and how I really poorly combine pop culture throughout my writing with the topics within eCommerce. That said, today we had Pharrell in hot water for releasing the $1M handbag - yes you read that right.
Listening to the brilliant "Smartless" podcast with Michael Stipe this week it reminded me again of the place music holds in my own inner monologue - that unfiltered place where I go to switch off myself but also for some fun. Right now, there is a sameness in LI content and news that makes it hard to understand new ways to deliver new messages. Old dogs and new tricks are clearly misaligned. But, this fool wanted to try anyway. Before we get into the inevitable naval gazing that will land post #BFCM we should start with a little nostalgia.
2023 - what did you promise?
#AI #Profitability #growth #stability #CBT
and more. What a let down you were/are. Now, not making light of global human challenges, which remain existential, I thought it would be interesting to look at those things that did happen but through the seasonal lens of Christmas Songs - the theme to my favourite time of the year. Grab some Gluhwein, eggnog, hot chocolate or whatever makes you happy and whistle your way along this bad office party playlist and join me in the review of 2023.
All I want for Christmas (is your marketing budget allocation) - Mariah Carey - Retail Media Networks message to the FMCG brands.
The growth of
#RMNs
as they are now fashionably called is one of the ongoing areas of interest. Grocery spending continues to thrive (especially online) as struggling consumers divert discretionary spend to essentials. The brands themselves, in an effort to stay on shelf, or satisfy some JBP request from a platform is a difficult watch from the sidelines.
The platforms (many of them) provide little analytics or performance capability and their pricing seems inextricably linked to the price of oil. This old favourite seems like it is well positioned to last beyond Christmas and will be rolled out in 2024 again.
(Not) Driving Home for Christmas - Chris Rea
The cost of living crisis that has been a daily struggle for us all has made many people make some difficult choices. In a recent consumer sentiment report from the US (
The Conference Board
) citing that people are making the choice to drive rather than fly this Christmas due to the increased costs of travel. This is worth noting if you are devoting marketing spend into audio this year. Christmas lists, podcasts and all that good media space will be up for grabs. get in early.
Do they know It's Christmas Time at all - Band Aid
Not discounting this Christmas? Not participating in Black Friday on moral high grounds - well  you can forget about growth at all for 2023. The sheer pomposity of such decision making makes you wonder if these people want to be in business at all in 2024.
Holly Jolly Christmas - The Buble Version
Canada's finest Christmas crooner this year may only be their top 5 exports. Lagging marginally behind Ryan Reynolds and the seasonal favourite Will Ferrell (Buddy the Elf), we see a new Canadian darling emerge in the ill fitting man tights that we call Shopify. Impressive results in their recent earnings calls saw growth, clarity of purpose and the promise of many more glasses of Koolaid (I mean "cups of cheer") to follow in 2024. They had the drinks flowing in LA at their enterprise summit where they told the world they were gunning for enterprise. All the while, hiding their incoming price hikes in the cliff notes of a certain blue notebook. The proof of the pudding will be in the eating and it seems 2024 will let us know if they put too much sherry in the pudding and we are all left with a post Christmas Shopify Hangover.
Christmas Vacation From Lampoons Christmas - Buy Now Pay .. Whenever
The BNPL craze that has been ripping it's way through the world of commerce has created a frenzy not seen since the Beatles on Johnny Carson all those years ago. As great as the Beatles were (are and always will be), they were gone, almost as soon as they arrived. Yet in this short period of time managed to impress us, drive us wild, excite us, empty our wallets and then eventually leave us to pick up the pieces. Sure we had Sir Paul and Ringo in new guises and bands but it was just never the same. With credit card debts hitting $1T and BNPL being used to pay for household groceries, you wonder when the
"Bigger than Jesus"
moment will come for BNPL. (The loose musical inference here is take a vacation from paying, yes I am reaching, but this is all happening in real time, bear with me).
Blue Christmas - Elvis Presley
The retailers. Let's not forget the shit they have been dealt over the last 5 years. Spare a moment. In all seriousness I mean this. It is a tough business on a good day, but with the flexibility and agility required over the last few years, it is a wonder how they keep they going. This year promised so much at the start.
#ASOS
were only going to 20% off in Jan. By Feb it was 70% and the slow precipitous fall further and further into discounting continued. Excess inventory, minimal margin - more, new channels to learn and less time to get it wrong.
And now the winter of Discount tents, I am living that one.
Last Christmas - Wham
The Amazon conundrum - last year it was all rosy in the garden. But a few policy changes later and I can no longer even access my account - WHT Amazon. I have been a loyal seller for years and you just kick me off platform? Why? This list, this song, goes on, in perpetuity every year - this tune is timeless.
The Fairytale(s) of New York - The pogues
VC money has flooded into SaaS, tech and last mile now for too long. 2023 is the year that puts an end to this non virtuous cycle of non performance. Growth charts that looked "Handsome or pretty" and felt "Queen of New York City" are now very much in the drunk tank. Across many industries the message "Won't see another one" ring true all too well and not even a cameo from Matt Dillon can influence change here.
Christmas in Hollis - Run DMC
The old Christmas Adidas classic as told by influencer rap super group, Run DMC is a reminder of the power of celebrity ringing through in 2023. From Taylor Swift to Kim Kardashian and lest we forget Logan Paul and KSI - Prime is a phenomenon. Nothing like it,ever.
I wish it could be Christmas every day - Wizzard
The rise and rise of TikTok - to their seller base that get this right it feels like Christmas every day. It has been a really strong year by the entertainment platform and it seems like it was written in the lyrics. Don't believe me?
"When the kids start singing and the band begins to playOh, I wish it could be Christmas every dayLet the bells ring out for Christmas"
And there ends part 1 of the year of ecommerce in Christmas songs.
What did I miss? What themes?
#retail #usretail #ukretail #strategy #christmas #marketingstrategy

title: First class used to be just a better meal, now it's a better way of life.
pullQuotes: First class passengers, we apologise profusely that you have to live through this negative customer experience. We know you don’t really care anyway. Whatever your title, we got you covered. Alot of VPs, SVPs, Heads of in this cabin and we will not lie, it looks cosy and paid for by someone else. Maybe you rode in on your airmiles. We have not switched off comms to the second class citizens in economy either. We want them to feel like they are on the same journey. They are not. Most will not make the destination, many will turn back and others, well we will have to recover the black box to see how it all went wrong. We call your offering our joint business plan, cos, well, you know the lingo. We know we had you at JBP.
excerpt: Buckle Up for E-Commerce 2024: A message from your in flight team. Good Evening Passengers, this is your captain speaking from the flight deck of "By The Seat of your Pants Air", where our motto is, “We might not always know where we're going, and
_body:
Buckle Up for E-Commerce 2024: A message from your in flight team.
Good Evening Passengers, this is your captain speaking from the flight deck of
"By The Seat of your Pants Air", where our motto is,
“We might not always know where we're going, and we don’t even where if we will get there, wherever there is!”
We’re about to take off into the wonderfully unpredictable skies of online retail. So, fasten those seatbelts – it's going to be a bumpy, yet hilariously entertaining ride. Some notes before we make this journey into 2024.
Seat Belt Sign On - Do not take yours off
Due to the nature of the weather in front of us, we are saying that in flight seat belts must be on at all times. Radards indicate alot of turbulence in front  of us. A christmas of low pressure and the headwinds of economic downturn make for some uncomfortable watching ahead.
The Class System
We are operating in a 2 or 3 class flight tonight. We no longer try to hide it. For our first class passengers we will be sending you a complimentary crafted, digital first care package outlining your flight ahead. For those of you in economy, listen up. Given you cannot afford all of our services your journey is going to be alot different:
In flight entertainment
- Your channels will be limited. You will be operating the same channels you have always enjoyed. They just cost more than they did on your last flight. Also, you cannot select when you watch them. They will be largely linked to your prime account just to make things easier for you.
Your meals:
Due to budgetary constraints, at meal times you will have to select which of our three options you might want. Not all 3 at once, you cannot afford them Select wisely but do not forget just how much you hated our pasta lunch on the last flight. You will probably take it anyway because our revamped chicken bake is not as appetizing as we present it. If you are greenwashing and have dietary requirements, please let us know and we can sneak you the good stuff when no one is looking.
Baggage:
Our eagle eyed observing crew noticed you over packing your carry on luggage to avoid paying for the excess. Rather than put the baggage in the hold, we decided just to offload some of your packing paying little or no attention to essentials or maybe those nice to have destination bits. Sorry, something had to give. However your own lack of attention to detail gives us hope that you may not even have noticed had we not said anything. You will only know when you miss it.
Seating and your family
: Here at ecomm airlines we know you that being together, side by side may not be essential for the duration and we are happy to offer hybrid seating. Enjoy and connect with your family or friends through our in flight comms platform. 60% of the time, it works, all the time. Silos may happen on your journey and thats ok, just ask your seated neighbour where the lifejacket is, bearing in mind it may not be under your seat. And if you are using an agency for this service, cover your own ass first, blow up your own life jacket too.
International Travelers:
If you intend on traveling across borders you are on your own when it comes to customs services. We get you there, you need to do the rest. We are not even sure what the rest is.
Icelandic: Ef þú ætlar að ferðast yfir landamæri ertu á eigin vegum þegar kemur að tollþjónustu. Við komum þér þangað, þú þarft að gera afganginn. Við erum ekki einu sinni viss um hvað restin er.
Japanese: 国境を越えて旅行する場合、税関サービスについてはご自身で行ってください。私たちがあなたをそこまで連れて行きます。残りはあなたがする必要があります。残りが何なのかさえわかりません。
There may be mistakes in the above as we did just about enough with Google Translate to get you there.
Bathrooms:
We have done our utmost to provide a personalised service for you. We can definitely provide male/female services. We do know that most people from 13 - 75 enjoy using soaps and toilet paper. We know a few other things about you, but this should be enough to get you through the basics. You can take your own route to the bathroom walking up either aisle to get the same result. Finally as we have a diverse policy team you can either sit down or stand up whilst you pee. We won’t judge.
Rebooking:
All the way back to the start for you. We will not make this part easy for you. We cannot even guarantee we will have this flight in stock next year. So when you think about your next flight, shop around.
First class passengers, we apologise profusely that you have to live through this negative customer experience. We know you don’t really care anyway. Whatever your title, we got you covered. Alot of VPs, SVPs, Heads of in this cabin and we will not lie, it looks cosy and paid for by someone else. Maybe you rode in on your airmiles. We have not switched off comms to the second class citizens in economy either. We want them to feel like they are on the same journey. They are not. Most will not make the destination, many will turn back and others, well we will have to recover the black box to see how it all went wrong. We call your offering our joint business plan, cos, well, you know the lingo. We know we had you at JBP.
This message will also be delivered through video display, in flight ads, and in some airports that you are not even visiting - that is how different your experience is going to be. And should we uncover new technology during the journey, we have preselected the opt in option so you have something to talk to your linkedin friends about.
Seat Belt Sign:
What seat belt. We have your armchair set to recline. We have switched off the ability to feel turbulence. We have added in long term budget to offset this and bought some air-miles and water conservation back from other third parties to give you a neutral carbon footprint. Your team size on return, may be a little smaller, but don’t worry, they are in economy for the next one and won’t feel the pinch too bad.
Seating
: Where you are going you don’t need seats. Hop from Air BnB to your nearest WeWork and Uber yourself to the nearest morning ice baths. If there is not one nearby, you have gone to the wrong destination.
In flight entertainment:
There are no limits. Just pick a channel, pick a show and go for it. Do not be afraid to test and fail even on repeat. One of the them will stick.
Meals:
A la carte everything with a personal chef on hand to deal with your whims. Portion size is adjusted to your diet type, time of day and you can even enjoy our special “Happy Hour” - eat the little guy’s lunch special. With unlimited porn star martini chasers too.
Baggage:
A hearty congrats to your for packing so nimbly and light. Your Rent the runway account also means you can hire designer on the run. No brand out of reach. And your RTR account ensures your own personal brand is right on circular righteousness.
Seating and your family :
It is your we value, not your family. Our flights might keep you away from your family for long periods, but think of the perks you can get with your airmiles to keep them happy.
International travelers:
Everything will be rooted to your bank of choice in country. Our tax compliance team have the tech to mean they worry about your pennies whilst you focus on lbs. All messages will autotranslate and be presented in formats of your choosing when meeting with your international delegate partners.
Bathrooms:
Your bathroom is fully personalised - connect your spotify account to your shower for optimal music indulgence choice. Water temperature will be set ot your optimum body requirements based on your fitbit outputs and your “Peloton Quotient” (The Peloton Quotient is an intelligence we designed to determine your % chance of heart attack based on a number of key factors from your lifestyle). Our on board physician can help with any mediation at this point, should it be required. They are seated in Keto Coroner ( a little doctors joke, we are told).
Rebooking:
No need. Your journey is just consistent and budgets pretty healthy from where we sit. We will keep the engines turning in wait and you can ride your gulfstream through even the toughest of headwinds.
In conclusion, dear passengers, thank you for choosing BYSPAir. We may not always get it right, but we promise to make the journey memorable – with a hint of sarcasm, cynicism and a dash of pop culture references. And remember, in the world of online retail, every landing is a “sale”!
Yes, this is a satirical look at the year ahead, but I already wrote about this earlier this year. If you want to read it have a look here.
eCommerce, The Retail Apocalypse and The third industrial Revolution. The 2023 version

title: Hype is overrated. 2024, the year of the eCommerce Renaissance.
pullQuotes: It has very little to do with ecommerce
- there, I said it. Let's look loosely at the real reasons for it:
excerpt: When I wrote this first in 2019, it read - "We urgently" need to reframe how we think about #ecommerce . I now have reset this mania to become a more considered approach. But that is only for those who can afford to do so.
_body:
When I wrote this first in 2019, it read - "We urgently" need to reframe how we think about
#ecommerce
. I now have reset this mania to become a more considered approach. But that is only for those who can afford to do so. Time will not be our friend in 2024. All you have to do is look at the volume, depth and breadth of information already been levelled our way. We are 6 days in. But we knew this, right?
False dawns and the light before the storm.
We have been on a road to purpose for the last 3/4 years with many trying to force sustainability claims into their marketing. According to the
RetailX
Global report from November, only 22% of the top 1000 leading brands publish an ESG or CSR policy on their sites. Only 4% of them share details of the suppliers or manufacturers. In France, Macron passed legislation around visibility for brands. It is overreaching (kinda) but a clear statement, to me. Coupled with the fact that Shein sold over £1.2B in 2022 in the UK leads me to the conclusion, that we as consumers don't really care about the catch all phrase, sustainability. Not really. The way this will change for businesses, will be through legislation. In an election year, anything is possible. (Side note: Facebook algo improvements are being hinted at and expected to see a rise in performance. They would need to have this ready before the bulk of election ad spending happens. Cooincidence?)
This leads me to a point to be discussed another day. The challenge for retail and more so for ecommerce, is that we are as blind as we ever were to consumer behaviour. We still know relatively little. Partly, because, we as consumers do not either. Discovery is a passive experience of knowledge transfer and rarely borne out of need. This is, to me, the single biggest challenge of our industry. So where does that leave us? Back where we are, building better, realistic, sustainable (growth side) businesses.
Back to 2019.
Chicken Little famosly said the sky is falling and ran aimlessly sharing his message with anyone who would listen. Today, he/she would be an influencer. But doomsday is not where we find ourselves. We are in limbo, figuring our what is next but in the meantime there is enough fear now to suggest that the stationary will react.
It has never been more abundantly evident to me that we need to view the function of ecommerce as a utility, in the same way electricity was adopted used to power the second industrial revolution.
RetailX Report 2023
Utility is ok. It got us to here but the most successful tech is tech we deal with in our daily lives. It is actually easier to craft user experiences for tv streaming, or mobile phone providers. There are a limited set of tasks you want to accomplish with each so it is inherently easy to get better experiences. Ecommerce does not enjoy this luxury - too many entry and exit points. Experiences are therefore, disjointed.
In the report, Ian and the team challenge retail to craft better experiential tech. With investment drying up, this is where real ingenuity will be formed. No more half baked attempts at personalisation or loyalty. No, not this time. Real, meaningful and new tech is what we need. This I agree wtih. But in the age of passivity and ever connecting devices, I wonder will utility alway trump experience. Afterall, convenience and personal care and growth are current mantras. It is hard in this environment to create groupthink and understand what is better for the collective rather than the individual.
Back to 2019
Colin Lewis
taught me about a think or two about research, though I never admit it. And weirdly,
interviews
I watched over 15 years ago with
Pharrel Williams
, Kobe Bryant, Tiger Woods and many more lead us to understand that a healthy respect for our past, helps us to understand our future - or at least gives us lessons. Listening to them and how they talked about those who marched before them was, to me, what set them apart. If you listen to
Hans Zimmer
talk about Leonard Bernstein and what he learned about the craft, the mindset and the clues left behind for others to follow, it opens your mind to the possibility that maybe history has eschwed some lessons on us.
There are some parallels and inverse parallels to the industrial revolution and it is in this context that I now view the world of commerce. Lets look loosely a the linear or parallel lines:
Up to the 1870's in Great Britain, electrical generators were starting to be used, usually by the early adopters, those who benefited economically and those who could afford it. It took 40 years almost before the economies of scale arrived and in 1910, the first "powering" of a residential area was delivered using only a single power station.
When we think about the importance of broadband rollout for countries in order to achieve the full true power of the internet and how it can serve a fundamental purposeful use for society.
The use of the word society is not misplaced. The origins of the internet, and its utopian place is ultimate freedom, access and transparency. If you unclear on this I suggest you read the
Cluetrain Manifesto
, (thanks
Chris Byrne
)its updates and digest - couple this read with Thank you for being late by Thomas Friedman and you can start getting a sense of where this is going. With history we learn that revolutions take time - the early adopters absorb the wealth, power and control early and then as govts figure out how best to harness the power of the revolution, then the power is put into the hands of the people.
Cluetrain Manifesto - Just a snapshot of the theses
The Internet is enabling conversations among human beings that were simply not possible in the era of mass media.
As a result, markets are getting smarter, more informed, more organized. Participation in a networked market changes people fundamentally.
In just a few more years, the current homogenized "voice" of business — the sound of mission statements and brochures —will seem as contrived and artificial as the language of the 18th century French court.
Companies can now communicate with their markets directly. If they blow it, it could be their last chance.
Companies that do not belong to a community of discourse will die.
These were penned in 1999. Bear that in mind.
What has been most startling about this revolution, is that the power is already in the hands of the many. We have to closely watch Moore's law to see just how quickly our revolution is happening.
What does this have to do with ecommerce?
The IoT is what. While we scramble to figure out how to set up our Shopify/BigCommerce stores or understand which social channel has the best engagement rate (thanks Rand Fishkin for sharing yesterday) the IoT folks are looking beyond the here and now.
eCommerce is going to blend into our surroundings and become a passive part of our lives in the same way electricity did - moving from generators to mini solar panels in our homes. This is already happening.
The inverse relationship we have with the industrial revolution is migratory patterns In the mid-18th century, about 15 per cent of the English population lived in urban areas; by 1900 this figure had increased to a whopping 85 per cent. Today we have virtual teams, remote teams and a desire for the "where" not to be as important as the actual output. The outputs themselves are largely intangible and therefore require no person present, if not only to receive the service, benefit for which they signed up to. Interesting shifts in just 200 years.
The Retail apocalypse - that old chestnut (if we talk about it enough, it might just happen in that exact way)
It has very little to do with ecommerce
- there, I said it. Let's look loosely at the real reasons for it:
Outdated business models
Too many outlets
- group profits kept many doors open, when they should have been shut. I would suggest looking to Schuh as a retailer who has got alot right. Investment early in ecommerce technologies - note my language and made service impeccable. Does sound like any other retail giant? And they also made a conscious decision not to appear on every UK high st, instead opted to use their tech to access new geographies and markets. They also turned loss into profits or cash recovery using marketplaces. Hardly groundbreaking, but just darn smart. Bravo Schuy.
Poor governance
-- Corporate governance 101 - have the board members largely not just shifted left at the table like a bad version of speed dating. There have been the equivalents of oligarchs in retail whose views on the world had not really changed for decades. It is not surprising to see the removal of these teams now and replacement with new blood - who fail in their early tenure while they unravel decades of ravelling. Is the same not happening in the old Ad game too ?
Poor adoption of retail technologies and over investment in stock
. Rather than solve customer problems and present options, they have allowed payments companies, delivery companies and social media to force their investment strategies. They have not roadmapped this themselves yet. This is most evident in the #Amazon competitor - Walmart. They don't have that clear roadmap themselves instead they are buying and acquiring in the hope they cobble this together right - in the same way one writes a dissertation or thesis these days - they are generally the best combination of articles you can find, edit and replace with your own words without being caught plagiarizing.
I don't know why I left the best until last.
Marketing and advertising have been bastardised
and amalgamated into this industry we call digital marketing. I have thought alot about this over the last number of months. Why do we get this so wrong. Always.
Marketing should be the combination of people who frame a brand proposition relative to a customer desire/need/connection. If this goes wrong, there is no point in embarking on the rest. This insight (from data, not gut) should inform the channels within which your customers are playing. Quick hospital pass to the advertising team now - Media buyers, Adwords specialists, content writers and so on. Connect the dots in the most profitable way you possibly can and if you find you are not, you talk to your marketing team and figure out where this is going wrong, amend, move on and remeasure. Now back to marketing - what it is the next plan.
We have got to address the team structures to get this right. We have got to invest in training internally to empower people with product knowledge and commercial knowledge to make decisions and take actions where they can influence control, debate insight and share knowledge in a constructive environment. The comes the creativity, the fun, the funFear. However...
Creativity needs a muse - for the true genius creatives, I am at a loss to understand what that may be, but for poets like Kavanagh and Yeats and the likes, it came from the banal, the every day and the things that midered them. In retail and ecommerce it comes from panic, mistakes, fear or a place of complete control, knowing the bases are covered. It rarely occurs when we are coasting along, in fact it never does.
Retail is not dead, the business model needs to change. The retailers need to work more closely with brands, manufacturers and customers to figure out what consumers really want. Maringalising those less powerful on the supply chain, in today's world, is an opportunity missed. Retail is a wonderful industry in a world full of consumers, the hedonistic mantra, of bigger, faster, more has never been more feverish. Our capacity to process information is greater than it has ever been and our inability to pay attention and take time make the challenges even greater. For those, not yet engaging in adoption of #ecommerce in whatever guise you need, maybe look differently at your business or market. Map it backwards to 25 years, look to the competitive forces who Porter did not account for (disruptors) and plan for how you want to engage them. Then, breathe, move forward and repeat this process of reflection forever.

title: Leap Year 24: The love story of Johnny Castle and Frances Houseman. IYKYK.
pullQuotes: Where is my beige iridescent lipstick? - Seems like a thing a TikToker might say,but no, it was Big Sister Lisa.
Nobody puts baby in a corner.
I carried a watermelon.
excerpt: Strap in for this one. Today, I will be quoting, among many other nostalgic confines of my head and heart, Dirty Dancing. What place has this on LinkedIn. Apart from a dazzling display of the class system in effect, it was the first DVD, I
_body:
Strap in for this one. Today, I will be quoting, among many other nostalgic confines of my head and heart, Dirty Dancing. What place has this on LinkedIn. Apart from a dazzling display of the class system in effect, it was the first DVD, I put on for my now wife. I was tipsy and trying to impress her. It failed but was a talking point, is a talking point.  Classic, lesser known quotes like
Where is my beige iridescent lipstick? - Seems like a thing a TikToker might say,but no, it was Big Sister Lisa.
Class systems tend to box us consumers into buckets. They way we think about ourselves, our society our place in it and what standards we should expect from each other. This man made system is being broken down and broken apart in many aspects of life right now. And to be clear, I am not equating ecommerce to this in an attempt to trivialise anyones struggles, but look at all of the movements that have occured and are ongoing. People fighting their corner for the speaking box to make change to make life better, yet here in eCommerce, just shy of 30 years of the retail version, we sit on our hands like Frances Houseman. Today I speak for Frances Houseman because:
Nobody puts baby in a corner.
The evidence is irrefutable. It is there, in plain sight. We care or choose not to look or take action. I spoke before of a class system in eCommerce. Let's just say I was right. (Depending on how you read that line, i seem like an arrogant ass*ole!). Read it the other way and then follow me for a few mins. This is not my doing, blame
Ian Jindal
(again) and his accomplice,
Mark Pigou
.. For what it is worth, this should be a discussion at
Shoptalk
Europe. We have a class problem. But we know that right?  For 10 years now, the team have not just been telling us this, but breaking it down as to why this is so. I first wrote about it in 2016 - the audience was tiny, but I have been observing its development since then. Today, I am not making the case for this, I am presenting the evidence. Evidence that can and should facilitate change.  But first. A public service announcement. (PSA). This is opinion not science backed by evidence.
https://www.popsugar.co.uk
“A good question is not concerned with a correct answer. A good question cannot be answered immediately. A good question challenges existing answers. A good question is one you badly want answered once you hear it, but had no inkling you cared before it was asked. A good question creates new territory of thinking. A good question reframes its own answers. A good question is the seed of innovation in science, technology, art, politics, and business. A good question is a probe, a what-if scenario. A good question skirts on the edge of what is known and not known, neither silly nor obvious. A good question cannot be predicted. A good question will be the sign of an educated mind. A good question is one that generates many other good questions. A good question may be the last job a machine will learn to do. A good question is what humans are for.  •”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
Are we using information in the right way to shape how our businesses operate?
Let's use the RetailX report to build evidence and see if we view things in the right way. I amusing specifically the Global Elite Top 1000 and the UK Top500 reports as my guides. 10 years of curated info. When we decouple our businesses into processes we find ourselves packaging them up neatly into functions and the reports focus on
Customer Value Chain
Product Value Chain
Operations Value Chain
Capital Value Chain
Sustainability or Greenwashing as we know it better
Elephanty in the room time, only 5 of 1000 retailers surveyed in 2023 made the Elite bracket. Combined revenues of around $180M. Carrefour alone contribute just under 50% of this under. eCommerce is a strong growing part of the business - Zara says at least 30% of all revenues come through online.  Other noteworthy characteristics:
They have many channels of distribution, physical and digital.
Strong brand positioning and stronger proposition.
Growth in ecommerce is/can be linked to a demographic rather than business model adaptations.
(At the end of the day, everyone on the top 1000 list is really just trying to sell stuff. Just in different ways, to the same people).
An emerging aspect I will not go into today is the development of media networks - this is changing the types of business functions and teams to run them. It is generating new revenue and poses the question, "Are they even retailers at that point, in that function?" Probably not, but it is worth a note - here is where Walmart drive revenue outside of retail:
Business Mix
- Diversified Income - Higher growth businesses: higher margins than retail, growing faster. bends margin curve upwards. global advertising grew 28% to 3.4B. Walmart us marketplace revenue grew 45%, with more than 35% orders fulfilled by WFS. Global Membership up 20% - there are few retailers with a profile likethis.
Product Mix -
Expanding ecom assortment important, mostly in gen merch. markpetplace key here - extended digital shelf gives them moreways to compete (this is replicable if your audience is big enough).
Geographic Mix
- Expansion, acquisition and #CBT.
Productivity from Supply Chain
Back to the list - I mention Walmart as you willstart to see some of this happening in some of the Top 100. For many it has started already. At a glance through the list the following have started marketplace offerings - Next, Target, Darty, La Redoute, QVC, Shein. Some are marketplaces - Amazon, Zalando, Mercadolibre. Some are expandinginternationally and appearing where the fit is natural Sephora, Douglas, Lego. Why these examples? Retailers/Brands can not survive in the long term on just retail revenues.
https://www.linkedin.com/in/colinlewis/
The above is the best - where can we a $5M per year turnover business get to? This, in part, is why subscription strategies are favored. They are new,clean revenue. But what emerged, for me, during the Walmart earnings calls was that retail revenue alone will not get us scale or profits, unless we are in the Elite.
How do we change the approach we take? For the majority these ambitions need to be grounded in "Better Retail".  Better in every facet.
Product value Chain
The product value chain measures how retailers create, plan, buy, move and sell products. The items that together affect net margin. This is particularly important in light of the fact many brands/retailers have been discounting since October.
Exhibit A
Lego, a leader in the RetailX product value chain, maintains its wide appeal with adults as well as young people by diversifying its product ranges, making its sets inclusive as well as relevant by collaborating with movies such as Harry Potter, Star Wars and, more recently, celebrating 100 years of Disney. Lego has movies and TV shows.
Pricing Strategies
Retailers selling different categories in different regions have taken a range of decisions around how they approach full pricing and how and when they carry out promotional activity. As Nike reported for the three months to November 2022, “rising costs are an issue for the company, as gross margin decreased 300 basis points to 42.9%, primarily due to higher markdowns to liquidate inventory, particularly in North America”.
CONVERTING CUSTOMERS WITH PRODUCT INFORMATION
The depth of the information will vary by product category, while the extent to which a potential customer looks at the information will depend on their product knowledge, interest and individual shopping journey. These are your basics, this is where you increment your way out of this mess. Scarily in the results though the median score of 3.0 has remained the same for 520 of these retailers. Someone forgetting the "Control your controllables" mantra.
HIGHLIGHTING PRODUCT CHOICE
Since 2022, the biggest change has been in the number of ecommerce sites showing customers alternative products when they are browsing. This
has seen a 31 percentage point decline from something that 72% of Global Elite retailers did in 2022 to just 41%
in February 2023. In all, 507 retailers were measured by the RetailX research team in both years.  We are doing less to compete and yet we expect to grow.
Did the pandemic make us lazy? What have we been doing. Some blame new generational cultures on workplace attitudes.
I carried a watermelon.
See these attitudes have been around since the late 50s. (Thank you Dirty Dancing).
ENABLING CUSTOMERS TO CHECK STORE STOCK
The number of omnichannel retailers giving customers a way to view whether an item is in stock in a particular store remains unchanged since last year. It is still a service offered by a minority of retailers. Of the 507 members of the Global Elite 1000 that have stores and were assessed in 2022 and 2023, just 12% show levels of store stock on their ecommerce site.
We are running faster to stand still. We can action these. We can remedy this.
The product value chain remains one of those areas in terms of performance where we can do better. To do better we need to think differently. Merchandising, for me is the skill businesses of all sizes should be focused on. Not just one part of it, but all parts. Merchandising is multi faceted.
You just put your pickle on everybody’s plate, college boy, and leave the hard stuff to me.
Operations Value Chain
The operations value chain measures how retailers handle order management and orchestration through the sales cycle, all actions that affect profit per order. Bread and butter this is called in some jurisdictions.
Leading retailers in the operations value chain are predominantly multichannel retailers.
Here ends the debate on many of the DTC conversations. What is #DTC not? A business model. It is a channel for retail to reach customers directly. It is the place that brands go to either live or die.
HOW GLOBAL RETAILERS HANDLE RETURNS
Recently, retailers have begun charging customers for product returns in order to reduce the level of returns but also to cover some of their costs. For example, fashion brand Zara started charging customers for product returns in May 2022. In the UK, a charge of £1.95 is made for shoppers returning unwanted goods via a third-party delivery point. However, there is no fee for shoppers returning goods to stores. This is sensible business decision making, stepping towards profits. This is not a poor customer experience. FWIW, I think free returns is mad - just the thought of it.
Capital Value Chain
The capital value chain measures how retailers convert all capital into profit or capital growth, items that together affect return on investment and share price. Revenue only shows one part of the story. Costs relating to customers, products and operations as already discussed in this report all impact on final profits and the sustainability of a business over the longer term. Without profit – and capital to reinvest in the business and ensure cash flow – a business will need to look to other measures for capital, such as investors.
Alot of external forces now means we cannot control these costs:
Wars
Inflation
Elections
Strikes
For many, these are insurmountable costs. But this may be where ecommerce can change for people. Small, independent fashion retailers, do social really well -they connect, they get it and there are no mental hurdles to overcome. Is TikTok your first stop? Is it your only stop? Is this where your investment of time, effort and money goes? Conversion rates of 1% will notget your accountant too excited and calls for killing marketing spend will be on the weekly.
Determine your own type of ecommerce. Do it for Frances.
Sorry for the disruption, folks, but I always do the last dance of the season. This year somebody told me not to. So I’m gonna do my kind of dancin’ with a great partner, who’s not only a terrific dancer, but somebody who’s taught me that there are people willing to stand up for other people no matter what it costs them. Somebody who’s taught me about the kind of person I wanna be. Miss Frances Houseman.
Greenwashing, Sorry, I meant Sustainability. Sorry, not really sure what that means.
Legislation, consumer pressure and brands’ own desire to make a change are driving sustainability measures and new business models. Unless y ou are designing business policies to help restructure your business, you are most likely greenwashing. In the RetailX brand report, pre Christmas, it was reported that only 11% of the Elite 1000 had published policies on ESG or CSR. Unless you are designing policy, you are kidding yourself. Policies do something controversial and I will quote
James Byrne
of
Faerly
here. (A small, few person operation working from the town I grew up in) where they are truly committed to bring better retail to the environment. Everything they do. I asked James once, does this make decision making harder? My thinking was more barriers and a need to be creative. James' reply, "No, it's easier. We know what we can/cannot do".
I know what you are thinking, if you have read this far.
The reports signpost all of the decisions that we make. It is also a clear statement to show us we cannot do everything, everywhere, all at once (thanks
Colin Lewis
) . But we can have a long term plan (called a strategy) and we can use tactics to get there. Retail, for the large ones of you, revenue diversification if key. This is built on operational excellence and designing experiences that go beyond personalisation. What is interesting in the composition of the list is that 4 of the top 5 are brands. They are customer centric. They start there and build out. They have clear propositions (Ye trainer firesale aside) and know how do execute campaigns. Their retail model is a series of checks and balances.
I continue to think we need to figure out new ways to utilise ecommerce along that journey.
“We are morphing so fast that our ability to invent new things outpaces the rate we can civilize them.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
Conclusion
Johnny and Baby met in the summer of 1963 at the Kellerman resort, in the Catskills mountains. It took time for them to meet, dance, fall in lust, fall in love and learn how to Tango. And this is where we currently find our star cross lovers Retail and eCommerce. Johnny ripped up the rule book to win over the lady who won his heart, taught him to be strong, be better and almost broke his back (are  you listening ecommerce?) And Baby, a family legacy talent broke down the barriers of convention, persuaded her family she could not only love but dance too. And in the end, they all danced in rhythm and harmony, not knowing what the winter of 63 might bring (it was bleak) but they had broken the mould for those that followed after. That and left us with an awesome soundtrack on the way.
The path to retail and eommerce harmony is stillvery much back in the summer of '63.

title: Profits as Prophets: It's only after we've lost everything that we're free to do anything.
pullQuotes: Gordon Newman
Meanwhile, 2023 LVMH , €86.2bn rev, €22.8bn profit , 25% margin"
Retail Media, as a solution is temporary for many. Making profitability a challenge.
excerpt: Lack of profitability is not exclusively an ecommerce problem. For the last 2 years ecommerce has been washing away the sin of being loss making and promising to do better. It’s penance, shrinking budgets, cost cutting and a really poor narrative that ecommerce is somehow
_body:
Lack of profitability is not exclusively an ecommerce problem. For the last 2 years ecommerce has been washing away the sin of being loss making and promising to do better. It’s penance, shrinking budgets, cost cutting and a really poor narrative that ecommerce is somehow a pariah. There is plenty of sanity in the messaging, but the over reaction to performance, marketing and brand activity become ever more unhelpful the more we write about it. What if the strategy is all wrong. Let they without sin, cast the first stone. Let the games begin.
Winning margins are fine. See below.
Courtesy -
Colin Lewis
Imagine what it is like being a small to medium size retailer. These guys have/are divesting revenue streams away from core retail income due  to  the fact, by itself, it is not very profitable, or at least highly risky. We will have to come  "Back to the Future" in a little while. First a trip in our Delorean to a time when ecommerce was technically harder but actually was easier.
For the purposes of this and to avoid this being a Scorcese length epic, I need to generalise a tad, grouping categories together to provide better context.
It was acceptable in the 80s - Calvin Harris
Early, mid 90s ecommerce was plucky and really crude. Legislative changes on how commerce could be conducted in 1995 paved the way for Jeff Bezos on his Amazon vision. It was other structural changes that allowed this growth to continue and without them, we may not have ecommerce as we know it. In  1998, the purchase and download of electronic stamps meant printable, downloadable labels were possible. 1999 saw the launch of Alibaba and Napster was created which is a step we forget. This was the beginning of online communities, the idea of discovery and a sense of democratization in action. The  first platform started emerging too, ATG started selling decorative items for the home online. Domain values started to rise in alignment with their importance to search activity - 1997 business dot com was purchased for $149,000 and then sold for $7.5m  in 1999 to eCompanies only to be sold in 2007 for $345M.
It was around then that eCommerce companies were experiencing higher uptakes from customers looking for something different to the high street. This is a key factor in its success at the time. I started my career in the same year, no coincidence.
2007 was in fact a pivotal year for the future of ecommerce - slight digression.
Excerpts from "Thank you for being late, Thomas Friedman - Updated edition 2017"
Apple Launched the iPhone
Facebook and Twitter went Global
Kindle and Android were released
AirBnB was founded
Google bought Youtube
IBM created it's AI super friend to Bill Gates - Watson
To give further clarity.
Mobile, in hand technology. Internet everywhere.
An always on, connected, sharing community starts. Now over 2B strong.
Operating systems that helped spark 3rd party development and entrepreneurship.
The idea of category disruption through better commercial realities.
Understanding the role TV and Media has  in our lives. Or making it that way.
Today, everything add AI.
eCommerce at the time
It was possible to get healthy double or even triple digit growth during this period. Why?
Less competition.
Availability of items you could not access elsewhere.
Potential for marketplaces to provide international markets.
Commercial propositions were well considered and well executed.
More complex tech stacks meant longer rollouts and constant roadmaps, IT blocks for key trading periods and in most cases, strong architects mapping the solutions. In short, time to market was slower and better thought out.
Consumers liked the variety and the novel experiences.
Consider the landscape today
Competition is everywhere and in abundance.
Sameness of product and offering makes online shopping cumbersome and dare I say boring. (Side note: Does Amazon win because it does funcationality best?) .
Marketplaces have been underutilised.
Many brands today, dropship,create a brand in 24 hours or were forced online beacuse of COVID.
The simplicity of tech set up has created this false narrative that quick and easy is better than slow and difficult. It is also too cheap. But then if it were not, Moore's Law would be wrong.
Consumers are passive.
We have become consumers of media and to be frank we have all of the shit that we need to get by in life.
Our customer today is complex and in many markets preoccupied with someone who has already caught their attention:
Amazon has 1,363 e-commerce facilities in the US and more than 1.5 million workers around the world.
Eight in 10 US shoppers are Amazon customers, and they place an average of 72 orders per year.
Amazon
's average customer is a white Gen X woman who earns about $60K per year and spends $2,662.
Entire countries fail to compete with this.
The average online spending in 2023 ranges from €816 for Ireland to €2,120 for Germany. Purchase frequency varies from 16 orders annually for Belgium to 42 for the United Kingdom
.🇩🇪 Germany: €2,120 for 35 orders
🇬🇧 UK: €1,866 for 42 orders - favouring cheaper items
🇫🇷 France: €1,756 for 27 orders
🇮🇹 Italy: €1,112 for 21 orders
🇪🇸 Spain: €907 for 20 orders
🇳🇱 Netherlands: €1,147 for 19 orders
🇧🇪 Belgium: €1,071 for 16 orders
🇦🇹 Austria: €1,582 for 25 orders
🇮🇪 Ireland: €816 for 18 orders
Retail by it's nature, is dependant on us doing what Fight Club said we shouldn't.
The things you own end up owning you.
Advertising has us chasing cars and clothes, working jobs we hate so we can buy shit we don't need. We're the middle children of history, man. No purpose or place.
We've all been raised on television to believe that one day we'd all be millionaires, and movie gods, and rock stars. But we won't. And we're slowly learning that fact.
Opportunity was everywhere in those heady days. You just need to look back at headlines of growth, success and conquering the word. There was rarely a reference to profits, but should have been but something greater was happening.
New wealth was being created. This is how economies grow. Money flooded into brands and aided the growth and there was this new tech scene emerging. "Ecosystems" were emerging and curiousity around what technology could achieve became  even sexier during the financial crisis of 2008. What a time to work in eBay - wow, excess inventory everywhere. eBay was recession proof. That was then and this is now. We emerged from those days with startups, incubators, new tech conferences and the idea that the water was more than warm, we should all jump in.
Meanwhile, retail continues. Retail cycles did not change, we had summer, Christmas and maybe Jan sales but the merchandising cycles remained the same and to alot of CEOs this was comforting. Most retailers then and now retrieve their unprofitable year in peak trade. Think about that, think about the risks involved and how this has almost, always been the way. Peak sales and Christmas being the saviours of retail.
But you are in retail, why are you bashing it? I am not. Retail is changing and it is out of necessity, not out of vision. This, new retail, is however and elitist sport. Like Rugby back in the early 2000's, reserved for those who could afford it. Now, a sport of the wider community.
The New World of Retail and Why most cannot access it.
Gordon Newman
Meanwhile, 2023 LVMH , €86.2bn rev, €22.8bn profit , 25% margin"
(This is important because now we need ecommerce to work)
Some Headlines:
UK: 13.03.24 Morrisons pulled a £1bn loss against revenues of £18.4bn.
UK: 11.03.24 Matalan profits plummet. EBITDA down to $124m against revenues of £1.15bn or profits of 0.1%
US: NYSE moves to delist retailer Express
US: Macys shutters 150 stores/ Zulily goes out of business
Walmart earnings were quite telling. They have successfully builtgrocery from a crazy vision in the late 60s to make this a recurring revenue stream. Sprinkle in other categories, seasonal events and you have the Walmart retail margin.
Walmart are smart. They started divested income streams and talk openly about this.
Business Mix
- Diversified Income - Higher growth businesses: higher margins than retail, growing faster. bends margin curve upwards. global advertising grew 28% to 3.4B. Walmart us marketplace revenue grew 45%, with more than 35% orders fulfilled by WFS. Global Membership up 20% - there are few retailers with a profile likethis.
Product Mix -
Expanding ecom assortment important, mostly in gen merch. markpetplace key here - extended digital shelf gives them moreways to compete (this is replicable if your audience is big enough).
Geographic Mix
- Expansion, acquisition and #CBT.
Productivity from Supply Chain aided by AI.
Just beacause you think you can box, does not mean you get in the ring with Ali. Not everyone can be Walmart, in fact almost no one can. Not many retailers can be a last mile company. Almost all get this wrong and empty their pockets whilst doing so too.
Retail Media, as a solution is temporary for many. Making profitability a challenge.
An emerging aspect is the development of media networks - this is changing the types of business functions and teams to run them. It is generating new revenue and poses the question, "Are they even retailers at that point, in that function?"
It is a worrying trend that is emerging. Become a marketplace, add a media network, problem solved. But what next? Why is this not possible for most? Let's present some evidence: From my annual Hat Tip to
Ian Jindal
and
Mark Pigou
and all the team
RetailX
a look at the Global Elite top 1000.
The Global Retail Market grew to $2.83 TN. Inturbulant times, a salient message from Nike VP Matthew Friend - " Focus on what we can control".
Global companies have achieved mixed results in the last year but their plans to capitalise on what they can control, capture market opportunities and continue to invest is what sets them apart.
DTC vs Omnichannel - Let's be frank, this should not be a debate.
#DTC
is not a business model. But for context, omnichannel retailersdominate the top 100 positions. Common traits - reach, volume, online and offline sales, cross border trade and leadership vision.
4 of the 5 "Elite" are brands. Shein make the top 150, no room for Temu - yet. Shein really only entered mature markets in 2021. Shein are investing in the right areas for long term success. Expect to see them move higher in 2024. Anyone doubting their creds, do at your peril.
Of the top 1000
43.8% are brands
27.6% are marketplaces
28.6% are retailers
In the light of traffic value:
Marketplace 77.9%
Retailers 7.3%
Brands 4.8%
Do we need more marketplaces - probably not.
Can we sustain them? No. Inside all of this, we need to also look at the providers. How do they continue to make money from retailers and brands who cannot make profit, how squeezed will they become? With VC money drying up and gathering "powder" the battle for mid market will be a blood bath over the next few years. Shopify have been the most successful in realising their strength is in the divergent revenue streams it has built. Notably Shop Pay.
So where does this leave us on the profitability conversation I started with? Thomas Friedman said of his findings,
“If you keep your economy open, keep it flexible, keep it as deregulated as possible. These opportunities, when they come, you’ll be able to jump on them,” he concluded.
This afternoon in the US there will be a vote on whether or not to carry legislation to look at closing down TikTok. In the EU, we are looking at continuing anti trust cases (rightly so) against techs largest operators who largely shape the world we exist in. We have union strikes, wars and inflation economics happening all at once. We have failing commitments to environmental governance and compliance. We are consumers who are tired and broke and trying to figure out who we are again.
eCommerce has potential to be better.
But in its fight for finding profits, it is not alone. It's transparency and simple paths to markets make it a competitive place where product market fit, for most, would fail on day 1. Yet we persevere.
Technology needs to find a place where it problem solves again. Convenience is not always a problem, nor is speed. Less haste is hard to find when the world spins so fast and we consume so much info daily. In the cold harsh review of the pandemic, we slowed down, sped up and did what we needed to survive. The skills we acquired during those formative years will again prove useful as we take on the next 10 years. The pioneers of early ecommerce are getting to the sunsets of their careers and are blissfully thinking of that cocktail by the pool or the world trip they always planned. The next wave of ecommerce will be more concise, compact and more on demand. It will exist in the devices around commanded by necessity over want.
Singer Brandi Carlile - "The Eye"
You can dance in a hurricane But only if you’re standing in the eye. I hope that it is clear by now that every day going forward we’re going to be asked to dance in a hurricane. (Now Friedman) set off by the accelerations in the Market, Mother Nature, and Moore’s law. Some politicians propose to build a wall against this hurricane. That is a fool’s errand. There is only one way to thrive now, and it’s by finding and creating your own eye. The eye of a hurricane moves, along with the storm. It draws energy from it, while creating a sanctuary of stability inside it. It is both dynamic and stable—and so must we be. We can’t escape these accelerations. We have to dive into them, take advantage of their energy and flows where possible, move with them, use them to learn faster, design smarter, and collaborate deeper—all so we can build our own eyes to anchor and propel ourselves and our families confidently forward.”
