Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
excerpt: “Since it is the last scarcity, wherever attention flows, money will follow.”― Kevin Kelly, The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future A Satirical Soirée: Economic Luminaries Debate the State of Retail and E-commerce in 2025 New York City, February 12,
_body:
“Since it is the last scarcity, wherever attention flows, money will follow.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
A Satirical Soirée: Economic Luminaries Debate the State of Retail and E-commerce in 2025
New York City, February 12, 2025
– In an unprecedented convergence of minds, I had the distinct pleasure of hosting a dinner party featuring some of history's most renowned economic thinkers. The guest list included Sir Thomas More, John Stuart Mill, Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, George Bernard Shaw, William Herschel, Nikolai Kondratiev, Wilhelm Roscher, John Dewey, Charles A. Beard, Thorstein Veblen, Alfred Marshall, John Maynard Keynes, Milton Friedman, Naomi Klein, and, making a grand entrance, former President Donald J. Trump. Yes, this appears to have been well researched. What could go wrong?
(Authors note: I had to wikipedia most of these names, and after dinner, I know even less about them.
)
As the evening unfolded, the conversation naturally gravitated towards the current state of retail and e-commerce, particularly in light of recent trade tariffs and their impact on supply chains and consumerism.
Prepare for a lot of economic puns.For this, I am sorry, not sorry.
State of the (E)Nation Address: The Great E-commerce Circus of 2025
Delivered by Vinny O Brien, E-commerce Consultant and LinkedIn Spammer, to a Room Full of Dead Economic Legends Who Are Somehow Still More Relevant Than Most Modern Pundits. Their words, not mine.
Esteemed guests, intellectual giants, and one particularly orange-hued former president.
Welcome to New York City, (I picked New York as not everyone had been, i thought the place woudl set a tone. I was wrong) the land where dreams are made, rents are absurd, and e-commerce is currently tap-dancing on a high wire over an economic abyss. It's 2025, and oh, what a time to be alive! Or in some of your cases, sort of... conceptually alive.
Ecommerce today is like a teenager with a credit card or a BNPL account (more on that later) and no impulse control. Sales are booming, logistics are crumbling, and consumers are more confused than ever. Supply chains? Tighter than Veblen's definition of pecuniary emulation. Tariffs? More unpredictable than Keynes's mood swings. And don't get me started on Temu and Shein’s whack-a-mole strategy with de minimis exemptions—a loophole now closed faster than Friedman's disdain for government intervention.
Inflation is up, consumer trust is down, and the only thing more inflated than prices are tech CEOs' egos. Note, many are Billionaires - economists, love this kind of stuff. None predicted it though.  Amazon is still the towering colossus, now delivering existential dread within 24 hours.
Shopify? Still helping SMBs live the dream of working 80 hours a week to avoid a 40-hour job.
And Meta? Oh, they’re too busy building virtual malls in the metaverse where no one shops.
One Big Question: The outlook for 2025? It has changed since NRF.
Picture a rollercoaster designed by Kondratiev himself: long waves of growth followed by sudden plunges that make Marx scream “I told you so!” from the afterlife. Tariffs on Chinese imports are wreaking havoc, turning every container ship into a floating financial crisis. Retailers are scrambling like Marshall calculating elasticity, while consumers are left wondering why their $5 Temu t-shirt now costs $15. (it takes a lo to pun this much).
But fear not! Said the NRF.
Resilience is the name of the game. We're seeing brands innovate, adapting like Roscher would advise, and exploiting crises in ways that would make Naomi Klein write another book. The future is uncertain, the challenges are immense, but if history (and Veblen’s snarky observations) teach us anything, it's that commerce, like human folly, is eternal.
So buckle up, dear guests. Tonight, we dissect the chaos, reminisce about the days when tariffs were mere textbook entries, and debate whether any of this madness is, in fact, progress.
I would love to hear your insights !! Let the intellectual brawl begin!
Cheers to the past, the present, and the profoundly Perplexity future. Now, you don't want to hear from me any more. I will defer to you my guests to let me know if Shirley Bassey was indeed right and are we seeing a little bit of history repeating.
Some say, A Modern Utopia?
Sir Thomas More, observing the skyline from the penthouse where we dined, remarked, "I envisioned a Utopia, but this metropolis exceeds even my imagination." To which John Stuart Mill replied, "Indeed, but with greater freedom comes greater responsibility, especially in commerce." These are not so much insights as context setters. You know, like the rails in bowling.
The Great Tariff Debate Begins
Karl Marx, never one to shy away from critique, opens, "The bourgeoisie has once again imposed measures to protect their capital, this time through tariffs that burden the proletariat." Friedrich Engels nodded in agreement, adding, "These trade barriers disrupt the global supply chain, leading to scarcity and inflated prices for the working class."
Milton Friedman interjected, "Trade barriers are indeed detrimental. As I have long advocated, free markets should dictate the flow of goods, not governmental interference." He glanced pointedly at Marx, who just smiled.
A String of Conversations: The Dinner Table Dynamics
George Bernard Shaw, with his characteristic Irish wit, quipped, "It appears we've traded one form of madness for another. From the lunacy of laissez-faire to the insanity of interventionism."
Lots of soundbytes but not much substance yet - but amazing how real the soundbtyes echo in modern headlines.
Alfred Marshall, ever the pragmatist, noted, "The elasticity of demand will determine how consumers respond to these price changes. Some goods may see a significant drop in quantity demanded."
A Wonder years Inner Monologue Moment: "Oh F*Ck, I thought to myself. It is 2024 but on steroids. Thankfully Klarna just announced a partnership with JP Morgan"
John Maynard Keynes leaned forward, "In the short run, these tariffs may protect domestic industries, but in the long run, they could lead to a decrease in overall economic welfare."
Naomi Klein, referencing her seminal work, commented, "This is reminiscent of the 'Shock Doctrine'—using crises to push through unpopular economic policies. The current trade tensions are no different."
Former President Trump, never one to miss an opportunity, declared, "These tariffs are making America great again! We're bringing jobs back and standing up to unfair trade practices."
Thorstein Veblen, observing the spectacle, mused, "It's all a display of conspicuous consumption and vested interests. The leisure class thrives while the common man suffers."
Real-World Impacts: A Contemporary Analysis
Recent reports have highlighted the tangible effects of these policies. Alot of people speak about it, we all have opinkions. The imposition of tariffs by former President Trump on goods from Canada, Mexico, and China has led to increased prices for consumers. Some immediage and some to come. Because of the changing nature of all of this, what it has done more than anything.
Investments in AI - $1T wiped off the US stock exchange in one day. Why? Let's quote Top Gun, Goose over to you "It was inverted".
“A universal law of economics says the moment something becomes free and ubiquitous, its position in the economic equation suddenly inverts. When nighttime electrical lighting was new and scarce, it was the poor who burned common candles. Later, when electricity became easily accessible and practically free, our preference flipped and candles at dinner became a sign of luxury. In”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
Uncertainty.
Brands like Lululemon and Aritzia, though Canadian, produce most of their goods outside of Canada and might not see significant price hikes. However, the repeal of the de minimis exemption, which enabled tax-free import of goods under $800, could lead to higher costs for retailers and consumers, causing confusion and an increase in prices.
Additionally, the global fashion supply chain is undergoing significant changes due to the de minimis rule, which allows low-value parcels to enter the US duty-free. This rule has been exploited by huge numbers of companies but has had a particular spotlight shone up on it because of the rise of companies like Shein and Temu who continue to ship low-valued goods to the US in large quantities.
The suspension of the de minimis rule poses challenges, including backlogs at ports, increased tariffs, and additional compliance costs. Smaller e-commerce businesses and US luxury resale markets are particularly vulnerable. This situation may shift consumer behavior towards higher quality products and benefit domestic brands while pushing global brands to rethink their supply chain strategies.
History Repeating at 5G Speeds
As our spirited dinner party draws to a close, let us reflect on the parallels between historical economic thought and today’s e-commerce dilemmas. Kondratiev’s waves remind us that economic booms and busts are as predictable as your annual Amazon Prime Day splurge. Marx and Engels’ critique of labor exploitation is alive and well in the gig economy, where couriers race against time like it’s the Industrial Revolution on steroids.
But what’s accelerating this cycle? Enter Moore’s Law—predicting that computing power doubles roughly every two years. AI development has taken this to heart, making algorithms smarter, faster, and frankly, a little too eager to sell you things you don’t need at 2 a.m. AI-driven personalization is transforming e-commerce, from chatbots mimicking human sarcasm to product recommendations that know your preferences better than your therapist My therapist is pretty spot on, to be fair. We are having great conversations about AI but the speed at which it moves, means we cannto cultivate it.
“We are morphing so fast that our ability to invent new things outpaces the rate we can civilize them.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
Yet, with great power comes great disruption. AI is reshaping supply chains, optimizing inventory management, and, ironically, replacing the very consumers it targets with automated buying bots.
No body is talking about this.
The future of e-commerce? A battleground where AI algorithms outbid each other on your behalf while you binge-watch dystopian dramas,
Black Mirror much people?
In conclusion, dear guests and readers (if you are still reading this far), our dinner party has proven one thing: economic history is not just a series of cycles but a chaotic spiral now propelled by AI. Brace yourselves—2025’s e-commerce landscape will be one of hyper-efficiency, relentless competition, and, if Moore’s Law holds, increasingly existential product recommendations.
Farewell until our next dinner. Now, for some Irish coffees. “Is there any other kind” asked GBS.
The paths to our future are littered across our past.
“Over the next three decades, scholars and fans, aided by computational algorithms, will knit together the books of the world into a single networked literature. A reader will be able to generate a social graph of an idea, or a timeline of a concept, or a networked map of influence for any notion in the library. We’ll come to understand that no work, no idea stands alone, but that all good, true, and beautiful things are ecosystems of intertwined parts and related entities, past and present.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future

(Put on your best movie trailer voice,...... now) In a world where technology meets tradition, comes a story of love, laughter, and logistics. The wait is over. The giant has arrived. Amazon, the overseas behemoth, is coming to a small town near you in Ireland.
The prequels have not all been pretty, but Amazon and Ireland could be a match made in heaven. Get ready for a romantic comedy like no other, with drama, twists, and turns that will make you laugh, cry, and turn heads.
Will this unlikely union bring prosperity or chaos? Find out in 2025, when Amazon comes to a small town near you in Ireland. Coming soon to theaters everywhere. Don't worry, you won’t miss it!"
The Back Story (Building characters and players up)
Amazon entering Ireland is like every other Amazon entry to a market and unlike it too. Ireland is a small, island economy. As a retail nation we have a few major points that Amazon can erode over time, little by little:
We have a large amount of retail resellers.
We have many chain stores who are struggling in home territories. They are in Ireland as part of a failed product/brand extension. ASk people who have tried this before. In our heads it makes sense, on the  P and L, it does not. It never has.
According to best info, we have 217 retail parks in the country. If these were to be evenly distributed, this would be a park every 20km (rounded up). We have too many .
We have approx 24,500 retail stores in 2021. Categorised as follows:
Convenience stores and grocery make up 50% of our retail footprint. This is not the initial target but strategic acquisitions would make it interesting.
During COVID, we all proved we could build a Shopify store and run ads. Now the wheels have come off for many. There are plenty of influencer led brands emerged but as in other countries, do they have a life span. My view is influencer/celebrity brands should be run to sell trend based products, not to fill a category and hope you can expand outwards. We simply do not have the market to do it. When we go over the pond, we get overwhelmed. Let’s not forget Greater Manchester is bigger than Ireland. In the US, there are 143 “Ireland’s “ or cities with < than 6M people. That is a lot of demographic change, behavioural nuance and learning.
As I said, Ireland needed a Co-oP. It has landed. But I think it is worth breaking it down to see what this means for people. But a few key topics emerged for me and through the magic of cinema, I am going to bring them to life. Call this Episode 1.
The Curse of Prime Delivery - It’s Fast and we’re Furious.
In the high-octane world of retail, Amazon has been the undisputed champion of fast and free delivery, leaving competitors in the dust. Let's compare Amazon's impact on next-day and free delivery in the UK over the years, how retailers have responded, and the pressures it has imposed on decision-making.
Amazon's Turbocharged Delivery
Next-Day Delivery: Amazon's Prime service has revolutionized the delivery landscape with its next-day and same-day options. By 2024, Amazon delivered over a billion items in the UK within a day or the next, setting a new benchmark for speed
1
. This has forced competitors to rev up their engines, offering similar services to keep pace. In the US 200 prime members enjoyed the delivery of over 9BN parcels in 2024 or 1 per week. Prime and its penetration will be a key watching metric for those looking to impacts.
Free Delivery: Initially, Amazon offered free delivery on orders over £25. However, in a recent move, the threshold was increased to £35, pushing non-Prime customers to either spend more or face delivery charges
2
. This strategic shift aims to encourage more customers to join Prime, further solidifying Amazon's grip on the market. This is going to impact retailers around the country and opens up more discussion on buy online, pick up in store.
Retailers' Response: The Need for Speed
Retailers have responded by adopting faster delivery options, but many struggle to match Amazon's scale and efficiency. The pressure to offer next-day delivery has become a significant challenge, with missed deliveries costing UK businesses £1.6 billion annually6. To stay competitive, retailers feel they must invest in smarter logistics and warehouse operations, often at the cost of profitability.But do they need this? Is the smart move now FBA?.
Pressures on Decision-Making: The High-Stakes Game
Amazon's dominance has imposed immense pressure on retailers to adapt quickly. The dynamic pricing model and fast delivery expectations have forced competitors to be agile and responsive. However, this race for speed and price competitiveness can be a double-edged sword. While it drives innovation, it also risks undermining profitability and sustainability for smaller retailers.
The Obsession: A Noose for Others?
Amazon's relentless pursuit of speed and efficiency has become a benchmark that others struggle to meet. This obsession with fast and free delivery has created a high-stakes environment where smaller retailers may find it difficult to survive. The increased costs of maintaining such services, combined with the need to match Amazon's pricing strategies, can be overwhelming. In this "Fast and Furious" world of retail, you have to decide if you are Paul Walker or Vin Diesel.
"Retailball: The Art of Winning in a Changing Game"
In a world where the retail landscape is as unpredictable as a baseball season, one man, Jack Harris, stood at the helm of a struggling retail chain. Jack was the Billy Beane of retail, determined to challenge traditional methods and find a winning strategy amidst the chaos. His team, like the Oakland A's, was underdogged by the giants of e-commerce, particularly Amazon, with its unparalleled mindshare and distribution capabilities.
The Challenge: Amazon's Dominance
Amazon's influence on the retail industry was akin to a home run in the bottom of the ninth inning—it changed the game entirely. With its vast distribution network and innovative fulfillment strategies, Amazon had set a new standard for customer expectations. Traditional retailers, like Jack's chain, were left scrambling to keep up. The high operating costs, complex supply chain management, and the need for digital transformation made it difficult for brick-and-mortar stores to compete34.
The Opportunity Costs
Jack faced a dilemma similar to Billy Beane's in "Moneyball." He had to decide whether to invest in more physical stores or pivot towards a more digital strategy. Each choice came with significant opportunity costs. Expanding physical presence meant higher overheads and less flexibility, while going digital required a complete overhaul of their business model. Jack realized that the traditional retail model was no longer viable; it was time to rethink distribution and focus on profitability rather than sheer store count. This is the conversation going on in stores all around the country now. 90% of those present at the partner day last week said, they were not even after taking the first steps. There is my worry.
The Sunk Costs
Many retailers were clinging to their existing strategies, much like Beane's reluctance to let go of underperforming players. Jack understood that past investments couldn't dictate future decisions. He needed to cut losses and adapt to the changing retail landscape. This meant embracing Amazon's strengths, not fighting them. Jack considered partnering with Amazon or leveraging its advertising platform to reach a broader audience.
The Comparative Advantage
Just as the Oakland A's leveraged players' unique skills, Jack sought to identify his chain's comparative advantages. They excelled in providing personalized customer experiences and curated product selections, something Amazon couldn't replicate. By focusing on these strengths, Jack aimed to carve out a niche in the market where his stores could thrive alongside, rather than against, Amazon's dominance. It is not necessarily how you have done business to date, it’s how you expand on how did things, being key.
The Statistical Discrimination
In "Moneyball," statistical analysis revolutionized player selection. Jack applied a similar approach to his retail strategy. He used data analytics to understand consumer behavior, optimize inventory, and tailor marketing efforts. This data-driven approach allowed him to make informed decisions about store locations and product offerings, ensuring each store was a home run in its market.
The Principle-Agent Problem - The Night Agent
Jack faced the challenge of aligning his team's goals with the company's overall strategy. He needed to motivate his staff to embrace change and work towards a more efficient, digitally integrated model. By empowering them with the tools and training necessary for success, Jack ensured that everyone was working towards the same objective: winning in the new retail game.
As Jack navigated the complex world of retail, he realized that success wasn't about beating Amazon but about finding a way to coexist and thrive. By leveraging Amazon's strengths while focusing on his own comparative advantages, Jack created a winning strategy. "Retailball" became a story of innovation over tradition, where the underdog retailer found a way to stay in the game by embracing change and optimizing for profitability in a rapidly evolving retail landscape.
Jack Harris and his team embody the spirit of "Moneyball," using strategic decision-making and resource allocation to navigate the challenges posed by Amazon's dominance. By focusing on their unique strengths and adapting to the changing retail landscape, they find a path to success in a market where traditional models are no longer viable.
Rightsizing Retail Stores
On Saturday last, I spoke with
Bobby Kerr
(Thanks @john fardy). The role of down sizinig or exiting a market is not truly rtold through occupancy figures. Jervis Streeet shopping centre is to be sold for 50% of its highest valuation despite, occupancy not being a probelm at all. Over 35% of the retail outlets are food chains. Jervis itself is in close proxiomity to Arnotts and other affordable stores. It is also a terrible looking building. There is no "Gra" in this place whatsoever. Experiential, it aint.
The reality is that the retail industry is undergoing a significant transformation, with many brands reassessing their store counts due to over-supply and distribution challenges. This trend is evident in the rapid pace of store closures across the U.S., with about 15,000 retail stores expected to close in 2025, significantly higher than the 7,325 closures in 2024. This shift reflects a broader strategy to optimize retail operations, focusing on profitability and efficiency rather than extensive physical presence.
Key Factors Influencing Store Closures
E-commerce Growth
: The convenience and competitive pricing of online shopping have led consumers to shift away from traditional brick-and-mortar stores.
Economic Pressures
: Inflation, supply chain disruptions, and changing consumer spending habits have strained retailers’ profitability.
Overexpansion
: Some retailers expanded rapidly without sustainable demand, leading to financial overreach.
Sustainability and Consumerism
Using sustainability as a lens, it's clear that consumers are increasingly questioning whether they have too much stuff. The fast fashion industry, in particular, is under scrutiny due to its environmental impact and unsustainable practices. Fast fashion encourages overconsumption, leading to massive textile waste—Americans generate about 82 pounds of textile waste annually. This has prompted consumers to favor brands that prioritize sustainability, with 70% willing to pay more for sustainable products.
Fast Fashion at Risk
Fast fashion brands are facing significant challenges due to their unsustainable practices and the growing demand for eco-friendly products. Brands like Quiz, a UK-based clothing retailer, have struggled in recent years.
Quiz clothing once posed a model for balance and growth. And Allbirds SEC S-1 Filing presented a case for utopian commerce. Both are now floundering with Quiz in adminstration and Allbirds in a turnaround strategy. Pray for Allbirds.
Quiz: A Timeline of Challenges
2020
: Quiz underwent a restructuring, renegotiating rents after lockdowns damaged sales. At this time, they adopted a healthy approach to convessions and internationalization.
2023-2024
: Quiz faced declining sales, with UK online operations severely impacted by economic pressures. Despite a 12% increase in international demand, overall sales declined.
December 2024
: Quiz warned of running out of cash by early 2025, seeking additional funding due to a significant reduction in revenue.
February 2025
: Quiz fell into administration, with Teneo handling the process. This led to the closure of 23 shops and about 200 redundancies.
Allbirds: A Sustainable Model Under Pressure
Allbirds, known for its sustainable footwear, initially thrived with a strong brand identity and commitment to eco-friendly practices. However, the brand has recently faced declining sales and store closures due to supply chain disruptions and shifting consumer behaviors. When they filed they S-1, pre IPO, they had a Utopian looking business model.
Their wrong decisions,
now a glorious cautionary tale - stay in your lane

Ecommerce Strategies for Growth
Ecommerce plays a crucial role in retail growth, especially in expanding customer bases and international reach. Retailers must navigate challenges such as subpar on-site search functionality and adapt to shifting consumer behaviors. Successful ecommerce strategies often involve AI-driven personalization, mobile optimization, and omnichannel experiences.
It is not the be all and end all. Customer trends move quick, very quick. The idea of long term brands is a tough consideration.
Key Ecommerce Trends for 2025
Marketplaces
: Marketplaces continue to drive consistent growth, offering expanded product offerings, reduced operational costs, and improved customer experiences.
Retail Media
: Retail media strategies are becoming essential for targeted advertising and customer engagement
AI Integration
: AI is increasingly a core strategic pillar for enhancing customer experiences and operational efficiency.
Sustainable Ecommerce Practices
As consumers become more environmentally conscious, sustainable ecommerce practices are gaining traction. These include eco-friendly packaging innovations, green supply chain management, and energy-efficient data centers. Retailers can leverage these practices to reduce environmental impact, boost brand loyalty, and potentially increase profits.
As I come back to reality, I am thinking.
Rightsizing Retail Stores
: How can retailers balance physical presence with ecommerce strategies to optimize profitability?
Sustainability and Consumerism
: What role do consumers play in driving demand for sustainable products, and how can retailers respond effectively?Does it matter anymore? Is sustainability the new DEI.
Fast Fashion at Risk
: How can fast fashion brands transition towards more sustainable practices without sacrificing profitability? OR should fast fashion exist at all, is there a new way to deliver this.
Ecommerce Strategies
: What are the most effective ecommerce strategies for expanding customer bases and international reach in the retail sector? Internationalisation is one of the last growth pillars, where does it sit in the mix?

The Acceleration of Retail Decline in 2025
The first quarter of 2025 has already proven devastating for traditional retailers. After experiencing 7,325 store closures in 2024, projections indicate an astonishing 15,000 locations may shutter throughout 2025, offset by only 5,800 new store openings. Major U.S. retailers have announced a staggering 334.3% more closures and 29.6% fewer openings compared to the same period last year.
High-profile casualties already include Joann, which plans to close 500 of its roughly 850 stores nationwide as part of its second bankruptcy filing in less than a year. Similarly, Liberated Brands, operator of iconic surf and lifestyle brands Volcom, Billabong, and Quicksilver, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, resulting in the closure of over 100 retail locations across the country. Other prominent retailers, including JCPenney, Macy's, and Kohl's, continue to trim their physical footprints. It won’t at this point, IMO, be enough.
Perhaps most emblematic of the crisis is Party City, which filed its second Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2024, with plans to liquidate all 695 stores in early 2025. Meanwhile, The Container Store filed for bankruptcy protection in late December 2024, though it successfully emerged in January 2025 after restructuring its debt and transitioning to private ownership.
External Forces Driving the Retail Age of Enlightenment
The Relentless March of E-commerce
The shift to online shopping continues to accelerate, fundamentally changing consumer behavior patterns. What was once a gradual migration became a stampede during the COVID-19 pandemic, permanently altering shopping habits. Global e-commerce sales were forecasted to reach $6.09 trillion by the end of 2024, with expectations of growing to $6.56 trillion in 2025. This, thankfully, has not happened, but ecommerce growth continues upwards.
The "Amazon effect" remains potent, with reports suggesting Amazon generates more than half of all retail sales growth in the United States. Additionally, the proliferation of direct-to-consumer brands with hyper-focused product offerings and "authentic" connections to specific consumer groups has further eroded traditional retailers' market share.
Persistent Economic Headwinds
Despite moderating inflation, prices remain significantly elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels. Walmart's CEO Doug McMillon recently expressed disappointment at the current level of food inflation, noting that food-at-home prices have seen a staggering 25% increase compared to pre-pandemic levels.
The Federal Reserve's series of interest rate hikes between March 2022 and January 2024 has made borrowing more expensive for retailers, with the federal funds rate reaching a range of 5.25-5.50%. These higher rates, which are expected to persist through much of 2025, particularly impact debt-laden retailers unable to refinance at favorable terms.But then the ZIRP days created false economies. It seems now unless you are Ryan Petersen or Marc Lore, money is hard to come by.
Changing Consumer Preferences
Beyond the online migration, consumers have shifted their spending priorities. There's evidence of a move toward experience spending versus material goods, as well as preferences for casual fashion in relaxed dress codes. Additionally, inflation-weary shoppers increasingly seek the lowest prices, often turning to online channels to find the best deals.
The rise of "fast fashion" has also transformed consumer expectations around price, style turnover, and the shopping experience itself. These behavioral shifts have left many traditional retailers struggling to adapt their merchandise mix and pricing strategies.
We continually ignore the cries of - we have enough shit. Leave us alone.
Internal Factors Contributing to Retail Failures
The Debt Burden
Many retailers that have filed for bankruptcy in 2025 share a common problem: overwhelming debt. Joann carried around $1 billion in debt even after securing $132 million in new financing during its first Chapter 11 filing in 2024. Similarly, numerous retailers have struggled with overleveraged balance sheets and rising interest expenses.
A significant portion of this debt often stems from leveraged buyouts by private equity firms, which saddle retailers with debt that becomes unsustainable when sales decline or economic conditions worsen.
Ownership structures and their motives are the silent killer of retail.
1. Joann Fabrics: Private Equity Rollercoaster
Timeline
:
1998: Acquired 250 House of Fabrics stores, rebranded as Jo-Ann Fabrics.
2010: Sold to Leonard Green & Partners (LGP) for $1.6B, transitioning to private equity ownership.
2021: Returned to public markets via IPO ($12/share).
2024–2025: Filed Chapter 11 twice, re-privatized under lender ownership.#
Strategic Shifts
:
LGP’s leveraged buyout left $1B+ debt, forcing aggressive cost-cutting and inventory rationalization. Post-IPO, failed merchandising shifts (e.g., Halloween assortment timing) eroded sales.
Post-bankruptcy privatization prioritized liquidity over store closures, worsening operational inefficiencies.
2. Liberated Brands: Complex Equity & Licensing Struggles
Ownership Structure
:
Majority owned by HLB (private equity), 19.9% by Authentic Brands Group (ABG), and management.
Strategic Challenges
:Reliance on wholesale (50% revenue) clashed with fast fashion and DTC trends. License terminations for Volcom, Billabong (2024) crippled North American operations.
Private equity ownership focused on brand acquisitions (Spyder, RVCA) but failed to invest in e-commerce, leading to liquidity crunches.
3. Party City: Private Equity Debt/Death Spiral
Timeline
: 2012: Acquired by Thomas H. Lee Partners (private equity).
2015: IPO with 55% retained by THL.
2024: Filed Chapter 11, liquidated; IP sold to Ad Populum ($20M)
Strategic Missteps
: THL’s debt-heavy model ($14.5M lease liabilities) and overexpansion to 900+ stores left no liquidity for experiential pivots. Post-bankruptcy, assets were acquired by discount retailers (Dollar Tree, Five Below).
4. The Container Store: From Public to Private Survival
Ownership Journey
:
2007: Leonard Green & Partners took majority stake.
2024: Filed Chapter 11; emerged privately owned by lenders in 2025.
Strategic Adjustments
:
Post-2024 bankruptcy eliminated debt, secured $40M financing, and integrated Bed Bath & Beyond spaces via Beyond Inc. partnership. Shift to private ownership prioritized operational continuity over growth.
5. JCPenney: Mall Operator Rescue
Ownership Shift
: 2020: Acquired by Simon Property Group and Brookfield Asset Management ($1.75B) post-bankruptcy.
New Strategy
: Focused on smaller-format stores (667 locations) and “shopping excitement” through partnerships (e.g., Sephora-in-Kohl’s model). Leveraged mall operators’ real estate expertise to renegotiate leases.
6. Macy’s: Institutional Investor Pressures
Ownership Profile
: 70% institutional (Vanguard: 11.71%, BlackRock: 8.88%). - Next Stop?
Strategic Drivers
: Post-1994 Federated acquisition consolidated regional brands (e.g., Broadway Stores) into Macy’s East/West. Current omnichannel push (Bloomie’s small-format stores) reflects institutional demands for digital growth. Fucked, if you ask the layman.
7. Kohl’s: Institutional Ownership & Stalled Turnaround
Ownership
: 99.1% institutional (Vanguard, BlackRock).
Strategic Crossroads
: 2022 strategic review rejected Franchise Group’s $53/share bid, opting for partnerships (Sephora) and 100+ small store. Institutional pressure prioritized share buybacks over debt reduction, leaving vulnerability to retail headwinds.
Common Themes in Ownership-Driven Strategies
Private Equity Debt Traps
: Joann, Party City, and Liberated Brands collapsed under leveraged buyout debt, limiting agility during market shifts.
Post-Bankruptcy Privatization
: The Container Store and Joann used Chapter 11 to shed debt but face growth constraints under lender ownership.
Institutional Investor Priorities
: Macy’s and Kohl’s balance dividends/buybacks with omnichannel investments, often lagging behind DTC trends.
Mall Operator Interventions
: Simon/Brookfield’s JCPenney acquisition highlights real estate-driven restructuring over brand innovation.
The Ownership-Strategy Mismatch
While external forces (e-commerce, inflation) intensified, ownership structures dictated strategic rigidity. Private equity’s debt focus and institutional short-termism clashed with the need for digital/experiential overhauls. As Party City’s liquidation and Joann’s repeated bankruptcies show, traditional retail models falter when ownership prioritizes financial engineering over consumer relevance. The survivors? Entities like The Container Store and JCPenney, where ownership aligned with operational pragmatism over growth-at-all-costs.
Operational Inefficiencies
Poor retail management practices have plagued many failing retailers. These include inadequate inventory control resulting in underperforming merchandise and out-of-stock situations, understaffing to maintain short-term profits, and ineffective pricing strategies.
When Joann emerged from its first bankruptcy in 2024, it notably failed to close underperforming stores and continued to operate with tight liquidity—decisions that ultimately led to its second bankruptcy filing in January 2025.
Failure to Adapt
Perhaps most critically, many bankrupted retailers failed to effectively adapt to changing market conditions. Liberated Brands explicitly cited shifting consumer preferences toward "'fast fashion' and e-commerce as opposed to branded apparel and brick-and-mortar retail" as a key factor in its bankruptcy filing.Forever 21 anyone? Thanks NIck Kaplan for the in here.
The inability to develop effective *omnichannel strategies—seamlessly integrating online and in-store experiences—has left many traditional retailers at a severe competitive disadvantage. While consumers increasingly expect frictionless shopping experiences across multiple channels, many retailers have struggled to make the necessary technological and operational investments.
*The author apologizes for the use of the expression Omnichannel.
Is the Traditional Retail Model Fundamentally Flawed?
The mounting evidence suggests the conventional retail model may indeed be structurally unviable in today's environment. Traditional retailers are hamstrung by capital-intensive operations, with significant resources tied up in real estate and inventory—creating illiquid assets that limit flexibility. By contrast, online retailers operate with more agile, cost-efficient business models that allow for greater adaptation to market shifts.
The democratization of retail has also led to price transparency across markets, eliminating retailers' ability to charge different prices in different regions and driving global price equalization toward the lowest common denominator. This margin compression has made it increasingly difficult for traditional retailers to maintain profitability.
Tellingly, the retailers showing the greatest resilience during this "retail apocalypse" are those with distinctive business models: discount superstores like Walmart and Target, low-cost "fast-fashion" brands such as Zara and H&M, dollar stores, and warehouse clubs like Costco. These successful operators have reimagined the retail model to minimize fixed costs while maximizing value perception.
Rethinking Retail for Survival
For retailers to survive in this challenging environment, fundamental transformation is essential. Industry experts suggest several strategies:
Diversification and Adaptation
Successful retailers are diversifying their merchandise mix to appeal to a broader customer base and reduce dependence on single product lines. They're also embracing e-commerce and omnichannel strategies, developing user-friendly websites optimized for mobile devices and providing seamless shopping experiences.
Financial Restructuring
Retailers must maintain strong financial management practices, including regular monitoring of cash flow, accurate financial records, and realistic budgets. Many should consider preemptive debt restructuring before reaching crisis points that necessitate bankruptcy filings.Note the work that ASOS have done in the UK.
Asset Transformation
Perhaps most critically, retailers need strategies that transform illiquid assets (real estate, inventory) into liquid assets, freeing up capital to invest in growth initiatives and creating financial buffers against market downturns. This might include rethinking store formats, implementing more efficient inventory management systems, or even exploring sale-leaseback arrangements for owned properties.
The Empire Strikes Back: A New Retail Reality
The wave of bankruptcies and store closures in 2025 represents more than just another challenging year for retail—it signals a fundamental reckoning with a business model that increasingly appears misaligned with contemporary market realities. While some analysts project a potential decline in retail distress as vulnerable companies complete their restructurings, the underlying structural challenges remain unresolved.
For retail executives, investors, and stakeholders, the message is clear: incremental changes will not suffice. Surviving in this new retail reality requires reimagining core business models, embracing technological innovation, and developing more agile approaches to serving customers across multiple channels. Those unable to undertake this transformation may well join the growing ranks of once-iconic retailers that now exist only in retail history books.
The question has evolved from whether the traditional retail model is broken to how fundamentally it must be reinvented for a future that has already arrived.

_body:
Introduction: The Illusion of Simplicity
In the hedonistic times, we lived by the mantra, better, faster more. Now crippled by risk management, channel selection and the paralysis by analysis we are in a new battle. The battle for middle earth (yeah, I'm sticking with the motif) is one as laborious as the later stages ofg the LOTR books - the one where Frodo is in Mordor and it goes on and on and on. I read that and thought Tolkein made it so boring and over descriptive as to give the same sense of hopelessness and vastness that was being felt by his leading hobbits. You win Tolkein, you win.
The Heady 'Ol Days
There was a time when selling on Amazon was a revelation. You uploaded your products, flipped on the ads, and waited. It worked—until it didn’t.
Now, as we roll into 2025, we find ourselves in an ecommerce paradox. Amazon is still the behemoth, yes. But putting all your chips on a single platform feels like playing poker with your cards face up. It looks simple. It feels efficient. But it hides risk, caps growth, and keeps your brand playing defense instead of offense.
So, is a single-marketplace strategy efficient or lazy? Is multichannel expansion a growth engine or a chaotic mess of integrations, feeds, and false promises?
Let’s explore the data, the contradictions, and the reality of where the modern ecommerce brand finds itself—armed with more technology than ever, but stuck choosing between comfort and chaos.
Marketplace Pulse
provide the backdrop, as with so many great marketplace stories.
Me own work
Chapter One: Amazon, the Necessary Evil?
Let’s start where it hurts.
Amazon accounted for nearly 38% of all U.S. ecommerce in 2024. According to Wedbush, it’s expected to grow operating income by 24% in 2025, outpacing both Meta and Google. Its AWS division is booming. Its ad platform is now a cornerstone of its revenue model. It is, by every traditional measure, the smartest bet in town. Let's not even get into ad growth.
And yet, ask any ecommerce brand founder what keeps them up at night, and they’ll whisper the same fear: "What if Amazon changes the rules?"
Michael Jones, ex-CEO of CandleScience and former exec at Spoonflower, calls Amazon "
a beast you have to feed daily, but one that might bite you when you’re sleeping."
You can't argue with the scale. But you also can't ignore the risk:
Increasing seller fees
Limited brand control
Algorithmic favoritism
Buy Box volatility
And the terrifying "Account Health Suspension" roulette
Amazon works—until it works
against
you.
Brands like Anchor and Peak Design learned this early. They used Amazon as a launchpad, then sprinted toward diversification. Because at a certain point, survival depends on control.
But if Amazon isn't the final answer, what is?
Chapter Two: The Multichannel Myth... or Masterstroke?
According to Feedonomics, brands that operate across three or more channels see a 494% increase in order rate. Marketplace Pulse reports that brands on multiple platforms grow 2x faster than the ecommerce average.
Your customer is hiding in plain sight
The story isn’t just statistical. It’s strategic.
Take Anker, the portable charger giant. It didn’t become a billion-dollar brand by going all-in on Amazon. It expanded into Walmart, Best Buy,
Target.com
, and even specialty marketplaces in Europe and Asia. Its brand equity is now divorced from any single platform.
Or look at Govee, the smart lighting brand. It started on Amazon, but it didn’t stop there. It built its DTC store, then expanded into niche home improvement marketplaces and now dominates lighting categories on
HomeDepot.com
and
Lowes.com
.
The lesson: complexity, when managed well, becomes a moat.
Chapter Three: Growth vs. Efficiency—A False Binary
Here’s where many brands get stuck. The
Nick Kaplan
algorithm.
They think multi-marketplace selling means blowing out the budget. It doesn't. It means reallocating smartly. NRF’s "Five Forces" report reframes this well: in 2025, the measure of brand health isn’t profitability—it’s
efficiency.
GMROI (Gross Margin Return on Inventory)
nCAC (new Customer Acquisition Cost)
Retention Rate
These aren't anti-growth metrics. They’re smarter growth metrics.
The brands winning in 2025 will be those who don’t cut spend—they optimize it. They invest in tools that let them scale product listings, localize feeds, test channels, and syndicate content at speed.
Take a page from Caraway, the DTC cookware darling. It scaled from 1 to 7 marketplaces in 18 months by using tech like Feedonomics and ChannelAdvisor.
It didn’t add headcount. It added capability.
Complexity isn't the problem. Poor prioritization is.
Chapter Four: Technology Is the Multiplier
Remember when listing on a new marketplace meant custom dev work, a six-month timeline, and a stiff drink? Not anymore.
Modern commerce platforms offer plug-and-play integrations. API-first tools like Feedonomics, Plytix, and
Cart.com
act as your central nervous system. They let brands operate with the agility of a startup and the scale of an enterprise.
This is where the "Feedprint" concept matters. Think of it like your distribution DNA. The more channels you syndicate to
intelligently,
the more chances you have to win—without burning budget or bandwidth.
Marketplace optimization has become the new performance marketing. Titles, tags, categorization, stock syncing—they're all levers for discovery and margin.
The question isn’t "Should we add another channel?" It’s: "Why haven’t we already?"
Thanks to
Feedonomics
for the above.
Chapter Five: The Platform Portfolio Play
Let’s make it simple.
The most successful brands treat platforms like stocks. They diversify. They hedge. They learn the rules of each exchange and trade accordingly.
This isn’t just about revenue. It’s about defensibility. In M&A, a diversified channel mix adds to your multiple. In a downturn, it spreads risk. In a pricing war, it gives you options.
Brands that lean into channel complexity don’t just survive. They scale. New channels - provide new opps.
Chapter Six: So, Is Growth Worth It?
Let’s stop pretending this is a trick question.
Yes, growth is harder. Yes, complexity is real. But in ecommerce, standing still is falling behind.
[Insert GIF: Shark swimming forward with caption “If you stop, you sink”]
The real risk isn’t expansion. It’s irrelevance.
2025 isn’t about who sells the most on Amazon. It’s about who shows up where the customer actually shops. And guess what? They’re everywhere. Temu. TikTok. Google. Kroger. You name it.
Growth isn’t the enemy. Poor execution is.
Conclusion: Customers Are Hiding in Plain Sight
As RMW Commerce says, "The customer is hiding in plain sight."
Your job is to stop hiding from them.
The brands of tomorrow are building Feedprints, not footprints. They’re leveraging AI, not fearing it. They’re optimizing channels, not obsessing over vanity metrics.
So, is one marketplace enough?
Only if you’re okay with one outcome: limited growth.
Choose complexity. Choose growth. Choose relevance.
And maybe, just maybe, stop feeding the beast without feeding your brand.
