In the midst of a mercantile war not seen since the turn of ther 20th century, we are faced with challenges. The US has long been a mecca for manby EU brands looking to scale through commerce, it always proved elusive. Too big. In most practical ways but in terms of understanding the mindset it needs to survive, not succeed in North America is not one that sits well on EU sensibilities, or anyone with a risk profile that is geared towards sleeping well.
Tariff Wars:
Motivations - possible
Straight up control and a thought process that tariffs can grow the wealth of the nation.
A desire to do deals on global debts
Devaluing the almighty dollar- who would have the balls to make the default global fallback currency something else?
Whatever the desire, it leaves us all floudnering. What, instead of waiting (like we always do), we decided to manage or own path. What if we remembered Harley Finkelstein told us Shopify are only 1% of global retail revenues and that only 14% of that comes through cross border. The vehicles are desire, local knowledge is well designed, but is the knowledge evenly distributed?
These are not easy decisions or small ones, but need to be made. There is no short termism allowed. Not anymore.
You are not serious people.
Global brands today face an
Odyssey-like journey
in expanding through cross-border e-commerce. The rewards – access to new customers and revenue streams – are vast, but so are the challenges at each leg of the voyage. This mini white paper charts the current landscape, obstacles, required tools, team makeup, success stories, and new horizons of cross-border e-commerce, framed as a heroic journey for brand leaders and tech executives.
The Call to Adventure: Global Cross-Border E-Commerce Landscape
Global cross-border e-commerce revenues by region (2019 vs 2023). Europe leads in total cross-border sales, while Asia-Pacific has seen the fastest growth.
The
cross-border e-commerce market is booming
. In 2023, worldwide cross-border online sales
surpassed the $1 trillion mark
, recovering from a post-pandemic dip and resuming steady growth). Projections show global cross-border e-com revenue reaching about
$1.1 trillion in 2024
as international online shopping becomes the norm . This growth is fueled by consumers increasingly willing to buy from overseas for variety and price advantages. In some countries,
over 80% of online shoppers purchase from abroad
– for example, more than
eight in ten
Austrian e-buyers shop internationally . Small markets often rely on cross-border shopping to access brands not present locally, and even in larger markets like the U.S., consumers are turning to foreign platforms for deals amid inflation. Living in Ireland I can testify to this.
Importantly,
regional dynamics vary
. Europe currently contributes the most to cross-border revenues globally (about $469B in 2023), thanks to many countries trading with each other across relatively open borders.. Asia-Pacific, meanwhile, has seen the fastest growth – cross-border sales there nearly
doubled (+96%) between 2019 and 2023
, reaching ~$300B . This surge is driven by emerging markets coming online and by influential new players.
Global marketplaces and integrators
are central to this landscape:
Amazon and Alibaba
dominate much of the cross-border market, leveraging vast logistics networks to ship worldwide. Amazon’s cross-border activities (through its global marketplaces and programs like Global Selling) are a
core component of its revenue (
enabling millions of merchants to reach customers abroad. Alibaba’s AliExpress and newer entrants like
Temu (Pinduoduo)
and
SHEIN
have rapidly gained international traction by offering ultra-low prices and aggressive social media marketing. For instance,
Chinese platforms now account for 1 in 3 online purchases in Spain
, demonstrating their quick rise in Europe.
Leading e-commerce markets
reflect these trends. The
United States is the single largest origin of cross-border e-commerce
– U.S.-based sellers shipped roughly
$605 billion worth of products to foreign consumers in 2023
(owing largely to giants like Amazon and eBay). “Greater China” (mainland China/Hong Kong) is the next largest exporter at about $158B, though this number is diluted by Chinese firms routing sales through overseas hubs (SHEIN, for example, bases operations in Singapore). On the flip side,
demand is global
: the top import markets for cross-border e-com in 2023 were the
UK (≈$109B), Japan ($92B) and Germany ($87B)
, followed by Canada, France, and India. It’s noteworthy that
India and Brazil now rank among the top 10 importers
of cross-border goods – a sign that emerging economies are embracing international online shopping at scale. Overall,
cross-border consumer behavior has shifted
to normalize international purchases. Shoppers increasingly prioritize
availability and price over borders
, hopping on marketplaces or merchant sites abroad if it means finding the right product or deal. Executives must recognize this
call to adventure
: global consumers are out there, and they are buying. The stage is set for brands to venture beyond their home markets.
Is international ubiquitous purchasing a problem?
Same problem everywhere means race to the bottom in terms of pricing. Should a differentiation strategy be employed? INcreasingly, I think so. For the long term among you, this can be the only way forward. It is also where margin lives and hides. It has no past, so no incumbency. Building futures is easier than removing legacies.
Trials and Tribulations: Current Cross-Border Challenges
Every Odysseus faces monsters – for cross-border sellers, these take the form of
tariffs, taxes, compliance hurdles, and complex logistics
. In recent years,
tariff wars have raised the cost of serving key markets
. The U.S.-China trade war, for example, imposed steep duties on categories from electronics to apparel, squeezing margins for brands sourcing in China and selling to the U.S. Market uncertainty persists: even eBay has warned investors about
“uncertainty around U.S. tariffs and de minimis changes” in 2025
). (De minimis refers to the import duty exemption threshold – currently $800 in the U.S. – which lawmakers are considering lowering to curb low-value Chinese shipments.) Such policy shifts could suddenly make it more expensive and paperwork-heavy to fulfill small orders into the U.S., a market many international DTC brands covet.
Tax and compliance friction
are perennial challenges across all corridors. Brands must navigate a patchwork of regulations: differing VAT/GST in each country, customs documentation requirements, product standards, and data laws. Over
40–50% of organizations worldwide say classifying products with the correct HS (Harmonized System) codes is a major challenge
() (). Without accurate HS codes and paperwork, shipments can be delayed or fined. Indeed, customs delays plague many cross-border operations – nearly
half of Asia-Pacific companies (48%) report frequent delays due to incorrect documentation
, versus about one-third in Europe and North America (). Compliance burdens have grown recently: for example, the EU ended its €22 VAT exemption, meaning
100% of imports into Europe now require VAT collection
(even low-value goods) – a new hurdle that brands and marketplaces addressed with tools like IOSS (Import One-Stop Shop).
Legislative differences
also add friction: Europe’s strict data privacy (GDPR) can affect email marketing and customer data use across borders; certain products (e.g. cosmetics, electronics) face different safety certifications country by country. Each new market can feel like navigating a new legal maze.
Hand-in-hand with compliance are the
operational complexities from first mile to last mile
. Shipping internationally is substantially more complex than domestic fulfillment.
Sellers must get products export-ready in the first mile
– proper packaging, documentation, and often consolidation for overseas transport. Then comes international transit (ocean or air freight), customs clearance, and the
“last mile” in the destination country’s delivery network
. Each leg can introduce delays or quality issues. In many cases, brands rely on multiple partners – freight forwarders, customs brokers, local couriers – which increases coordination complexity. Different countries have varying address formats and delivery preferences (locker boxes, pickup points, etc.), which brands must accommodate for a good customer experience.
Returns logistics
are another beast: handling international returns or exchanges can be costly and slow, leading some merchants to refund without requiring a return. All these moving parts drive up cost:
cross-border shipping can be 3-4x the cost of domestic
, and surcharges (fuel, remote area fees, etc.) add up. It’s no surprise that in a recent survey,
“cost of shipping” was the top disruption 67% of Middle East & North Africa e-commerce firms expected to worsen ()
– reflecting global inflation in logistics.
Finally,
geopolitical and legislative “storms”
loom over cross-border trade.
Trade tensions
(like US versus the world) create uncertainty in supply chains and often provoke retaliatory regulations.
Brexit
introduced new customs borders between the UK and EU, complicating what was previously intra-EU trade (). Regions also impose new e-commerce laws – from India’s data localization rules to Europe’s sustainability regulations (e.g. packaging waste requirements) – that companies must monitor closely. In sum, the cross-border journey is fraught with trials:
tariffs, taxes, compliance paperwork, shipping delays, and high costs
are the
Scylla and Charybdis
through which brands must skillfully steer. The key is to anticipate these challenges and build resilience into operations. For instance, many merchants keep individual order values low to minimize duties – in fact, about
79% of cross-border purchases into North America and Europe fall below duty de minimis thresholds
(), a strategy that could be upended if laws change. Successful navigation requires not only willpower but also the right tools and allies, which we examine next.
What happens after May 2nd?
Tools and Tech for the Journey: Software & Infrastructure Needs
Odysseus had his ship and sword; a modern cross-border enterprise needs its
software and infrastructure stack
. Scaling internationally without the right tech is like sailing without a map. Key needs include
localization, customer service, automation, and region-specific marketing capabilities
.
Customer experience localization is paramount.
Shoppers are far more likely to buy (and stay loyal) if the experience speaks their language – literally and figuratively. Brands therefore need
multi-language customer service tools and content management
. This ranges from having websites/apps translated into local languages, to supporting multiple currencies, to customer support via chat/email in the customer’s tongue. For example, in regions like the Middle East or Latin America,
cultural and language barriers
are cited as a top concern by over 30% of companies () – meaning a lack of localization can directly hurt sales. Solutions like AI-powered translation (for product descriptions, FAQs, and even live chat) can help smaller teams cover more languages. Many brands invest in
localized sites or microsites
per region, or leverage geolocation to show the right language and currency automatically. On the customer support side, tools such as helpdesk platforms with translation features or third-party BPO call centers can ensure 24/7 support in local languages.
Payment localization
is another must-have infrastructure: offering local payment methods (like Klarna in Europe, Alipay in China, cash on delivery in some Mideast markets) and displaying prices in local currency with duties/taxes included builds trust. Without these, even interested foreign consumers might abandon cart.
Beyond localization,
communication and marketing automation
tailored to different regions is critical. A global marketing team needs the ability to segment audiences by country, send region-specific campaigns, and comply with local contact regulations.
Email marketing systems and CRM
should allow segmentation for time zones and languages – e.g. scheduling a promotion to hit inboxes at 10am local time in each region.
Personalization engines
can use regional behavior data to recommend relevant products (for instance, promoting winter coats to Canadian shoppers while showing summer attire to Australians at the same time of year). Marketing teams also benefit from
centralized dashboards that track regional performance
– so they can compare, say, conversion rates in Germany vs. Japan and tweak strategies accordingly. Automation can also handle complexity like
localized pricing and inventory
: if you maintain separate inventory pools or warehouses per region, your e-commerce platform should route orders to the correct fulfillment center and display accurate stock levels per region.
Order routing and OMS (Order Management Systems)
become vital infrastructure as you scale cross-border, to optimize delivery times and costs by fulfilling from the best location.
Another growing need is for
retail media and localized advertising tech
. When expanding abroad, brands often rely on major marketplaces or retailers for distribution – and success partly means
mastering the ad platforms on those channels
. For example, advertising on Amazon (sponsored products) or on regional marketplaces (like Mercado Libre in Latin America or Zalora in Southeast Asia) can make or break your visibility. The rise of retail media networks means brands must allocate budget and creative to ads on partner sites and apps. Notably, retail media has exploded to become about
20% of all digital ad spend worldwide in 2024
with global retail media ad spending growing ~18% YoY. This underscores that
brands need tools to manage ads across multiple retailer platforms
in different countries. Investing in a retail media management platform or agency expertise for each key marketplace can greatly enhance performance. Likewise,
social media and search advertising
should be localized – e.g. using WeChat or TikTok in APAC, or region-specific influencers who can authentically promote the brand. Marketing automation tools that integrate local ad channels (like Baidu SEO for China or LINE messaging in Japan) help central teams coordinate campaigns that resonate locally.
Lastly, don’t overlook
compliance and backend systems
.
Tax automation software
(such as Avalara, Vertex, etc.) is crucial to calculate and collect the correct VAT/GST/duties at checkout for each destination – avoiding nasty compliance issues later.
Trade compliance systems
can automate HS code classification and screen for restricted items to certain countries. And robust
analytics
are needed to monitor cross-border performance – e.g. identifying if delivery times are lagging in one region or if return rates are higher in another, so you can react. In summary, the tech stack for cross-border must enable
seamless localization, proactive customer service, efficient logistics, and targeted marketing
across borders. Many solutions exist (often cloud-based or provided by ecommerce platforms), but the onus is on leadership to assemble the right “ship” for the journey. With the right infrastructure, brands can navigate complexity at scale – turning what could be a chaotic voyage into a well-charted course.
Crew and Competencies: Team Requirements for Cross-Border Success
Even the best ship needs a capable crew. Successful cross-border e-commerce requires a
team with diverse roles and expertise
– a combination of global vision and local know-how. Many companies stumble here: it’s common to have
gaps
in expertise when first expanding internationally. Identifying and filling these roles is crucial to execute your strategy.
First, leadership must assign clear
ownership of the cross-border initiative
. This often means a
Head of International E-Commerce
or
Global E-Commerce Director
(if the company is large enough) who coordinates all cross-border efforts and is accountable for growth abroad. Under this leader, several key roles are needed:
Logistics & Operations Manager (International)
– responsible for the end-to-end supply chain of cross-border orders. This person handles warehouse strategy (e.g. when to open an overseas fulfillment center), shipping carrier selection, customs broker relationships, and return logistics. They ensure the first mile to last mile pipeline flows smoothly. For example, if orders to the Middle East are seeing delays, this manager investigates and might contract a new local last-mile carrier. They often coordinate with 3PLs and integrators; in a sense, they are the
navigator
keeping the ship on course.
International Marketing Manager
– responsible for customer acquisition and growth in target markets. This role localizes campaigns and messaging, overseeing country-specific marketing calendars, promotions, and possibly managing local agencies or partners. They need to understand local culture and channels (e.g. knowing that in Germany, consumers respond to different messaging than in the US, or that in China, one must leverage WeChat and local influencers). Often, successful firms hire
regional marketing leads
or country managers who report to the international marketing head – for instance, a lead for Europe, one for APAC, one for the Middle East, etc., who can execute on the ground. This team crafts the brand story in each market, balancing consistency with cultural relevance.
Localization & Customer Experience Lead
– driving all aspects of localization (site/app translation, product content, sizing guides, customer support) and ensuring a great CX for international customers. This role might manage a team of translators or work with localization vendors. They also train customer service reps or chatbots to handle multiple languages. Essentially, they champion the perspective of the foreign customer within the company, making sure everything from the website copy to the return policy is appropriate locally. A common gap is underestimating this – many companies start by simply translating their site via Google Translate and find it’s not enough. A dedicated lead ensures a professional localization effort. They also monitor international CSAT/NPS scores to identify pain points for overseas shoppers.
Customs & Compliance Specialist
– focusing on the nitty-gritty of international trade compliance. This role ensures the company complies with import/export regulations: correct tariff codes, import licenses if needed, labeling requirements (e.g. language on product packaging), and tax rules. They keep track of changes like new EU VAT rules or US de minimis law changes. When expanding to a new country, the compliance specialist assesses legal feasibility (can we ship this product there? what regulations apply?). This position is often filled by someone with logistics or legal background. Small firms may outsource this to consultants or rely on partners, but as volume grows, having in-house expertise saves costly mistakes.
In addition to these core roles, successful cross-border teams tap into
regional expertise
. Some hire local country managers or advisors – essentially guides native to the market who know the terrain. For example, a brand might have a China e-commerce consultant or a small team in-market to handle local partnerships and feedback to HQ. Moreover,
customer support staff
fluent in target languages are needed (whether in-house or via a service provider) to respond to inquiries in local time zones.
IT and analytics support
is also important – the tech team must ensure the e-commerce platform supports multi-country operations, and analysts should track international KPIs closely.
Many organizations initially lack these dedicated roles, with domestic teams trying to cover international tasks “off the side of their desk.” This often leads to errors and slow response to issues.
Successful firms recognize the need to fill the talent gap
. For instance, over
56% of retail/manufacturing companies now engage in cross-border e-commerce sales
, which has driven a surge in demand for e-commerce localization specialists and international logistics managers. Leading brands often partner with experts while they build internal talent – e.g. contracting a global e-commerce solutions provider (like Global-e or eShopWorld) that can handle many aspects, and learning from them. Over time, however, building an in-house “centre of excellence” for cross-border is invaluable. Teams that coordinate across functions – marketing, ops, customer service, compliance – in a unified international division tend to execute better. Regular syncs between the global team and local market teams (or distributors) ensure alignment.
In short, your cross-border crew should include
strategists (to chart the course), operators (to row the ship), and local guides (to avoid shoals)
. With the right people in the right roles – and clear mandates for each – the company can respond quickly to overseas market dynamics. They’ll know how to execute an international promotion, how to solve a customs holdup, and how to wow a customer 5,000 miles away. With a strong crew, the ship is well-equipped to reach its destination.
Stories of Success: Case Studies in Cross-Border E-Commerce
What does a successful cross-border journey look like in practice? Let’s look at a few “heroes’ journeys” – companies large and mid-market that have traversed this terrain and thrived, offering lessons to others.
Gymshark: From UK Garage to Global Fitness Phenomenon.
This athletic apparel brand began as a UK startup in 2012 and achieved unicorn status by leveraging cross-border e-commerce early. By 2015,
Gymshark was shipping to 131 countries
, tapping into the fact that cross-border e-commerce was growing twice as fast as domestic at the time. Without a single physical store, Gymshark built a global community via social media (especially Instagram) and sold directly online worldwide. Key to its success was
localized marketing and strategic ops
: Gymshark’s youthful branding translated well across markets, and they used influencer partnerships in different countries (e.g. fitness YouTubers in the US, Europe, and Asia) to build awareness. Operationally, Gymshark initially fulfilled all orders from the UK, but as demand surged in the U.S., they partnered with a U.S. 3PL (Radial) to stock and ship locally, significantly cutting delivery times. This hybrid model – a lean central team with outsourced logistics in target markets – allowed Gymshark to
provide 2-3 day delivery in key regions and smooth returns
, replicating a local-like experience. The lesson from Gymshark is the power of
digital-native global expansion
: a strong brand story and social media prowess can create global demand, but backing it with regional fulfillment and customer experience is what sustains the growth.
Nike: Speeding Up a Global Digital Rollout.
Nike is a global giant, but even it faced challenges in cross-border e-commerce. In the early 2010s, Nike’s country-specific e-commerce launches (e.g.
nike.com
in Japan, China) took 18+ months each, with heavy investment. To accelerate, Nike partnered with cross-border integrator
ESW (eShopWorld)
to rapidly stand up direct-to-consumer online stores in multiple countries. This “plug-and-play” approach allowed Nike to leverage ESW’s localization, payments, and fulfillment infrastructure instead of building each from scratch. The result was a much faster deployment of localized Nike e-commerce sites across dozens of markets – achieving in a few months what previously took years. Nike’s bold strategy shows how even large firms can adopt a
”digital expansion SWAT team”
mindset: by using an experienced partner, they filled gaps in internal capability (like local payment processing, duty calculations, etc.) and scaled their
direct
reach to consumers globally without waiting to develop everything in-house. The payoff has been huge: Nike now enjoys robust online sales in markets where it has no stores, and it controls the brand experience end-to-end. The takeaway is that
speed to market and local finesse
(via partnerships or acquisitions) can be a winning strategy, even for the biggest brands. In a fast-moving global market, first-mover advantage in capturing online consumers can’t be understated.
SHEIN: Fast Fashion Conquers the West.
No cross-border discussion is complete without SHEIN, the Chinese fast-fashion upstart that took the world by storm. Founded in China, SHEIN had virtually no domestic market (China has its own giants) – so from the outset, it was built as a cross-border enterprise, selling into the U.S., Europe, and beyond. Through a combination of ultra-low prices, an endless stream of new styles, and savvy TikTok/Instagram marketing,
SHEIN’s revenue skyrocketed from an estimated $2 billion in 2018 to over $30 billion in 2022
, with the vast majority of sales in North America and Europe. Its mobile app became one of the most downloaded in the U.S. for shopping. SHEIN’s success rests on
world-class logistics and data-driven merchandising
: it built a supply chain that could ship individual packages from factories in China to Western customers in as little as 10 days, at virtually no shipping cost to the buyer. By strategically using chartered air freight and local distribution partnerships, SHEIN made cross-border shipping appear invisible. On the front end, SHEIN localized content in multiple languages and tuned its app’s algorithm to show trending products tailored to each region’s tastes. They also navigated tariffs cleverly by shipping many small packages (often below de minimis thresholds) and even set up warehousing in key countries to forward-deploy popular products. A key lesson from SHEIN is the importance of
understanding the global consumer psyche
– they tapped into Gen Z’s desire for trendy, affordable clothes and delivered it across borders in a way that felt native (local pricing, free returns, engaging local influencers). However, SHEIN’s rise also highlights potential pitfalls: it now faces scrutiny around sustainability and regulatory compliance (issues that become amplified at scale). Still, its meteoric growth underscores that a
born-global approach
, if executed with relentless efficiency, can disrupt incumbents. Traditional retailers now watch SHEIN as the benchmark for reaching young consumers worldwide through e-commerce.
Anker & DJI: Niche Electronics Go Global via Marketplaces.
A pair of Chinese manufacturers, Anker (portable chargers/accessories) and DJI (drones), illustrate how even mid-sized companies can become global leaders by leveraging cross-border channels.
Anker
entered crowded electronics markets overseas by focusing on quality and winning customer trust on platforms like Amazon. They invested heavily in R&D to ensure their chargers and cables outperformed others, and it paid off – Anker’s products gained a reputation for reliability, reflected in strong reviews. This built a loyal fanbase globally, all through e-commerce. By listing on Amazon in the U.S. and EU, Anker sidestepped the need for physical distribution networks. They then expanded to their own DTC site, using social media and tech expos to build brand recognition. Today, Anker is a top-selling charging brand in many countries – a testament to
product excellence and savvy use of marketplace infrastructure
(Prime shipping, reviews, etc.) to go global.
DJI
, on the other hand, created a new product category (consumer drones) and
had
to go global to find its market. DJI leveraged both DTC and reseller partners worldwide. It localized its marketing for hobbyists, filmmakers, and enterprises, highlighting different use cases in different regions (e.g. aerial photography in the West, industrial uses in other markets). By setting up regional offices for support and training while selling primarily through online channels, DJI achieved dominance with reportedly
70%+ global market share in drones
. Their story shows the value of
innovation and timing
– with a unique product, they captured global mindshare early, and then maintained it through strong after-sales support and community building (e.g. online forums, ambassador programs) across borders.
Temu: New Challenger on the Scene.
Finally, consider Temu, a very recent entrant (launched 2022 by Pinduoduo) that exemplifies the rapid rise possible via cross-border e-commerce today. Temu is a bargain shopping app offering a cornucopia of low-priced goods shipped from China to the U.S. and Europe. In less than two years, Temu has achieved massive scale – by mid-2024 it was reported that
34% of U.S. consumers were buying from Temu at least once a month, surpassing eBay’s 29%
in a survey (. Such a feat – overtaking an incumbent’s engagement levels – was accomplished through aggressive social advertising (think Super Bowl ads and viral TikTok hauls),
gamified promotions
, and rock-bottom prices often subsidized by the parent company. Temu piggybacks on a well-oiled Chinese supply chain and logistics network (including guidance from its sister company Pinduoduo) to sell everything from clothing to electronics overseas. Its rise shows that
the cross-border market still has room for disruptors
, especially those who innovate on price and customer engagement. However, Temu and similar fast-growth players face challenges in sustaining quality and navigating regulatory crackdowns (the U.S. government is eyeing de minimis abuses that apps like Temu allegedly exploit).
For established brands, Temu’s story is a wake-up call:
competition in cross-border e-commerce can come from unexpected places
. It reinforces the need for constant innovation in customer acquisition and value proposition when operating globally.
These case studies – spanning apparel, footwear, electronics, and marketplaces – highlight a few common threads.
Success in cross-border e-commerce is achievable for both upstarts and giants
if they leverage their strengths and adapt to global dynamics. Key learnings include: start with a digitally-driven approach and build a community (Gymshark, SHEIN); ensure operations can deliver on the promise (SHEIN’s logistics, Nike’s partnerships); prioritize quality and trust to stand out (Anker, DJI); and don’t be afraid to disrupt the status quo (Temu). Each “hero” encountered setbacks, but they adjusted course – a mindset every brand should embrace. Cross-border growth is rarely linear, but as these examples show, the journey can yield transformative results for those who persist.
New Horizons: Alternative Growth Markets Beyond the US
For many Western brands, the first instinct for cross-border expansion is to target the
U.S. market
(if they aren’t U.S.-based already). The U.S. is indeed huge and relatively homogenous, but it is also highly competitive and increasingly costly to serve (due to tariffs, rising customer acquisition costs, etc.). As the cross-border landscape evolves, it’s wise to look at
alternative growth markets beyond the U.S.
, which may offer big opportunities with less saturation. In this final leg of our Odyssey, we identify some regions that global brand leaders should have on their radar, supported by data and trends.
Europe – Intra- and Extra-EU Opportunities
:
For North American brands, Europe remains a very attractive next step – it’s the
largest cross-border e-com region
by revenue, and European consumers are accustomed to buying internationally (both within Europe and from the U.S./Asia). The EU’s single market makes scaling across multiple countries efficient – once you localize for key languages and set up an EU distribution node, you can serve 27 countries with relatively little friction (post-Brexit UK requires separate handling, but is itself a top market). Data shows the
UK, Germany, France, and Italy
are among the top destinations globally for cross-border purchases – so demand is there. However, success in Europe means addressing local nuance: e.g. accepting payment methods like SEPA or Klarna, complying with stricter privacy and sustainability rules, and competing with strong local e-commerce players (like Zalando in fashion or MediaMarkt in electronics). Still, Europe’s high internet penetration and affluent customer base make it low-hanging fruit for brands that can navigate its regulations. Many mid-sized U.S. brands have found Europe to be a lucrative second home – for instance,
Allbirds (US shoe brand) operates e-commerce in 30+ European countries
and even opened stores in UK/Germany after seeing strong online demand . The takeaway:
Europe is a mature market worth pursuing
; the cross-border consumer there is alive and well, and even
expects
international options when domestic selection is limited.
Asia-Pacific (APAC) – Beyond China’s Borders
Asia-Pacific is a diverse mix of markets at different stages of e-commerce development, but many are in high-growth mode. Southeast Asia, in particular, has been dubbed the “next frontier” – countries like
Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Philippines
boast young, mobile-savvy populations coming online rapidly. E-commerce in SE Asia has been growing ~20-30% annually, accelerated by marketplaces like Shopee (from Singapore) and Lazada (Alibaba-owned). Cross-border plays a big role here: consumers often buy from China-based platforms for affordable products, but they also crave Western brands. For example, Singapore and Hong Kong (advanced economies) are major hubs where
cross-border spending is high
– Singapore is actually the 3rd largest origin for cross-border exports in some analyses (partly due to re-export activity). For brands, APAC outside of China represents a chance to get in early in fast-rising markets.
Australia
is another market often overlooked – it’s an affluent, English-speaking country where e-commerce is well-established, and Aussies frequently order from the US/UK. The
Asia-Pacific region saw 96% cross-border growth from 2019-2023, outpacing the Americas
, showing the momentum. However, each APAC market requires localization (language for Southeast Asia, sizing and content for cultural fit, etc.), and logistics can be tricky due to less developed infrastructure in some nations. Many brands partner with regional e-com enablers or list on marketplaces (like selling on
TMall Global to reach Chinese consumers without a local entity
). It’s worth noting that
Chinese consumers
themselves are a huge opportunity via cross-border (despite China’s import regulations, demand for foreign goods like luxury, baby products, and health supplements is strong on platforms like Tmall Global and JD Worldwide).
Japan
is also a top import market (second only to the UK in cross-border spend, ~$92B in 2023) – Japanese consumers value quality and will pay premium for trusted foreign brands, though market entry is complex. The big picture:
APAC offers high growth potential
– brands willing to invest in understanding local markets (or working with local partners) can ride the wave of a burgeoning middle class coming online.
Middle East & North Africa (MENA): New Digital Consumers.
The Middle East has come into focus as a promising e-commerce region. Led by the Gulf states (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar) with their high GDP per capita, the region has rapidly adopted online shopping, especially in the wake of COVID-19. What’s striking is how
cross-border oriented MENA’s e-commerce is
: nearly
29% of online sales in MENA are cross-border transactions ()
, as local product availability is sometimes limited and consumers shop abroad for variety or price. Popular categories include fashion, beauty, and electronics from Western brands. MENA consumers are also very optimistic about e-commerce growth –
83% of organizations in MENA expect cross-border e-com market growth in the next 24 months ()
, one of the highest confidence levels globally. We are seeing global players take note: Amazon acquired Souq (a regional marketplace) and launched
Amazon.ae
and
Amazon.sa
,
noon.com
has grown as a local marketplace, and brands like
Nike, Adidas, and IKEA have expanded online offerings in the Middle East
. To succeed in MENA, brands should consider localizing to Arabic (at least for key markets like Saudi Arabia and UAE) and understand local payment preferences (cash on delivery is still significant, though shifting to cards/wallets). Logistics can be challenging but have improved with carriers like Aramex and DHL extensively serving the region. Also, cultural considerations (modest imagery, local holiday campaigns around Ramadan, etc.) go a long way. Some mid-sized Western brands partner with regional distributors or platforms (e.g. using a service like Namshi or Ounass for fashion) as a stepping stone. With its young population and high social media usage, the Middle East is a ripe ground for
social commerce and influencer-driven cross-border sales
. As political barriers gradually lower (e.g. new trade ties between Israel and Arab states could open new customer pools), MENA stands as a bright spot for those looking beyond the usual suspects.
Latin America – The Sleeping Giant
Latin America has historically lagged in e-commerce adoption due to infrastructure and payment challenges, but this is quickly changing.
Brazil, Mexico, and others saw a pandemic-fueled jump in e-commerce
, and now LatAm’s e-com growth often outpaces the global average. Cross-border is a big component of this, since many global brands don’t have local operations. In fact,
Brazil now appears in the top 10 cross-border import markets (≈$33B in 2023)
, reflecting how Brazilians are buying from overseas online. MercadoLibre dominates as the local marketplace, but Amazon is expanding its presence too. For brands, LatAm does present hurdles: customs in countries like Brazil can be slow and unpredictable, and duties can be high, which historically deterred cross-border purchases. However, improvements are underway (Brazil has simplified low-value import processes, for example). Payments have gotten easier with fintech – more consumers have access to international-capable cards or alternative payment methods.
100% of Latin American e-commerce organizations surveyed expected cross-border growth to continue
(), the only region to hit 100%, which indicates a consensus that the market will keep rising. Argentina, Colombia, Chile and others also show e-commerce promise. U.S. brands find LatAm appealing because of geographic proximity – shipping from U.S. to Mexico or Brazil is often quicker than to Europe or APAC. Additionally, there’s cultural affinity for U.S. brands in many Latin countries. To tap LatAm, brands may use
cross-border shipping programs
(for instance, some U.S. retailers allow international customers to buy on the U.S. site and use a third-party logistics provider to handle customs and last mile). Over time, as infrastructure improves, we can expect Latin America to account for a larger share of global online sales. For now, it’s an emerging opportunity – perhaps not as immediately large as Europe or APAC, but one with a high growth ceiling and relatively underserved demand in certain categories.
In looking beyond the U.S., brands should adopt a
portfolio approach to markets
– balancing mature, easier-to-enter markets with high-growth developing ones. The
alternative markets mentioned (EU, APAC, MENA, LatAm)
each require a nuanced strategy, but all share a common trait:
significant consumer eagerness for e-commerce
. Moreover, diversifying globally can mitigate risk. If tariffs or competition squeeze margins in one region, revenue streams from another can compensate. Many European brands, for instance, found solace in APAC markets during periods when U.S. trade policy was unfavorable, and vice versa.
As with any odyssey, venturing into new lands requires preparation: understanding local regulations, forging alliances (with local partners or platforms), and sometimes adapting the product offering. But the data and trends make one thing clear –
growth is not limited to the United States
. In fact, some of the fastest e-commerce growth is happening elsewhere. The journey might take you to new continents, but those who venture wisely often find rich new customer bases waiting.
And now, what choices do we have - tomorrow will be telling - deals to be done or not. A new world order, so long predicted and feared comes to pass.
Conclusion:
The cross-border e-commerce odyssey is a multi-stage journey – from recognizing the global opportunity, to overcoming challenges, equipping the right tools and team, learning from trailblazers, and exploring new markets. Brands that succeed in this journey tend to be those who embrace a
global mindset
while executing with
local precision
. The landscape is dynamic: trade winds shift with geopolitics, new digital platforms emerge, consumer preferences evolve. Yet, the trajectory is unmistakable –
commerce without borders
is becoming a norm. As a global brand leader or tech executive, now is the time to plot your course. The opportunity is evolving and expanding every day. Those who navigate it with resilience and resourcefulness – much like our metaphorical Odysseus – will find themselves not only surviving, but thriving, in far-off markets.
Cross-border e-commerce truly is an odyssey worth undertaking. Bon voyage – and may your journey lead to prosperous new shores, guided by the insights and strategies we’ve charted above.

_body:
You're Sarah, founder of Evergreen Essentials, a DTC brand you've nurtured from your garage to a $130M ARR powerhouse over eight years. Your 87-person team is celebrating the finalization of your Spring/Summer 2026 collection – designed in-house, manufactured in Guangzhou. Then President Trump's "Declaration of LiberF*ckinAtion Day" tariffs hit. Overnight, your 24% profit margin evaporates as Chinese import duties skyrocket to 125%.
The DTC Cash Flow Crunch: When Tariffs Meet High-Growth Brands
Your supply chain manager calculates the new landed costs (direct from their hospital bed in Cedars) – you'd have to raise prices 38% to maintain margins. Your marketing team says that would tank conversion rates. Your CFO looks shell-shocked. Just when Ol’ Peter had gotten his head around ROAS. FML 🍆he wrote to his wife. (
He hasn’t yet mastered emojis. That is in the May TikTok masterclass)
.
"We have three containers arriving next week," she says, staring at her laptop. "That's $780,000 in tariffs we didn't budget for. And we've already committed $2.4M to the Spring/Summer production run."
This poisoned chalice was no one choices or blinkered view. It is a day working with Andre the Giant, trying to keep up with his red wine intake on Princess Bride. Welcome to the great DTC cash flow crunch of 2025.
The Silent Killer of DTC Brands
Cash flow mismanagement has always been the silent assassin lurking in the shadows of even successful DTC businesses. As Dinko Kolev recently observed: "Most D2C brands don't fail because they have a bad product. They fail because they run out of cash".
A brand can have incredible products, strong demand, and substantial growth – yet still collapse when cash gets squeezed from multiple directions. Think of it as drowning just a few feet from shore: you can see safety, your business fundamentals are solid, but you simply can't bridge the gap. Now, from the unseen horizon, a Tsunami is rising.
Studies show half of the UK's small businesses fail within the first three years because of cash flow problems. In the US, ineffective cash flow management is cited by 60% of SMBs as a major challenge that significantly increases the risk of business failure. When cash is king, many DTC brands are finding themselves suddenly peasants in their own kingdom. Blessed are the meek according to Monty Python or was it the Greeks - their cheese prices have gone nuts.
How We Got Here: The DTC Growth Formula
For the past decade, DTC brands operated on a relatively straightforward playbook:
👕 source affordable products (primarily from China),
🖥️ create a beautiful Shopify store,
👀 master Meta and Google ads,
🚀 and scale customer acquisition.
As you grew, you'd establish inventory financing to support larger purchase orders. The model worked brilliantly for thousands of entrepreneurs.
Between 2018 and 2024, an entire ecosystem of financial products emerged to support this growth model. Shopify introduced Shopify Balance, giving merchants "a clear, holistic view of exactly how much money is flowing in and out of their business" and faster access to sales funds. Amazon launched cash advances between $500 and $10 million to merchants without fixed terms or credit checks. Specialist DTC financiers like Wayflyer deployed over $5 billion to brands worldwide.
This financing ecosystem became the lifeblood of the DTC economy. Rather than waiting weeks for inventory to sell through and generate cash, brands could access capital immediately, allowing them to place larger inventory orders, expand marketing campaigns, and grow faster than traditional cash flow constraints would allow.
The Financial Triple Threat - The Unholy Triumvirate
But now the DTC sector faces a perfect storm of financial pressures:
Tariff Shock
: Trump's Liberation Day tariffs have created what the industry is calling a "doomsday scenario" for U.S. ecommerce brands reliant on Chinese production. Duties on Chinese-manufactured goods have reached 125% in some categories.
Rising Customer Acquisition Costs
: After iOS privacy changes and increasing digital ad saturation, the cost to acquire customers has steadily increased, squeezing margins from the top line.
Supply Chain Instability
: Global logistics networks remain vulnerable to disruption, with lead times and shipping costs fluctuating unpredictably.
Edward Upton, who has worked with over 3,000 DTC brands on Shopify (or so he says), puts it bluntly: "Winning the category for your Shopify app is a prize worth fighting for - but you'll need to invest outside of the app store to win". The same principle applies to DTC brands themselves – winning requires investment, but investment requires cash, and cash is precisely what's in short supply.
Harley under Pressure. Harleys Under pressure.
From one Harley
ARIS, April 11 (Reuters) - Sales are brisk at the Villiers-Sur-Marne Harley-Davidson dealership outside Paris, where French bikers reckon they had better hurry if they want the American motorcycle of their dreams before trade war puts them out of reach.
"It's now or never," said 55-year-old carpenter Stephane Roger as he inspected the gleaming machines. He had been thinking about buying a Harley anyway, he said. But when he heard the news of U.S. President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, he figured he had better hurry.
To Another
For Shopify, these challenges create cascading risks. In Q3 2024, Shopify reported impressive 26% revenue growth and a 19% free cash flow margin, marking their sixth consecutive quarter of greater than 25% revenue growth. But what happens when thousands of merchants suddenly face existential cash crunches?
Shopify's financial stability depends on its merchant ecosystem. The company's Balance offering now provides eligible Plus plan merchants with competitive 3.96% APY reward on savings. But when merchants aren't saving – they're scrambling – those financial products change from growth drivers to risk exposures.
Let's run (from) some numbers:
If 10% of Shopify's merchant base experiences severe cash flow constraints due to tariff increases, how quickly could that impact Shopify's quarterly results? The company reported $94.5 billion in gross merchandise volume (GMV) in a recent quarter. Even a 5% reduction in GMV due to merchant distress would represent a $4.7 billion hit.
The Unspoken Risk: Inventory Hostage Situations
Here's where things get especially dicey. Many DTC brands' balance sheets are dominated by inventory – often 60-70% of their total assets. When tariffs suddenly increase, that inventory becomes what finance professionals might call "hostage capital." You've already paid your manufacturer, but now you need to pay an additional 25-125% in duties to get your goods into the country.
Unofrtunately my budget would not let Margot Robbie break it down for us.
This creates a brutal catch-22: you need the inventory to generate sales to create cash flow, but you need cash flow to pay the tariffs to get the inventory. It's like needing a job to get experience, but needing experience to get a job – except with millions of dollars at stake.
For brands with razor-thin cash reserves, this single shock could be fatal. A KPMG survey found that only
20% of non-finance executives are very confident their business accurately measures true DTC profitability.
(Here is your opportunity
Thomas Gleeson 🦸
and
Richie Graham
)
If you don't know your true profitability, how can you possibly navigate a tariff storm?
The Wayflyer/Clearco Dilemma
Revenue-based financing (RBF) providers like Wayflyer proudly promote that they've deployed billions to DTC brands. Their model is elegantly simple: provide upfront capital, then collect repayment as a percentage of daily sales. As Wayflyer states on their website: "If the business slows for a month or stock doesn't arrive on time, RBF protects you and your business".
But what happens when thousands of businesses all slow simultaneously due to a systemic shock like new tariffs? RBF providers base their underwriting on historical performance – they're betting that past performance predicts future results. Tariffs fundamentally break that model.
Wayflyer's pitch highlights "limited risk" because they "don't secure against your inventory”. That's great for merchants, but potentially problematic for financiers when inventory becomes the central problem. If inventory can't enter the country without additional capital, and sales depend on that inventory, the RBF model faces unprecedented stress tests.
The Consumer's Double Squeeze
Meanwhile, consumers face their own financial pressures. If DTC brands are forced to raise prices to accommodate tariffs, they're asking consumers to absorb those costs during a period of already heightened inflation concerns.
The appeal of DTC has always been better products, often at better prices, delivered with better experiences. When the price advantage disappears, what remains of the value proposition?
Some brands may seek an escape hatch by shifting production or targeting European markets. As one report suggests: "Amid the fallout from these U.S. import taxes, a promising solution is emerging across the Atlantic: Europe is a haven for lower tariffs, cheaper ad costs, and robust consumer demand".
The Warning Signs To Watch
For investors, suppliers, employees, and customers of DTC brands, what are the early warning signs of cash flow distress? History tells us to watch for:
Extending payment terms to suppliers
– pushing from net 30 to net 60 or beyond
Flash sales and heavy discounting
– sacrificing margin for immediate cash
Reduced ad spend
– pulling back on growth investments
Inventory stockouts
– inability to maintain stock levels
Delayed product launches
– pushing timelines on new releases
Looking at our fictional Evergreen Essentials, Sarah now faces impossible choices. Cut the Spring/Summer line completely? Attempt to renegotiate with Chinese suppliers? Rush to find alternative manufacturing in Vietnam or India (where everyone else is also rushing)? Take on emergency financing at punishing rates?
As Sarah opens Shopify Balance to check her current cash position, she realizes she has exactly 42 days of runway before making payroll becomes impossible. The clock is ticking.

_body:
We rely on the weather for so many things, but at its simplest, and for most people, we wake up hoping for sunshine. It just makes life easier. Too many days here in Ireland, we wake up robbed, not by the weather, but by the forecast. We are used to rain and wind and the land of four seasons in a day, but it is when we get our planning wrong that it screws with the head. But, as the saying goes, there is no bad weather, just bad clothes.
No such thing as bad weather, just bad clothing.
What the heck has this got to do with #ecommerce ? Forecasts. They are unpredictable, but we use the unpredictable to forge our decisions, even when there are many other scenarios we can plan for. Rick Watson scared the "bejesus" outta me today-delinquencies on credit cards are at their highest since 2012.
Since that post US household debt has risen to over $18Trillion - Jan 2025
The cost of living is not leveling off, and another Rick-ism shook me recently too-over 50% of US households could not sustain a one-off $400 extra bill on a monthly basis. We are stretched, we are squeezed. Retail is already facing a crisis, and we have not yet really spoken about it. The growth model is broken-too many costly stores and we, the consumer, have enough stuff. Layoffs continue and yet we trudge on.
Two or Multi-Tier System of Commerce In effect (2025 version, Boom)
Just because you think you can box, doesn't mean you get in the ring with Ali (Mohammad Ali for those too young to know).
For the last few years, I have watched how large ecommerce now dwarfs the SMs from the SME sector. And it is tough going for those in that bracket, so much so that I am beginning to think the SM is for sado-masochism. We tend to want to learn lessons the hard way. Let's look at this:
Amazon introduces free shipping.
Smallco Meeting - Monday 9am - "I see Amazon just offered free shipping. I think we should too. Their service is awesome." ... case closed.
Three years later
Smallco - Our cost base is too high. Free shipping our customers love, let's cut our brand video we were gonna shoot. Better yet, let's fire our brand manager.
2023 - Amazon increases shipping thresholds for free grocery delivery.
2023 - Amazon introduces €1.99 charge for same-day service.
2023 - Amazon earns approx $40B in ad revenue, new revenues, profitable, new revenue streams.
This is a dumb scenario outlook but it is A-typical of how we make decisions over the last 10 years or so.
Strategy is Wrong. We Are Diagnosing the Wrong Thing.
We don't need to panic. What is forcing decisions is largely cash flow and financing, not shifting consumer behavior (pandemics aside). Let's review this point.
https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/ecommerce-percentage-of-retail-sales
https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/ecommerce-percentage-of-retail-sales
Image courtesy of
MobiLoud
- thanks
Eric Gopeesingh
And as reported by Statista Market Insights, between 2017 to 2022, offline sales started at 90.6% and decreased to 86.4%, signaling a shift in shopping preferences. Meanwhile, online sales began their journey at 9.4% in 2017 and climbed to 13.6% by 2022.
Update for 2025:
By 2024, ecommerce penetration in the US reached a record 22.7%, and in Europe’s five largest economies, online sales now account for 16% of all retail sales, projected to reach nearly 21% by 2029.
The split of revenue pre- and post-pandemic is growing at a modest rate. What does that not tell us? It should be helping us understand that there will be a gradual shift into how and where people are consuming products over the next 4–5 years, similar to what happened pre-COVID. Driving this are not really consumer behaviors, they are changes in the infrastructure of how we live.
Today, we have Tariffs. And Govt ineptness.
The Biggest eCommerce Markets of Europe
The biggest ecommerce markets of Europe are the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain, which doesn’t come as much of a surprise since these countries also have the highest Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of the continent.
https://ecdb.com/blog/top-online-stores-in-europe-key-players-market-shares/4647

for the image.
Amazon's German and UK domains take the top 2 spots with 2023 net revenues of US$17.36 and US$16.61 billion, respectively.
Apple.com
and
shein.com
follow with net revenues of US$9.36 billion and US$9.09 billion, respectively.

make up the middle tier of the ranking.

round out the list.
To grasp the shift in online and offline retail, we must examine the evolution of online shopping in these major economies, their current status, and future projections.
Update for 2025:
In 2024, online sales in Europe’s “Big Five” markets hit €389 billion and are forecast to reach €565 billion by 2029, with online’s share of retail sales set to rise from 16% to 21% over that period.
The Case for the EU
Shopify reported their 8th straight quarter of growth greater than 35% last week. In the EU. This is despite them stumbling and falling and doing very little to support the market. Hat tip to all you SI and agency folk out there - your commissions should not be capped either APP lovers.
We Need Our Own Version of Ecommerce – Introducing the "Goldilocks Effect"
I won't go full Tom Cruise on this one-the man is pretty damn committed to his stunts. Have you seen his helicopter jump in the last Mission Impossible? Wild. But he does, like me, think about them for some time. I have maintained, rightly or wrongly-probably rightly, that because of the external forces we should now start developing roadmaps and plans to tie in with your strategy. Strategy needs to be beyond sales numbers FYI.
How can we shape these thoughts? Interesting report on Germany. A massive EU market. So different in its composition to the US and the UK. Yet a massive growth pillar for many folks. Germany has a rich history of multi-generational, family-run businesses. It makes decision-making quick but gathering trust can be key. But many are built on solid financial foundations so the things that don't make sense, usually don't, so don't happen. So when people say to me, "How is that feckin' possible?" you have got to ask yourself that actual question.
Entering the German Market-Marketplaces
By 2020, marketplaces accounted for 60% of all ecommerce transactions. In Germany, there were three dominant players: Amazon, eBay, and Otto.
Update for 2025:
In 2024, marketplaces in Germany generated €44 billion in sales, up 4.7% year-over-year, and now account for 55% of the ecommerce market.
Amazon.de
remains the market leader, with over 90 million monthly visits, followed by
eBay.de
(30 million),
Otto.de
(20 million), and
Zalando.de
(18 million).
https://ecdb.com/blog
Price Strategy something even Mike H could agree with
Idealo analyzed more than 1,700 product categories to find out how often Germany’s biggest online marketplaces offer the cheapest price on the German price comparison platform
idealo.de
. Across all product groups, the “big four”-Amazon, eBay, Otto, and Kaufland-offered the cheapest price in only 22% of cases. In a compelling 78% of cases, someone else had a better best price offer.
The biggest disparities are in drugs and health-expected, given how cross-border trade impacts. Interestingly, there is no single category in which the big marketplaces generally win the price battle. Yet there are some categories in which they at least hold their ground, such as the car & motorcycle category, where the big players offer the best prices in at least one-third of cases. Another notable segment is the fashion & accessories category.
This is the only product category in which the gap between the leading players and smaller marketplaces is less than 20 percentage points: the “big four” secure 44% of price comparisons in the fashion category.
Predicting the Weather Is Tough-But Planned Dressing We Can Do. What Channels to Go After-Let’s Go Against Conventional Wisdom for a Minute
Let’s go where our customers are. Let’s foster loyalty. Customers (we) are not loyal. We make decisions on a whim.
Depends on what we are presented with, how we are feeling at that time, external factors, weather, is it Friday?-will determine our steps, almost without consciousness. Brand marketing is so damn tough and the battle for attention is constant. (This is before we think about our teams and their skills to do all of this.)
Maybe our job is better distribution. Not to be everywhere, but to have a better footprint than competitors. Chances are if you are the following business with the profile attached, you will struggle to last beyond 2025:
UK pureplay seller
Revenue < £2M pa
Conversion rate 2.5%RMW
Channels in play – Meta/Google
Not selling on marketplace
Data I shared previously from
Conjura
shows this segment shrinking. You cannot buy your way out of this inertia.
But maybe, just maybe, you decide to reduce budget on these contracting markets for two years and focus on placing that budget into EU expansion. Many thoughts here (product curation, production, etc.) but let’s look at the opportunity for a second. Let’s see what our competitors are doing and what can we do to become front of mind in a better way. This is what Mike would want me to say.
Channels
Multichannel strategies provide more room for growth. We can grow more in other countries to fuel our slow burn at home. Based on over 15,000 channel feeds, 50 countries, and 20 sectors, we see three or more channels in use in more than 50% of brands. In a report by Pipecandy in 2022, we saw that US DTC brands who engage in multichannel marketing and selling observe a 4X greater conversion rate than those in DTC only.
Today, customers use an average of almost six touchpoints, with 50% regularly. Using more than four. It’s worth mentioning that by expanding to three or more channels, companies can boost their order rate by a substantial 494%. - RMW Commerce - Your Customer is Hiding in Plain Sight, white paper for
Feedonomics
Feedonomics
Feedonomics calls this their client “Feedprint.” Think of it as your distribution planning toolkit. The larger your Feedprint, the greater your returns. Marketplaces are a critical source of growth and expansion. Feedonomics customers on marketplaces grow 2x more than the ecommerce growth rate (20.5%).* It is not enough to sit on your products and hope that they bring through sales.  Consideration has to be given to the optimization techniques required to thrive on each of the different marketplaces, of which there are many.
Privacy and Retail Media
The two biggest shifts we face in the next few years. These are not negotiable, but remain navigable. But we have got to plan for them. This means we will need the infrastructure to allow this to happen, easily, to fail easily, and to move on with clear information.
Update for 2025:
New privacy laws are coming into effect in 2025, significantly impacting how social media platforms and ecommerce businesses operate. Restrictions on data collection may limit hyper-personalized ad campaigns, forcing marketers to explore alternative strategies such as contextual advertising or first-party data collection. However, these changes could foster greater trust between brands and consumers, with transparency and ethical data practices becoming a competitive edge.
Retail media continues to grow rapidly, with global ad spending hitting $140 billion in 2024. Amazon alone commands a third of global retail media spending-approximately $46.9 billion.
https://www.warc.com/newsandopinion/opinion/amazons-gravitational-pull-is-shaping-the-development-of-retail-media/en-gb/6412
The platform’s e-commerce domination may be stifling hopes of a multifaceted worldwide retail media market, a new Global Ad Trends report finds.
Our large institutional platforms are under pressure for performance and will struggle to meet our growing demands. Is it too much to ask that, we as an industry, surpass 5% conversion for the next 10 years? Instead, we will meander at the same rates we have for the last 10.
So from COVID to Tariffs, we remain out of control. Not "out of control" rather we operate within boundaries of trade and ways of living that are not conducive to modern commerce. When I wrote this, I was not friends with
Nick Kaplan
but I have come to love his perspective on such matters and this is a guy with trading in his DNA. It sits well beside his love of food, healthy debate a devout love of friends and family but like some kknowledge and talent, we have a generational, gravitational and inherent understanding. Nick, today I present to you the case for new thinking and the day we think about the Goldilocks effect - enjoy your morning brew.
Vidhi Choudhary
this is the start of our colaboration - Back to the Future and a new view on commerce.
