_body:
Moat Wars: How Frasers Group Is Building an Amazon-Like Empire While The Hut Group Drowns
Post Brexit British Retail has had a hard time but there have been some success stories and potential success stories along the way. My focus is on THG and Frasers. Both started with their own Logan Roy and are now playing out like the real story and the story that could have been two contrasting corporate stories unfolding with remarkable parallels to HBO's hit show Succession. Frasers Group, under the strategic leadership of Michael Murray, is methodically constructing Moat Wars: How Frasers Group Is Building an Amazon-Like Empire While The Hut Group struggles. (relative to its early meteoric rise).
Meanwhile, The Hut Group (THG), once the darling of the London Stock Exchange, is struggling to prevent its once-vaunted moat from drowning its own prospects-reminiscent of  Cousin Greg's bumbling attempts to secure his position.
"You can't make a Tomlette without breaking some Greggs"
Knowing plenty about THG, but not enough about Frasers, I wanted to know how these two retail giants have taken dramatically different paths, with Frasers emerging as possibly the UK's most evolved retailer while THG fights for relevance in a rapidly changing landscape.an Amazon-like ecosystem that strengthens with each acquisition and initiative-much like Tom Wambsgans' calculated rise to power.
Meet the Cast: Introducing Our Retail Protagonists
The Hut Group: Digital Ambitions and Public Market Struggles
Founded in 2004 by Matthew Moulding, The Hut Group (THG) emerged as one of Britain's most promising e-commerce success stories. At the time, I was working at eBay and Dougie, sat next to me said, I got a new account. We didn’t really realise how good this was to be.
Initially focused on entertainment products - they used a VAT rate from Jersey where their DC was to house products form their recent distressed purchase - Zavvi. Zavvi were then, through eBay able to sell new PS and Xbox releases for 1% below the market. Strategic advantage too. This was formative, as was their approach to store building - hiring dev grads from the newarby Manchester Uni, they build stores for all their distress purchases. I remember 14 eBay shops under their mgmt at the time of my leaving, contributing approximately £30M per annum. Then, THG expanded into beauty and nutrition through acquisitions and organic growth, building brands like Lookfantastic and Myprotein into significant digital players. This blew up and a bigger ambition was the follow. The company's September 2020 IPO was London's largest in seven years, valuing the business at £5.4 billion and seemingly cementing Moulding's vision of a vertically integrated e-commerce empire powered by proprietary technology.
Like Cousin Greg's early appearances in Succession-awkward but seemingly full of potential-THG initially captured investor imagination with its ambitious vision. Moulding positioned the company not as a mere online retailer but as a technology platform company with its proprietary Ingenuity e-commerce solution at the center. "We're building the world's most advanced e-commerce ecosystem," Moulding declared at the time of the IPO, echoing Greg's characteristic overreaching statements. Also known as Project Strathearn.
However, THG's journey as a public company has been turbulent. Its share price has plummeted by more than 80% from its peak as investors questioned its governance structure, the true value of its technology platform, and its ability to maintain margins in an increasingly competitive e-commerce landscape. The company that once seemed poised to redefine British e-commerce now faces existential questions about its business model and future direction. Moulding has a hate hate relationship with the investment world too and has been publicly decrying the treatment of British brands on the exchange. Not without merit, but his position and rhetoric suggests all is not well. Suggestions of a coup de tat in the last few years have gone quiet and their numbers softened. Divestments and a split in the structure suggests another path forward is needed. More to come.
Frasers: From Discount Sports to Retail Ecosystem
In stark contrast stands Frasers, the company formerly known as Sports Direct. Founded by Mike Ashley as a single sports shop in 1982, the business expanded into a discount sportswear empire before embarking on an ambitious transformation. Following the acquisition of the struggling House of Fraser department store chain in 2018, Ashley renamed the company Frasers Group and began articulating an "elevation strategy" to move upmarket.
The appointment of Ashley's son-in-law Michael Murray as CEO in 2022 accelerated this transformation. Under Murray's leadership, Frasers has pursued strategic acquisitions across multiple retail categories while investing in premium experiences and digital capabilities. Should have chosen THG? No? Too soon? The May 13th 2025 announcement of a retail media network represents the latest step in building what increasingly resembles an Amazon-like ecosystem spanning physical and digital retail.
Like Tom Wambsgans' progression in Succession from corporate outsider to calculated player, Frasers has evolved from a company once dismissed for its no-frills approach to one increasingly respected for its strategic vision.
Murray said in a recent interview,
"We're not just building a portfolio of retail businesses; we're creating an interconnected ecosystem where each element strengthens the others".
And they are not here to f*ck around.
The Tale of Two Business Models
THG: The Digital-First Vertical Integration Play
THG's business model was built on several key pillars that initially attracted investor excitement: (The “We can do everything approach”) or Ingenuity.
Vertical integration
: The company controls the entire value chain from product development through manufacturing, marketing, and fulfillment to direct customer relationships.
Proprietary technology
: The Ingenuity platform, which powers THG's own brands and is offered as a service to third parties, was positioned as a key differentiator and value driver.
Digital-first brands
: With names like Lookfantastic, Myprotein, and ESPA, THG built a portfolio of online-focused consumer brands with strong direct relationships with customers.
International expansion
: The company rapidly expanded globally, establishing operations across Europe, Asia, and North America.
Acquisition strategy
: THG used both private and public capital to acquire complementary brands and technologies to expand its reach.
This strategy is what might be called the "Greg approach" to business-ambitious but perhaps naively so, attempting to do too much without adequate foundation. As Greg once said in Succession, "I'm just trying to stay ahead of the curve here," THG likewise attempted to position itself ahead of retail trends, only to find itself overextended.
The challenges with this model became apparent after the IPO. Vertical integration requires significant capital investment and creates fixed costs that can be difficult to adjust during downturns. The technology platform, while impressive, faced skepticism about whether it truly deserved the valuation multiple of a SaaS company rather than a retailer. Most critically, the governance structure-with Moulding serving as both CEO and Chairman initially and maintaining a "golden share" with veto power-raised concerns about oversight and accountability. Onboarding became a challenge - not because results could not be achieved - but cost. IPO that’s expensive.
Frasers: The Physical-Digital Hybrid Ecosystem
Frasers' business model presents a striking contrast:
Strategic acquisitions
: The company has methodically acquired businesses across the retail spectrum, from discount sports (Sports Direct) to premium fashion (Flannels) to gaming (GAME) and cycling (Evans Cycles).
Elevation strategy
: Rather than remaining in the discount segment, Frasers has progressively moved upmarket, cultivating relationships with premium and luxury brands.
Physical retail focus
: While investing in digital capabilities, Frasers maintains a strong belief in the value of physical retail spaces as brand showcases and customer touchpoints.
Opportunistic approach
: The company moves decisively when it identifies undervalued assets or strategic opportunities, as seen in its acquisition of House of Fraser out of administration.
Ecosystem development
: Increasingly, Frasers views its diverse businesses as parts of an interconnected whole rather than standalone operations.
"Ooh, nice vest, Wambsgans. It’s
so
puffy. What’s it stuffed with, your hopes and dreams?"
This approach mirrors Tom in Succession-initially underestimated but increasingly revealed as strategic and opportunistic.
"I've been watching you all my life. I've been playing the game since I was born," Frasers has studied the retail landscape carefully and positioned itself to capitalize on both traditional retail strengths and emerging digital opportunities.
Retail is in Frasers DNA - this is a primary competitive advantage - cannot be bought or sold.
Yesterday’s
announcement of a retail media network
exemplifies this approach. By creating an advertising platform leveraging customer data from across its ecosystem, Frasers is following Amazon's highly profitable playbook of monetizing customer attention and information. As retail analyst Jonathan Chen observed, "Retail media networks are essentially a way to extract more value from existing assets-customer traffic and data. They represent one of the highest-margin opportunities in modern retail".
Frank! It hasn't been the same without you. It's been better.
Matthew Moulding: The Founder Who Wouldn't Let Go
THG's governance structure and leadership approach have been central to both its rise and subsequent challenges. Matt, who founded the company in 2004, has maintained tight control throughout its journey from startup to public company. Even after the IPO, Moulding initially served as both CEO and Chairman, while retaining a "golden share" that gave him veto power over key decisions.
This founder-centric approach has advantages in terms of vision and decisiveness but has raised significant concerns among institutional investors accustomed to more traditional governance structures. After sustained pressure, Moulding eventually relinquished the Chairman role but has remained firmly in control as CEO and the company's largest shareholder.
"‘Control the narrative.’ You probably yell that when you c-m. ‘Oh, control the narrative! Oh, control it. Control the narrative!’"
Moulding's leadership style combines entrepreneurial vision with hands-on management. He is known for being deeply involved in operational details and maintaining close relationships with key employees. This approach helped build THG from scratch into a significant player but has proven less suitable for a public company requiring transparency and independent oversight.
Like Greg's tendency to overreach beyond his capabilities, Moulding's ambition to position THG as a technology company rather than "just" a retailer may have ultimately backfired by creating expectations the business couldn't meet. As one analyst noted after a particularly disastrous investor presentation in October 2021, "They pitched the company as a SaaS business to get a SaaS multiple, but the market has decided it's actually just a retailer with lower margins".
Let the minutes reflect that Logan Roy shoved his boot up Frank’s ass.
The Murray-Ashley Dynamic: Strategic Evolution
Frasers Group presents a different leadership model that has evolved over time. Founded and built by Mike Ashley, the company was long synonymous with its controversial founder, whose brash style and unconventional business practices often generated headlines.
However, the appointment of Michael Murray-Ashley's son-in-law-first as "Head of Elevation" and later as CEO in 2022 marked a significant pivot. Murray, with a background in property and retail development, brought a more polished approach focused on premium experiences and strategic growth.
The transition has created an interesting dynamic where Ashley remains the company's largest shareholder and a significant influence but has stepped back from day-to-day management. This arrangement provides continuity while allowing for evolution in style and strategy.
Murray's leadership approach appears more methodical and ecosystem-focused than either Ashley's previous direction or Moulding's at THG. As he explained in a 2023 interview, "We're building a retail group for the future-one that leverages physical spaces, digital capabilities, and strategic partnerships to create value across categories and price points".
This leadership evolution mirrors Tom learning to navigate complex organizational politics while gradually implementing a coherent long-term strategy. Or looked at another way, playing boar on the floor.
"I'm playing a long game here,"
Frasers likewise appears focused on building sustainable advantages rather than chasing short-term wins or headline-grabbing moves.
She’s bought a lucrously capacious handbag.
Understanding the May 13, 2025 Announcement
On May 13, 2025, Frasers  announced the launch of its retail media network, a platform allowing brands to advertise across its physical and digital properties using the company's first-party customer data for targeting. This move represents a significant strategic development with several important implications:
New revenue stream
: Retail media networks typically generate high-margin revenue from existing assets (customer traffic and data).
Enhanced partnerships
: The offering creates new ways for Frasers to collaborate with brand partners beyond traditional wholesale and retail relationships.
Data monetization
: The initiative transforms customer data from a cost center to a profit center.
Competitive advantage
: Few UK retailers have developed comprehensive media networks, giving Frasers an early-mover advantage.
The announcement specifically mentioned capabilities including:
Digital display advertising across Frasers' websites and apps
In-store digital signage opportunities
Targeted email marketing campaigns
Sponsored product placements in search results
Cross-category customer insights and targeting
Performance measurement and attribution tools
Murray framed the initiative as a natural extension of Frasers' ecosystem strategy: "Our retail media network leverages the strength of our diverse brand portfolio and customer base to create new value for our partners and shareholders. This is about monetizing assets we've already built while enhancing the customer experience through more relevant, targeted messaging".
The Amazon Parallel
Frasers' move into retail media explicitly follows Amazon's playbook. Amazon's advertising business generated over $40 billion in revenue in 2023, making it one of the company's fastest-growing and most profitable segments. By creating its own version, Frasers is positioning itself as perhaps the UK retailer most explicitly modeling itself after Amazon's ecosystem approach.
Retail media expert
Colin Lewis
: "What makes retail media networks so valuable is that they combine the targeting capabilities of digital advertising with the purchase intent data only retailers possess. When someone is actively shopping, they're far more likely to convert on relevant advertising than when they're just browsing social media".
For brand partners, retail media networks offer several advantages over traditional digital advertising:
Access to first-party data in a post-cookie world
Direct connection to consumers at the point of purchase
More measurable ROI through closed-loop attribution
Integration with trade marketing and retail partnerships
Tom would say, "Sometimes you have to make friends with the money." Frasers' retail media network creates a new way for the company to generate profit while strengthening relationships with the brands that stock its stores and websites.
How Amazon makes money - lots of it.
The Moat Theory: Different Approaches to Competitive Advantage
THG's The Dinosaur is having one last roar at the meteor before it wipes him out.
The concept of an economic "moat," popularized by Warren Buffett (now retired :) ), refers to a company's ability to maintain competitive advantages over rivals to protect long-term profits and market share. THG attempted to build its moat through several key elements:
Proprietary technology
: The Ingenuity e-commerce platform was positioned as a unique asset that powered both THG's own brands and could be offered as a service to third parties.
Vertical integration
: By controlling everything from manufacturing to customer relationships, THG aimed to create efficiencies and customer experiences that competitors couldn't match.
First-party data
: Direct relationships with consumers across multiple categories created valuable data assets for personalization and targeting.
Category expertise
: Deep knowledge of specific verticals like beauty and nutrition was meant to create specialized advantages.
However, this moat has proven less defensible than initially thought. Several factors have eroded THG's competitive position:
Platform commoditization
: E-commerce technology has become increasingly accessible, with platforms like Shopify offering sophisticated capabilities to businesses of all sizes.
Rising customer acquisition costs
: Digital marketing expenses have increased across the industry, compressing margins for direct-to-consumer businesses.
Category competition
: Established players and new entrants have improved their digital capabilities, eroding THG's early advantages.
Capital intensity
: Vertical integration requires significant ongoing investment, creating a cash drain during challenging periods.
Speed to new geographies did not happen.
THG built a moat that requires continuous investment to maintain-like Greg's persistent need to prove himself in Succession despite repeated setbacks. As one analyst observed, "Their moat turned out to be more like a money pit, requiring constant capital just to stay competitive". F you Shopify.
Talent and culture are challenges too - but for another day, maybe over a beer.
Frasers' Amazon-Like Network Effects
Frasers appears to be building a moat more similar to Amazon's-one that becomes stronger over time through network effects, scale advantages, and ecosystem synergies. Key elements include:
Physical-digital integration
: Leveraging stores as fulfillment centers, showrooms, and customer acquisition tools while using digital to drive traffic and enhance experiences.
Multi-category presence
: Operating across numerous retail categories creates cross-selling opportunities and economies of scale.
Strategic real estate portfolio
: Prime locations acquired opportunistically (often through distressed sales) provide physical touchpoints that are difficult to replicate.
Brand relationships
: Increasingly strong connections with premium and luxury brands create differentiated offerings.
Retail media network
: Monetizing customer attention and data creates a new high-margin revenue stream.
Like Tom's gradual accumulation of power, Frasers has methodically added capabilities that strengthen its competitive position. Each acquisition and initiative appears designed not just as a standalone business but as a component of an interconnected ecosystem where the whole exceeds the sum of the parts.
My digestive system is basically part of the Constitution
Retail analyst Maria Jenkins:
"What's impressive about Frasers' approach is how each part reinforces the others. Their stores drive online sales, their online presence drives store traffic, their data improves merchandising, and now their media network will monetize customer attention. It's becoming a virtuous cycle similar to Amazon's flywheel".
The British Retail Landscape - Cold and Inhospitable. Checks out.
During the writing of this, I was reminded in a discussion of M&S, Next, Boots and more and for comparative purposes, I am including some of them to see why I think Frasers moat stands up, firguratively and literally.
Frasers vs. Next: The Digital Transformation Race
What is this, McCarthyism? I'm not declining. I'm just not clining
Next plc has long been considered one of the UK's most forward-thinking retailers, with a successful catalog business that transitioned effectively into e-commerce. It’s a business who has just upped its profit forecast for the year like the single biggest F*ck you to everyone else out there. They too, are long term players and thinkers. Like Frasers, Next operates across multiple categories and price points, with a strong physical store network complementing its digital presence.
Key comparisons:
Digital transformation
: Next began its digital journey earlier through its Directory business, but Frasers is accelerating faster through acquisitions and investments.
Third-party brands
: Next has developed a sophisticated marketplace offering carrying hundreds of external brands, while Frasers has focused more on owned retail concepts. (2015)
Financial services
: Both offer credit to customers, enhancing loyalty and providing additional revenue streams.
Real estate strategy
: Next has been selectively reducing its store portfolio while Frasers continues to expand strategically, particularly in premium locations.
International approach
: Next has built a substantial international online business, while Frasers remains primarily UK-focused despite some European operations.
Next CEO Simon Wolfson has been widely praised for his methodical approach to balancing physical and digital retail. However, Frasers' more aggressive acquisition strategy and ecosystem development may provide it with greater scale and diversification advantages in the long term.
Frasers vs. Boots and Superdrug: The Health and Beauty Battle
With its ownership of premium beauty retailer Flannels and investments in the beauty space, Frasers increasingly competes with health and beauty specialists Boots and Superdrug. This comparison reveals important differences in approach:
Store experience
: Boots is investing heavily in store renovations while Superdrug emphasizes value; Frasers focuses on premium experiences through Flannels.
Loyalty programs
: Boots Advantage Card and Superdrug Health & Beautycard are among the UK's most established loyalty schemes, areas where Frasers has opportunity for development.
Private label strategy
: All three are expanding proprietary brands, though with different positioning and price points.
Healthcare services
: Boots leads in pharmacy and healthcare services, areas where Frasers has not yet ventured.
Digital capabilities
: Varying degrees of online-offline integration, with Frasers potentially gaining advantages through its ecosystem approach.
It will be interesting to see how Frasers approach this category if at all - it is tough, fast paced and where THG operate well.
Frasers vs. JD Sports: The Sportswear Showdown
Sports Direct, Frasers' original business, competes directly with JD Sports in the sportswear retail space. This rivalry has evolved as both companies have expanded their ambitions:
Brand relationships
: JD has cultivated stronger relationships with Nike and Adidas, securing better allocations of premium and limited products.
International expansion
: JD has moved aggressively into the US market through acquisitions like Finish Line, while Frasers remains more UK-centric.
Target demographics
: JD focuses on fashion-conscious youth while Sports Direct emphasizes value and breadth.
Acquisition strategy
: Both companies have been acquisitive, but with different targets-JD focusing on similar sportswear specialists while Frasers diversifies across categories.
Premium strategy
: Frasers has moved upmarket more aggressively than JD through concepts like Flannels.
This comparison with JD Sports highlights both the origins of Frasers and how far it has evolved beyond its discount sportswear roots. While JD Sports remains focused primarily on sportswear and streetwear, Frasers has diversified across multiple categories, reducing its dependence on any single market segment.
I'm the eldest son. And I must be considered, and I need to be taken into account
https://gifdb.com/gif/cousin-greg-hirsch-succession-syu8z1z9lthk6fld.html
THG's Leadership Journey
Matthew Moulding (2004-Present)
2004: Founds The Hut Group
2010-2019: Leads multiple funding rounds, raising capital from investors including KKR and Blackrock
September 2020: Takes THG public in £5.4 billion IPO
October 2021: Faces investor backlash following presentation on Ingenuity business
November 2021: Steps down as Chairman but remains CEO following governance concerns
2022-Present: Attempts to stabilize business amid falling share price and take-private speculation
Moulding's leadership style combines entrepreneurial vision with hands-on management and tight control. Like Greg in Succession, Moulding's approach has generated both spectacular successes and significant setbacks. As mentioned already, his decision to position THG as a technology company rather than a retailer created initial excitement but ultimately led to disappointment when the technology components failed to demonstrate anticipated value.
As one corporate governance expert noted, "The very qualities that make founder-entrepreneurs successful-conviction, control, and vision-can become liabilities when running a public company requiring transparency and accountability".
Frasers' Leadership Evolution
Can I just be your fun guy in Uruguay?
Mike Ashley (1982-2022)
1982: Opens first Sport & Ski shop
2007: Takes Sports Direct public
2018: Acquires House of Fraser, begins premium push
2019: Appoints Michael Murray as "Head of Elevation"
2021: Announces succession plan with Murray becoming CEO
2022: Steps back to Deputy Chairman role while remaining controlling shareholder
I'm not saying I'd make a better CEO. That's unsaid.
Michael Murray (2019-Present)
2019: Joins as Head of Elevation
2022: Becomes CEO at age 31
2022-2024: Accelerates premium strategy and ecosystem development
May 2025: Announces retail media network initiative
Ashley built the business through opportunistic acquisitions and a focus on value retail, while Murray has emphasized premium experiences and ecosystem development. Unlike the Roy family drama, however, Frasers appears to have managed this transition relatively smoothly, with Ashley supporting Murray's elevation strategy while maintaining influence as the company's largest shareholder.
Blind Spots and Opportunities
Is Greg necessary?
THG's Potential Redemption Path
Despite its challenges, THG retains valuable assets that could form the basis of a turnaround:
Brand portfolio
: Ownership of successful D2C brands like Myprotein and Lookfantastic with loyal customer bases.
International presence
: Established operations in multiple markets providing diversification.
Technology platform
: Even if overvalued, Ingenuity has real capabilities that could be repositioned. In the current environment this is tough and their divestment strategy places this at the center of a challenge to be addressed.
First-party data
: Valuable customer information across beauty and nutrition verticals.
Fulfillment infrastructure
: Investments in automated warehousing and logistics.
A potential redemption strategy might include:
Governance reform
: Complete separation of Chairman and CEO roles and elimination of the golden share to restore investor confidence.
Business simplification
: Clear separation of technology and retail operations with transparent reporting.
Strategic partnerships
: Rather than going alone, partnering with complementary businesses.
Cost restructuring
: Addressing declining margins through operational efficiency.
Focused growth
: Concentrating on proven profit centers rather than expansive vision.
THG might benefit from a similar recalibration-acknowledging it is primarily a retailer with good technology rather than a technology company that happens to sell products. This thought, will not succeed in North America - they need a new map.
Frasers' Emerging Challenges
I don't care what you think. You're a tribute band.
While Frasers' strategy appears more robust, it faces its own blind spots and challenges:
Integration complexity
: Managing numerous acquisitions creates operational challenges and potential inefficiencies. In an age of efficiency, this is a concert.
Brand relationships
: Premium brands remain cautious about association with the Sports Direct heritage. But Murrary is turning the tide significantly here. PLus Money talks.
Leadership transition
: Michael Murray is relatively untested as a public company CEO. Public scrutiny leads to different needs when it comes to decision making. Murrays challenge is in front of him.
Economic headwinds
: Premium and luxury focus may be vulnerable during economic downturns. Ask LVMH.
Digital competition
: Pure-play e-commerce specialists continue to grow market share. Omnichannel and rise of marketplace and Retail Media ni Niche Categories means the survival of the fittest will be those who develop network effects better. With physical stores at their disposal, I think Murray has built well.
International strategy
: Limited success outside the UK to date.
Opportunities for Frasers include:
Loyalty program integration
: Creating a cross-brand loyalty program to increase customer lifetime value.
International expansion
: Applying the ecosystem model in selected international markets. Plenty of cautionary tales exposed above. Be great in you own country and more opportunity will fall.
Financial services expansion
: Leveraging customer relationships for higher-margin services.
Subscription offerings
: Developing a Prime-like membership program.
Further vertical integration
: Expanding private label offerings across categories.
The company's ability to maintain focus amid rapid expansion will determine whether its moat becomes truly Amazon-like in its defensibility.
Is Frasers Building the UK's Amazon?
Frank! It hasn't been the same without you. It's been better.
The Amazon Flywheel vs. Frasers' Emerging Ecosystem
Amazon's business model is famously built around a "flywheel" effect where each element reinforces the others:
Lower prices lead to more customers
More customers attract more sellers
More sellers create greater selection
Greater selection brings more customers
Scale enables lower cost structure
Lower costs enable lower prices
This core retail flywheel has been enhanced by additional elements like Prime membership, fulfillment services, and advertising, each creating their own reinforcing effects.
Frasers appears to be developing its own version of this flywheel:
Strategic acquisitions provide diverse customer touchpoints
Diverse touchpoints generate valuable customer data
Customer data improves merchandising and targeting
Better targeting enhances customer experience
Enhanced experience increases customer loyalty
Loyal customers shop across multiple Frasers brands
Cross-shopping improves economics
Better economics fund further acquisitions and investments
Retail media network monetizes customer attention
Media revenue funds premium experiences and lower prices
The addition of a retail media network is particularly significant, as advertising has become one of Amazon's most profitable business segments.
Frasers is positioning itself as perhaps the UK retailer most explicitly modeling itself after Amazon's ecosystem approach.
Key Differences: Scale, Focus, and International Presence
Ken did great. It was Tom who farted in his s--t.
However, important differences remain:
Scale
: Amazon operates at a much larger global scale, serving hundreds of millions of customers.
Technology investment
: Amazon invests billions in technology R&D, including areas like AI and robotics.
Logistics network
: Amazon's fulfillment network is vastly more extensive, with hundreds of facilities worldwide.
Third-party marketplace
: While Frasers carries many brands, it has not yet fully developed a marketplace model like Amazon's.
International presence
: Frasers remains primarily UK-focused despite some European operations.
Prime equivalent
: Frasers lacks a membership program with Amazon Prime's breadth of benefits.
These differences suggest that while Frasers may be the most "Amazon-like" major UK retailer, it remains focused on retail rather than becoming the "everything store" that Amazon represents.
My view is that the retail media network announcement indicates that Frasers understands a key aspect of Amazon's success-that the most valuable parts of retail may not be selling products but
rather monetizing the ecosystem built around those sales.
The Future Retail Landscape: Questions and Outlook
Key Questions that spring to mind
As these two retail approaches continue to evolve, several questions emerge for industry observers:
Is vertical integration a strength or a burden in modern retail?
THG's model suggests the latter, while Frasers' selective integration appears more sustainable.
How important is physical retail in building a defensible ecosystem?
Frasers' continued investment in stores suggests they remain crucial touchpoints.
Can British retailers successfully build Amazon-like ecosystems, or is this a fool's errand?
Frasers' approach suggests a middle path may be viable.
What role will retail media networks play in determining winners and losers?
Early movers like Frasers may gain significant advantages.
How important is leadership continuity and governance in retail success?
The contrasting approaches of Moulding and Murray offer different models.
Can premium and value retail coexist effectively within the same corporate structure?
Frasers' strategy depends on this being possible.
Will international expansion become necessary for long-term survival?
Both companies face UK market saturation challenges
The Most Evolved Retailer?
Is Frasers the most evolved retailer in the modern context? The evidence suggests it may indeed be the UK's most forward-thinking retail group, combining elements of:
Amazon's ecosystem approach and media monetization
LVMH's premium brand management
Walmart's operational efficiency
Inditex's vertical integration
Best Buy's store-as-showroom concept
What makes Frasers particularly notable is not any single innovation but rather its comprehensive vision of retail as an interconnected ecosystem rather than a collection of separate businesses. Under Murray's leadership, the company appears to understand that the future of retail is not about choosing between physical and digital, value and premium, or products and services-but rather about creating a system where each element reinforces the others.
I'm like a plane. I never stop moving forward.
Moats That Protect Versus Moats That Drown
The contrasting journeys of Frasers Group and The Hut Group offer valuable lessons for retail executives, investors, and industry observers:
Ecosystems over platforms
: Frasers' integrated ecosystem approach appears more defensible than THG's platform-focused strategy.
Physical-digital balance
: Rather than choosing between channels, the most successful retailers are finding ways to make physical and digital retail reinforcing.
Governance matters
: THG's unconventional governance structure ultimately undermined investor confidence despite operational successes.
Strategic patience
: Frasers' methodical "elevation strategy" demonstrates the value of consistent execution over flashy but unsustainable growth.
Data monetization
: The retail media network move suggests that the most valuable asset in modern retail may be customer data and attention rather than products or even platforms.
The retail media network announcement may just be Frasers' "king-making" moment-the move that solidifies its position as Britain's most evolved retailer in the Amazon age.
Will Frasers Group truly become the UK's Amazon? Can THG find a path to sustainable growth and investor confidence? And how will competitors respond to these contrasting retail approaches? There is no end here - just Succession.
You can't make a Tomlette without breaking some Greggs.

The Need for (Re)Speed
When Pete Mitchell and Nick Bradshaw walked into that famous bar they didn’t realise the irony their shoulder tap and bad song would have for the resale ecommerce market, in particular eBay.
eBay, you’ve lost that re-lovin’ feeling, whoah that re-lovin’ feelin. You’ve lost that lovin’ feelin’ now you’re gone, gone gone, whoah oh oh.
eBay, eBay, i’d get down on my knees for you
If you’d only pre-loved me, like you used to… End.
eBay has a big challenge to solve - buyer or seller. Age old, but now they have a challenger - Vinted and they have taken the problem and “inverted” it. No, I seen them do it. Alot of press given to Vinted in the last 2 weeks. Some of it justified, some under scrutiny but they are making waves in Europe. Mostly because they sided with the buyer and are creating the experience with them in mind. eBay were the 2nd highest trafficked site in the world for 20 years until last December. Now, they languish in 3rd. Once Maverick, now more Goose. Iceman is dead and the Hangman is the new Wingman - Sounds Ominous. But, Pete Mitchell is still here… after all these years.
https://bit.ly/43j8doQ
How Vinted Outmaneuvered eBay in the Battle for Preloved Fashion
Written by an eBay alum who’s watched the dogfight from both the cockpit and the control tower.
The Original Top Gun (2005–2015)
eBay’s Golden Era: Leather Jackets, Listings, and Legacy - I wore them all - listings FYI, was a cheap belt brand.
In the early days of ecommerce, eBay was Maverick.
Cocky.
Fast.
Unconventional.
And the king of preloved everything—from Beanie Babies to Burberry blazers.
eBay pioneered the consumer resale market before sustainability was sexy. It made “garage sale culture” global. Its UX wasn’t perfect, but it was thrilling: the countdown, the bids, the sniping tools. This was
commerce with adrenaline.
But over time, eBay grew up. Or rather—grew old. The once-thrilling fighter pilot became the airline pilot. Dependable, maybe. But no longer dangerous.
Enter Vinted – A New Wingman in Town
Top Gun: Maverick
“It’s not the plane. It’s the pilot.”
https://bit.ly/4k6m1dl
Just as eBay was working on B2B platforms, AI tools, and legacy inventory clean-up, a startup from Lithuania said, “Hold my depop.”
Vinted came in
low altitude, no fees, no frills.
It spoke the language of a generation that grew up on TikTok thrift hauls and Depop dopamine. And it made three very simple moves that changed everything:
1. Mobile-First Everything
While eBay was still clinging to desktop-era workflows, Vinted delivered the cleanest listing flow in resale. Upload. Tap. Swipe. Sell. Done.
2. No Seller Fees
Vinted made money from buyers,
not sellers.
That broke the old eBay model—and won seller loyalty instantly.
3. Community Culture Over Transaction Engine
Vinted didn’t just host listings—it built an identity. It
felt
like a place to swap clothes with friends. eBay? A place where vintage handbags go to die… slowly… over 30 days… with a starting bid of €1.
You’ve Lost That (Re) Loving Feeling
The Sequel Struggles of the OG
eBay still has firepower—there’s a lot of experience in that cockpit. But experience isn’t relevance. And relevance is everything in resale.
You never close your eyes any more when I kiss your lips.
Just like the bar scene in
Top Gun: Maverick
, eBay tried singing to its audience again. Loyalty programs, better search, more AI. But the buyer (in this case, Gen Z) had already moved on. They’re over at Vinted, getting dopamine hits and five-star reviews from people who say things like “Great vibes. Fast shipper.” (could be call signs in another world).
And while eBay is still the best place to find rare collectibles, it’s just not
fun
anymore. It's the “dad marketplace”—reliable, full of history, but desperately in need of a reboot montage.
https://bit.ly/3SHs63G
The Final Dogfight – Market Share, Mindshare, and Mission Drift
“It’s not just about selling. It’s about belonging.”
Vinted has already outflanked eBay in several markets, particularly in fashion-forward, sustainability-conscious Europe.This is well documented but have a look here.
Take us there Rooster. Here’s what the radar shows:
Category
eBay
Vinted
Mobile UX
:  Clunky (but improving) Clean      VS      native, addictive
Fees (Sellers)
:                             Yes                   VS           No
Audience Demographic
: Millennials + Gen X     VS       Gen Z + Millennials
Perceived Culture
: Auctions, old-school, clsoed  VS  Swapping, fun, community-led
Brand Vibe:
Amazon’s slightly cooler cousin       VS       TikTok meets Etsy meets WhatsApp
eBay’s moves—acquiring marketplaces like TCGPlayer, investing in authentication services—show it still has fuel. But in the day-to-day world of everyday clothes and casual clear-outs, Vinted owns the skies.
Will the Real Maverick Please Stand Up?
The comeback depends on risk, not nostalgia.
If eBay wants to be
Top Gun
again, it can’t just tweak search algorithms and call it innovation. It needs to:
Kill seller fees
(or rethink them dramatically)
Simplify mobile workflows
to match the dopamine cycle
Invest in brand narrative
—show up where Gen Z lives
Stop chasing enterprise sellers
when the battle is in the bedroom closet
https://bit.ly/3FdD2TH
The Danger Zone Is Crowded
Vinted isn’t just eBay’s only rival. Poshmark, Depop, Vestiaire Collective, and even TikTok Shop are entering the resale dogfight.
But Vinted has one thing they don’t: A clear sense of purpose, a sticky user loop, and a younger audience it hasn't yet disappointed.
eBay still has altitude. But if it wants to win this sequel… It better learn to fly like it’s 2005 again.
Want to talk more about how marketplaces grow, fade, and pivot?
Join me here:
https://vinnyobrien.substack.com/
#marketplaces #resale #vinted #ebay #TopGun #ecommerce #digitalstrategy #fashiontech #MaverickVsGoose
