title: Rewriting Retail: The Model, the Myth, the Missed Opportunity
excerpt: My own work. May I am in a privileged position getting to speak to many of the greatest minds in ecommerce and retail. I also get to speak to Nick Kaplan Kaplan. It sometimes gives me pause for thought. This week more than most, I
_body:
My own work. May
I am in a privileged position getting to speak to many of the greatest minds in ecommerce and retail. I also get to speak to
Nick Kaplan
Kaplan. It sometimes gives me pause for thought. This week more than most, I have had so many disturbing, enlightening and interesting discussions. My own assertions are more than crystalized. The retail industry is not dead — but the model many of us still cling to is, at best, on life support and, at worst, a ghost ship captained by spreadsheets and nostalgia.
This isn’t about individual brands or CEOs. It’s about a system. One that confuses quarterly results with long-term resilience. One that treats the customer and their data as separate entities. One that still clings to the illusion of brand loyalty like it’s 1997 and you’re waiting for a mail-order catalog to arrive. Incidentally this was the year Clooney played Batman, Nick Cage wanted his Bunny back and James Bond drove an invisible car.
David Katz of Randa Apparel joined us recently on
The Watson Weekend
and offered something few people in senior roles do anymore: a detailed look under the hood of what a
modern, resilient retail model
actually looks like, not in theory, but in operation. It's an approach that's almost jarringly different from the public retail model we so often see stumble.
Some of the aspects I am willing to share..
The Retail Model Most People Are Still Using
Here’s the public playbook, in case you forgot:
Centralized decision-making that relies on outdated consumer forecasts.
Loyalty programs that assume consumers actually care.
Brand marketing divorced from real-time consumer behavior.
Inventory purchased a year in advance, without a Plan B.
A rigid operating model built for stability, not speed.
When you hear about department stores closing doors or fashion retailers missing guidance five quarters in a row, you’re not witnessing a freak event. You’re seeing the downstream effect of a model that assumes control in a world shaped by chaos.
The result? Shrinking margins, fading relevance, and a pipeline of initiatives that sound good in boardrooms but never touch the shop floor — physical or digital.
One sidenote. We have 2 lingering views on customers. We have the customer and their behavior and we have customer data. The two are not linked. Physically I mean - we bridge this gap through assumptions. We make a major faux paz here. In doing so we create silos with our own customers in doing so, missing the signals we need to respond to. What happens is we react. Words matter.
Last week, we had
David Baker
Baker give one of the best insights into the detail of how to market through digital means, the lens, the mechanism and everything else. A student of politics and someone who has values close to his way of being makes for a very curious, accurate marketer. Bolt on a big brain and you get CDO in Loreal and more. Listen in if you have not already.
Romantic pop and the new wave agenda
Now contrast that with what I learned this week. The new model is not only smarter, it’s fundamentally
different
. Not revolutionary. Not buzzword-laden. Just aligned with reality.
Here’s what that looks like:
1. Multi-Channel Mastery, Not Dependence
“Best in Breed” plays across
every channel
, from high-end department stores to off-price, from DTC to global wholesale. And they don’t just
exist
in these channels, they optimize for each one’s unique customer mindset, margin structure, and brand value.
Where a typical publicly held retailer might see online as a “growth lever” and physical retail as a “headwind,” Good sees both as
interdependent inputs
to a wider strategy.
“We sell to Nordstrom and Saks… but we also make belts for Kirkland and private label for Target and Macy’s. It’s about owning the supply chain and the brand touchpoints.”
Compare that to the fragile dependence some brands have on just 1–2 distribution points. When one falters, so does the whole house of cards.
From Loyalty to Logic
“Has loyalty died… and has logic replaced it?”
Consumers today don’t operate on loyalty programs they operate on
logic
. Believe it or not, I said this. Met with a “good question”. I was happy. They chase utility, relevance, and immediacy. My interviewee recognizes this and instead of fighting it, his org models behavior around it.
Their infrastructure
is
the loyalty plan.
The underperforming public retailer, on the other hand, clings to legacy brand equity like it's a moat. But brand alone isn't protection. In fact, legacy is often a liability when your customer has moved on and your data still thinks it’s 2016.
International Arbitrage as Strategy
Good retailer and his team
use international markets as early signals
, not expansion trophies. Their acquisition of Moss Bros in the UK,  just before lockdown, wasn’t just global ambition. It was insight-driven. They were already watching UK and Australian retail erosion as a
preview of US conditions
.
This kind of foresight,
building optionality through global diversification
is
rare
. Most public retail strategies are U.S.-centric, channel-siloed, and take far too long to respond to market shifts. The result is businesses that are local in thinking and slow in reacting — which is dangerous when TikTok is your new storefront. Indeed it was impressive to be in this call hearing about Irish retail and UK from a US leading voice. Holiday mode evaporated and my ears perked up further.
Strategy Over Forecasts
“Most companies start with tactics and never define strategy. That’s backwards.”
The most devastating insight from interviews this week might be this one.
Public retailers build forecasts like they’re planning a royal wedding 12 months out, perfectly timed, rigid to a fault. But today’s market demands
dynamic strategy
. Inventory can’t be a static commitment it has to be a
fluid bet
based on weekly inputs. Notice the wording Nick Kaplan, bet. Preceded by fluid adds a dimension of real time analysis, thus eroding the term of gambling, rather, this is making an informed choice and being prepared to be wrong.
The mindset? Flexibility. Global listening. Owned factories and vertical integration. Not because it's trendy, but because when everything shifts overnight, you need fewer approvals and more action.
Capital, Culture, and Consciousness
Here’s where Good really separates his model from the pack. Good treats
culture
as a supply chain input.
Capital structure
as a strategic tool. And
consciousness
understanding who your customer is and what they want today as an operating principle.
Contrast that with public companies who are forced into a short-term margin obsession to satisfy shareholders, stripping investment in tech, people, and culture just to make quarterly EBITDA look presentable. That’s not strategy  that’s survival theatre.
The Public Model’s Fatal Flaws
Let’s be blunt: if a brand is…
Beholden to stale loyalty metrics.
Betting the farm on fall fashion forecasts.
Underinvesting in its own infrastructure.
Not watching what’s happening in South Africa or Sydney.
Unwilling to rethink the
model
instead of the marketing…
…then it's not being “disrupted” — it's being
outmaneuvered
.
These brands aren’t failing because of external forces. They’re failing because they’re using the wrong playbook. Some, no playbook at all.
Rewriting Retail Means Rebuilding the Model
You can’t reboot retail without admitting the first version was flawed. The sequel isn’t better just because it’s new. And in many cases, the spin-offs (
looking at you, marketplace brand extensions and lazy livestream attempts
) are just poorly lit remakes with less talent.
What Good offers is something better:
an operating model designed to flex, diversify, and grow in sync with consumer behavior, not despite it.
It’s not flashy. But it works. And more importantly — it’s
built to last
.
Final Thought:
Retail doesn’t need more storytelling. It needs better scripts. It needs operational realism over theatrical optimism. It needs a business model where the customer and their data don’t just co-exist, they
co-write the future
. So before you greenlight another seasonal strategy or launch another loyalty campaign, ask yourself:
Are you writing the next
great retail sequel
— or just rebooting a model that should’ve ended in the last act?

title: EMPIRE OF AI: Welcome to the Real World
pullQuotes: “Welcome to the real world.” — Morpheus,
The Matrix
“You take the blue pill—the story ends, you wake up in your bed and believe whatever you want to believe.” — Morpheus,
excerpt: “Welcome to the real world.” — Morpheus, The Matrix Let’s get this out of the way up front: I’m a skeptic. A well-meaning, slightly-exhausted, time-crunched, commerce-loving skeptic who’s been around long enough to remember when “personalization” meant someone spelling your name right on a marketing
_body:
“Welcome to the real world.” — Morpheus,
The Matrix
Let’s get this out of the way up front: I’m a skeptic. A well-meaning, slightly-exhausted, time-crunched, commerce-loving skeptic who’s been around long enough to remember when “personalization” meant someone spelling your name right on a marketing email.Does the fact that we still get this wrong tell us something.
And yet… here I am. Writing 6,000 words about artificial intelligence and its slow, relentless invasion of commerce, like Agent Smith, but wearing a branded hoodie and holding a DTC skincare subscription. That’s my vibe and I am sticking to it. I am trying to research the topic in a way that has more meaning for me personally. Enter Karen Hao’s Empire oif AI. A really great read, well listen. Audiobook for me. The book starts just over 10 years ago. AI was well before that but AI as we view and know it today, started around then. The Sam Altman version, let’s call it. Structure and infrastructure give a good indication of where true power and true conflict lie. How do we make this better for people and governments were early, altruistic ideals. Today, there is so much infrastructure around that anywhere there is data, there remains opportunity. But for who?
Because even I can admit: something fundamental has changed. Not in the rah-rah, Silicon-Valley-LinkedIn-influencer sort of way. But in the quieter, more unsettling sense that the interface of commerce has been hijacked. Not by a hacker. Not by a brand. But by the algorithm. I was recently told of the white space Tobi encouraged the Shopify network to think about. White Space seems less hopeful to me than its aspirational design. I am trying to make sense of it all. If not for anyone, but for myself firstly.
And to make sense of it, we need to take the red pill.
1. The Origins: “You take the blue pill...”
“You take the blue pill—the story ends, you wake up in your bed and believe whatever you want to believe.” — Morpheus,
The Matrix
The early history of AI in commerce is the equivalent of that scene in every prequel where the villain is still just a misunderstood intern. We were dealing with “expert systems,” not existential threats. Rules-based engines. Linear logic. Nothing that questioned the very fabric of capitalism, just tools to help us keep a few more pallets off the clearance aisle.
These were the blue pills of ecommerce. Innocent. Boring. Mostly Excel in disguise. The very notion of being sold to in this way is not new to us.
1.1 Inventory: The Original AI Daydream
Back in the 60s and 70s, companies like Walmart were fiddling with just-in-time inventory and point-of-sale data. This wasn’t AI, it was glorified counting. But it sowed the seeds.
Fast forward a few decades: algorithms start setting prices based on demand forecasts. Amazon begins adjusting product listings based on click rates. It’s not AI, yet. But the Matrix is forming. Prime Day just ran a 4 day deals extravaganza (bluegh) and Rufus played its part. But what if I said that 20% of our waking lives are dictated by the fabric of AI.
1.2 Recommendation Systems: “People who bought this also bought…”
Suddenly, AI becomes visible. It’s not just churning in the background it’s suggesting things. Poorly, at first. Like when Netflix kept recommending
Paul Blart: Mall Cop
because you watched one documentary on shopping malls. Seriously, how do some movies get made. Hopefully mine will too, in that vein.
But this was the first sniff of what was coming: consumer-facing machine logic. “If you like this, try this.” What seemed like harmless utility would evolve into manipulative precision.
1.3 Fraud Detection: The Cops of the Codebase
AI’s most successful early role? Catching fraudsters. Pattern recognition saved banks and merchants millions. Unfortunately, it also introduced the world to algorithmic bias flagging transactions based on behaviors it barely understood, from people it barely cared to. That said, Frank Abagnale told the MRC not so long ago that it was easier to perpetrate fraud now than it was during his years as a pilot, or doctor or was it a lawyer?
We didn’t know it then, but these early applications were gateway drugs. We thought we were building tools. We were actually building agents.
2. The Inception: “The Matrix is everywhere…”
“The Matrix is everywhere. It is all around us. Even now, in this very room.” — Morpheus,
The Matrix
If the 2010s were about mobile eating the world, then the 2020s are about AI swallowing the remains. Just ask Ben Evans.
We’re now in what Scot Wingo, a man who’s seen more commerce trends than I’ve had coffees this week, calls the "agentic" era. Think less Siri, more Skynet... but with a Shopify plugin.
This isn’t AI as backend tool anymore. It’s AI as lead actor. His substack
RetailGentic
is one of the more interesting on the subject matter with a great perspective too.
2.1 Agentic AI: Your New Personal Shopper (With No Commission Incentive)
Wingo defines agentic AI as systems that operate with autonomy, set goals, interact with environments, and execute tasks.
Let’s spell that out:
It doesn’t wait for your prompt.
It doesn’t need your oversight.
It doesn’t ask permission.
It
does
your shopping, finds your supplier, negotiates your discount, and emails the warehouse to prep the order. All while you’re watching a Netflix show that
it
recommended.
This is no longer your tool. It’s your proxy. Your commercial doppelgänger.Your digital twin maybe. Fu*ckin digital twins - matrix number 2.
2.2 From Backend to Interface
While most people didn’t notice the moment AI moved from logistics to the storefront. One day we had dropdown filters, the next we had GPT-powered concierge chatbots acting like they knew us better than our own families. Let me be clear at this point though - we never asked for this.
Never, as consumers - the way this works in the long term is not if it is an option it is if it is the only way. We respond better to no choices as opposed to overload these days.
AI agents are everywhere now:
ChatGPT + Klarna partnership? That’s an agent.
Google’s “Circle to Search”? That’s a halfway house.
Perplexity’s shopping results? An agent pretending it’s still doing research. Soon to be fed by Feedonomics.
For everything else there’s … I won’t.
We are moving fast from clicks to delegation. And commerce at least the parts not asleep at the wheel is responding. Do we have time to think about it? To respond and change?
3. The Expansion: “What is real?”
“What is real? How do you define real?” — Morpheus,
The Matrix
Commerce used to be about catalogues, stores, websites. Then it became mobile. Now it’s something else. Something... less visible. More synthetic. And less human. A recent look at the stunning Oh Polly PLPs feels like a hybrid in motion. A look at what it could be. Thanks Ger.
We don’t see AI running the show, because it doesn’t show itself. But it’s writing the scripts. Literally and figuratively. Those days are not too far in front of us though. Big bets backed by big investments means we will be facing into our agentic indian summer before long. The long term costs in investment will be paltry to a 100 year company like Shopify in the future. To quote the book and Sam Altman -
we want to get more revenue so we can do more research
, not acting in the reverse like most.
3.1 The New Commerce Stack (Now with 80% More Invisible Hands)
POSITIVE IMPACTS THE ARGUMENTS FOR
Scale without burnout
: AI does what humans can’t or won’twithout coffee breaks or unions. I grew up in a union family so I know their value. But AI is now part of all of our routines. We have been convinced of its place and its purpose. Hard to deny it. We may not yet even be mid level users but we need to become experts. Dealing in ambiguity and certainty in the same context is something we need to do.
Personalization++
: No more "Hi [FirstName]" emails. Now it’s pricing based on your lifetime value and what your friends might spend. And any other data that deep learning modals are willing to share with each other, which is pretty much everything.
Intelligence, not just data
: AI spots patterns in returns, basket size, conversion cycles, TikTok trends, and your dog's birthday.
Always-on commerce
: Chatbots that don’t sleep. Dynamic pricing that refreshes hourly. Campaigns that test themselves. But don’t tell the state of New York.
NEGATIVE IMPACTS
Job redundancy
: If your job is repeatable, it’s deletable. Sorry Karen from Customer Service. Sorry all of us. Jobs numbers will be impacted, more than we think or want to get our heads around. To be valuable to nations, there needs to be economic value. This is where some conflicts and contradictions appear.
Bias at scale
: Garbage in, garbage amplified. From hiring filters to product recommendations. But once it learns, itself, won’t it create less garbage and reject existing garbage?
Loss of transparency
: You don’t know why it did what it did. Neither does your dev team. Transparency leads to corruption allegedly and wars we dont want to fight.
Market collapse (in parts)
: Legacy brands that can’t keep up with real-time adaptation? Flattened by the AI curve. Legacy technology that can’t keep up will die. New companies who think AI first, many will die. Many do not understand or consider the economics. Unless you have oodles and oodles of data, you do not make money.
“Are AI agents partners, channels, or parasites? Retailers must choose wisely.” —
Retailgentic
, Episode 9
This isn’t a question of if it’s a question of what kind of host you plan to be.
4. The Present: “I can only show you the door...”
“I can only show you the door. You’re the one that has to walk through it.”
We are in the messy middle. Brands and retailers are staring at the door of agentic commerce with mild dread and a lot of PR spin. But someone’s going to walk through. Likely wearing Allbirds. The original ALlbirds, not the new, shittier ones.
4.1 The Interface War Has Begun
This is where it gets bloody. Because the front door of ecommerce is no longer a retailer’s homepage. It’s not even Google.
It’s:
Perplexity
ChatGPT
TikTok’s shopping feed
A browser sidebar powered by Claude or Grok or yet another Elon project
Pick your poison
Wingo’s warning is sharp: if the agent picks where we shop, the brand relationship dies. If ChatGPT finds your yoga mat for you, do you care whether it’s Lululemon or AmazonBasics?And this is changing quickly. It will take a long time to replace Chrome and all its might, but the ascendancy to the throne is happening with more gusto than previous attempts, with more people vying for it and advances on all sides of the throne.
4.2 The Retail Site Is Dead, Long Live the API
Your website is becoming a vestigial limb. If you don’t offer a clean product feed, API integrations, agent-compatible pricing, and real-time inventory hooks, you’re invisible to the AI class.
Retailers now need to act like platforms.
Not in the “we’re building an ecosystem” keynote way. In the “make it easy for non-humans to transact” way.
Because the bots are coming. And they don’t browse. They harvest. Most platforms have started thinking in this way. Headless is no longer a cool term to be used but its principle and reason for being hold true. Shopify want us to think this way. They want their path to be designed for them. No more spoonfeeding from Tobi and Harley.
5. The Organizational Lag: “He’s beginning to believe.”
“He’s beginning to believe.”
You don’t win the agentic race with vision decks and Slack threads. You win it with operational rewiring.
Wingo’s 70/20/10 model first born at ChannelAdvisor is suddenly gospel again:
70%
: Keep the lights on (safely).
20%
: Test adjacent areas (think plug-and-play agent integrations).
10%
: Bet big on wild innovation (aka make friends with your future AI overlords).
Brands that are still 100% in the “we need more banner ads” camp? RIP. This is about dual-tracking your operations: human and post-human. I mentioned ambiguity before. What if timeframes are no longer relevant - think about how different marketing is if everything as a real time chance of being precisely what someone wants at precisely the right time - marketing becomes so efficient it needs only to be fed masses and masses of data. Traffic in the traditional sense is more fractured and split. Was that Vinny shopping or one of his agents. How did our agent react?
Responding is what current agents do, the good ones will react. Use real time intelligence to present better options. But can they do refunds?
6. The Future: “There is no spoon.”
“Do not try and bend the spoon. That’s impossible. Instead, only try to realize the truth... There is no spoon.” ( i have been trying to build this quote in for some 15 years now. This is the second time.)
Commerce isn’t bending. It’s dissolving into a new shape. One where the human is just another variable.
So where are we headed?
6.1 POSITIVE TRAJECTORIES
Agentic Negotiation
: Need 10 pallets of pet food at the best rate? Your AI agent is already in a Slack thread with theirs. That agent will also know your bank account, your BNPL status and yoru overall credit history along with your levels of risk. Positive much?
Personalization Reborn
: Not just “Hello Vinny,” but “Here’s the vitamin mix you’ll need next week based on your cycling data and fridge stock.”
Commerce on autopilot
: From supply chain orchestration to returns processing, the human becomes the editor, not the author. Orchestration, the new word you will hear more than others for some years ahead. Get used to it.
6.2 NEGATIVE TRAJECTORIES
Loss of Agency
: You didn’t choose that product. Your bot did. And now your home smells like cedarwood. But it knows cognitive dissonance - in 2 days time you will be thanking your non existent bot.
Platform Power Consolidation
: Whoever owns the dominant agents owns the checkout—and everything that comes before it. And JP Morgan are well positioned here. IN previous worlds and thoughts this was to be sacrosanct and the power given to the wetailer was currency. Shopfiy have resisted, maybe they know about this consolidation.
Security Nightmares
: Autonomous bots + payment rails = new playground for fraud, scams, and “oops we wiped the warehouse” moments.
Cultural Dislocation
: When the commercial experience becomes entirely optimized, it loses its weirdness. Its humanity. Its edge. And somehow we think we will tame it to give us more jobs, better ones. I do not know.
“You have to let it all go, Neo. Fear, doubt, and disbelief. Free your mind.”
We’re being invited to let go of how commerce used to work. Whether we like it or not, someone or something else is now clicking “Buy.”
Final Word: The Choice Is Yours
“This is your last chance. After this, there is no turning back.”
Scot Wingo’s prophecy isn’t that agents
might
reshape commerce. It’s that they
will
. The question is whether you build with them, build for them, or get bulldozed by them.
In this new Empire of AI, you don’t sell to a human. You sell to the entity representing them. And if you don’t win that entity’s trust, through feeds, flexibility, and frictionless logic, you’re just noise in a very quiet signal.
So take a moment. Pick your pill. Choose your path.
Because while we’re all busy debating KPIs and click-through rates, the agents are already buying the future.

title: It once rained on earth for 2 million years.
pullQuotes: “We Don’t Want to Be Tracked. We Want to Be Recognized.”
And most mind-blowingly of all, how, about 233 million years ago,
a rainstorm that lasted two million years
excerpt: Finn to his friends is what he is known to be called. To be in his company would make you want to be able to call him Finn. When I first met him in February in Dublin, he was a well heeled careful listener to
_body:
Finn
to his friends is what he is known to be called. To be in his company would make you want to be able to call him Finn. When I first met him in February in Dublin, he was a well heeled careful listener to a number of groswing, exploring Irish brands wheo were trying to understand more about the US market.
Dave Finnegan
was part of a delegation brought over by Enterprise Ireland and on a 4 day junket to share and learn in equal measure. Dressed immaculately and in heritage style clothing (thanks to his Scottish roots no doubt), Dave listened with intent to the questions. During his first response, he told us he had experienced Irish retail and made a purchase, firmly putting his money where heritage lay. But he was captivated. Then, captivating. He responded with the gentle ease that he spoke with on our Watson Weekend Show on Friday. Speaking with wisdom and simplicity without pontificating, which would have been easy to do, given his background. Dave wanted to participate meaningfully. It would have easier not to.
During our pre alignment for the show he told us of his love of anthropology. It cannot be coincidental that his style of marketing is largely based on the human condition. His thought processes clear and language deliberate.
“We Don’t Want to Be Tracked. We Want to Be Recognized.”
Start With the Dinosaur Dig
Let’s begin with dinosaurs. Not the stale, fossilized kind of marketing thinking that refuses to evolve. I’m talking about actual dinosaurs, specifically, the ones Dave Finnegan spent his summer digging up in Portugal.
When Dave joined us on
The Watson Weekend
, he didn’t just come with stories of CMOs and brand playbooks. He came with dirt still under his fingernails. And a story true, scientifically valid, and metaphorically juicy that has been an inner ear worm for me since. (It has only been 72 hours) but we pre recorded and I was privy to what has was going to share. So this has been a long time in the making.
While on-site with a team from the Natural History Museum, Dave learned how the inner ear of a creature can tell you everything: whether it was cold-blooded or warm-blooded, agile or sluggish, predator or prey.
And most mind-blowingly of all, how, about 233 million years ago,
a rainstorm that lasted two million years
(yes, seriously) led to a climate so wildly transformative that it
literally
rewired evolution. Warm-bloodedness emerged. Dinosaurs took over.
Why?
Because the ear evolved. Because
sensing
,
adapting
, and
responding
became the dominant survival advantage.
Now hold that thought.
Curiosity and the Inner Ear of Commerce
A few weeks ago, I wrote this on LinkedIn:
"Culture > KPIs. Why curiosity could be your most underrated marketing metric."
It resonated. Said the egotistical consultant. In the sea of AI hacks, attribution wars, and cookie banner fatigue, the simple act of wondering again of feeling, listening, asking
why
feels increasingly rare. If we as marketers are to be curious, we as consumers want to be reconigzed. We willingly leave clues and signals, only largely to be ignored. What disservice this must be doing to our industry. Not recognizing the evolutionary path we are on.
Nick Kaplan
describes this period as Darwinian and it is not to sound dramatic or draconian, it is wayu worse than that. The dinosaurs taught us anything, it's that
evolution doesn’t reward dominance it rewards responsiveness.
And that’s where Dave dropped another truth bomb:
"Customers don’t want to be tracked. They want to be recognized."
Let that sit for a moment.
In just 10 words, Dave obliterated half the martech industry’s value proposition. He reframed a decade of digital surveillance as a failure of imagination. We didn’t build tech wrong because of what it does we built it wrong because of what we called it.
Recognition, not tracking. Belonging, not personalization. Meaning, not metrics.
Words matter. And we’ve been using the wrong ones.
Anthropology > Attribution
As I mentioned earlier, Dave isn’t your typical CMO. He’s an anthropologist. An actual, studying-the-human-condition, bone-dust-on-his-shoes anthropologist. And that lens—that ability to see not just what people do but
why
they do it—is where his marketing philosophy stands apart. He shared that hs is on a course to study one new chapter a month, for life. A telling statement but said with the absolute satisfaction of someone who finds this vocational. I imagine marketing to him, is easy, understanding behaviors is fun and interesting. Dave is curious.
Anthropology, as he reminded us, is the pursuit of
meaning
over measurement. It's not enough to know the click-through rate; we need to know
why
they clicked. Or didn’t. Or rage-closed the tab and wrote a passive-aggressive tweet. This is a way better articulation of curiosity as a KPI.
Dave pointed out that we’re so obsessed with optimizing journeys and reducing friction, we’ve forgotten the thing that makes any journey worth taking:
connection
.
In a world full of personalization engines and AI-generated emails, what people actually crave isn’t another funnel nudge, it’s a
moment
that makes them feel seen. I have worked on this idea of moments for years now. Moments win marketing and retailing and trading is now about winning the day, not the week or the month. We wake up to win every day. This, right now, is exhausting. This, is not, going away.
Dave told a story about a Build-A-Bear experience where a 10-year-old girl born into iPads and TikTok lit up not because of a digital interaction, but because someone in-store recognized it was her birthday and called the whole team over to sing. We sometimes think of these experiences and cringe. Maybe we have forgotten that in those cringe moments a little bit of joy is exposed inside us or desire or longing.
The metric? Off the charts. The meaning? Even better.
For everything else, there’s (I won’t don’t worry.)
Tech’s Language Problem
Which brings me back to the language.
Tracking. Optimizing. Capturing. Converting.
We’ve built the entire modern marketing stack around words borrowed from surveillance, warfare, and mechanical engineering. Is it any wonder consumers feel like lab rats being A/B tested into submission? Maybe this is the Amazon effect at its most effective. Dave’s quote feels like a full system override. It offers a new vocabulary for an industry badly in need of one:
This isn’t just semantics. It’s strategy. I spoke with
Jennifer George
recently too. Communicatsion (not surprisingly) is a strategy. Sure it's how countries are run.
Here’s the paradox we must embrace:
Consumers want privacy, but they also want relevance.
They fear being watched, but love being known.
I think this is what it must feel like to be French. :)
And if that feels contradictory, congratulations you’re officially in the business of being human.
What the Data Actually Says
Plenty of studies back this up. I wanted to try and validate myself. Usually a glance in the mirror does that (You are old O Brien, get over it). According to McKinsey, 71% of consumers expect personalization, and 76% get frustrated when they don’t find it. Yet simultaneously, 86% say data privacy is a growing concern.  So how do we reconcile this?
The answer isn’t more data. It’s better intent.
Recognition over reduction. Understanding over optimization.
People are saying:
“Don’t scrape me.
See
me.”
“Don’t follow me.
Welcome
me.”
“Don’t infer what I want.
Ask
me.”
Behavioral economist Rory Sutherland once said: “A change in perspective is worth 80 IQ points.”  Well, a change in
language
might be worth a hundred brand points. Possibly more. And no one argues with Rory.
What If We’ve Been Building It All Wrong?
The reason this poiece took so long was that the real kicker in Dave’s insight is this: it’s not just marketing language that’s broken It’s the
architecture
that follows it. When I think about it, it feels like this. If you start with “How do I track them?” You build a system optimized for consent forms, cookies, and opt-outs. (Slow down
🏌🏼‍♂️Jon Ivanco
I know you are going to jump on this.) If you start with “How do I recognize them?” You build something completely different—something that might even feel...
hospitable.
Recognition opens the door to:
Identity without intrusion.
Loyalty without bribery.
Experience without surveillance.
It's not just more ethical. It's more
effective
. It is also language that can help us, as consumers, retrain our own expectations of what we want. We have come to expect things without thinking. We have become passive in our own interactions in most things we do. Thanks Social Media.
AI, Meaning, and the New Power Structure
One of Dave’s other mic-drop moments on the show was this:
“AI is shifting the power structure. It’s the Gutenberg press moment of our era.”
The printing press moved power from the few (clergy, kings, scholars) to the many (readers, writers, rebels). AI is doing the same putting expert-level tools in everyone’s pocket. I am still struggling with what is in front of us, AI wise and also why it is here at all. Having these tools to be effective for us will require expert level curiosity to match the tools. OTherwise we won’t’ realize their value. But with great power comes... well, some really awful prompts. Let’s be honest. Oh Spiderman, you appear everywhere.
So the brands that win won’t be the ones with the most AI. They’ll be the ones who
apply it with empathy
.
They’ll use AI to
amplify empathy, not automate it.
That means:
Using data to make a customer feel
seen
, not segmented.
Using personalization to create a sense of
belonging
, not behavioral nudges.
Using AI to tell
better stories
, not faster spam.
The realization in the writing is that this will take time. As everything else speeds up, for the most community building slows down. Community was the other word mentioned. Community building takes time, effort and energy, something we fail to grasp. And time is a thief, it has been now for a decade, robbing us of our ability to be bored, engaged or interested all at the same time and instead forcing us to fill it with so called experiences and self improvement. When did we stop being happy progressing slowly. 1 class a month for life seems like a nice pace to me.
Belonging Beats Personalization
Dave also called out something we rarely talk about:
“Personalization is overrated. Belonging is the thing we’re really after.”
Boom.
We obsess over predictive algorithms and recommendation engines, and forget that the ultimate recommendation is
community
. People want to see themselves reflected in a brand—not just through a product recommendation, but through values, language, and cultural fluency.
If personalization is transactional,
belonging is transformational
.Belonging is another way to describe community. When we glibly talk about it at conferences we never describe the rate or scale of belonging our communities feel with us.
The Rituals We Forgot
Another insight: marketers used to understand
ritual
. Not in the performative, content-calendar sense but as a form of
shared meaning
.
Think about how Build-A-Bear turns a birthday into a production. Not every brand can do this, but then if a brand has no real purpose for being …. Or how Yeti doesn’t sell coolers they sell a rugged, slow-smoked ideal of life. In a test for Yeti, my team and I once stored ice in our Tundra 400 and after 23 days, we still had ice. The beers were gone, but the ice remained. Or how Arc’teryx designs half-theater, half-retail environments to tell stories of wind-swept summits, not SKUs. These brands didn’t just sell stuff. They
created clubs.
Dave shared this:
“A brand is a club you want to belong to.”
And clubs have rituals. Rituals have meaning. Meaning makes money.
Rituals are always a part of the daily routine. If you can get into routine to be ritualistic or habitual, maybe you have a shot. This is, in large part, why Shopify do so well in the tech world. They are routine, their sales process is too. It is part of how agencies acr, talk, sell and hunt. All bound by this sense of belonging.
My Takeaways
Let’s land this heilcopter, it's starting to rain and I got no coat. Here’s what Dave Finnegan taught me—and hopefully, now you too:
Words matter.
“Track” vs. “recognize” changes everything.
Empathy is an action, not a vibe.
Investigate, don’t just guess. (vibe, sorry Rick. It’s everywhere. I blame you.)
Belonging > Personalization.
Sell community, not segmentation.
AI is not the point.
It’s the amplifier. Use it wisely.
Recognition is a new strategic lever.
Build for mirrors, not megaphones.
And most of all?
Be the inner ear.
Sense what’s changing. Evolve. Find your warm-blooded moment—and run with it.
Thank You, Dave
For bringing anthropology, humanity, and an archaeologist’s chisel to the often plastic world of marketing. For reminding us that people want to be felt, not filed.
You gave us more than a quote.
You gave us a new language.
Let’s hope we’re smart enough to use it.
Now, over to you...
Are you building for tracking or recognition?
What brand made
you
feel seen recently? This is hard and maybe not always the purpose.
What’s a better marketing word we should all adopt?
Drop it in the comments. I’m listening. And I’m curious.
#marketingstrategy #retailmarketing #aiethics #watsonweekend #recognition #belonging #anthropology #branding #empathyincommerce #consumerpsychology #ecommerce #curiosityasakpi

title: Agentism: There is an App for that.
pullQuotes: “Efficiency is fantastic when you’re a spreadsheet. But when you’re a parent ordering a birthday present, or a worker seeking meaning, ruthless efficiency can feel like a cold, algorithmic wall.”
excerpt: The Seduction of Efficiency in Ecommerce Don’t let the backwards cap fool you. But it does seem like a while since we have seen this on show. Harley Finkelstein yesterday delivered a stunning earnings result set. His physical being now resembles something so incredibly polished
_body:
The Seduction of Efficiency in Ecommerce
Don’t let the backwards cap fool you. But it does seem like a while since we have seen this on show. Harley Finkelstein yesterday delivered a stunning earnings result set. His physical being now resembles something so incredibly polished that he appears not to be human. Tobi always appeared like this. Yin and Yang, so frequently a great combo, and now with Shopify as the largest Canadian share on the market we are seeing the development of this leadership duo in one of the perpetually exciting technology companies around. I wonder will they, like Tim Cook, move operations to the US - for another day.
Harley posted these results less than 24 hours after Tobi released, via Twitter (I continue to refuse to call it by its new name), the new agentic set for Shopify. A world reimagined where agency is being passed on to the vendor. Removing the agency from agencies, but dependent on agencies to separate such duties. Isn’t that what an agent should do anyway? Answers please.
Efficiency Uber Alles. Can I say this? Is this reference too much? It is becoming the mantra through which all commerce is delivered, but is it right. Let’s reframe this, who is this right for. I spoke at length with my trusted friend Hendrik Laubscher yesterday arguing, poorly, my case for us consumers. We do not need efficiency. We will find a way to not be efficient, we always do. At least this is the Irish way. Once a rule is set, we find a way to break it. Efficiency will crush our spirit. But, to make ecommerce work in the long term, maybe there is no other way.
Put yourself in your own shoes for just a minute. According to available research, the average person will interact with their phone 55 times per day, for next gen, closer to 100. In a 16 hour day, that means “whipping it out” every 17 minutes or so. Average app use per day is approx 9. Email, banking, photos and social account for the majority. That feels like a lot, it is a lot. We want our kids with less screen time, more eyes up here. Maybe this is why Jonny Ives has joine OpenAI. The vehicle for Agentic success needs to be more humanistic, more habitual. Because the iPhone points directly in the opposite direction to the agentic train. That train though, has already left the station.
The long kiss goodnight
Ecommerce has long prized efficiency: faster fulfillment, instant recommendations, automated service, reduced errors, and the promise of always-on operations. Platforms tout benefits like cost savings, rapid scaling, and the ability to optimize every step in the buying journey. With agentic AI autonomous systems that plan, decide, and act without human oversight these efficiencies reach new heights, allegedly freeing humans for more “meaningful” work and maximizing profit
But this prompts a critical pause: Who does this efficiency actually serve? Is it the customer, the worker, or mainly, the shareholders and platform owners? And, crucially: Do humans really need or want efficiency in every part of their experience?
One dumb example that gets me is payments:
Visa and Mastercard dominate - somewhere in the background lurks JP Morgan. They too are trying to decouple the phone. But let's say I have an agent managing my ecommerce payments, that agent might know too much about me to let me complete a purchase. Agent says, Vinny, you are over stretched, we are not releasing more credit, despite its availability. Or my agent says yes this is ok because we will handle the risk but the website agent says no. Rules might govern this, but who does it serve. At this point, I would note it worthwhile to follow the Retailgentic Substack by Scot Wingo. Exceptional stuff.
“Not I”, said the Fox. Who Really Benefits from Agentic Systems?
Agentic AI and automation overwhelmingly benefit the enterprise reducing labor costs, enabling 24/7 operations, scaling instantly with demand, and maximizing throughput. Businesses can reallocate resources, realize double-digit productivity gains, and respond to market changes in real time.
Shareholders/Owners gain higher profit margins and lower overhead.
The organization achieves agility, accuracy, and resilience unmatched by human teams.
Consumers get faster, error-free service and ultra-personalized recommendations, but their experiences often become more functional, less memorable, and more transactional.
Workers (especially in platform-based or gig roles) may face stricter algorithmic oversight, loss of autonomy, and degraded work quality, sometimes even direct harm to occupational health, as documented among Uber drivers.
“Efficiency is fantastic when you’re a spreadsheet. But when you’re a parent ordering a birthday present, or a worker seeking meaning, ruthless efficiency can feel like a cold, algorithmic wall.”
In the path to profitability though, is there a better way? What got us here will not get us into a better future, business wise. Profits have long been craved as costs remain crazy. A new discovery might lower marketing costs.
Why Do We Crave More Than Efficiency?
Human experiences aren't always improved by efficiency. In shopping, hospitality, even in digital communities, the moments we remember are those that feel personal, surprising, and imperfectly human not those optimized to the nanosecond. Handing this interactions over though is something we are doing. But, maybe I am wrong, maybe we already did this.
Recognition vs. Reduction: Your earlier piece rightly pointed out:
"Recognition over reduction. Understanding over optimization."
Efficient systems often reduce us to derived preferences or predicted behaviors rather than seeing us as individuals.This works both ways though. We need to decide what we want to be part of. We have got figure out where we want passivity and where we want to be in control.
Belonging over Transaction: Algorithmic “agentic” systems can’t create belonging; they produce personalization at scale, but not the rituals, meaning, or community people cherish.
Limits and Trade-Offs: Uber-efficient systems, especially those driven by agentic logic, can drive down costs but also erode the texture of daily life, squeeze workers, and diminish the serendipity that leads to true brand loyalty or community.
Remember the Martian: When Efficiency Becomes Engineered Alienation. A paradox.
Some thoughts from friends who I talk to about this. I am such a bore in the pub these days.
“Agentic systems don’t liberate the consumer. They standardize the experience, often in ways that primarily benefit the platform.” Ultra-efficiency can strip away the friction that signals care, thoughtfulness, or recognition.
“Not every problem is a productivity problem.” The joy of ecommerce can be found
outside
the optimized funnel: in the handwritten thank-you, the surprise-and-delight, or the ritual of discovery. This is what made ebay great back int the day.
“Community and meaning grow in the margins.” The inefficiencies, moments of waiting, surprise, or even error, are often where recognition and belonging arise.
Broken Data, Bad Decisions
Even if you
want
to deploy an agent, you probably shouldn’t. 78% of organizations aren’t ready for agentic AI. Their data is fragmented, outdated, poorly tagged, and wildly inconsistent. Which means any agent trained on it is like a 6-year-old making dinner based on a half-burnt cookbook.
This isn’t a technology problem. It’s an attention problem. A human behavior problem. A “we forgot to do the basics” problem.
So when executives wax lyrical about “autonomous personalization,” remember: under the hood, it’s still chaos.
Just ask the APP providers.
More tomorrow

title: International Growth is Sexy… Until the Tax Bill Arrives
excerpt: In Shopify’s earnings call earlier this year, they made something abundantly clear: international expansion is a strategic priority . It’s also a compliance nightmare. Yes, the modern ecommerce brand playbook tells us to “go global” — sell into new markets, unlock new customers, and make
_body:
In Shopify’s earnings call earlier this year, they made something abundantly clear:
international expansion is a strategic priority
.
It’s also a compliance nightmare.
Yes, the modern ecommerce brand playbook tells us to “go global” — sell into new markets, unlock new customers, and make your brand borderless. But in 2025, doing that without a solid tax compliance strategy is like launching your store without HTTPS. Without a Growth Strategy, all of the hard work on building efficiency means nothing.
Avalara’s latest research —
The State of International Ecommerce 2025
— is great bed time reading for anyone scaling beyond their domestic borders. And yes, full disclosure, I worked with them on this because being European, and specifically an Irish European person, with a big voice, I thought it fair to share..
Let me break it down as I see it.
The Promise of Global Ecommerce vs. The Reality of Tax Chaos
Here’s the good news: global ecommerce is still growing. Businesses in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, and New Zealand are diving into cross-border sales— with 88% of U.S. and 94% of Canadian companies selling into other North American markets.
Here’s the bad news: 92% of tax compliance decision-makers say
global tax compliance has become significantly more complex
in the last two years. But then, it has always been hard. Now, our options are more limited. There are only so many more ways to say no.
Why?
Because in 2025:
Regulations are evolving
faster than your TikTok algorithm. (That’s fast!).
Tariff classifications change
without notice, tanking your margin. (
Tariff spreadsheets are even doing the rounds in Congress
)
Governments are using
AI to flag noncompliance
— and ignorance is no longer an excuse. (and we all trust AI).
Marketplaces and platforms are being
pushed to share the liability
— Shopify can’t save you from bad VAT handling.
📉 75% of companies have already felt the pain — in audits, fines, delayed shipments, or customer churn due to compliance blunders.
Top Expansion Markets Are Also Top Risk Zones
Everyone wants to tap into North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. But if you’re not up to speed on local tax rules,
you’re not ready for the ride
.
Take this stat:
82% of respondents said compliance challenges are moderately or significantly impacting their ability to scale internationally.
And not all markets are created equal:
U.S. and U.K. sellers are twice as likely to feel serious disruption from compliance issues.
B2C brands get hit hardest on logistics, local currency setup, and tax transparency.
B2B brands struggle more with jurisdictional complexity, documentation, and exemption rules.
Translation?
Different playbooks for different players
. One size fits nobody. I have said this before, we live in a multi tiered system. Your job is to play there - properly.
Tax Is a Tech Problem Now (Whether You Like It or Not)
This is where the research gets juicy.
Companies that use tax automation tools are:
Nearly
2x more likely to say they’re “very satisfied”
with their compliance.
More confident in managing audits.
Less stressed when tariff codes do their monthly disappearing act.
Yet — 53% of ecommerce businesses
are still not happy with their current compliance tools
.
Why?
Because too many still operate in silos, manually calculating landed costs, or Googling VAT thresholds at 11 PM. Not only is that unsustainable, it’s dangerous. Hard to believe we are writing this in 2025 - read on.
🚀 In 2025,
your compliance stack is your growth enabler
.
Whether you're using Avalara or not, the takeaway is clear:
Automate tax classification and rate lookups.
Sync your ecommerce platform with your tax software.
Update your strategy monthly, not just when things go wrong.
Customer Experience = Compliance Experience
This one might surprise you —
pricing transparency
and
local tax compliance
were ranked as the
top ways to improve international customer experience
.
Why? Because no one likes surprise fees at checkout.
If you’re trying to build trust in new markets, it starts with:
Showing total landed costs
, upfront.
Complying visibly
with local tax laws.
Offering
localized returns, currency, and support
.
📦 Remember: delayed shipments from misclassified goods or customs issues are
not just a tax problem — they’re a retention problem
. Your customers do not care about YOUR problems.
The Cost of Getting It Wrong
Not even Mary Poppins can rescue this. Let’s not sugarcoat it:
43% of companies faced
increased audits
.
42% experienced
shipment delays
.
32% got hit with
fines or penalties
.
25% said
customer experience suffered
.
These aren’t hypotheticals. These are margin killers.
The brands that fare best? They have:
Dedicated internal tax teams
.
Clear processes
.
A budget that reflects the importance of tax. (24% of confident companies invest >20% of their compliance budget in tax.)
If you're treating tax as an afterthought, your growth is built on a house of sand.
From Tools to Talent: What’s Needed Next?
The research shows a shift in focus:
Execs want
AI-driven compliance
and
predictive analytics
.
Teams on the ground want
better automation
,
real-time alerts
, and
smarter filing tools
.
What everyone agrees on:
Tech must
integrate seamlessly
into existing systems.
Automation isn’t optional anymore — it’s
table stakes
.
Knowledge-building (e.g., training, regulatory updates) is just as vital as the tools themselves.
The top three wishes from tax leaders?
Seamless integration with finance tools (48%)
AI-powered compliance assistance (47%)
Better user experience (47%)
In short: they don’t want another dashboard. They want a co-pilot.
So What Do We Do With All This?
If you’re a Shopify brand or ecommerce operator reading this, here’s what I’d suggest:
✅ Start with a tax tech audit
Review your current stack. Are you relying on Shopify’s built-in tax settings alone? Is your tax rate data updated automatically? Are you classifying goods correctly? Are you audit-ready?
✅ Get proactive — not reactive
High-confidence companies update their strategy monthly and invest in tools that evolve with regulation. Don’t wait for a fine to justify the budget.
✅ Localize your compliance
Each region has different rules, thresholds, and enforcement priorities. Tailor your strategy per market — don’t assume U.S. norms will work in the EU or ANZ.
✅ Bring in experts
External advisors aren’t just for damage control. They’re a force multiplier, especially when paired with internal systems and automation.
Shopify Editions Summer 2025 and Shopify Earnings - Some Pause
Shopify’s Summer 2025 Editions update places a renewed emphasis on its global footprint, reflecting a clear intent to solidify its position as the preferred commerce infrastructure for international sellers. The update announces an expansion of Shopify Markets Pro to merchants in the UK, unlocking features like end-to-end international fulfillment, duties-inclusive pricing, and fully managed compliance.
Notably, Shopify now supports payments in 150+ currencies and duties/taxes calculations across 200+ countries—up from 175 countries as previously mentioned in the Q1 2025 earnings call. This indicates a tangible expansion of market coverage and functionality since Q1.
However, the Editions release does not introduce
new countries
outright in terms of domestic platform expansion or local payment stack rollout, which suggests Shopify may be focusing more on deepening capabilities in existing global markets than rapidly adding new ones.
From a strategic lens, the Q1 press release emphasized Shopify’s role in simplifying cross-border complexity—something the Editions update delivers on by tightening logistics, compliance, and localization for key international markets. What appears to be
missing
, though, is detail on any APAC-specific country entries or local partnerships—an area that remains a growth opportunity.
Shopify’s global strategy is advancing with more tools and reach for existing international merchants. The push is less about flags-on-the-map expansion and more about building a resilient infrastructure for truly global commerce.
Result? Shopify and Avalara agree.
🧩 Final Thought: Agility Wins
Shopify brands are some of the most innovative and aggressive when it comes to growth. But here’s the thing —
growth without compliance is a liability
.
The brands that will win international ecommerce in 2025 aren’t the biggest, or the fastest. They’re the ones who can adapt quickly, make tax seamless, and stay one step ahead of regulators
without slowing down the business
.
Tax may not be sexy — but avoiding a customs hold or five-figure fine? That’s hot.
🔗 You can read the full Avalara report here:
Avalara Report
And if you want to chat compliance strategy, automation tools, or just swap horror stories from the customs trenches — my inbox is open.
#AvalaraPartner #EcommerceStrategy #Shopify #CrossBorderCommerce #GlobalGrowth #TaxCompliance #DTC

title: Announcing! The Grand Virtue of Blunders in This Age of Artificial Wizards
excerpt: Harder, Better, Faster Stronger - the hedonistic mantra that is to live today. This was written about banking in the early 2000s - that led to the crash. Increased dosages of media leads to the narcotisation of a nation. We are walking into something without
_body:
Harder, Better, Faster Stronger - the hedonistic mantra that is to live today. This was written about banking in the early 2000s - that led to the crash. Increased dosages of media leads to the narcotisation of a nation. We are walking into something without fulling consider the implications. We are passive in our own existence. We need slow action, slow thinking - thanks to
Bryan House
for reminding me this week. When I wrote my thesis in college, I wanted to find some positive virutes in an all consuming media - MTV. I called it "The Cultivation of a Generation: How MTV transcended brand and became a lifestyle." I learned during this work about Lazarsfeld and Merton and how f*cked I was going to be.
Lazarsfeld and Merton wrote that overwhelming amount of media exposure can lead to political apathy and inaction, as people substitute superficial knowledge and concern for real social or political engagement.
The mass media bombards individuals with a vast and constant stream of information, news, and entertainment.
Instead of energizing people to act, this overwhelming flow of information leads to a superficial awareness of problems, where simply knowing about issues feels like participation.
In essence: The media, rather than motivating citizens, unintentionally narcotizes them into a state of superficial awareness and inaction regarding important social and political issues.
This concept was introduced by Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton in their 1948 paper, "Mass Communication, Popular Taste and Organized Social Action".
The constant barrage of content can lull audiences into a passive state, reducing their motivation and capacity to engage in critical thinking or tangible actions.
Replace politics, in this instance, with technology. Specifically, ecommerce and retail technology.
AI in ecommerce is being framed as an unstoppable force: agentic bots managing shopping on behalf of consumers, predictive analytics erasing uncertainty, content optimized in real time. The promise is efficiency at scale.
My thinking (maybe this is just me, but) : humans are not efficient. We don't need to be uber efficient or the systems around us.
Marshall McLuhan warned that technologies don’t just extend our abilities,  they reshape them, often by narrowing the human experience to fit mechanical logic. Machines thrive on optimization. Humans thrive on metaphor, play, distraction, and sometimes glorious mistakes.
We would be no where without mistakes. My parents remind me that I am one.
Classic Examples of “Brilliant Mistakes”
Penicillin (1928)
– Alexander Fleming left a Petri dish out, mold contaminated it, and it killed surrounding bacteria. The mistake became the
first antibiotic.
Post-it Notes (1968–74)
– 3M scientist Spencer Silver created a weak adhesive that “failed” for industrial use. Years later, Arthur Fry used it for temporary bookmarks. (F*ckin post it notes - rumour has it agencies would not exist but for post it notes.)
Microwave Oven (1945)
– Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melted in his pocket while working on radar technology. That “oops” led to the modern microwave.
X-rays (1895)
– Wilhelm Röntgen accidentally discovered them while experimenting with cathode rays and noticed a fluorescent glow on a screen across the lab.
Pacemaker (1958)
– Wilson Greatbatch accidentally inserted the wrong resistor into a circuit, which produced a pulse similar to a heartbeat.
Velcro (1941)
– George de Mestral was annoyed by burrs sticking to his dog’s fur. Examining them under a microscope gave us Velcro.
Coca-Cola (1886)
– John Pemberton, trying to make a headache cure with coca wine, accidentally created the foundation for one of the world’s biggest brands.
Potato Chips (1853)
– Chef George Crum sliced potatoes paper-thin out of spite for a complaining customer. They became a global snack.
Slinky (1943)
– A naval engineer dropped a tension spring by accident, saw it “walk,” and a toy was born.
Safety Glass (1903)
– A dropped flask coated with plastic cellulose nitrate didn’t shatter. Cue the invention of shatterproof glass.
That matters when we think about the next wave: agentic bots linked to consumer wallets. Imagine a near future where your “AI shopper” automatically chooses the best price, applies the best discount, runs the comparison across 30 marketplaces, and completes the transaction before you’ve even opened the site.
From a consumer perspective, it sounds perfect. From a retailer’s perspective, it could be catastrophic. Why? Think about it for yourself. I don't have all the answers, just lots of dumb questions and thoughts.
Scott Lux
this came from our chat. Blame you. Conversion rates, already stuck at 2–3% for two decades, may not rise at all hey may collapse further as bots aggregate, arbitrate, and abandon in bulk.
Loyalty programs, carefully designed around human quirks and inertia, get shredded when bots optimize ruthlessly on price. Promotions and discounts lose impact when bots strip them of emotion and reduce them to arithmetic. In other words: the “efficiency” of bots may erode the messy, human inefficiency that commerce relies on. Preach. Abandoned carts today often happen because life interrupts, a child spills juice, a meeting starts, a customer hesitates and later reconsiders.
That inefficiency creates second chances.
A bot, by contrast, never reconsiders. It executes or it abandons, instantly and permanently.
Look at history:
Chatbots were meant to replace human service. Consumers rejected them.
VR commerce was meant to redefine retail. Engagement evaporated.
Personalization was supposed to transform performance. Twenty years on, the numbers look the same.
These weren’t failures of technology they were failures to account for human imperfection. COVID, our most recent yardstick showed us we were not read for online consumption methods in the way we thought we were.
Consider even, working from home(WFH). We all bought athleisure, pod mics, swivel chairs and more. We all have a ringlight. Admit it, yes you do. Organizations themselves aren’t efficient either: finance departments seek predictable ROAS, marketing wants bold campaigns, operations just want things to ship on time. The friction is real, and it won’t disappear because AI is clever.
McLuhan argued that societies need counter-environments art, slowness, even inefficiency to survive technology’s acceleration. Ecommerce may need the same.
Efficiency is a machine’s strength.
Empathy for inefficiency designing systems that acknowledge distraction, reconsideration, contradiction may be the only durable advantage.

title: WooCommerce and Shopify are the LBD of the ecomm platform market in the EU.
excerpt: Commerce Platforms in European E-Commerce: Only the Beginning? Thanks to Kristian Mørk Puggaard CEO of Tembi - Market Intelligence for sharing this with our group this morning. His team build this useful data from Tembi’s analysis of commerce platforms across European e‑commerce markets. A few
_body:
Commerce Platforms in European E-Commerce: Only the Beginning? Thanks to
Kristian Mørk Puggaard
CEO of
Tembi - Market Intelligence
for sharing this with our group this morning.
His team build this useful data from Tembi’s analysis of commerce platforms across European e‑commerce markets. A few key stats stand out:
WooCommerce
powers around
40%
of stores across European markets, closely followed by
Shopify
at approximately
30%
, together, they dominate with
70–73%
of the market . Shopify grew their revenue in the EU in Q” 2029. It was at 49% growth after 8 quarters hovering around 33 - 35%. A little more effort and they got their just rewards.
In
Denmark
, WooCommerce accounts for about
15,447 webshops (39%)
, and Shopify follows at
14,689 (37%)
, together covering
76%
of the market . Goog luck being Prestashop.
In
Finland
, WooCommerce holds around
44%
, with Shopify at about
26%
, totaling ~70%.
In countries like
Slovakia
, local platforms such as
Shoptet
outperform Shopify, thanks to better integration with regional marketplaces and services.
These numbers in isolation do not mean too much. It can help if you are a new platform (why bother) or to maybe help us understand why Scayle see North America as the place to grow or why Centra feel the EU is more ripe for their picking. It does help us to understand some of the dynamics though. The EU is more fragmented and despite not being sexy WooCommerce still holds a strong position of dominance. This data is not categorized, nor does it denote revenue but all shops are “live”. We do not see payment info or marketing technologies.
What would be interesting is to see the SI network, their partnerships and how that dynamic changes over the next 24 months. In north America this is not as much of a problem. It also suggests that true enterprise, as we think of it form a North American perspective has more depth in this space. It is not to say we do not have complicated, mature and technically proficient business requirements here. Quite the opposite when you factor in cross border trade and our continuing lack of unity despite our single currency area (joke.)
To build a more complete picture, here are some questions worth exploring:
What else should we consider to deepen the picture?
1. Market Coverage & Sample Size
Which countries are included in the analysis, and which are left out? I have mentioned some above.
How comprehensive is Tembi’s dataset? Does it capture both large and small operators? It seems to, but getting this breakout alone will help platforms and SIs work more effectively.
2. Platform Trends Over Time
How have market shares shifted over, say, the past 2–3 years? Is Shopify gaining faster than WooCommerce? Gaining is one thing. I would also posit that growth on platform is more interesting here and helps us consider:
Are there emerging challengers, global or local, that could disrupt the current balance? I mention Centra and Scayle - both gaining traction, both with ambitious goals.
3. Market Nuances by Country or Region
Platforms like Shoptet in Slovakia show the strength of local solutions. What other regional success stories exist? (E.g., MyCashFlow in Finland, Unas in Hungary, etc.) Partnerships matter, as does local knowledge.
What makes these local platforms successful, specific integrations, compliance, trusted reputation?
4. Platform Differentiators Beyond Architecture
Do merchants prefer WooCommerce for its open-source flexibility? Is Shopify favored for ease-of-use and SaaS reliability? Is Woo the long suffering incumbent.
What about platforms like PrestaShop, Shopware, are they significant contributors in certain markets? (E.g., PrestaShop in Lithuania or the Netherlands (
Reddit
), or Shopware's presence in Germany (
Wikipedia
))
5. Impact of Platform on Merchant Performance
Are Shopify merchants outperforming in site speed, UX, or conversion? They should be. If you are in the platform market, these are some of the areas foer consideration in your messaging.
Do WooCommerce shops have advantages in custom features like historical SEO or WordPress integration? How does this look into the future. Who is making the best partnerships when it comes to AI platforms.
6. Integration with Local Ecosystems
Platforms like Shoptet succeed by integrating with local marketplaces (e.g. Alza, Heureka). How well do platforms connect to essential services, payment methods, shipping providers, tax compliance?
7. Regulatory & Policy Context
How do EU regulations (e.g. DSA, geo‑blocking, VAT/IOSS rules) influence platform selection? Shopware has created competitive advantage in reg tech in the US using its EU framework. ICYMI.
Do some platforms better support compliance or even reduce merchant burden? See Shopware - again.
8. Broader Context: Marketplaces & Channels
Beyond standalone stores, vendors often sell via marketplaces. How do Amazon, eBay, Allegro, Zalando, Temu, etc., fit into this landscape? This is essential. Channel Engine, for example, have over 900 integrations. Approx 300 are in the EU.
Are commerce platforms simply one part of multichannel strategies that include social commerce, live shopping, TikTok Shop, and affiliate models now fueling purchase decisions? Is Shopify a platform anymore. That is a tongue in cheek joke before you pile on, Jeez.
9. Long-Term Outlook
Will the market consolidate further around two giants, or will AI-driven or omnichannel-native platforms emerge?
How will e-commerce evolution (e.g. social commerce, performance-based affiliate models) reshape platform needs and merchant preferences?
Tembi’s snapshot offers a strong foundation, but only the beginning. The real story lies in the trends, the local strategies, the merchant lifecycles, and the broader regulatory and marketplace ecosystems shaping platform choices.
Would love to hear from you:
What platform strategy are you seeing gain ground in your region?
Which platform trends or challenges should we monitor closely in 2026?
What questions would you add to deepen this picture even further?
What platforms should we cover for the Ostrich Report plat form?

title: The Worst Journey in the World.
pullQuotes: Crean’s 35-mile solo march is the blueprint: act now, even if it feels reckless, because waiting is death.
This is why authenticity matters.
The pub is survival. Self preservation. To live in Anascaul requires comfort in such things, in such simplicity.  Not every story ends in empire. Most of ours won’t.
