_body:
“Tom Crean was the hardest man that ever came out of Ireland, a great lump of an Irishman, big-hearted, simple, and with a fund of humour.” Tom Crean (1877–1938) was an Irish seaman from Annascaul, County Kerry. Born into poverty, he joined the British Royal Navy at just 15. He wasn’t a public-school officer type like most explorers of the time, he was an ordinary sailor, with no wealth, no connections, and no status. Yet he went on to play central roles in some of the most legendary Antarctic expeditions ever attempted.
He showed up every time. Serving to his captain. HIs story is told in the book, Unsung Hero and Guinness (who else) brought him to public attention again in 2002.  He survived 3 expeditions to the South Pole. In itself, seems like a story only that could be told be a book. One of his greatest feats was the rescue of crewmen, walking on a 35 mile trek, in the Antarctic, with no equipment, to bring his friends home. He had walked for 18 hours straight.
Crean wasn’t the one who wrote the memoirs. He wasn’t the flag-planting leader. He was the quiet hand that got people home when the world was collapsing. He walked 35 miles alone across the ice to save his companions. He endured Scott’s doomed South Pole attempt, Shackleton’s
Endurance
disaster, and came back to Kerry to open a pub. He never claimed to be more than he was. Yet, without him, others would have died.
That’s small retail and ecommerce in 2025. Not glamorous. Not always in the headlines. Not the leader remembered in textbooks. But enduring. Quietly shaping the outcome. It is why the Struggle Bus exists.
The First Unicorn Expeditions
Robert Falcon Scott wanted the South Pole the way empires want headlines. It wasn’t survival he was after, it was victory. He gathered a caravan of men, ponies, dogs, and equipment,  too much equipment. The sledges were overloaded. The plan was ambitious and rigid.
When Amundsen beat him to the Pole, Scott pressed on anyway. On the return, his men began to collapse. Food ran out. The weather turned. One by one they died. And somewhere in that long retreat, Tom Crean turned back with two companions and found himself facing the unthinkable: they wouldn’t all make it unless someone walked alone. Thirty-five miles, starving, frozen, delirious. He did it, and the men he left behind lived.
Scott had the grand ambition. Crean had the instinct.
It’s the same today. Big retailers love the big march: 18-month plans, fiscal-year roadmaps, campaigns crafted for “brand consistency.” They’re Scott hauling too much weight into a blizzard. Small retailers are Crean: moving fast, adjusting, walking now because tomorrow will be too late. That’s why small brands go live on TikTok Shop this week instead of waiting for “channel approval.” They test Threads ads on a Tuesday. They try marketplaces the boardroom doesn’t recognise. Giants need committees; small needs only instinct. In an environment where discovery is being rewritten by AI and CAC is spiralling, instinct is survival.
Crean’s 35-mile solo march is the blueprint: act now, even if it feels reckless, because waiting is death.
Shackleton’s
Endurance
expedition set out with glory in mind: to cross the Antarctic continent. Instead, the ship was crushed in ice and the men stranded on drifting floes. Shackleton is remembered as the great leader who got every man home alive. But survival didn’t come from glory.
It came from improvisation. Innovation in any other language.
From men like Crean who hauled sledges, who kept singing, who kept morale from collapsing.
That’s the lesson small actors live every day. Big retailers are building
Endurance
ships: billion-dollar retail media networks, loyalty programs with hundreds of millions of members, robotic warehouses projected to cut costs by 25%. They’re efficient, impressive, enormous. But when the ice shifts, the ship splinters.
Small retailers improvise. Garage inventory one week, 3PL the next. A Shopify app swapped overnight when it stops working. Fulfilment flexed through drop ship or local courier. Indie X indie collaborations forged in DMs. It’s messy, but it works.
A Struggle Bus guest once told me, “We didn’t survive by being smart. We survived by trying everything until something worked.” That’s
Endurance
. The map fails. The ship cracks. You improvise, you sing songs to keep morale, you push forward. Giants think efficiency equals resilience. Crean knew better: survival is improvisation.
South Georgia Therapy Sessions
When Shackleton realised salvation lay in South Georgia, he picked five men to sail an open boat across 800 miles of Southern Ocean. Crean was one of them. The journey itself was insane: hurricane seas, frostbite, exhaustion. But it didn’t end there. Once they landed, Shackleton, Worsley, and Crean had to cross the island’s unmapped mountains on foot to reach a whaling station and summon rescue.
No maps. No precedent. Just instinct and endurance.
That’s what small retailers do when they operate in niches too small for giants to bother with. Giants want TAM measured in billions. Small players build profitably in “ugly” categories,  industrial parts, obscure hobbies, hyper-local products. They walk where no map exists because the giants don’t even look there.
This is why authenticity matters.
You don’t fake your way across unmapped terrain. You live it. Small brands win here because their stories feel human. They aren’t trying to appeal to everyone. They’re speaking directly to a niche, in its own language, with credibility that polished campaigns can’t replicate.
Beauty in the Dark?
This is one of the reasons I think that Beauty is emerging categories for standout brand leadership. Almost all the success stories come from a founder who new what the didn't have, couldn't get and wanted. They set off to do this. They understood from the inside out why they were dong the thing that they were doing and this permeates through all that they do and how the communicate this. Story is not always written and in many cases, today is through the lens. This type of authenticity is hard to replicate on the latest plant based trainers or the newest athleisure gear with tummy tucking support. Spare me. Sons, an Irish hair loss supplement, are bucking this trend. I know because I am in their discovery pool. Their story is told through barbers. Local therapy givers to many a man, the world over. Their potential limitless
until we launch a pill for that. Holding my breath for same
.
The indie beauty founder on TikTok explaining her serum in her own voice isn’t aiming for mass market. She’s speaking to her community. That’s Crean on South Georgia: not looking for a banner headline, just finding a way through the mountains.
The Solo Trek: The path forward to the way home.
If Crean is remembered for one thing, it’s this: the thirty-five mile solo march. His two companions too weak to go on, he left them in a tent and set out alone. No food, no sleep, sub-zero temperatures. Thirty-five miles of ice to reach help. He stumbled into camp delirious, collapsed, and then insisted rescuers return immediately to save his friends.
In this, there is no glory. There’s grit. And it’s a metaphor, of sorts, for small retail.
Because what is a founder answering DMs at midnight if not a solo march? What is packing orders in a garage, writing email copy by hand, fighting through another CAC spike, if not endurance at the edge of collapse? Or getting things wrong. The warehouse gets flooded and you need to back a tractor up to take orders out the second floor window so no rug get’s l;eft behind. Sound familiar Paul Valelly? Though, you are a team with a mission and a purpose, value set and move forward. Admirable and quietly go about being one of the best.
And consumers trust it. They trust founder replies more than call centres. They trust a human voice more than an outsourced script. They trust a story about survival more than a polished campaign.  That’s why indie brands breaking through get better PR than “Big Box does X.” The underdog narrative resonates because it feels real. Crean’s march resonates because it was real. He didn’t come back with a flag. He came back with his friends alive. Small brands win trust the same way. Not by shouting louder, but by
walking farther.
The Pub in Annascaul - Now up for sale.
After all the ice, after Scott and Shackleton and the impossible marches, Crean came home to Kerry and opened The South Pole Inn. A pub. No memoir. No lectures. Just a place to serve pints and live quietly. In this pub, there is history. For me personally and for all those that visit. Many black and white photos were brought from the British museum in Scotland, handpicked by my father in law, a keen adventurer and fan of the story before it was made cool.
The pub is survival. Self preservation. To live in Anascaul requires comfort in such things, in such simplicity.  Not every story ends in empire. Most of ours won’t.
Small retailers understand this better than anyone. They aren’t all chasing unicorn valuations. Many are building profitably in niches giants dismiss. TAM too small for Amazon is enough to sustain a family, a team, a community. Small businesses run “ugly” models that giants can’t justify,  and they do it profitably. Take my Struggle Bus Conversation with Tracey Smith - 130 years ago Foxford woollen Mills started with some key goals. Provide warm blankets to the Nuns that set this up and then to provide a livelihood for locals in the area. The job today has not changed much but there is a burden of responsibility on those walking through the doors today to honour those values and yet provide modernisation, new wave thinking and the chance for another generation to benefit for not wanting to outgrow ones place. That takes steel, determination, ambition and innovation. It remains one of my favourite learnings all year.
Small retail partnerships are more genuine too. I used to work in a small butchers in Kildare, Ireland. We rode the crest of the wave of oven cooking chickens for customers, realising quickly our customers wanted them stuffed, we need to adapt. We did. But instead of landing all the cost#, we spoke with the supermarket across the road. We saw they took away “almost stale” bread when new, fresh loaves arrived every day. It needed a home, where better than in the chicken. This was not our first innovation. Tills back then needed cash, our local church used to need to change the weekly collection pots into notes. It made sense that we both tradewares to avoid bank charges.  And so our needs were met locally but with innovation. It also provided me with a sneaky out, getting to know who said mass that week to complete the white lie to my parents.
The is the stuff of survival, not empire. Crean’s pub was no less heroic than his march. It was the same instinct: build something that lasts, even if the world doesn’t write books about it. Until they do.
The Struggle Bus Again
And that’s where I end up, back on
The Struggle Bus
. Back in those silences where founders admit that survival feels harder than strategy. That CAC is crushing. That customers don’t want to be tracked, they want to be recognised. That they don’t need scale, they need community.
Crean didn’t beat Shackleton or Scott. He didn’t become a household name. But he ensured survival.
Small retailers don’t beat giants. They don’t topple Amazon or Walmart. But they endure. And in enduring, they show us the traits that matter:
Move fast. Test this week, not next fiscal year.
Live in niches, speak the language, don’t chase mass market.
Let authenticity beat polish.
Lower overhead, higher creativity.
Pivot SKUs, pricing, messaging in days.
Tell human stories.
Be the indie breakthrough, not the faceless big box.
Get early on new formats,  live shopping, UGC, creators.
Avoid legacy, swap tools fast.
Forge genuine partnerships, indie with indie.
Build profitably in places giants won’t touch.
Choose community over scale.
Stay flexible on fulfilment.
Trust founder replies over call centres.
We hear and forget the expression right sizing, all of the time and yeat, it may be the love language of the small operator when it comes to commerce. Many are speculating today that maybe ecomm has had its day in the sun and it has plateaued. If so, there is no rocket ship, there is endurance. But the tasks still have to be done every day. Groundhogs even get bored. Right sizing may be the mental flex to get us into the right way to make decisions.
You are not global.
You do not need next day.
TikTok is your friend.
Not all technology will cost less than $50.
Your customers occasionally will shop elsewhere.
You can learn from Youtube.
You are competing with Amazon.
Comfort from salience. Sleep from the comfort. It is not rocket science as they say and it is not steering the ship rather, being part of the team. Survival not as spectacle, but as daily practice. Wax on, wax off, but colder, harder, lonelier.
Small doesn’t win against big.
But small endures. And in that endurance, we see the future of retail.
Thank you, Tom Crean: Unsung Hero.
His main expedition boats, incidentally were - Terra Nova (New Land). Discovery and Endurance.

_body:
I'm dying to see how this one ends Grab your passport and my hand I can make the bad guys good for a weekend
So, it's gonna be forever Or it's gonna go down in flames?
Friday discussions with
Dave Finnegan
(Finn) rarely end in room for anything other than introspection. I am glad he is not my therapist. Should I have one. Ireland veers towards Arthur Guinness and friends for that particular shade of sanity. I was in a meeting with
Gerard Keohane
in May. He spoke of conversations in the search for White Space. The place where revenue is earned. In thinking about this I got thinking about AI and inflation and other thoughts. AI is the definition of wealth of a nation – new revenue. However it is not being distributed back sovereignly, this, in my meagre mind is why inflation is impossible to control with conventional methods. New lines are drawn as new minerals are mined and extracted. This new world order is placing the burden on us all to think different, think quick, act different, act quick. It, is exhausting. It is too, exposing the fragility of both retail and ecommerce. No customer asked for it, but then we didn’t ask for electricity said Finn. I share the optimism for ingenuity in AI and agentism but in the hands of different actors with different agendas.
As it stands, across the industry we see, hear and now feel angst. In almost every conversation. We have to be optimistic, we defined this industry and learned to breath from within it. So we need to move forward with optimism of a better future. There are those among us who point to the history of how we got here. But there is something new and uneasy about the world of agentic and AI. Adam Smith though may have predicted this:
“The man whose whole life is spent in performing a few simple operations, of which the effects are perhaps always the same, or very nearly the same, has no occasion to exert his understanding or to exercise his invention in finding out expedients for removing difficulties which never occur. He naturally loses, therefore, the habit of such exertion, and generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become. ” ―
Adam Smith,
An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
Our industry has endure many supposed iterations – web 3.0, the metaverse and more. The roblox in me thinks this is different. Inflation is continuing to grow despite fiscal and monetary remedies. They only work if the producer pays their dues – this is not happening. The tax systems are well structured enough that the winners in this will be managing their own wealth and letting governments to flounder and try to help the rest of us. We are not going to need a bigger boat, we need to call Noah.
We are in the midst of a fast iteration of the ecommerce and retail industries, the idea of strategy is in there somewhere, but the next sale is the name of the game for the foreseeable. This affects us all in many ways. Thanks to Ger Keohane for the inspo here. Enter into White Space.
White Space: The Undefined Arena of Modern Commerce
We are in that rare season: as conferences line up in calendars, award submissions are being prepped, budgets are half‑spent, half‑planned, and every organization,  brands, system integrators, agencies senses that the ground underneath commerce is changing. Not broken. Not fully formed. But shifting. And what I want to do here is
name
the white space where so many of us are living now. The place between what was, what is, and what might become. I’m not trying to offer blueprints. I’m trying to map what I see: uncertainties, pressure points, glimmers of differentiation, and risk. Because if we can observe more clearly, maybe we can move with less regret.
The Nature of White Space
“White space” in this context is the stretch of territory between established business models and uncharted ones. It’s that zone where everything is up in the air, what revenue streams will stick, which platform bets pay off, whether first‑mover advantage is still a reliable edge, or whether it's being outflanked by fast followers who learn from others’ mistakes.If I were to quote Kevin Kelly, which I often do, I would say we are “Becoming” but it seems this is, a constant.
Key features of today’s white space:
Fragmentation but also gravitons
: Many actors, many platforms, many strategies. But certain platforms or marketplaces continue to exert gravitational pull.
Experimentation under pressure
: Brands and SIs trying new models (subscription, hybrid wholesale + direct, marketplace first, etc.) because status quo yields diminishing returns.
Unclear risk profiles
: Because the variables are more, the dependencies more intertwined (platform changes, consumer habits, regulation, global supply chain).
So: when brands, SIs, agencies say “we need to find where we earn revenue,” increasingly they mean:
we need to figure out what part of this shifting landscape we own, or can own
. And because no one fully owns it yet, there
is
opportunity. But opportunity comes with risk.
Brands: Between Glory and Grind
Brands are the centrepieces, in many ways. They’re under pressure from consumers, from marketplaces, from channels. They are pulled between the prestige of innovation and the grind of margins. Awards can be a good indicator that someone, somewhere is notcing the work. Next week is the culmination of 12 months graft in Ireland at the eCommerce awards. I was on the judging panel and reviweed almost 80 different applications. Another is the Leads Direct 60 list. This lens:
Lead’s Direct 60 List
. It recognises brand executives who are redefining go‑to‑market at heritage or non‑pure‑digital brands. The honorees are people who are
forcing
their organizations to evolve: using data more, changing supply chains, rebalancing between direct and wholesale, often rethinking brand values. (
The Lead
)
In my opinion this is what this tells us:
Innovation is no longer optional; it's table stakes for staying relevant.
“DTC” is less the only axis; many brands recognized are hybrid, or legacy brands trying to rebalance their portfolios. Easier said than done. But this sales game is a distribution one at its heart.
Recognition (awards, lists, speaking slots) is increasingly valuing adaptive leadership, not just growth or size. The people on the Direct 60 tend to be those who visibly are trying experiments,  whether they always succeed or not.
So for brands, the white space is being able to define:
which parts
of their revenue stream are under threat, which are ripe for growth, and which require reinvention.
But there are trade‑offs: high cost of experimentation; inertia; internal resistance; risk of cannibalising existing retail or wholesale sales; platform dependency. This list should be observed though for the work being done, it is where innovation lives IMO.
Some observations:
Many of the honorees are those who have pushed their companies beyond just adding a webstore. They are rethinking processes, supply chains, data, organizational structure. That suggests that future competition won’t be about who has the slickest UI or best campaign, but who can orchestrate across functions.
It also signals that direct‑to‑consumer (or hybrid) strategies remain central. Even for large brands heavily invested in wholesale/retail, direct remains in traction as a hedge or growth area.
Being on these lists confers visibility: for talent, partnerships, investment. Sometimes even more importantly, for internal buy‑in. When an executive is known as “on the Direct 60”, they more easily persuade internal stakeholders to invest in new tech, in riskier models.
But there is also selection bias: people recognized tend to be those who had resources to invest already; those in industries more visible (fashion, beauty, consumer goods) might get more attention. So it is a signal, not proof.
I will be watching this list and these people for the years ahead.  These signals are good signposts of where to hang your hat.
System Integrators: The Fork in the Road
I feel for you guys. Being told the cool aid is still refreshing while systematically seeing this place you occupy so well being reduced and redacted by prompts and vibe coding. Your years of experience in becoming commercial, great relationship builders, all for what? System Integrators (SIs) are not a monolith. The white space looks very different depending which type.
Two broad cohorts seem especially instructive:
Shopify‑native SIs
These are firms whose core competency, client base, and tooling revolve around Shopify. They often benefit from platform momentum, from Shopify’s own innovation (themes, apps, Editions, etc.), and from a relatively lower tech stack complexity per project compared to more enterprise setups.
Advantages:
Faster delivery, less technical risk per project.
Ability to productize services more easily: theme variants, app integrations, packaged migration, etc.
Lower barrier for smaller/mid‑sized brands wanting to test models.
Risks:
Platform dependency: changes in Shopify’s pricing, rules, terms, or direction can ripple materially.
Increasing competition: many agencies/SIs chasing same Shopify clients; downward pressure on price.
Sometimes a ceiling: more complex integrations, high volume operations or composable needs may stretch what Shopify (or the chosen tier of Shopify) can do without custom work or supplementary systems.
Non‑Shopify / Enterprise / Composable / Legacy Platforms
These SIs work with Adobe Commerce, Salesforce Commerce Cloud,
commercetools
tools,
VTEX
X,
BigCommerce
at enterprise level, in some cases custom‑built stack or headless / composable commerce. Some newcomers are making inroads namely
SCAYLE Commerce Engine
and Centra Why? Complexity is not a sales tool yet it is in this place that deals are being won. Fashion, more than most categories seek to win on experience. Websites are more function that form, just ask Amazon.
Advantages:
Greater potential control, bespoke architecture, ability to tailor deeply.
Usually higher margin per engagement (assuming client size, complexity).
Opportunity to lead in markets or segments underserved by off‑the‑shelf solutions.
Risks:
Higher cost, longer sales cycles, more risk in implementation.
More exposure to macro effects: supply chain delays, inflation, rising cost of talent for headless/composable architecture.
Fewer fast wins; harder to pivot if client changes direction (e.g., from wanting headless to wanting simpler monolith).
Putting that together: there is a bifurcation in risk profiles. Shopify SIs have lower risk if they scale repeatable wins, but possibly lower reward per deal and high competition. Enterprise SIs have higher upside in large deals, but heavier downside if mis‑estimate the client’s readiness or scope.
By observing marketplace data (e.g. Tembi’s platform usage in Europe), you see this play out: many webshops use leading “frameworks” (Shopify, WooCommerce) while thousands more use smaller or locally‑specialized platforms. That means there
is
white space in serving the ecosystems around those “other” platforms if you are willing to be geographically or technically broad.  So being small, being nimble and being open are currencies to survival. Look at the data.
Agencies: The Monetization Maze
What of the agencies. Many I know are hiring despite the writing on the wall. Agencies win by their people. Not their performance really. It is a rather transient relationship, swapping one out for another to try get something that does not exist. Work with good people who do good things. Live together, die together. The middle ground has left the building.
Agencies live somewhere between brands and SIs, sometimes overlapping both. The white space here is particularly complex, because agencies are trying to define what they
sell
, not simply how they produce.
Some dimensions:
Deliverables vs. Outcomes vs. Optionality
: Many clients still expect defined deliverables (site redesign, campaign, etc.), but more agency leaders believe clients increasingly want optionality: “Can you pivot if we want different channels?” “Can you adapt if Apple/Google changes privacy?” etc.
Productizing vs custom work
: Some agencies are offering fixed‑packages (e.g. subscription content, marketing automation, CRO, UX audit, etc.). Others keep custom high‑touch, which may give higher margin but less scalability. I hear of many developing LLM – bad idea for the masses.
Data & infrastructure debt
: To deliver more outcome than output, you need measurement, tech, analytics, possibly custom integrations. Those are cost centres. If clients are not ready to invest or sustain them, agencies take on risk.
Talent and specialization risk
: Keeping up with front‑end/trend, back‑end privacy and regulation, headless/composable, AI in marketing, delivery/distribution nuance, marketplace strategy — all these skills are scarce.
Thus agency risk profiles tend to be layered and non‑linear. A small agency focusing on creative/campaigns with local brands has a very different danger profile than a full‑service growth agency promising CRO + retention + paid ads + operations at scale.
Marketplaces: The Return of the Empire
My love language you might say but it is obvious to me. One of the clearest patterns in the white space is that marketplaces are not going away. In fact, even as “direct” becomes more hyped, marketplaces continue to dominate in terms of discovery, logistics leverage, consumer expectations.
From what Tembi’s data shows:
In Europe, many webshops still cluster around a few dominant commerce frameworks, but there’s also long tails of smaller platforms. This signals both consolidation at the framework level
and
fragmentation in the periphery.
The “size indication” + “growth predictions” data from Tembi illustrate which webshops (across platforms) are growing faster, investing in infrastructure, having high traffic, etc.
What that means is:
Marketplaces continue to try to capture more of the journey: discovery, fulfillment, logistics, last mile, returns. Brands that once thought “we must build direct to escape” find themselves racing not only other brands but the marketplaces’ own infrastructure and algorithms.
For some smaller brands or brands with limited distribution power, marketplace channels are essential, not incidental.
Marketplaces set standards: delivery speed, pricing transparency, customer expectations (returns, tracking). Brands that want to compete outside marketplace silos often find themselves benchmarked by what Amazon, Temu, etc. deliver.
Thus, the white space is not a zero‑sum between direct vs marketplace, but among different ways of
balancing
them: which product lines go direct, which go via marketplace; how to optimize logistics where marketplaces force a certain standard; how to use marketplace data to inform direct channel strategy.
First‑Mover or Fast‑Follower: A False Binary?
One of the questions that keeps coming up in my conversations: in white space, is first mover advantage always worth chasing? Or are we increasingly seeing fast followers (or late entrants) sometimes having the better hand?
GThings I notice:
The cost of first mover is increasing. The marketplace and platform rules change swiftly. So what was once an advantage (being the first headless commerce implementer in a region, for example) can also mean bearing all the risk: uncertain tooling, staffing challenges, performance bugs, mounting technical debt.
Fast followers can learn from mistakes: see what early adopters overshot on (feature complexity, cost, underuse) and refine. In environments where the infrastructure is improving, where platforms are announcing support, fast followers get to build on more maturity.
But in some cases, first movers still capture outsized “branding” or “mindshare” value: being the brand that “did it first” matters, especially for investors, for press, for partner perception. Also, if you can move first in a geography or niche where margins or competition are favorable, that can give lasting advantages.
The context matters: in sectors with high switching costs (e.g. enterprise commerce with headless architecture, complex integrations) being first mover gives you the chance to define standards, integrations. But in low switching cost settings (SMB ecommerce, small brands, low complexity), fast followers often do just fine—or better.
Thus, first‑mover is not inherently always superior. It depends on domain, scale, cost, risk tolerance, client or brand readiness, competitive pressure, regulation/trends.
Risk Profiles Across Sectors
Here, I have sketched (observationally) risk matrices. These are not scientific, but drawn from many discussions, real projects, announcements, and failures. Each sector gets rated in how exposed it is to certain risk dimensions. (High / Medium / Low). IN other words, your opinions will not be considered here – the bird has flown.
Market Fragmentation: The Micro and the Macro
I had a great conversation with
Kristian Mørk Puggaard
from
Tembi - Market Intelligence
last week. He confirmed something for me. Tembi’s intelligence illustrates a dual pattern:
At the macro level
, platform usage is consolidating. In Europe, in many markets, Shopify, WooCommerce (and a few others) dominate in terms of sheer number of webshops. (
tembi.io
)
At the micro / periphery level
, there’s a long tail: thousands of smaller platforms, local players, legacy custom builds. For those working in SIs, agencies, or tools, this long tail can be both opportunity (less competition, unmet needs) and pain (fragmented standards, fragmented skill requirements, patching together integrations).
Tembi also offers tools like the
Size Indication
(to score webshops by product variety, infrastructure investment, traffic, etc.) and
Growth Predictions
(to anticipate which webshops are likely to grow in the next 3‑6 months).
These make visible what white space might yield revenue: the growing webshops in under‑served platforms; smaller brands with traction; places where logistic/delivery demand will strain current services and open gap.
Another fragment: delivery & logistics. The Tembi “Delivery Pricing Trends” across markets (parcel box, parcel shop, home delivery) show that even common problems (cost of last mile, consumer expectations) vary widely, both in absolute cost and in volatility. Strategies that succeed in one country or segment may fail in another. (
tembi.io
)
But in delivering on all of this, we get overwhelmed by the speed of things, by the vastness of everything and yet innovation seems to mean to be willing to do everything, always. That’s the FOMO of not going to a conference and it is the anxiety created when we hear how others are doing it.
Is First Mover Advantage Always the Way?
Given everything above, my sense is: first‑mover advantage remains real, but is riskier, costlier, and requires certain conditions to pay off. Let’s think through those.
When first mover is likelier to benefit:
In markets/geographies where competition is low, regulatory or logistical infrastructure is lagging. If you can move first you shape expectations, build brand loyalty, learn what local constraints are.
In platform innovation phases: when a platform opens new APIs, tools, or editions. Being early can allow you to build expertise, positioning, internal capabilities.
When your organization has resilience: high tolerance for ambiguity, ability to absorb failures, enough financial/organisational slack.
When there is strong customer signal of unmet need — e.g. poor delivery, weak UX in certain regions, unaddressed marketplace integration issues.
When fast following, or deliberate waiting, may be smarter:
When the platform or technology is unproven, or standards are still shifting. Early adoption may mean paying for custom work, dealing with immaturity, being penalized for bugs or user experience gaps.
When cost of switching/migration is high: if you build one way and the platform changes significantly (e.g. Shopify changing core feature or pricing), or technological debt accumulates, being first could lead you to overpay or be locked in.
When many competitors are already testing: you can watch, learn, sometimes piggy‑back or improve upon others’ bets.
When internal readiness or culture is not aligned: if your team, your operations, your leadership is risk‑averse, or lacks data/infrastructure, being first may expose you to failure more than being a fast follower.
In short, first mover is not a universal advantage in white space; it’s conditional. Often, what's more critical is
execution speed, adaptability, clarity of ambition
, rather than simply being first.
Where Revenue is Being Made (and Threatened)
Here is what  counts, at least from the foks I am speaking with. This is  what I've observed, and heard in dozens of conversations:
Brands that have managed to make meaningful revenue shifts are those that combine direct + marketplace intelligently. Not “escape wholesale”, but “optimize across channels”.
SIs that succeed tend to be those that are helping brands with
optionality
: helping brands move between channels/platforms; making integrations easier; investing in modular architectures so that changes in marketplaces, consumer habits, privacy/regulation do less damage.
Agencies that are thriving are those who are comfortable with ambiguity: they are often mixing consulting/advisory with execution; doubling down on retention/supply chain/delivery customer experience; not just marketing funnels but what happens post‑purchase.
Marketplaces continue to grow, especially where they fill gaps (logistics, discovery, trust). Platforms like Amazon are obvious, but also others that combine localized marketplace + logistics + user trust.
Regions/countries with weaker infrastructure or less mature direct commerce often see more rapid marketplace adoption. Those same regions are where there remains relatively large white space — of brands, of integrators, of agency services.
Threats include: platform policy shifts, rising expectations (faster delivery, free returns), regulatory costs (data protection, cross‑border commerce), rising cost of talent, inflation in supply chain, customer acquisition cost rising in saturated digital channels.
Putting this all together, the white space isn’t neutral: some sectors are more exposed; some more rewarded. Below is a refined view of what I see as risk vs opportunity across sectors — again, observationally, not predictive.
Brands (mid‑size, digital native)
are in a sweet spot: lower legacy cost, more agility, potential to scale. But also risk of being squeezed by both ends: large incumbents with deep pockets, and small niche brands who move faster.
Brands (heritage / enterprise)
have more to lose — but also more resources. Their risk is mis‑investment: building direct channels that conflict with retail/wholesale, overestimating customer willingness for premium service or supply chain capability.
Shopify SIs
can scale via volume, replicate success, but risk margin erosion. Their opportunity is in specializing (performance, UX, speed, value add) or extending into adjacent services (fulfillment, logistics, retention).
Enterprise SIs
have the opportunity when brands begin investing for real in headless, composable, omnichannel, data capabilities. But most enterprise clients are either slow or cautious, so SIs must balance upfront cost vs proof of concept.
Agencies
: the best ones will be those that can combine creativity + technical / operational infrastructure. Those that stay only in marketing will increasingly be squeezed by performance demands, by commoditization of ad channels, by rising expectation around end‑to‑end experience.
Marketplaces
will continue to dominate discovery and expect loyalty, logistic scale. But they too are under risk: regulatory (antitrust, data), geopolitical, consumer expectations (speed, ethics), and perhaps saturation in some categories.
What We Are All Trying to Figure Out
Because white space is not defined, a lot of things are still unknown. Among them:
What does “good enough” look like for direct commerce in terms of logistics / delivery / returns? How fast is fast enough? How much free is free enough?
How will regulation shift the game: privacy, cross‑border tax, data sharing? How much cost will that impose?
Which platform architectures will become dominant (headless, composable, hybrid)? When does the technical debt of being early outweigh the benefit of being first?
How much will marketplaces squeeze margins vs provide scale? Where is the tipping point for brands between acquisition cost and marketplace fees / dependency?
What is the role of AI / automation in content / personalization / search / recommendations in the immediate future? Who leads: brands, agencies, platforms?
How will labor/talent markets behave: skills in performance, UX, headless tech, logistics, data science; how easy/hard will that be to acquire globally or locally?
We Are All Guessing, Informedly
If there is one thread through all this, it’s that no one fully knows what the “right answer” is yet. But many are trying, many are learning, some are ahead of others in seeing what kinds of bets might pay off. The white space is not a failing of strategy; it is the space where strategy must be remade continuously. First‑mover advantage matters, sometimes. Fast follower matters, often. Platform mattering is being redefined by regulation, by logistics, by consumer tolerance. Marketplaces aren’t the enemy; they are gravitational bodies whose pull you might harness or need to resist, depending on your angle.
For those reading this, who build, lead, design, consult, integrate: your best hope is not certainty, but clarity of choices. Keep sketching your map. Know where your dependencies lie. See where your capacities are weak. Observe where other people are going, not to copy, but to avoid dead ends or to find paths others overlooked.
Because in this space between maps, we are all explorers.

title: Ep. 74 – “Belts, Pants & the New Retail Trinity – David Katz Unpacked
excerpt: Joining Rick Watson and Jessica Lesesky on the Virtual sofa last week David J. Katz This was a fanboy moment having David on the show. Or Katz as I now call him in my head. His team said "Do not call him that". Fair point.
_body:
Joining
Rick Watson
and
Jessica Lesesky
on the Virtual sofa last week
David J. Katz
This was a fanboy moment having David on the show. Or Katz as I now call him in my head. His team said "Do not call him that". Fair point. But, David J. Katz is not your average CMO. He’s part fashion insider, part data scientist, part consumer-behavior whisperer. As EVP & CMO of
Randa Apparel & Accessories
, he steers marketing and growth for more than
35 powerhouse brands
including Calvin Klein, Levi’s, Tommy Hilfiger, Columbia, Cole Haan, Dickies and Haggar. Chances are you are wearing one of his products today.
Randa is the
world’s largest men’s accessories company
and one of the biggest women’s suppliers (minus handbags and footwear), with products sold everywhere from Nordstrom and Macy’s to Tractor Supply, Walmart and Costco. They also own
Haggar Clothing Co.
(26% of the U.S. non-denim pants market and the #1 sport coat brand by units),
Tribal Women’s Sportswear
(in 2,500 specialty boutiques), a JV stake in
Moss Bros.
in the UK, and even 50% of the two largest belt factories on earth (Guatemala and Chennai).
This is a company that literally controls the belt you’re wearing, the pants you’re in, and the jacket you throw over it, and yet Katz spends his time re-thinking the
model
, not just the merchandise.
The Backlot Dispatch - seen through the eyes of an everyman
What We Learned in This Episode
The model is brittle, not the consumer.
Katz argues retail isn’t “broken”, it’s the outdated financial and operational models that can’t flex fast enough. He’s showing that a 100-year-old company can still behave like a start-up if it questions its own assumptions about forecasting, ownership and distribution. Curiousity did not, as it happens kill all cats, just some.
Logic over loyalty.
Today’s shoppers chase value, culture and immediacy, not just logos.
Infrastructure may be the new loyalty program
. Katz’s teams aren’t lamenting the death of loyalty instead the use info and tools and they’re engineering relevance at speed.
Arbitrage as strategy.
Randa r
eads global signals in real time
(even planning inventory around Taylor Swift’s tour cities) and treats internationalization as a risk reducer, not a risk. That’s a lesson for any brand sitting on siloed domestic data. We are all believeers in Swiftonomics.
Forecast to flexibility.
Annual plans are dead weight. Katz urges brands to
build long-term strategy first and layer tactics later
. If you’re an operator obsessing over next quarter’s contribution margin while ignoring macro shifts, you’re building a paper ship for a storm.
The new retail trinity.
Culture, CapEx and consciousness: know who you are, what you can sacrifice, and how quickly you can respond. Katz frames it as an operating system, not a slogan.
Thinking about me, thinking about you.
David isn’t just giving conference platitudes. He’s running a portfolio that spans private label, licensed brands, vertical manufacturing, global JVs and mass/mid-market channels. When he says “flexibility beats forecasts,” it’s because he’s applying it to factories he partly owns and brands he licenses in dozens of countries.
For DTC founders, this is a warning shot: your Instagram halo won’t save you if your supply chain is brittle. For legacy brands, it’s proof you can pivot without blowing up your P&L. And for retailers, it’s a blueprint for treating infrastructure as loyalty making it so easy, reliable and relevant that customers keep coming back even when the logo changes. Music to the ears of
Nick Kaplan
From The Backlot - Some Meanderings
Some episodes feel like interviews. This one felt like alchemy. (No surprise)  David Katz didn’t just talk about belts, pants and jackets, he talked about the hidden scaffolding of retail, the code beneath the interface. This, he talks about with so much ease that it has got to be difficult. Listening to him, you realise retail isn’t broken; it’s brittle. He isn’t selling another “playbook”. He is though, making the whole structure more supple so it can flex without tearing.
He showed us that loyalty hasn’t died; it’s just wearing a different costume. Infrastructure, speed, and cultural fluency are today’s loyalty cards. He showed us arbitrage as a form of listening, reading the crowd in Melbourne to predict the crowd in Memphis, following the beat of a Taylor Swift tour like a travelling merchant caravan.
And the part that sticks:
a 100-year-old company behaving like a start-up
because it keeps its capital, culture and consciousness aligned. Discipline disguised as curiosity.
He left us with a simple provocation: if Randa can flex at scale, what excuse do the rest of us have?
Next Week - Kristen Wiley  of Statusphere
Friday 26th Noon Eastern Time. Beer o Clock on GMT.
🔗
Subscribe to The Watson Weekend on YouTube
to catch full episodes, backstage takes and our next guest reveal.👉
Subscribe on Youtube -Never miss a guest
About our Guest
David J. Katz is a fashion, retail, and consumer behavior expert. He is the Executive Vice President and CMO of Randa Apparel & Accessories (RAA), a global leader in lifestyle products, producing clothing and accessories for 25 owned and licensed brands, including Haggar, Calvin Klein, Levi’s, Tommy Hilfiger, Columbia Sportswear, Cole Haan, and Dickies sold through majordistribution channels worldwide.
David is an alchemist who uses data, insights, and technology to study and shape consumer behavior across thousands of physical and digital touchpoints. He is recognized as a retail industry influencer by The Wall Street Journal, CNN, CNBC, The New York Times, and Women’s Wear Daily. He is the co-author of the best-selling book “Design for Response: Creative Direct Marketing That Works,” a “LinkedIn Top Voice,” and a prolific writer and speaker on marketing, technology (including artificial intelligence), and consumer behavior.
David holds neuroscience and business administration degrees from Tufts University and the Harvard Business School. He is fascinated by the science of stimulus and response. Heunderstands what makes Pavlov’s dog salivate and what makes people buy.
P.S. ALCHEMY
:
A science or philosophy that transforms something ordinary into something extraordinary, often through mysterious means.

Kaylea Sepulvado
and
