title: A Catholic Woman and a Protestant Mason walk into a bar. The rest is history.
excerpt: My first in this series. The Struggle Bus is a place we create empathy through shared learning, laughs and cries. The idea is to give a platform to those who maybe don't get to share the stage at big conferences, who are not on rocket
_body:
My first in this series. The Struggle Bus is a place we create empathy through shared learning, laughs and cries. The idea is to give a platform to those who maybe don't get to share the stage at big conferences, who are not on rocket ships to the moon. They get the job done, because they have to.
Wool, West of Ireland & the Yellow Brick Road of E-Comms.
Guest Bio
Tracey Smith
Tracy Smith was the digital marketing manager at
Foxford Woollen Mills
in Mayo, Ireland. She runs e-commerce, social and email for a 133-year-old heritage brand that’s evolving into a lifestyle destination with cafés and contemporary throws. Not bad for someone who started as a law student, became a young mum, pivoted into business, and now leads digital transformation for one of Ireland’s most beloved names in textiles.
What We Learned
Heritage ≠ Static.
Foxford was founded in 1892 by a Sister of Charity and a Protestant mill owner on the River Moy. Tracy’s job is connecting that living history to a new generation without losing the soul.
Tiny Team, Global Reach.
Foxford ships to ~
12 countries
every month (Ireland, UK, USA fight for the #2 spot, then Germany, Italy, Japan) — with a team of…
Míse
(just me).
Rebrand Weight.
Tracy began in 2018 by simply telling customers what Foxford was already doing. By 2023 she led a full rebrand, balancing new customers and a fiercely protective internal culture.
Metrics that Matter.
Success isn’t just ROAS. Foxford measures
lifetime value
, engagement, and how closely they’re reaching target customers.
Survival Skills.
Motherhood taught her “respond, don’t react” a skill she uses daily to prioritise budgets, decide what to outsource, and keep her cool when tech and trends shift.
AI & Agencies.
She embraces AI as a tool and brings in agencies when a channel outgrows her bandwidth knowing when to let go is as important as knowing what to do.
Conference Frustration.
Big-brand case studies inspire but rarely match the reality of a 130-year-old company fighting for digital relevance from the west of Ireland.
Theme Song:
Elton John’s “Yellow Brick Road” — a bright but precarious path of stepping stones, which sums up the job of a solo e-com manager
From the Backlot – Producers’ Reflection
If you want to know what grit looks like in e-commerce, it’s Tracy Smith sitting in a mill built in 1892, shipping to a dozen countries, rebranding on a shoestring, and doing the jobs of an entire digital team. She’s proof that “innovation” isn’t just a Silicon Valley word,  it’s also a woollen mill in Mayo figuring out TikTok.
Her story reminded us why we started The Struggle Bus: to give a mic to the forgotten operators who keep brands alive between spreadsheets, warehouses and customer emails. Tracy’s road may be yellow brick, but every brick is a lesson in prioritisation, community, and sheer stubborn Irish ingenuity.
Tracy was the first person to put her hand up to take part. There was something in her location that was really intriuging. Many of us work where we are because it is where we are. Remote working improved the sorts of opportunities we can pursue. We are no longer limited to a "beggars can be choosers types roles". But there is something about recognising we do not need the limits. The other thing about this is the proximity to where we live in such an iconic brand in an area carries burdens of responsibility but offers a much more higher sense of belonging to a brand, knowing where you come from equips you to know where you are going. When the world turns as quickly as it does now, this sense of grounding can be helpful.
The power of possibility
What really drew me to empathising with Tracy was the place on the map idea. This is where I live in Kerry, Ireland . It is tiny. It is remote. My journey saw me work with General Motors, PepsiCo, BigCommerce and many more over the last 3 years. From here. Mindblowing.
All possible because of people who laid the path before me.
From Copper to Cloud: The Transatlantic Cable Story
In the mid-1800s the fastest way for a message to cross the Atlantic was still a steamship. It took 10–14 days. In 1858 a handful of Victorian visionaries, Cyrus Field in New York, the British Admiralty and the Atlantic Telegraph Company , laid the first transatlantic telegraph cable between Valentia Island, Kerry, and Heart’s Content, Newfoundland. That fragile copper line carried one stuttering signal for 27 days before burning out, but it proved the concept. By 1866 a more robust cable was live, reducing transatlantic communication from weeks to minutes. Kerry became a literal landing point for the information age.
Over the next century the west coast of Ireland became a landing ground for successive generations of undersea cables. Valentia was joined by other sites like Ballinskelligs and later
Ventry Bay
, which saw cables from the U.S. and Canada come ashore in the 20th century. These cables were the hidden nervous system of global finance, news and diplomacy; by the 1960s Ventry was part of a dense mesh of coaxial and fibre lines.
Fast-forward to today: the same Atlantic seabed is littered with fibre-optic bundles owned by Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon. The modern “cloud” literally lands in Ireland, from MAREA in Bilbao to Dunant and Grace Hopper into the UK,  because of the geography and cool climate for data centres. When you stream a video or send a Slack message to New York from Dublin, it rides the descendants of those Kerry cables. Valentia and Ventry are as much a part of the internet’s origin story as Menlo Park or Palo Alto.
So if you stand on the beach at Ventry and look west, you’re staring at the invisible trunk line of the modern web, a Victorian project that shrank the Atlantic and became the first strand of what we now call the internet.
My ecommerce reality
Those who think in terms of making the world better than the way they came into it. Not in the pursuit of wealth. It is kind of what our generation has strived to achieve. Not possible without the transatlantic cable which celebrated  its 125 birthday during COVID. And it is there I will leave this. When I first came here, I went to the opening of the Dingle Hub to celebrate the arrival of 1 GB fibre optic internet, presented to us by our now presidential candidate, Heather Humpries.  seemingly mind numbing PR exercise. It spawned a conference and have me the belief I can do this anywhere. We had Philip King (South Wind Studios) talk to us as part of it. His way with words is truly breathtaking and he told us his daiughters had emigrated to the US to pursue their careers, to have families and do things they could not in Ireland, until then. it was now possible for them to do this here and so his heart was filled with hope. Not expectation but now this reality could become real. The power of possibility.
Bio Tracy Smith
Tracey Smith is the Digital Marketing Manager at FOXFORD, but her journey here wasn’t your typical marketing career path. She began studying law before becoming a young mum, later pivoting to a business degree as a mature student. With a natural flair for writing and storytelling, she returned to do a Master’s in Marketing when her youngest was just one month old, travelling six hours a day, twice a week, to attend lectures. She graduated in 2016 and has since carved out her creative path in marketing.
At FOXFORD, Tracey leads the brand’s digital strategy across e-commerce, social media, and email, connecting a new generation of customers with over 130 years of Irish craftsmanship. Her role also spans traditional marketing, from retail campaigns and in-store activations to the launch of new stores and FOXFORD’s complete rebrand in 2023. Everything she works on reflects her deep appreciation for design, detail, and authenticity, with a strong dose of creative thinking
The Struggle Bus - Kindly Partnered wtih
Big shout-out to our partners who keep this bus rolling and the conversation free for the community:
Omnisend
for powering smarter email journeys.
Eurobase
⁠ - Ireland's best kept ecomm secret. Perfecting Global shipping for over 30 years. Making complex look simple. Stupid look good.⁠ De Minimis problems? Contact Julie Colclough
Strike Digital
⁠ Human First always (hope they sign up for season 2)
EVOLVE Commerce Club
for connecting the sharpest minds in retail and marketplaces. Our community partner.

title: Grosse Pointe Blank.
excerpt: Discoverability is a by-product of community. I didn’t search for it. It found me. A new emerging trend. Discoverability Beats Search. Arbitrage is everywhere only if you look for it. Daily Incrementality Compounds Into Durable Growth. A conversation with Trevor Testwuide, a few side notes
_body:
Discoverability is a by-product of community. I didn’t search for it. It found me. A new emerging trend. Discoverability Beats Search. Arbitrage is everywhere only if you look for it.
Daily Incrementality Compounds Into Durable Growth.
A conversation with Trevor Testwuide, a few side notes from the last few weeks building and now this. Our industry is morphing. It is becoming the worst and best version of itself all at once. A few conversations with friends will illuminate the discovery and search idea. This is by no way empirically proven, but I don’t know many who are not having this same discussion. At the same time we cannot predict the future, in fact the present moves so quickly that chasing the future is a lot like these old jokes from my first job - each brilliant in their own definition of futility:
“Get me a glass hammer.”
“Go into the kitchen and ask for a long stand.”
“I need a bucket of steam.”
Our successes are defined by what is in front of us and Kiri Master’s article and subtext today confirmed this. The idea of channels confuses the idea of omni channel - did anyone ever like the expression anyway? How we are discovering channels, how are we choosing to buy it and how are we choosing to get this delivered - quoting Jason Goldberg here. But it is the general idea that all operators should be thinking through.
Last week I spoke with Rhys Sandford selling 1000’s of packs of freeze dried sweets (candy to the lay American) on TikTok. Makes sense, doesn’t it. 1 customer bought 48 times in 6 months or 8 times per month or twice a week (roughly speaking. His methods recognize this view - Daily Incrementality Compouns into Durable Growth. There is that word again, compound. I blame  Suze Dowling for this. This is where this ramble started. I feel like that this is the quiet confession behind half the stuff sitting in your basket right now, those running shoes you didn’t know you wanted, the magnesium gummies your friend swears by, the niche kitchen gadget TikTok swore would fix your life. None of that started with you tapping into a search bar and typing “salvation, but dishwasher safe.” It started in the stream: a feed, a recommendation, a nudge from an algorithm that knows your 2am browsing sins better than you do.
For two decades we built commerce on
search
, harvesting explicit demand like farmers at peak harvest. This is how the industry wanted us to behave. But we are the people, we have the power, remember. It is said that 20% of Walmart's referring traffic comes from LLMs. What will we hear in the earnings calls? The center of gravity has shifted.
Discoverability
is now where growth lives: proactive, ambient, embedded in the places people already are. The edge no longer belongs to those who bid fastest on the keyword; it belongs to those who are
present
before the keyword exists.
Discoverability is a by product of community.
This is a structural re-write. Social feeds have become product search. AI assistants are turning queries into answers without clicks. Meanwhile, retail media buyers are abandoning vanity metrics for one idea that actually tracks to money in the till:
incrementality
. Shopper budgets. The daily lift. The compounding curve. The quiet math that turns a pile of small wins into a moat.
Remember there is no predicting the future, there is though what is shaping it. Here is my view.
Search vs. Discoverability: the demand you catch vs. the demand you create.
Search
is reactive: it waits for the user to declare intent. You pay to show up, you win or lose the auction, and you argue with attribution software about who gets credit at the afters.
Discoverability
is proactive: it manufactures intent upstream. Your product becomes the idea that happens to someone. It shows up in feeds, in recommendations, in “people also bought,” in creator content, in AI assistants nudging a short list.
This is a view I had a look for - to be the brain that I cannot be. And the shift is measurable:
Social is now a primary product-discovery surface for large swaths of consumers. HubSpot’s 2024 consumer trends work flat-out says it:
social media is the #1 product discovery channel
, surpassing search for many cohorts. (
HubSpot Offers
)
TikTok Shop is velocity. eMarketer estimated
100.7M U.S. social buyers in 2024
, with TikTok adding
~11.9M
new buyers that year alone. The discovery → purchase loop moved
inside
the feed. (
EMARKETER
) $6BN in revenue this year in the US.
Platform-run studies (always sprinkle salt) report eye-popping discovery claims, TikTok/GlobalData touts
83% of shoppers discovering a new product on TikTok Shop
, directionally right, even if you haircut it. (
TikTok Newsroom
)
Zoom out from “shopping” to information habits and the pattern holds:
online overtook TV as the UK’s top news source in 2024
, with
52% of adults using social for news
. For under-30s in the U.S.,
43% now regularly get news on TikTok
, up from 9% in 2020. Whether you sell moisturizer or micro-loans, your future customers live in streams that never touch a search bar. (
www.ofcom.org.uk
) In the US CTV advertising surpassed linear this year. This is no longer a discussion about channel separation. 80% of all data transferred and used online in North America is video or streaming.
Meanwhile, the old mall is renovating its atrium with LLMs. Google’s
AI Overviews
synthesizes answers above the blue links; Amazon launched
Rufus
, an AI shopping assistant that absorbs your intent and hands you options without a single comparison tab. The short version:
fewer clicks, more conclusions
, and the click-through you relied on becomes optional. (
About Amazon
)
Publishers and brands are already feeling the gravity: multiple independent reads show rising “
zero-click
” share and
material drops in referral traffic
when AI summaries appear, think
–25%
for many publishers, sometimes much worse—while Google publicly disputes the aggregate impact. Even if you believe Google, the strategic signal is obvious:
the answer plane is absorbing the query plane
. If you’re not discoverable
inside
that plane, you’re background noise. (
Digiday
)
Implication:
Search is still important, but it is becoming one stop in a wider
discovery web
. The winner is the brand that shows up early, often, and adjacently—across creators, feeds, recommendation rails, and AI assistants.
Incrementality: the only KPI that doesn’t lie to you
How do you define incrementality, I am not stealing thunder here but it is an interesting thing to think about. The successful business outcome from a marketing action, again compounded against everything else you do. The conversation has always been about attribution. It is a thoughtless conversation today. Attribution was required for managing media mix and making decisions of which, when why etc. Fact is today it is all those plates that need to be spinning, always. Arbitrage is where incrementality lives. This requires monitoring. It is where trends lay in waiting for virality.
Attribution can feel like a custody battle where everyone claims the same child. Incrementality doesn’t care. It asks a single question:
what changed
because
of this touch?
Marketers are getting religion on this:
eMarketer highlights
incrementality
as the KPI brands care about most in retail media, and notes that
only ~26%
of in-house teams actually run incrementality testing themselves. Translation: everyone wants truth; few have the lab coats. (
EMARKETER
)
The ANA/eMarketer read shows a discipline split: brands are increasingly
taking RMN measurement into their own hands
because they don’t trust the glossy dashboards.
41%
say RMNs are
worse
at measurement vs other channels;
39%
say
better
. That’s a coin flip. (
EMARKETER
)
Industry pieces hammer the point:
retail media’s future depends on proving incrementality
, not just ROAS cosplay. If your “lift” is just robbing organic or branded search, you laundered. (
Infillion
)
The question that will rise, with it’s answer (not in full). How to measure lift without nuking your campaign:
Holdouts & Geo Splits:
Randomized control groups, or geographic split testing, let you estimate causal impact.
Temporal Controls:
Pulse campaigns on/off against baselines when true randomization is impractical.
Synthetic Controls:
Use comparable cohorts (new vs. returning, high-propensity vs. low-propensity) to sanity-check your lift.
Cross-channel Guardrails:
If paid social “wins,” but branded search falls, you’ve probably just shifted credit.
The vibe shift:
Daily or weekly lift reads beat monthly retros by a mile. If you don’t measure often, you mistake
noise for signal
, and you’ll overpay to “win” what would have happened anyway.
Compounding 101: small daily wins → big weird outcomes
You already know compounding in finance. Apply it to discoverability.
+1% daily lift for 90 days
→
~2.45×
.
+0.5% daily for 90 days
→
~1.57×
.
A modest
+0.3% daily for a year
→
~2.98×
.
Small deltas, boring Tuesdays, multiplied relentlessly. The trick is not “one big hack,” it’s thirty little knobs you tune, metadata, thumbnails, creator whitelists, feed-friendly cuts, email subject lines, PDP load time, product graph relationships that together become a flywheel. We all know a company or two that use this flywheel mentality to good effect. Looking at you Amazon, Walmart and Shopify too.
Where does compounding actually show up?
SEO authority accrual
: content → links → rank → more links—less sexy than a viral, more permanent than your CPC. (And yes, SEO isn’t dead; it’s just more valuable for
non-answerable
queries and brand depth.)
Recommendation rails
: once your SKUs appear in “similar items,” you earn impressions you didn’t pay for, which drive engagement that justifies more impressions: rich-get-richer dynamics you kickstart with early signals (reviews, CTR, save-to-list, add-to-cart assist).
Creator ecosystems
: one mid-tier creator unlocks five micro-creators who copy the format; now you’re in the trend rather than buying pre-roll.
Counterintuitive truth:
Compounding also
buffers shocks
. If AI Overviews siphon some of your search clicks this quarter, the surface area you built in feeds and recs keeps water in the tub. Multiple reads show AI surfaces are growing referrals
some
, but not enough to offset zero-click search. Your best hedge is a discovery moat. (
Digiday
)
AI/LLM turn: assistants = the new endless aisle
Endless aisle and digital shelf - variations ont he long tail. The future of discovery looks less like ten blue links. It is more like a conversation with a competent shop assistant who’s eaten the internet for breakfast. Can I help you with your Cluetrain Manifesto?
Amazon Rufus
now sits in the app, fielding “I need a gift for a 7-year-old who loves dinosaurs and hates socks” and returning a tidy, shoppable shortlist. Here is
context
. Form builders everywhere rejoice - this is your bittersweet symphony. This is not PPC; this is
presence
. (
About Amazon
)
Shopify Sidekick
is evolving into a merchant-side consigliere, recommending apps, automating workflows, and (increasingly) making
proactive
suggestions. As that intelligence moves down the stack, the ecosystem itself starts
surfacing
the next best action: your job shifts from campaign runner to
graph gardener
. (
Shopify
)
Perplexity & co.
show an early pattern: yes, AI platforms are referring some traffic (Perplexity referrals up ~490% YoY in mid-2024), but it’s still small relative to search. The zero-click rise is real. In other words, assistants will be powerful, but you won’t always get the click. Design for
in-answer brand presence
and
multi-touch capture
. (
Adweek
)
Google AI Overviews
is the elephant: studies and trade-press analyses tie it to
increased zero-click rates
(Similarweb: 56% → 69% within a year) and
~1–25% or worse
traffic drops for many publishers, numbers Google disputes. Whether the precise figure is 10% or 25%, the directional lesson for commerce is the same:
don’t be the result under the answer
. Be part of the answer,
and
be discoverable elsewhere. (
Search Engine Roundtable
)
Strategy for the LLM era:
Answerable vs. Unanswerable
: For commoditized queries (“best 4K TV under €500”), LLMs compress the funnel. Invest in being the source that assistants cite (rich PDP data, structured specs, reviews, FAQs), and in
adjacent discoverability
(creators, lists, communities) where the assistant can’t fully replace the
feel
.
Evidence-rich content
: If assistants synthesize, you want to be the
evidence
, the guide, the teardown, the benchmark, the “we tried 7 humidifiers and here are the mold counts.” Assistants need sources; be the one they
must
include.
Own the graph
: Feed clean product data (attributes, compatibility, use cases) into marketplaces and your own site. If the assistant is assembling kits, your SKU should “connect” to more scenarios than the next guy’s.
Capture beyond the click
: More answers = fewer clicks. Your
direct capture surfaces
(email/SMS, community, content hubs, app) matter more. If you only play the last-click game, you’ll slowly starve.
Really though, if you were creating “middle of funnel “ content for the last decade, you are covered here, this might be the day that you win, or tomorrow, but one, that day is your increment. The more days we win, the better the outcome. Wasted effort, it was not. The internet is catching up with you.
A practical playbook: 30 levers that add up. Apologies for the playbook. But they work like Sex Panther.
Many sources can tell you all of this, but these were the basics of the WWW to begin with. We are dealing with platforms which survive on breakfast, lunch and dinner of structured data. The speed to get tehre has just been accelerated. Uptake was fast, very fast, dog year motions in effect. So, you don’t need a moonshot. You need a metronome. Here’s how to manufacture
daily lift
and let the compounding do its work.
Data hygiene & product graph
Attribute completeness ≥ 95%
for top 20% SKUs. Missing attributes destroy rec-rail eligibility.
Compatibility pairs & bundles
: add “works with X/Y/Z,” usage contexts, seasonal tags.
Reviews density
: seed early with post-purchase flows; pin most helpful; mine for UGC.
Media variants
: thumb-stopping primary image + secondary that shows scale, use, and texture.
Feed-native content
Platform-first creative
: 15–30s hooks cut for silence-on (captions), then audio-on variants.
Creator lattice
: blend mid-tier niche creators (authority) with micro-creators (volume).
Live & episodic
: appointment shopping beats one-off promotions; train the feed.
PDP speed & persuasion
Sub-2s LCP on mobile PDP
. Anything slower and your discovery tax becomes a bounce fee.
Evidence on page
: comparison tables, video “unbox/use,” “who it’s for vs. not for.” Assistants scrape these.
Recs & marketplaces
Similar/Complementary tuning
: A/B your “you might also like” modules; push profitable adjacencies.
Taxonomy sanity
: fix orphan categories; avoid duplicate nodes.
Marketplace storefronts
: curate collections around
use cases
, not just categories.
AI-era readiness
Schema markup
maxed: product, review, FAQ, HowTo, video.
Source-worthy content
: benchmarks, buying guides, teardown posts—stuff assistants
need
.
Assistant testing
: ask Rufus/Copilot/Gemini 50 real buyer questions monthly. Track if/when you appear.
Email/SMS/community
List accretion
as an explicit KPI for every discovery surface.
UGC loops
: creator features, customer spotlights, remix contests.
Post-purchase arcs
: onboarding → upsell → referral → review → community.
Measurement & governance
Weekly incrementality readout
with a one-page “what moved, by how much, what we do next.”
Holdouts by default
on RMN/social prospecting.
Attribution sanity checks
: if branded search drops when you spend more somewhere else, you probably just shifted credit.
In other words, give the platforms what they want and you will reap the benefits. Hacks are usually never a hack, it is someone who can provide you a step by step instruction of the thing you don’t want to do. Well guess what you gotta do? The thing you still don’t want to.
Points of view I have developed
“Search is over-resourced. Discovery is under-loved.”
“Incrementality daily or it didn’t happen.”
“Assistants are now an aisle.”
“Zero-click isn’t a debate. It’s table stakes.”
There are risks.
Good governance mitigates these - does not stop them, mitigates.
Risks, as I see them.
Platform risk
: algorithms rewire traffic patterns overnight. AI Overviews, TikTok tweaks, your garden needs many roots. Multiple independent reads show publisher traffic hits from zero-click surfaces; don’t pretend you’re immune. (
Digiday
) - Stay up to date, talk to professionals and remember AI evolves daily, the best professional you can consult, is yourself.
Measurement fiction
: incrementality is hard, and false confidence is worse than humility. If your methodology can’t survive a peer review from your CFO, it’s not incrementality.
Diminishing returns
: discovery lift plateaus. That’s fine. Compounding doesn’t require constant acceleration; it requires
consistency
.
Brand hollowness
: discoverability without a proposition is just impressions. You can’t optimize your way out of being forgettable.
Your 90-day discoverability plan (print this bit or list it or whatever, I am checking out).
Basiclaly, test, test and test again.
Week 0 (Set the lab):
Appoint a
Lift Czar
. One owner. One page each Friday.
Define
North Star
: incremental revenue per day vs. holdout, plus 3 supporting OKRs (rec-rail impressions, % of SKUs with complete attributes, weekly creator slots).
Build your
test calendar
: 2–3 concurrent tests/week, max. Assign owners, baselines, start/stop dates.
Weeks 1–4 (Graph & surfaces):
Take top 100 SKUs; get to
≥95% attribute completeness
; add use-case tags.
Ship
evidence blocks
: comparison tables and short “how it works” clips on top PDPs; add FAQ schema.
Launch a
creator lattice
(10–20 micro-creators) with consistent format and weekly beats.
Weeks 5–8 (Assistant & rails):
Run a
50-question assistant test
(Rufus/Gemini/Copilot) for your category. Track presence & citation. Fix missing attributes and FAQs that block inclusion. (
About Amazon
)
A/B
rec-rail configuration
to push profitable complements; monitor dwell time and attach rate.
Expand
UGC loops
: post-purchase review incentive → best-of montage in feed → PDP embed.
Weeks 9–12 (Scale & codify):
Promote winners into
always-on
sequences.
Formalize
weekly incrementality
cadence (geo/holdout/temporal) and kill three lowest-lift efforts.
Build a
discovery dashboard
: daily lift, assistant presence score, rec-rail share-of-shelf, creator cadence health, list growth.
Rinse, Repeat and Rinse again.
Frequently argued objections - answers from postcards
“Search still drives most of our sessions.”
Cool. The past is big. The future is bigger. When Ofcom and Pew say people are consuming more via online/social streams uiand when social buyers cross 100M in the U.S., you don’t wait to be late. You seed now. (
www.ofcom.org.uk
)
“AI traffic is tiny.”
Yes, and it’s growing fast, while zero-click rises. You don’t optimize for 2030. You make sure your data, evidence, and brand are
in
the answer layer so you’re not starting from zero in 18 months. (
SE Ranking
)
“Incrementality is too hard.”
So is bankruptcy. Start simple: one weekly holdout. If you can’t prove lift on a prospecting campaign, it’s not a growth lever, it’s a line item.
“We don’t have creators.”
Borrow them. Micro-creators are plentiful, affordable, and better at platform grammar than most agencies. You’re not buying celebrity; you’re buying
pattern
.
The moral of the story (and the fun bit)
Search is a faucet, or tap to us EU people. Turn it, traffic spills. Useful, but fragile. We can create fragility or build against it.
Discoverability is a garden. You plant, prune, water, and build the soil. It’s slower at first. But it weathers storms. It creeps into the cracks, the rec rail here, the carousel there, the assistant’s shortlist on a Tuesday at 11:32pm when someone wonders if a better night’s sleep can be ordered by Friday. (What is the reference to 11.32 on Tuesday I hear you say).
And
incrementality
is the gardeners’ calendar. Not vibes. Not “we feel busier.” Just the
daily difference between what happened and what would’ve happened anyway
. Add those differences up, and in 90 days you won’t recognize your baseline.
The LLM era won’t kill search; it will demote it from King to Chamberlain. Answers move up; clicks move down; discovery happens where people are, not where you wish they were. The brands that win will be present in that answer layer
and
present in the feed that made the answer feel familiar.
So here’s your dare: run the 90-day plan. Measure lift weekly. Cut losers mercilessly. Promote winners immediately. Fix the boring stuff. Court the creators. Feed the assistants evidence. Water your garden.
Then come back and tell me your tide didn’t rise.
Notes, receipts, and rabbit holes
Social is #1 product discovery channel (HubSpot 2024). (
HubSpot Offers
)
U.S. social buyers hit ~100.7M in 2024; TikTok added ~11.9M buyers (eMarketer). (
EMARKETER
)
UK: Online overtakes TV for news; 52% use social for news (Ofcom 2024). (
www.ofcom.org.uk
)
U.S.: TikTok is now a regular news source for 20% of adults; 43% for under-30s (Pew 2025). (
Pew Research Center
)
Google AI Overviews associated with higher zero-click and reduced referrals (Similarweb / eMarketer / SEJ); Google contests the aggregate impact. (
Search Engine Roundtable
)
Perplexity referrals growing off a small base (Adweek); AI platforms sending more traffic but not offsetting zero-click (Digiday). (
Adweek
)
Amazon
Rufus
rolls out as generative AI shopping assistant (Amazon). (
About Amazon
)
Retail media measurement skepticism; incrementality ascendant (eMarketer, ANA). (
EMARKETER
)
Only ~26% of in-house teams run incrementality tests (Funnel/Ravn via eMarketer). (
EMARKETER
)

title: Influence Without the Middleman: Statusphere Is Rewriting Marketing.
excerpt: Micro-Influencers Gone Wild - Watson Weekend Ep 75 - From the Producer's Desk. Joining Rick Watson and Jessica Lesesky on the virtual sofa last week with Kristen Wiley Forget mega-influencers and million-dollar photo shoots. Kristen Wiley built Statusphere on the radical idea that influence can
_body:
Micro-Influencers Gone Wild - Watson Weekend Ep 75 - From the Producer's Desk.
Joining Rick Watson and Jessica Lesesky on the virtual sofa last week with Kristen Wiley
Forget mega-influencers and million-dollar photo shoots. Kristen Wiley built
Statusphere
on the radical idea that influence can be scaled like a supply chain, predictable, measurable and fast. In this episode of The Watson Weekend, we go inside her playbook for turning hundreds of micro-creators into a brand’s secret growth engine. It’s part marketing, part logistics, and part quiet rebellion against the old pay-per-post model. If you’ve ever wondered how to cut through rising CAC without cutting authenticity, this is the conversation to binge.
Statusphere is different - Human touch overlay on tech and AI. The Netflix Twist.
Scale-on-demand:
“We’re the only platform that can get
1,000+ creators posting
with
< 1 hour
of setup time.”
Validated and kinda nuts.
Creator economics:
Brands
set a single rate
;
all creators are paid the same
(free-market model for
micro/nano
creators). Transparent and fair.
Network maturity:
Kristen’s been in the space
since 2010
(blog → PR → agencies → Statusphere). This is important as Kristen understands platforms.
Career mix:
~
20%
of creators
aspire
to go full-time; most have day jobs (teachers, doctors, lawyers, etc.).
Built by creators:
~50%
of Statusphere’s creator-side team are
creators themselves!
Vetting depth:
Multi-step screen incl. fraud/quality checks,
last 30 posts
brand-safety scan, and a
human final review
.
Precision matching:
Each creator completes a profile with
300+ data points
(e.g., hair type & curl pattern, sensitive skin, pets, Costco membership). This is insane.
Enterprise proof:
Working with
P&G
and other
large enterprises
that need “
thousands of creators
” at once.
Brief discipline:
Brands must define
objective content requirements
(e.g., “show product in first 30s”) — software
auto-rejects
non-compliant posts.
Community flywheel:
Cast wide (1,000 creators) → identify
top performers
→ add to a
brand community
→
re-engage
(send gifts, iterate).
Social SEO use-case:
Brands deploy Statusphere to
rank for key searches
on TikTok/Instagram with community-sourced content.
AI stance:
Platform is
human micro-influencers only
; AI is fine for
unpublished UGC/editing
, not as fake “people” selling skincare.
Attribution realism:
“
Love–hate
” — no channel tracks perfectly; optimize for
measurable momentum
, not mythical precision.
What We Learned
From Pay-Per-Post to Product Seeding.
Kristen explained why traditional influencer marketing is broken and how seeding product with micro-creators flips the model from “renting reach” to “owning a network.”
Scaling Authenticity.
Statusphere’s system automates matching and shipping so a brand can activate hundreds of creators at once without losing the human touch.
Data + Community.
The platform’s real edge is not just shipping boxes, but analysing which creators actually drive conversion and feeding that back into campaigns.
Influence as Infrastructure.
Wiley argues that in a world of algorithm churn, building your own seeding network is like owning your own factory,  it’s a loyalty plan for attention.
Brands love to be subjective — ‘be funny,’ ‘be engaging’ — but what does that even mean? We force them to think critically about what’s actually important. If everything’s important, nothing’s important. Our software auto-rejects posts that don’t hit the objective content requirements, so the creators still have freedom but the brand gets consistency.”
Thinking about me, thinking about you.
Influencer marketing is the
now
, and what Kristen is doing with Statusphere gives us a lens into infrastructure. Her model is a signal: the shift is from paying for attention to
owning
pathways of attention. Remember
PESO
?
Here’s how it lands, with proof from what’s happening in the field:
Nano & micro-creators deliver outsized ROI.
Recent studies show that campaigns built around smaller creators can generate up to
10× ROI
compared to big-name influencer campaigns. (
Marketing Dive
) That validates Kristen’s thesis: you don’t need celebrity reach if you build the right network and measure performance.
Brands are reallocating budgets toward creator media.
At SXSW in 2025, marketers from Crocs to Southwest talked about shifting dollars from traditional digital ads into influencer/creator media, because it can hit the same reach with more efficiency. (
Marketing Dive
) That’s exactly what Wiley is betting on,  the era when creators are central, not peripheral.
Micro/nano influence is rising in importance.
Retail Dive flagged that micro- and nano-influencers are becoming a bigger lever for authentic connection, especially as user-generated content pushes trust over polished campaigns. (
Retail Dive
)
Brands must let go of control to gain authenticity.
Reports show that many brands are still trapped in commanding content,  but when they cede creative freedom to creators, engagement (and conversion) improves. (
Retail Dive
)
Seeding is evolving into “reverse seeding.”
In influencer marketing circles, there’s growing discussion about flipping the playing field: starting with gift / sampling programs that then evolve into paid collaborations once alignment and efficacy are proven. (
Influencer Marketing Hub
) Kristen’s model seems built for that leap: you don’t bet big until you’ve proven the creator works.
When you tie Kristen’s ideas to these trends, the takeaway is bold:
“This is not a sideline tactic. “
From the Backlot (Producers’ Meanderings)
Some guests talk about influencers like a line-item; Kristen talked about them like a supply chain. Listening to her, you realise influence isn’t just a campaign,  it’s an asset or a distribution network.
It’s a reminder that the future of marketing might not be more ads, but better infrastructure for advocacy. And like any good Watson Weekend, it left us wondering what else in commerce could be rebuilt from the ground up if we stopped renting and started owning.

👉

Bio - Kristen Wiley
Kristen Wiley is the Founder and CEO of Statusphere, a platform that helps brands generate thousands of high-performing influencer posts—without the manual work.
A former creator and longtime influencer marketing expert, Kristen built Statusphere to eliminate the friction marketers face when trying to scale. Today, brands use the platform to get guaranteed posts, instant usage rights, and complete campaign execution—powered by AI and first-party data. Her mission: to build the influencer platform every marketer wishes they had—one that actually does the work.

excerpt: Ep. 76 – Click, Cart, Repeat with Kiri Masters. We were thrilled to have a long time friend on the show, Kiri Masters. Not long after here move back from Australia to the US too. Kiri Masters is the founder of Bobsled Marketing , creator
_body:
Ep. 76 – Click, Cart, Repeat with Kiri Masters.
We were thrilled to have a long time friend on the show, Kiri Masters. Not long after here move back from Australia to the US too. Kiri Masters is the founder of
Bobsled Marketing
, creator of
The Retail Media Breakfast Club
, a columnist for
Forbes
, and a leading independent voice in the retail-media/marketplace world. She’s been inside the boards and dashboards of brand and retailer ad networks for years now she’s translating that insider math for the rest of us.
Kiri is consistent - her work tells us this.
The House Is Divided:
Retailers’ media and merchandising teams are in open turf wars both want control of digital shelf space and data.).
Retail Media = Black Box Marketing:
Brands are still buying media without full visibility into placement or outcomes. Transparency gaps are now retail media’s biggest PR problem.
AI Is Collapsing the Funnel:
OpenAI’s new checkout tools and Visa/Mastercard’s agentic payment pilots show commerce is moving inside conversations.
Walmart’s Already Building It:
The retailer is testing AI agents to handle purchasing, fulfillment, and recommendation logic a signal of mainstream adoption.
Discovery Is Dead; Recommendation Wins:
As LLMs and social algorithms decide what we see, ad budgets will follow utility and data interoperability, not traditional eyeballs.
Trust Will Be the New Currency:
Agentic AI threatens to blur authenticity and Kiri’s right that real human creators could become
more
valuable in the chaos.
Regulators Are Moving In:
Shopify has already limited how agentic bots operate on stores, while financial institutions debate fraud and consent rules.
The Next Big Risk:
If attribution stays broken, and automation drives spend, brands could lose not just control of their media and the logic behind it.
What We Learned
Conflict in the House
Retailers built ad networks to squeeze more margin, but often end up with
internal tug-of-wars
. Merch, ops, and media teams frequently compete over audience, inventory, and outcomes. Sometimes the same product is being “sold” as ad space and as goods  and the tension is structural.
AI Is Rewriting the Ad Game
The shift toward
agentic commerce
where AI agents transact, choose, and optimize for you threatens to collapse the classic retail funnel. Kiri argues that as LLMs aggregate product data and suggestions, they’ll reroute “ad spend” toward utility and interface, not just eyeballs.
Retail Media Beyond the Shelf
While on-site ads (sponsored products, banners etc.) are the first thing people think of,
off-site activations
(using retailer audiences to power ads on CTV, social, search) are quietly as large and often undercounted.
Demand for Transparency is a Paradox
Retailers and brands say they want full visibility (log files, placement detail), but in practice many brand-side buyers settle for a “black box ROAS” model handing over spend and asking “what did I get?” later.
Creative Meets Prompting
Expect tools tied into GPT / Gemini to auto-generate headlines, captions, and even shots fed by product, attribute, and context metadata. It’s not about reinventing creative; it’s about rethinking how you brief creative.
The Resilience of Identity & Loyalty
Even as agents and algorithms mediate discovery, people will still pick brands when something “feels right.” Price parity may become a commodity, but identity, experience, and frictionless fulfillment remain human.
Brands love to be subjective ‘be funny,’ ‘be engaging’  but what does that even mean? We force them to think critically about what’s actually important. If everything’s important, nothing’s important. Our software auto-rejects posts that don’t hit the objective content requirements, so the creators still have freedom but the brand gets consistency.”
We then ask them, get me results in 1 month, or else…..
Thinking about me, thinking about you.
Media is part of the product architecture. If Kiri is right, every SKU, every PDP, every ad unit and every brand story will be embedded in a system of continuous commerce. Making it more useful and purposeful in an agentic world.
For brands: media budgets will begin to flow toward
systems that integrate
, not just placements that perform. For retailers: your ad network is only as good as your data interfaces, your customer trust, and your ability to absorb transactional friction. For markets: we’re entering a phase where
recommendation engines
, not discovery engines, will decide what we see  and maybe what we buy.
From the Backlot (Producers’ Meanderings)
Talking with Kiri felt like stepping into the control room of a machine that’s still being built: half hardware, half hallucination. She bears the scars of building in ad tech,  the compromises, the vendor pitches, the politics but she also sees the promise: a system that doesn’t just push ads, but
enables intent
.
If every operator now is fiddling with bidding strategies, Kiri is already building the next layer: what happens when the ad becomes the interface? We leave this conversation both smarter and a little spooked.

Kiri was the founder of Bobsled Marketing, an agency focused on retail media and online marketplaces. Bobsled was acquired in 2022, and Kiri is now host of the ‘Retail Media Breakfast Club’ - a daily podcast and newsletter focused on the retail media landscape. She is also a contributor to Forbes and WARC.

_body:
Squarespace Refresh 2025 & the Hidden Value of Incrementality
There’s always money in the banana stand.  If you’ve watched
Arrested Development
, you know the line. If you’ve run a business, you
feel
the line. The trick isn’t just that the money exists, it’s that most companies don’t know where it’s hiding.
At
Refresh 2025
, Squarespace has just unveiled a shiny package of new features, AI-driven tooling, and the promise that your business can not only stand out, but scale, all on a single platform. Who doesn’t love these? On the surface, it’s a design upgrade. Underneath, it's not just about proving that the banana stand exists. It's about showing businesses where it is, how to reach it faster, and how to make it work harder for them/their growth.. Right now, this, is the only job. Compound growth is the only growth you should be focused on. Remember that movie, Everything, Everywhere All at Once? It was some sort of twisted analogy for describing the role of the ecommownerpreneur. #justcoinedthis.
Squarespace: Where They Stand
Before I unpack the new features, let’s set the scene with their last available numbers (remember, they went private in 2024 under Permira, so the information below is pulled from past public reports and 3rd party resources):
Customers / Subscriptions
: ~4.9 million unique subscriptions.
Revenue
: ~$1.12 billion annual run rate.
Employees
: ~1,700+ globally.
Websites Live
: ~6.6 million (with millions more historically churned or migrated away).
Geography
: Dominant in the US (~70%+ of users), but present in 200+ countries.
This isn’t your indie-blogger’s web builder anymore. This is a scaled, mature SaaS platform fighting for margin in a brutally competitive ecosystem. This is more than Shopify FYI. (Customers, I mean).
What Refresh 2025 Is Selling
Squarespace’s update isn’t just new fonts and templates. The big plays are:
Blueprint AI
→ build sites faster with machine learning scaffolding. Building is only phase 1, or foundations in building terms. Weird, huh.
Beacon AI
→ personalized guidance and optimization for entrepreneurs and SMBs. The job, today, yesterday and tomorrow. Be great at this, above all else.
Design Pro Moves
→ block animations, transforms, granular mobile tweaks. Can’t afford an agency? Not able to think and design because it costs too much? Those days are gone. Time to dream again. Because, we can.
SEO / AIO Additions
→ automated, context-aware optimization baked into site builds. The black box days are coming to an end.Ongoing optimisation is always going to be there. You no longer need to fear or interpret it. Just get things done.
It’s a clear shift from
DIY website builder
→
guided digital business partner
. Although the language is a little lame, you get the picture.
Translation: Squarespace is betting the next wave of value comes not from
what
you build, but from
how you optimize it over time
. In my words,
Incrementality.
The Age of Being Found ( Not Just Built )
For most entrepreneurs, time is oxygen. You either spend it creating, or you spend it being found. Squarespace’s new AIO suite collapses that trade-off. In a world where customer journeys now begin inside the chat box of ChatGPT or the search bar of TikTok, visibility is no longer just SEO it’s LLM-SEO: structured data and contextual understanding by machines deciding who gets seen first.
For small businesses, that’s existential. The brands that appear in AI results aren’t shouting louder; they’re teaching the algorithms who they are. AIO gives SMBs that blueprint  turning search from a black box into a daily habit.
The New Discoverability Dividend
Optimization is a part of marketing. In the Agentic World, Entrepreneurs need a co-pilot that keeps them visible while they run their business. Beacon AI and AIO are aiming to reclaim hours lost to guesswork and Google forums.
Just as good design once separated the pros from the amateurs, smart discoverability will separate tomorrow’s visible brands from the invisible ones. That’s the compounding play here: every small tweak teaches the algorithm who you are, stacking momentum quietly in your favor.
Why Product & Service Firms Should Care
Here’s the thing: this story and every other one like it right now (if you are allergic to them, do not go on LinkedIn, i repeat, do not go on LinkedIn.) It’s a
signal to anyone running a product or service business with recurring revenue
.
If you’re a
service company
(agency, consultancy, professional firm): your value lies not in the first delivery, but in the incremental improvements, retention, upsell, and optimization.
If you’re a
product company
(DTC brand, SaaS vendor, subscription platform): the real margin isn’t in the flashy launch but in the micro-adjustments that keep users sticking around.
Refresh 2025 is a reminder: every business has hidden levers. Find them, or lose to the ones who do.
Always Money Somewhere
Back to Arrested Development: “There’s always money in the banana stand.”
In commerce terms:
That “banana stand” might be your
pricing model
.
Or your
customer retention play
.
Or the
AI-powered add-on
you free for all existing users.
The problem is that most leaders chase the wrong levers. They see big launches, headline features, loud announcements. But the hidden money sits in the cracks,  incremental lift from the small, compounding changes. This is not just midweek wine talking, this is something I talk about every day. In fact, this was yesterday -> See below.
Incrementality: Lessons From Grosse Pointe Blank
In this essay I used
Grosse Pointe Blank
as a frame for talking about
incrementality
,  those small, daily decisions that,
when stacked, alter your trajectory.
Squarespace’s move is exactly that. They’re not reinventing themselves. They’re compounding: adding AI here, a design edge there, a guidance nudge elsewhere. Each is small. Together, they reposition the platform for another 5 years of relevance.
The lesson for you:
stop looking for your moonshot and start stacking your small shots
.
What to Watch Out For
Not every banana stand is full of money. Sometimes it’s just rotten fruit. A few watch-outs from the announcement:
AI Hype Over Substance
→ Shiny AI assistants can flop if they don’t deliver real lift.
Complexity Creep
→ Power features risk overwhelming the simple-creator base. Despite how much thought Squarespace has put into making them as intuitive as possible.
Margin Pressure
→ AI compute isn’t free, and these costs need to be passed somewhere. Right now, unlike others, this is free for existing users.
Churn Risk
→ unless these new features stick, customers can and will jump to Shopify, Wix, or Webflow.
Squarespace is betting that more guidance = more retention. That’s the banana stand they’re trying to unlock.
Closing Thought
The real question isn’t what Squarespace shipped, it’s what
you
are ignoring in your own business.
Where is your hidden banana stand? What incremental moves are you stacking? And most importantly — do you even know where the money is hiding?
Because trust me: it’s there. It always is.

title: Ep. 83 – The Forecast is in and it is Inevitable
pullQuotes: “We are morphing so fast that our ability to invent new things outpaces the rate we can civilize them.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
excerpt: Predictive Retail, Pattern Recognition, and the Rain That Never Ends. If you’ve ever worked in retail long enough to feel that strange mix of déjà vu and whiplash, John Andrews has probably helped you make sense of it. He’s one of the original thinkers behind
_body:
Predictive Retail, Pattern Recognition, and the Rain That Never Ends.
If you’ve ever worked in retail long enough to feel that strange mix of déjà vu and whiplash, John Andrews has probably helped you make sense of it. He’s one of the original thinkers behind influencer marketing — long before “creator economy” became a conference track. From
Walmart
to
Collective Bias
to his latest company
Cimulate
, John’s career has been about connecting dots most people don’t even see.
John’s not a futurist. He’s a pattern reader.  And this week, he helped us see how retail keeps repeating itself: faster, louder, and more automated.
We prepared to come into this one ready to talk about predictive analytics.  We left talking about
human adaptability
.
“We are morphing so fast that our ability to invent new things outpaces the rate we can civilize them.”―
Kevin Kelly,
The Inevitable: Understanding the 12 Technological Forces That Will Shape Our Future
1. The Retail Feedback Loop Is Too Slow
John made the case that retail has fallen into a data trap. too many dashboards, not enough decisions.
“Retailers collect an ocean of data,” he said. “But by the time they analyze it, it’s already out of date. You can’t swim in that ocean  you have to surf it.”
His message for practitioners was blunt: the companies winning aren’t necessarily
smarter
they’re just
faster at acting on imperfect information.
This is the exact message I was experiencing at Rithum live last week. We don’t need better insights, we need better decisions.
2. Predictive ≠ Prophetic
Cimulate doesn’t promise prophecy; it promises
probability
. Probability though, requires you to act. So be careful what you wish for.  John compared it to meteorology  the idea isn’t to know exactly when it will rain, but to prepare your supply chain, inventory, and campaigns for when it inevitably does.
“We’re not trying to predict the future,” he said. “We’re trying to understand which version of it is most likely  and build muscle memory around that.”
That means teaching organizations to operate in cycles, not campaigns.  Retail is a live feed. It is your own, daily, working Truman show - being held up for you to beat you with, to make you feel great and just when you think you are getting out, boom.
3. The End of Channel Thinking
This is another emerging conversation theme among the more salient observer. John said one of the biggest mistakes he still sees from brands is “channel ego.”  Everyone wants to own a moment, a platform, a pipeline and the consumer doesn’t care where they buy, only
why
they buy.
“The shopper doesn’t think in channels. The shopper thinks in missions,” John said. He argues that the true measure of omnichannel maturity isn’t being everywhere it’s being
useful
everywhere.
For practitioners, that means inventory visibility, price consistency, content parity, and fulfillment logic all have to speak to each other. Your internal silos can’t be louder than your customer’s intent.
4. Retail Media: The Double-Edged Sword
John didn’t hold back on retail media either  calling it both a revelation and a risk.  It’s the first time in history that
every
retailer wants to be a media company, but
the infrastructure isn’t ready for that ambition. This means on all sides of this coin, there can be only one winner.
“When every retailer becomes a publisher,” he said, “t
he customer becomes the ad unit. That’s a problem.
”
Practitioners need to treat retail media not as a growth hack, but as a
coordination layer
connecting merchandising, marketing, and operations.  If those three don’t align, retail media becomes a very expensive distraction. Which, this writer, feels it will become and we will be having this argument for the next 18 months.
5. Retail Darwinism
Origin of the species, John wasn’t there, but he has hindsight and for looking ahead, this can be 20:20 vision. And in this part we hear perhaps John’s best line of the episode:
“Retail doesn’t reward the smartest company. It rewards the company that learns the fastest.”
Cute soundbyte that it may be, it’s a survival law.  He called it
Retail Darwinism
: adapt or evaporate. To thrive in this climate, he said, retailers should:
Shorten feedback loops between decision and action. (I reported on this in the temu story - wanna know more? Ask me - 40,000 units in 2 months, themes nice apples.)
Replace post-mortem reports with
live adjustment meetings.
This is that decision marking thing again.
Make failure cheap and reversible.
Incentivize learning velocity, not just sales velocity
The faster your organization metabolizes mistakes, the more resilient it becomes.es spend, brands could lose not just control of their media and the logic behind it.
Thinking about me, thinking about you.
In my Substack essay,
“It Once Rained for Two Million Years on Earth,”
I wrote about how change doesn’t always come as a shock — sometimes it comes as a slow, unrelenting drizzle that never lets up.
That’s where we are in retail.  We’re in a
precipitation cycle.
Everything looks the same from day to day, but underneath, the ground is shifting. John’s world of predictive modeling isn’t about beating the storm it’s about learning to live inside it. Adaptation and moving forward become hard when everything is moving so quickly around us.
And that’s the real lesson for every retailer, brand, or founder reading this:
You can’t wait for the rain to stop. You have to build your business to
breathe underwater.
The future isn’t a forecast,it’s a fluid.
From the Backlot (Producers’ Meanderings)
Rick called this episode “what happens when weather meets retail.”  Jess described it as “the calmest apocalypse she’s ever heard.” I just think it was
truth with a side of thunder.
John Andrews reminds us that the best operators aren’t the ones predicting trends. They are listening for pressure drops.
If you’ve been feeling the fatigue of constant change, his advice is simple: stop treating volatility as a bug. It’s the environment. And if you can’t control the forecast, at least learn to sell umbrellas.

title: Where’s all good marketing gone dead, In the Heart or in the Head?
pullQuotes: “There is no mass media.”  Mark Weinstein, Hilton’s CMO, said it and he’s right.
What you do for my pocket is more impactful than why you source rubber using a mash up of

panda poo, only picked before 10am due to the texture being better in morning than afternoon, mixed with the discarded eggs of the Shinatogi Salmon, who naturally displace a portion of their eggs to create more fertile water for their growing spawn and 98% rubber.
excerpt: Loyalty, the choice of a new generation I fell in love with Minnie Driver’s character in Grosse Point Blank the first time I saw here and it was this line, for some inane reason that did it. Since I wrote about it recently, the line
_body:
Loyalty, the choice of a new generation
I fell in love with Minnie Driver’s character in Grosse Point Blank the first time I saw here and it was this line, for some inane reason that did it. Since I wrote about it recently, the line reemerged and now I keep turning over in my mind like a coin that won’t stop spinning:
“There is no mass media.”  Mark Weinstein, Hilton’s CMO, said it and he’s right.
We’ve moved from the shared living room of culture into a thousand rented bedrooms. Marketing has become more tribal, more atomized. And so have we. It has also, lets’s be really clear narcotized. We consume, don’t seek. This is why discovery is starting to move into search territory. I am careful not to say replace. I am under the watchful gaze of
Mike Ryan
.
But here’s the question I can’t shake, the one I’m putting to you today like a radio caller on line one:
If there’s no mass media, where does mass emotion go? Rather, where has it gone?
Because if marketing is dying, I’m not convinced it’s in the spreadsheets. It’s in the silence. It’s in the part where brand marketers stopped
feeling
anything. Now, let me preface this. We tried. Goddamnit we tried, we greenwashed like crazy over the last 5 years. Yet in a 2024 study of 1000 top EU brands by internet retailing, only 11% of those brands had a published CSR or ESG policy. Riddle me that. Smaller, DTC brands shifted to sustainability. The most meaningless word in the English language. Personally, I prefer the Japanese version I looked up 持続可能性 - has way more meaningful. Even the Gaelic words for it have more meaning. It has become a trap. And the go to marketing dictat. I blame Simon Sinek. RIght now, for me this is what is true:
What > Why
What you do for my pocket is more impactful than why you source rubber using a mash up of
panda poo, only picked before 10am due to the texture being better in morning than afternoon, mixed with the discarded eggs of the Shinatogi Salmon, who naturally displace a portion of their eggs to create more fertile water for their growing spawn and 98% rubber.
The Death of the Middle and the Rise of the Micro
Once upon a not-so-distant past, brand loyalty was a steady hum in the background predictable, habitual, baked into our consumption patterns like Sunday dinners and TV reruns.Gen Z doesn’t have reruns. They have the
refresh
button. They move in micro-truths, micro-moments, micro-loyalties. They are micro movements. The power of the indviidaul is more important than the collective - the hope that what is trending is the new movement. What happens when the trending stops? Does the movement?
Happy Rex Manning Day
They are allergic to the mass-produced even when they buy from it. They might wear Nike, but they’ll tell you they don’t trust corporations. They’ll use Amazon, but call it “late capitalism” while they do.
So yes, Weinstein is right again: tribalization isn’t just happening; it’s the new terrain. Tribes don’t eliminate mass culture, right now, they remix it. They localize it. They turn global stories into smaller, more emotionally resonant versions.
If mass marketing is dead, then micro empathy is the new oxygen.
Loyalty: Dead, Rebranded, or Reincarnated?
Did it ever exist? For this DJ, no. Pause
Here we break for a trip down memory lane
A
disc jockey
,is a
professional button presser with delusions of musical deity
.
They are the self-anointed
conductors of vibes
, armed with a playlist suspiciously similar to Spotify’s “Top Hits of 2010–2020” but rearranged like Picasso rearranged faces for “artistic effect.”
A DJ’s main skills include:
Pretending to twist knobs
that aren’t actually connected to anything.
Wearing headphones on only one ear
for reasons science cannot explain.
Gesturing to the crowd
like Moses parting the Red Sea every time a bass drop approaches.
Their natural habitat is the
dark, sticky-floored nightclub
, where they stand atop a small altar of electronics while the crowd below worships them for playing a slightly sped-up version of a Dua Lipa track.
They describe themselves not as people who “play music,” but as
“curators of sonic journeys.”
Translation: they know when to hit “next” and raise their hands simultaneously.
And let’s not forget the holy trinity of every DJ’s vocabulary:
“Yo, can I get more bass in the monitor?”
“You feelin’ it tonight, Tralee?”
“Make some noise!” (as if the room wasn’t already doing exactly that).
In short: a disc jockey is
a philosopher with beats instead of thoughts,
a
modern shaman with a USB stick,
and a
demigod of delayed gratification
, forever chasing the mythical “drop” that never quite lands as hard as they think it did.
Back to the programme.
Back to loyalty, the word we throw around like a dog-eared coupon.
Erdly’s comment from RetailWire was as impactful and smooth as a Mark Knoppfler chord change:
“Loyalty has moved from ‘points and percentage-off’ to a broader promise of recognition, access, and community.”
Recognition. Access. Community.
It’s not a program anymore; it’s a promise. The points-based loyalty model the cold, algorithmic form of affection is becoming a relic. You don’t earn loyalty now; you
perform
it.
Neil Saunders says discount-driven loyalty is fleeting. True. Because loyalty built on savings is transactional a marriage of convenience.
Shep Hyken’s warning is sharper still:
“Don’t confuse a repeat customer with a loyal one.”
That line should be printed on every marketer’s dashboard. Because loyalty is no longer a behavioral outcome it’s an emotional alignment. A customer might come back again and again, but they might be loyal to the
experience
, not the brand.
And Charles Ehredt brings it home:
“Loyalty is fundamentally a value exchange... a sense of belonging, access, special opportunities.”
Loyalty, then, is not about locking in. It’s about letting in. It’s about being seen and being known the primal need that outlasts every ad format.
Now, I see where they are going, but I raise your loyalty hand and I am playing my ace in the hold. Agentic is logic over empathy. Convenience over love. Agentic, if to be successful, can only come from the user. The user has different need states and they are contingent on how you feel on any given moment. Not the promise of community. Detail - you might want to feel part of a community cos you had a shitty day. You might want your peers to know you got that Google Garage cert (I failedf one today in fact). But they do not work in moments of impulse or discovery. Reminds me of that classic - Mad about the boy… Next up on our playlist, if I ever get back to my show.
The Agentic Question: Can AI Feel Anything?
Now, enter the agentic, AI-first world. The tools promise optimization, prediction, automation but here’s the dilemma:
can a brand be emotionally intelligent if its voice is algorithmic?
I’m torn. On one side, AI gives brands the ability to scale intimacy to send a “personal” message to millions. On the other, it risks reducing emotion to pattern recognition.
The more we teach machines to know us, the less we might
recognize
ourselves in what they say back. Unless, as Sam wants, we share our fantasies with them, all of them. Imagine your CoPIlot picking out a fleshlight for you or a something that fits your sordid fantasies, just appearing? Or worse, sexting you cos y ou had that bad day. Agentic, in these instances will struggle and limit marketers powers. I cannot be certain or this, only hopeful.
Agentic marketing might make loyalty more efficient but efficiency is rarely what wins hearts. Preparedness, yes. But not passion.
That’s where I think the new marketing divide sits:
The
head
wants precision, optimization, ROI.
The
heart
wants belonging, voice, meaning.
When AI automates the head, who’s left to speak for the heart?
Daily, the New Monthly?
I said this yesterday or was it last week - the timeframe melds and so does my ability to hold logic. There’s a new tempo to marketing. The monthly campaign calendar feels like a fax machine now. Brands are learning that in 2025,
planning is less important than preparedness.
Consumers’ attention spans are unpredictable chaotic, even and cultural moments happen in real-time. The new playbook isn’t “plan, brief, launch.” It’s “listen, respond, evolve.”
Daily is the new monthly.
The brands that thrive are those that can pivot mid-sentence, that can go from meme to message before the conversation shifts.
Identity crisis much. Because if you don’t know who you are as a brand, how can you improvise without losing the plot? After 2025, We are walking into a year defined by pressure. Inflation fatigue, channel saturation, too many subscriptions, too little soul. The consumer isn’t just squeezed they’re
shrinking back
.
They’re editing their brand relationships like they’re cleaning out a cluttered closet. “Do I really need this? Does it still fit me?”
That’s the climate brands are facing: the great emotional unsubscribe.
And while software companies will pitch dashboards and partnerships promising agility and preparedness, the truth is simpler:
The brands that win in the squeeze are the ones that stay human.
The ones who pick up the phone when the world goes quiet. The ones who show up, not just send. Because marketing isn’t dead. It’s just tired of pretending to be clever when it’s supposed to be kind.
Head or Heart?
So, where is marketing dead in the head or in the heart? Maybe the head’s overloaded too many metrics, too much noise, not enough meaning. Or maybe the heart’s just burnt out bruised from too many fake “authentic” moments and soulless “purpose-driven” taglines.
Either way, resurrection won’t come from technology alone. It’ll come from the same place marketing was born:
the tension between attention and affection.
Maybe the job now is to reconnect the two.  To make preparedness emotional. To make data empathetic. To make loyalty
felt
.
Because the future of marketing isn’t automation or surveilance.
Remember, It’s recognition.
And it’s time we remembered what that feels like.

title: Zeds Dead baby.
pullQuotes: Be the tortoise.
It’s the cult of
A-word marketing.
excerpt: Zed’s Dead Baby. From A to Z(ed). Actually A is, A is dead. Heuston, we have a problem. And it is the letter A. A, the first letter of the alphabet. The start of everything. Alpha. A for ambition, for audacity, for “a strategy.” Not
_body:
Zed’s Dead Baby. From A to Z(ed).
Actually A is, A is dead.
Heuston, we have a problem. And it is the letter A.
A, the first letter of the alphabet. The start of everything. Alpha.
A for ambition, for audacity, for “a strategy.” Not strategy. You see strategy and a strategy are different. In a world where words matter, letters like days, matter more.
Strategy
A strategy
These days, A stands for
absence
.
Strategy has left the building. The lights are still on, the dashboards are still blinking, but the grown-up conversation left hours ago. In ten years of consulting with brands, founders, and SaaS dreamers, I can count on one hand the number of times I’ve seen a real, defined strategy. Not a deck called “strategy.” And let me preface by saying it is hard, it is misunderstood and I don’t even get to do it much. Strategy feels like a constraint rather than a freedom. A way to cull opportunity rather than nourish it. When I say strategy it is not a wish list of tactics dressed in McKinsey drag. I mean
a coherent way to deal with a challenge
.
That’s what strategy is. Just ask
Colin Lewis
. And he just loves the Oxford Comma. He even gives a f*ck about it, much to the liking of Vampire Weekend.
And
a strategy
, the definite article that no one bothers with anymore, is the set of analyses, concepts, policies, and actions that respond to that challenge. The difference between “strategy” and “a strategy” is the difference between philosophy and plumbing. One is abstract; the other actually carries the water. Reminds me, the chatGPT response I got to fixing my cistern flush system left me wanting yesterday and with a lot of excess I was not expecting.
Most brands today are standing in puddles, wondering why they’re wet. Just like me.
The world of commerce has become a casino of tactics. Every spin of the algorithm feels like destiny. We measure performance in sprints and panic in slides. We don’t diagnose; we deploy. Speed is everything. Accuracy is the ugly cousin. “Be agile,” they tell us, as if agility is a substitute for direction. Agility without strategy is just frenetic movement, a hamster in performance-marketing sneakers. And I don’t say sneakers lightly. I am becoming more amnericanized by the z.
I see it every week: founders who confuse
activity
for
strategy
. Drowning in dashboards, fighting fires that shouldn’t exist, and mistaking a Facebook ROAS spike for proof of purpose.  It’s not their fault entirely. The system rewards motion over meaning.
Be the tortoise.
Look around.
DWe have quarterly capitalism baked into our DNA. We celebrate revenue graphs like ECGs, praying they keep pulsing upward even if the body underneath is already brain-dead. Donald Trump, of all people, once suggested scrapping quarterly earnings reports. For once, the man might have stumbled onto something. I should have followed with useful as he stumbles into things the whole time, usually himself. But, truth is, you can’t build anything lasting if you’re judged every ninety days. You can barely build a habit.
Most SaaS sales cycles are longer than that. We forget this. Unless you are in it. But it is important. Some brands take that long just to figure out what their customer actually wants. But Wall Street and venture capital don’t care. They want the hit single, not the album.
The 100 year Canadian Behemoth saving the little guy
I keep thinking about Shopify. The company says it’s building a “1 000-year company.”  It’s a ridiculous, glorious, almost medieval idea. It’s also the most strategic statement in modern tech. Because it says,
we are not here for the quarter; we are here for the century.
It’s an act of rebellion against short-termism. Oh how rebels love the short term.
I sometimes imagine Tobi Lütke standing before his shareholders after a rough quarter, saying softly, “I do not care what you think. I care what the world will think in 2125.” I really believe he would take a stance like this. Will he actually do that? I don’t know. But the sentence itself is a guardrail. It’s the difference between
a strategy
and
a story about strategy
.
Meanwhile, back in brand-land, the tactical delusion continues.
Picture yourself: Teams gather for “strategy days” that produce nothing but slide decks. The real problem, as I wrote once on a napkin somewhere between Dublin and Heathrow, is that
strategy and tactics have become interchangeable nouns.
It is amazing what 2 large glasses of Malbec become - usually, the bits that didn’t make it in Jerry Maguire.
The more fragmented our channels get, the easier it is to confuse the two. Instagram becomes the strategy. TikTok becomes the strategy. “Launch on Amazon” becomes the strategy.
The DTC playbook I worked on with Colin Lewis lays out nine clear pillars, Platform, Project, Partner, Payments, Performance, Profile, Products, Propositions, People. Nine Ps that, if treated strategically, form a symphony. This has become my own way of making sense of the world. It is my “thinking fast” framework.
Yet in most boardrooms they’re played like nine separate Spotify tracks on shuffle. Someone says “we need content,” another says “we need conversion,” and before long you have a beautifully optimised funnel with absolutely nothing flowing through it.
Because nobody paused for the first P that matters,
Purpose. This emergence of a new 9 is something I didn’t envision, and 10 Ps really skews my square. Will need to think about this.
In theory, every brand should begin with
diagnosis
, defining the nature of the challenge. Then an
approach
, a way of responding to that challenge. Then
actions
, the coherent set of tactics that bring it to life. Diagnosis → Approach → Actions. Three A’s. The holy trinity. Except most teams skip the first two because they’re messy and uncomfortable. Diagnosis sounds like “analysis” and analysis sounds slow. Approach sounds like “consensus” and consensus sounds expensive. So they jump straight to Actions. Always-on, AI-optimised, algorithmically-aligned Actions.
It’s the cult of
A-word marketing.
We’ve built an altar to agility, automation, and analytics. We pray to attribution models and worship dashboards as if they were commandments. And yet nobody can answer the simplest strategic question:
What challenge are we actually solving?
