_body:
WELCOME TO THE TRIPLE-SHOT PODCAST ERA
There’s a moment every creator
(It is easier than trying to actually explain to my Mother what I do)
hits where they stop, look around, and think:
“
How the hell did I get here, and why are there so many microphones?”
I’ve reached that moment.
In the past two years, what began as a few scattered ideas across WhatsApp chats and late-night Google Docs has evolved into
four distinct shows
, each with its own personality disorder, fan base, and running jokes that make sense only to the chronically online corner of retail tech.
And now, because ambition is a disease and bandwidth is imaginary , I’m moving the V Spot Nearly ECommerce News to a
three-day-a-week publishing cycle
across all channels.
3 episodes a week. Across three channels. Backed by Substack. And pushed into LinkedIn.
It’s basically a small media network at this point, except you can still DM me at 11pm and I will still reply like an idiot.
This next phase comes with something new:
👉
I’m opening 1–2 sponsor slots for a 10-week run.
👉
Every episode = LinkedIn + Substack + show mention.
👉
Two episodes per week, every week.
If you’re the kind of company that loves ecommerce, loves a theme, and doesn’t take yourself too seriously, then congratulations:
You’re my people.
But before we get to sponsorships, let’s take stock. Let’s lay the whole thing out — the shows, the guests, the energy, the growth.
Here it is. My whole messy, joyful, slightly unhinged media universe. Feel free to bookmark it, print it, or literally burn it after reading. I won’t blame you.
THE SHOWS — IN ALL THEIR GLORY, CHAOS & COMMUNITY
1. THE STRUGGLE BUS
Ecommerce empathy, founder therapy, and the occasional cry-laugh.
Tagline:
Because ecommerce is not a lonely place — it just feels that way until someone tells the truth.
This is the show where ecommerce veterans come to confess, founders come to decompress, and marketers come to realise they’re not the only ones living inside an always-on panic room. It’s tender, it’s honest, it’s messy, and it punches way above its weight in raw humanity.
Guests so far include:
Chloe Pascal
, Global Head of Marketing, Nosto – dissecting team leadership, creative restraint, and burnout.
Nick Kaplan
, Co-Founder, Fashion / Retail Operator – deep dives into strategy, empathy, and the actual human cost of growth.
More founders, operators, and unfiltered industry voices who are brave enough to talk about what actually goes wrong.
Where to listen:
🎧
Amazon:
http://bit.ly/4nUHjfh
🍏
Apple Podcasts:
https://bit.ly/48b5bXa
🎵
Spotify:
https://bit.ly/485Co6l
▶️
YouTube:
https://bit.ly/43mWVkb
This show is a warm pint of honesty mixed with a stiff shot of Irish sarcasm. Your sponsors here need heart, humour, and a tolerance for the truth.
2. THE OSTRICH REPORT
Marketplace madness with Hendrik Laubscher the show nobody asked for but everybody ends up listening to.
Tagline:
Data nerds. Gossip columnists. Feathered chaos.
This is
the
global marketplaces show for people who love cross-border intrigue, billion-dollar valuations built on vibes, and watching Hendrik drop acronyms like confetti.
It’s fast. It’s global. It’s nerdy with style.
Guests so far include:
Max Sinclair, Founder of ZOMA
— unpacking marketplace infrastructure and the future of AI-driven commerce.
Endless rants, insights, predictions, and feather-ruffling takes from Hendrik himself.
Where to listen:
🎧
Amazon:
https://music.amazon.com/podcasts/a6b52b48-d6a0-437f-a1db-af78918e186b/the-struggle-bus-ecomm-nearly-news
🍏
Apple Podcasts:
https://apple.co/47zGjIu
🎵
Spotify:
https://bit.ly/47TmAlV
▶️
YouTube:
https://bit.ly/4nWYSLz
This is for sponsors who thrive on global trade, wild data, and a bit of marketplace chaos.
3. THE WATSON WEEKEND
With Rick Watson and Jessica Lesesky — retail’s therapy session disguised as a podcast.
Tagline:
Retail headlines, sanity checks, and sarcasm — shaken, not stirred.
This is the flagship. The big one. Rick, Jess, and I dive into everything from AI nonsense to supply chain meltdowns to the soft-launch nervous breakdowns happening across retail.
It’s part therapy, part industry analysis, part stand-up comedy from people who should really know better.
Guests include:
Dave Finnegan
, tech anthropologist and experience guru.
James Lang (Ulta Beauty)
— the philosopher-practitioner of modern retail intelligence.
Matt Ezyk
,
Rob Garf
,
Suze Dowling
,
Lee Trotter
, and others across our ongoing “retail showdown” episodes.
This is where sponsors get
maximum reach
, maximum chaos, and the most caffeine-per-minute ratio in ecommerce media.
4. THE V SPOT (Nearly Ecommerce News)
Your daily dose of ecommerce mischief.
Tagline:
The news show no one asked for, but everyone quotes at conferences.
This is satire with teeth. The Stephen Colbert of commerce. A 20–40 second burst of takes nobody else is bold/stupid/hungry enough to say out loud.
Where to watch/listen:
🎧
Amazon:
https://bit.ly/480rUnM
🍏
Apple:
https://apple.co/4nR03ft
🎵
Spotify:
https://bit.ly/43p9HP7
▶️
YouTube:
https://bit.ly/47TmQRV
This show is for sponsors who love personality-driven content and aren’t afraid of a little chaos in their marketing diet.
THE SPONSORSHIP OPPORTUNITY
Ten weeks. Two episodes a week. Three shows. One absolutely feral media ecosystem.
Across the ecosystem, sponsors get:
✔ One mention in each episode (twice per week)
✔ One Substack placement per episode
✔ One LinkedIn newsletter / post mention per episode
✔ Integrated themes — not generic ad-reads
✔ A brand presence woven into the story, not tacked onto the end
I want sponsors who:
love this industry;
love a joke;
love a theme;
and most importantly —
don’t take themselves seriously.
The shows are serious
about the work
, but never serious
about themselves
. That’s the whole point.
WHY AM I DOING THIS?
Because the industry is changing — fast. The stories are getting bigger. The audience is growing. And frankly, the world doesn’t need another beige, half-asleep ecommerce show reading stats from a PDF.
What people want — and respond to — are:
voices
opinions
humour
honesty
storytelling
and a place where industry people can feel something other than KPI-induced paralysis.
That’s what these shows do.
And that’s the kind of sponsors I want riding shotgun.
IN CLOSING BURN AFTER READING
This whole thing started with a few notes scribbled on my phone and a desire to make content that didn’t feel like homework.
Now it’s:
4 shows
Across all major platforms
With global guests
A growing community
And a ridiculous sense of fun
I’m proud of what’s been built. I’m proud of the people who’ve come on the shows. And I’m unbelievably grateful for the people who listen.
If you want in for the next 10-week run — as a sponsor, collaborator, guest, or chaos enthusiast — reach out.
Just don’t take it too seriously.
After all…
this is retail, not religion.
And if you really want to follow instructions:
You can always
burn after reading.

title: Black Friday 2025: She’s brought a ludicrously capacious bag. What’s even in there? Flat shoes for the subway? Her lunch pail?

_body:
Logan Roy is turning in his cold grave.
“Anyone who believes that I am getting out, please shove the bunting up your ass.”
The numbers tell one story. The signals, another. Amazon, you go first.
AI Chatbots & Agents accounted for $14.2bn in global sales, $3bn in the US alone.
AI-referred traffic to retailers surged 805% YoY.
Rufus usage surged 70% in just two weeks leading to Black Friday. At this rate, the AI assistant could mediate the majority of Amazon sessions by Q1 2025 (which Amazon will actively encourage, given Andy Jassy revealed that Shoppers using Rufus are 60% more likely to convert).
How is this even quantified? First of all, the time period, it is more than a weekend. Defining finally what we know for years, Black Friday is more than a weekend. But, did they influence search, in the same way impressions are calculated or did Rufus aid the end to end sale? Unlikely. Rufus, right now feels more like a fluffer. The Fluffer that killed attribution. If you don’t know what a fluffer is, don’t AI or LLM it. Googling it is bad enough.
“He’s selling me things I want at a fair price. So what’s next? Fellatio?”
We now live in this post truth world which makes some of this reporting quite hard and almost meaningless, but we are focused on signal not noise, so lets move on. On paper, Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2025 looked like a triumph. This is according to, well everyone, even Shopify. $11.8 billion spent online on Black Friday. A projected $14.2 billion on Cyber Monday. New records, new headlines, new victory laps.
But it didn’t
feel
like a boom weekend. Retailers looked wrecked. Consumers looked bored. And somewhere in the middle of all that fatigue, a quiet power shift happened:
This was the year agentic AI claims it started running the show.
The Black-and-White Numbers: Record Spend, Hollow Demand
Let’s start with the scoreboard.
Adobe Analytics
: U.S. online Black Friday sales hit
$11.8 billion
, up
9.1%
year-over-year, with peak spending at
$12.5 million per minute
between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.
Salesforce
tracked
$18 billion
in U.S. online sales and
$79 billion
globally. They told us that there was $17.3 billion spent on cyber monday? That’s a lot of mixed pallets. Global online sales were up 5.3% through 12 p.m. ET (1700 GMT), according to the data firm. It expects online spending to rise 6% to $52.7 billion by the day’s end.
Shopify merchants
generated
$6.2 billion worldwide
, peaking at
$5.1 million per minute
. Cyber Monday not yet available. They could not access their admin panel at the Sphere.
On the surface, that looks like a healthy, resilient consumer.But underneath, the story bends:
Order volume
:
-1% YoY
Average selling price
:
+7% YoY
Units per transaction
:
-2% YoY
Average discount rate
: flat at
28%
, exactly where it was in 2024
In-store traffic
:
-3.6%
, per RetailNext
As Salesforce’s Caila Schwartz put it:
“On the surface, sales were strong, hitting $18 billion, a 3% jump year-over-year. But with the average selling price for goods climbing 7%, U.S. shoppers continued to feel the bite of inflation.”
Translation: Consumers bought
fewer things
, paid
more
for them, and didn’t get better deals than last year. Dollars grew. Demand didn’t.
The Exhausted Retailer, The Fatigued Consumer
I’m not saying I’d make a better CEO. That’s unsaid.
If retailers sounded tired this year, it’s because they are. Before I go further, I want to state my hugest of respect to retailers and brand owners. Staying the course this year was a lesson in necessity being the Mother of Survival. It used to be invention but Mothers can change their mind like that because they are, Moms.
A survey by AlixPartners found that consumers were already experiencing
“discount burnout”
before Black Friday even began. Weeks of “early access” sales, multiple Prime Days, and permanent discount ecosystems like Temu and Shein have done their job: they’ve trained shoppers to assume everything will be on sale, all the time.
There’s no urgency left.
“Black Friday used to be the highlight of the sales year. Today, retailers live in a permanent state of discount promotions,” — Dave Smallwood, Mollie
That exhaustion is starting to show up in behaviour too. In the UK,
76.79% of independent retailers
boycotted Black Friday altogether, up from
69%
last year, citing squeezed margins and “unsustainable” pressure to constantly discount. And where do we go from here? Agents will surely be on this mandate too. Right? But we will have other variables. Yeah right.
I never intended to soil these halls. - Cousin Greg.
Marshal Cohen
of
Circana
a nailed the mood:
“We’ve kind of put ourselves in an interesting position of making Black Friday very important, but not as engaged and not a frenzy and not as much of a purchase urgency that we’ve seen in years past.”
And the “meh” feeling on the deals? That is not just my sat in Kerry point of view:
Average discounts slipped from
35% in November 2024
to
34% in November 2025
.
Electronics peaked at
29% off
, down from
30.1%
the prior year.
The promotional landscape has flattened into beige. Everything is “on sale” and nothing feels special.
When Shopify Went Dark: Do Rails Still Matter?
Then came Cyber Monday’s jump scare. At
6:45 a.m. PT
, right in the teeth of one of the biggest online shopping days of the year,
Shopify went down
.
Merchants couldn’t log in.
Point-of-sale systems froze.
Admin dashboards simply disappeared.
Downdetector recorded roughly
4,000 outage reports in the U.S.
and
2,500 in the UK
at the peak. The culprit: a failed
login authentication flow
that locked merchants out of their own operations for about
5.5 hours
. These numbers are not equivalent to huge % of thier merchant base, but still to each of them, this was what they had been building up to. This is the biggest deadl, they are /were the biggest loser.
One merchant summed it up bluntly:
“Shopify going down on Cyber Monday has got to be one of the biggest fails of the year.”
Markets noticed. Shopify’s stock fell
3.8–3.9%
following the incident. Estimated merchant revenue losses landed somewhere between
$15–30 million
. Shopify acknowledged the issue by mid-afternoon and reported recovery, but the real damage was psychological:
Merchant trust took a hit.
Investor nerves were rattled.
And everyone was reminded how much of ecommerce is now single point-of-failure infrastructure. But that is changing. We are developing standards and protocols.
Does this break Shopify long term? Probably not. The platform still powers
over 10% of all U.S. ecommerce transactions
.
But symbolically, it matters. A company who has placed so much strategic emphasis on POS as a lever will face many questions about its reliability at the negotiating table next year. I am sure the team as Estee Lauder had a few nervous chuckles throughout the day. Latency at checkouts is not something retailers love, because, we the consumer, hate a line.Their response was in stark contrast to their drum banging about big numbers everywhere and I expect that they will say it is much ado about nothing and file this along side their tariff commentary this year.
Negotiate a bit of a Gregxit.
The rails of the last era of ecommerce briefly buckled under pressure, right as the rails of the
next
era, built on agents and AI interfaces, carried on unaffected.
The Agentic Takeover: When AI Starts Taking Credit for Everything
This for me, is where the story flips.
It seemed like traditional ecommerce metrics stagnated yet
AI metrics went vertical
. And I am sure we haven't even heard all these tales yet. JK Rowling could be brought in, but I would love to see MIchael Lewis get his hands on them.
A few numbers:
AI traffic to U.S. retail websites surged
805% year-over-year
(Adobe).
Traffic from AI-powered sources like
ChatGPT
and
Perplexity
increased
752% vs October 2024
(BrightEdge).
Salesforce reported that
AI agents influenced $14.2 billion in global sales on Black Friday alone
.
Shoppers arriving via AI services were
38% more likely to convert
than non-AI traffic.
In other words: the “who sent this customer?” question is increasingly being answered not with “email”, “search”, or “social”, but “some agent”.
And then there’s
Amazon Rufus
.
250 million customers
used Rufus in 2025.
Monthly active users:
+149% YoY.
Interactions:
+210% YoY.
On Black Friday:
Amazon sessions that used Rufus
and resulted in a purchase
doubled (
+100%
) vs the trailing 30 days.Sessions
without
Rufus were up only
20%.
Amazon projects Rufus will generate
$10 billion in incremental annual sales
. Rufus isn’t just a helpful search box anymore. Bopring and repetitive as it it, It now:
Remembers your account and context.
Adds items directly to cart.
Tracks prices over
30- and 90-day
windows.
Uses
Lens Live
for visual search.
And offers a
“Buy for Me”
feature that can purchase from
non-Amazon merchants
on your behalf.
This is no longer a recommendation engine.As Salesforce’s Caila Schwartz put it:
“This holiday season proves that AI is no longer just a cost-saver it’s now a major revenue engine.”
We’ve crossed a line: AI is no longer just advising the shopper; in many cases it’s doing the shopping.
Says who? There are so many questions to be answered here but with so many platforms building the narrative will this go away. And begs a question for me is an Agentic sale = to an ecommerce sale? Are they reported to differently? As OpenAI prepare to open the ads floodgates, I think 2026 will be as much about the revenue landgrab over attribution as something we need to trouble ourselves with.
If it is to be said, so it be, so it is.
TripleWhale Meet MobyDick.
Thomas Friedman Was Right (Again)
If this all feels bigger than “some new tools”, that’s because it is. Thomas Friedman saw this coming almost a decade ago.
What am I gonna do with a soul anyways?
In
Thank You for Being Late
, published in
2016
(first version in 2014), Friedman argued that
2007
was:
“the single greatest technological inflection point since Gutenberg.”
He pointed to what incredible emergences were  clustered around that year:
The
iPhone
Android
YouTube
being acquired by Google
Facebook
going global
Twitter
launching its own platform
IBM’s Watson
stepping into the spotlight
The
Kindle
The birth of
AWS
as the backbone of the cloud
The concept for
Airbnb
And the internet crossing
one billion users
And the Spice Girls had a reunion. Which mirrors today - Spooky.
That cocktail, he argued, had reset the speed of the whole system.
But Friedman’s more important move was
what came after the bang
. He described
three giant accelerations
reshaping society:
Technology
– driven by
Moore’s Law
, making computing exponentially cheaper and more powerful.
The Market
– globalization, connecting more people and businesses into one interdependent system.
Mother Nature
– climate change and environmental stress acting as another accelerating force.
His central challenge for the coming era was simple and brutal:
How do we turn
AI into IA
,
Intelligent Assistance
,
Intelligent Assistants
and
Intelligent Algorithms
, so more workers and consumers can ride the curve rather than be crushed by it?
He was articulated 11 years ago what is happening now. It was not if, it was when. The groundwork is done. Our Laborforce is being redefined and the way we need to loOtherwise ok forward along with it.Otherwise, they do, eat our lunch.
The future of workforce development must embrace intelligent algorithms to bridge the gap between skills and labor market demands. By focusing on mastery and providing access to critical resources, we can unlock potential talent that traditional systems may overlook.
That question, asked around
2014–2016
, has a partial answer now.
The AI-to-IA transition Friedman imagined is
manifesting in commerce first
—in the form of
agentic systems
:
Rufus
dadds to cart, tracks prices, and completes purchases.
ChatGPT’s Instant Checkout
transacts.
This is the logical endpoint of his thesis: not just smarter software, but
software with agency in commercial flows
.
Later in the book, Friedman warns that technology will accelerate:
“at a pace the average human cannot keep up with”
and argues that our task is to:
“learn faster and govern smarter”
if we want any hope of matching that acceleration.
Black Friday 2025 is what it looks like when the technology outruns our measurement, our attribution models, and maybe our mental models of how commerce works.
When I think about this, it frames where we need to be in 2026. Our job involves long term thinking, historically first and then we switch to the short term. Friedman lights the way.
The workforce is undergoing a transformation not due to automation alone, but due to the need for innovation in labor, education, and lifelong learning. An honest conversation about the future of work is necessary as we move away from outdated expectations of job security and stable middle-class jobs.
Changing Landscape of Work Historically, it was possible for average workers to secure good livelihoods through typical education and hard work, but this era is ending. The traditional pathways to stable middle-class jobs are diminishing, compounded by rapid innovations and the globalization of labor markets.
Workers today must navigate a landscape where being average is insufficient. Reimagining Skills and Learning In this new economy, individuals must commit to lifelong learning. Those who succeed will need to adapt and enhance their skills continuously to remain relevant. Self-motivation, creativity, collaboration, and essential technical skills have become paramount for future success in the labor market.
Rethinking Social Contracts To thrive, we need to rethink the social contracts among students, educators, employers, and governments. This involves recognizing human capital as a key asset and investing in it across all levels. Every participant must engage in mutual understanding and support to prepare for the challenges ahead. Emergence of Intelligent Assistance Intelligent technologies must be harnessed to create intelligent assistance that can enhance learning and job performance.
Companies like AT&T exemplify this through platforms that support lifelong learning and help workers adapt to new job requirements while providing a framework for skill development. Case Studies of Success Programs like LearnUp and LaunchCode exemplify how intelligent networks and algorithms can assist job seekers in acquiring the necessary skills and securing employment without traditional degrees.
These platforms emphasize mastery over credentials, making it possible for individuals to demonstrate their skills and find suitable employment.
The Losers: The Consumer and Traditional Attribution
I have of late decided not to tarry too much with hope.
Retail Dive called it plainly: the biggest Black Friday loser this year was
the consumer
.
Shoppers paid
7% more
for the same goods.
They bought
fewer units.
Discounts were flat to slightly worse.
And they leaned harder into debt to make it all work.
Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL)
use hit
$747.5 million on Black Friday alone
(+
8.9% YoY
). Adobe projects
$20.2 billion
in BNPL spending over the full holiday period—up
11%
from 2024.
Meanwhile,
FICO
plans to start integrating BNPL data into credit scores from this fall. Today’s “easy” instalment plan is tomorrow’s reduced borrowing capacity.
The second big loser is
traditional ecommerce attribution
.
73% of customers
now use multiple channels during their shopping journeys.
AI is increasingly mediating those journeys—researching, recommending, and even transacting within a single conversational interface.
The old playbook was:
See ad → click thing → buy thing → credit the last click.
That world is gone.
As one analysis put it:
“Just because something is easy to measure doesn’t mean it’s driving growth. Most marketing attribution models overvalue channels with clear click-through paths and undervalue the marketing activities that shape demand.”
Now imagine:
A shopper asks ChatGPT for gift ideas.
Gets a recommendation.
Clicks through to Amazon.
Uses Rufus to refine options.
Lets an AI agent handle the purchase timing based on price tracking.
The order is routed, fulfilled, and updated by logistics AI.
Who gets the credit?
The retailer?
The marketplace?
The agent?
The original content that inspired the query?
This is where the 2026 Media Battle is won.
When the entire journey lives inside agents and platforms that don’t neatly expose “clicks”,
the existing attribution infrastructure goes blind
.
The Shift Is Here: Two Scoreboards, Two Realities
Hanging around, like the threat of nuclear war.
Put the traditional metrics and the agentic metrics side by side:
Traditional Commerce Metrics – 2025 Black Friday/Cyber Period
Order Volume: -1% YoY
Units Per Transaction: -2% YoY
In-Store Traffic: -3.6% YoY
Discount Rates: flat at 28%
Agentic Commerce Metrics – 2025 Black Friday
AI Traffic to Retail Sites
:
+805% YoY
AI Referrals (ChatGPT/Perplexity)
:
+752% vs October 2024
AI-Influenced Global Sales
:
$14.2B on Black Friday
Amazon Rufus Users
:
250M
,
+149% MAU
,
+210% interactions
Conversion via AI Traffic
:
+38% vs non-AI traffic
The dollars grew because
prices went up
and
AI drove conversion
. The human signals of demand—
units, orders, footfall
—shrunk.
Friedman warned that technology would race ahead:
“at a pace the average human cannot keep up with”
The real question he posed was whether we could:
“learn faster and govern smarter”
to keep our institutions, our regulations, and our mental models from falling too far behind. Black Friday 2025 says, quite clearly:
commerce has already moved on
, even if our dashboards haven’t. Most probably because the Shopify outage won’t let you. Sorry, I will stop that now.
Shopify’s Cyber Monday outage is the metaphor of the moment: the infrastructure that powered the last era of ecommerce briefly failed under strain. The agents? They just kept shopping.
Where This Leaves Us: Commerce, Kicked to the Curb
I hope this wasn’t just another Black Friday recap. :
Traditional ecommerce and its attribution frameworks didn’t die this weekend
but now there are questions without answers.
Agents stole the scene but, did they?
We are moving, from
consumer-driven commerce
to
agent-mediated commerce
. Fu*ck, has it come to this? The consumer still “decides”, technically. But more and more, those decisions are being framed, filtered, sequenced, and sometimes executed by systems that sit between the human and the brand.
For retailers, marketers, and platform builders, the question going into 2026 isn’t:
“What was our Black Friday ROAS?”
It’s:
Are we still optimising for clicks and channels, or are we designing for a world where most of our customers’ decisions are mediated by agents that don’t care about our funnel at all?
Black Friday 2025 may be remembered as:
The weekend the consumer
paid more and got less
,
The weekend
retailers felt exhausted and discounts felt beige
,
And quietly, the weekend
commerce changed hands
.
2026, I declare you the year of Boar on the Floor.

title: 2025 Gaslit everyone.
pullQuotes: “How do we compete in a world where consumers now expect this level of agility and cultural fluency?”
excerpt: Art and Commerce converged to tell a tale. A look at the top 100 songs according to Rolling Stone for 2025 makes it seem like our artists were one step ahead of us. Thought artists usually are, right? They soundtracked the year giving us more
_body:
Art and Commerce converged to tell a tale.
A look at the top 100 songs according to Rolling Stone for 2025 makes it seem like our artists were one step ahead of us. Thought artists usually are, right? They soundtracked the year giving us more than the Demon Hunters Kpop earworms Soda Pop or Golden (try get them outta your head now). But Here are some of the eye catching titles, even though, I admit, to not listening to all of them:
End of the World
- Miley Cyrus. In her own unique fashion, this is an Ode to her Mom. But it was the most played song of April 2025.
Lost in Translatio
n - Kasey Musgraves - providing a cross cultural love tune.
Loco
- Netón Vega - A cyclical tune much like a recession which doesn't happen.
RunitUp
- Humankind - the consumer credit story of the year.
Anxiety
- Doechii - the score to the consumer sentiment, or so we thought, those crafty buggers, they just kept running it up. Apparently this was written in 2019 and didn’t get the pick up it needed so the rerelease was needed. The back catalogue as we call it. Nice if you can get away with it - many did.
There are so many more I could have used, the Lambrini girls were right on the nose with their song earlier this year. We also had straight line was a lie, a cop out track for all the removed forecasts in Q3/4 and
Incomprehensible
- the Flexport musical.
We are into the top 50 now, so sit up straight as we get to the good stuff.
Imaginary Playerz
, a Cardi B banger which summed up the Platform switching narrative for ecommerce in 2025.
Elderberry Wine and Pour the Henny
for all the battered agency front liners still trying to beat the Algo on December 9th 2025.
Earlier this year, which seems like a fog, but we had Guiturricadelafuente drop the tune,
POrt Pelegri
, which was apparently a notional safe haven for inbound stock that knew not where to drop stock during the Tariff Wars. Symbolical and practical this port was the one place where growth went to live, not die.
Stateside
and
Don’t let the bastards get you down
were Irish Rebel songs that were written by Warehouse operatives during this turbulent period also. Just kidding, but they could have been, thank you Margo Price.
Yamaha, Sports Car
and
Nokia
were nostalgic tunes reminding us of the place that consumerism occupies in all of our wallets. The Weekend gave all PE backed brand owners their private anthem -
Cry for Me
. How do we work with them at all is the Christmas version, a TikTok sensation.
Back to friends
by Sombr was the post coital message sent by DJT to all who crossed him and came back when the booty call inevitably came a few weeks later. Pharrell prodigies Clipse maybe had what should be our closing line,
So be It
- AKA Amen in Bible speak. This is the hand we are dealt, now play ball.
We are into the top 20 now and gaining pace to see what was the gas light song of the year as seen through ecommerce.
Sally, When the wine runs out
a reminder that there are generations living better and without the fear of Kombucha. Hayley Williams went old-school with “
Mirtazapine
” highlighting the impact of GLP 1 on retail sales and how grateful we are for all that excess skin on display.
No list of songs of the year would be complete without Sabrina Carpenter -
Manchild
was a powerful pop number about someone with too much power, too many decisions to make and many of them self serving. Who could it be? The art is is your own answer. Swiftie gave us her Eras tour, not just one song, but a reminder of how modern economics works.
At 5, it’s Kehlani with
Folded
, that is the reiterate the feeling we all had around discounting this Black Friday. Isn’t everyone else doing it? And at 1 it is
Abracadabra
by Gaga, who else a song about the magic of margin protection, one minute it’s there, the next, it’s gone. Like magic.
Songs of the year tell us one side of the coin, but we do need to look deeper. Gartner cannot point us there, even though they try, not with huge effort, but they try. Then all of the platforms and technologies telling us how great they are through data threy produce. About as useful as the Klaviyo attribution modelling, but these are not the stories we should be looking to. Yes, they might justify some investment stories for you, or benchmark you but what are, us consumers, doing that we should be paying attention to.
2025. The Year the Consumer Took Back the steering Wheel
Why 2026, and everything that comes after, belongs to behaviour, not technology.
Every December, commerce does what commerce always does: it gazes lovingly at its dashboards and declares that the future will be determined by whoever ships the most AI features, lands the biggest retail-media deals, or bulks up their platform roadmap with enough slides to blind an IKEA lighting department. (Now on sale at 35% off * does not apply to all ranges). It’s comforting, in its own way. Technology promises certainty. Dashboards promise control. Roadmaps promise linearity in a world that’s anything but. But that’s th new normal, non linear behaviour. Means that tracking that course needs to change too.
And yet one of the most important documents I’ve read for 2026 is not a tech forecast at all. It's a behaviour map. A psychological climate report. A mirror held up to the people who actually decide the fate of our industry: we the consumer. We have this strange dichotomy: we act one way yet train ourselves to think in another altogether.
Euromonitor International
’s
Top Global Consumer Trends 2026
is everything most trend reports are not. It is not vibes-based. It is not stitched-together conference rhetoric. It is not a series of hopeful predictions wearing the jacket of data. It is a rigorously constructed, globally sampled, cross-verified survey-led analysis across 40 markets, 5 major longitudinal consumer datasets, and category-level spend intelligence sweeping every region and income band. It’s the opposite of wishful thinking.
And this matters, because brand leaders right now, if we’re being honest, are tired. Not in the melodramatic “burnout” sense, but in the slow erosion way. If this were a song, there are plenty of ideas up above, but I digress, as usually, I do. They are planning for a future that refuses to stay still for longer than a quarter. Burdened by marketing by accounting cycle - that is what reporting has become. Not to decry the importance of control and planning and certainty. But marketing effectiveness does not fit in this precise way. Square peg, meet round hole. They’re trying to answer boardroom demands with tools that feel increasingly divorced from lived human behaviour. They’re trying to decipher signal from noise in a world where noise
is
the signal.
So this report lands as a reminder that the centre of gravity has always lived with the human being clicking the button, closing the tab, ignoring the push notification, doom-spending at midnight, or unsubscribing in a fit of clarity. Although the little Agentic Elf in me suggests differently. Elves, what do they know?
This isn’t a story about 2026.  It’s a story about who gets to define the next decade in commerce. A paradigm shift, a power struggle, the space where the Boar on the Floor squeals and we all watch on. Spoiler Alert: it’s no longer the platform.
Comfort Zone ,  When a Global Population Quietly Says “No More”
The report opens with a statistic that should stop any ambitious brand strategist mid-slide:
58% of consumers now report moderate to extreme daily stress
, and
two in five
feel under
constant
pressure just to keep life moving. Not occasionally. Not seasonally. Constantly. I think I am one of those people, but I do it like the duck.
That line hit me like a hammer because it mirrors something I’ve heard all year in founder conversations, podcast interviews, DMs and conference corridors: people are
tired of performing competence
. Tired of pretending to be optimised. Tired of living inside productivity theatre. Pause for a moment the word constant means our work has to be relentless just to keep up. No one day is good enough, no one hour. We are the constant.
Euromonitor’s data shows that roughly two-thirds of consumers now actively seek to simplify their lives, not as a lifestyle flex but as a coping mechanism. Homes becoming havens. Routines becoming rituals. Spending shifting toward protection and emotional quiet. The
USD 377.2B
global market for "natural" products? That’s not a trend, it’s a search for safety. And more than
2 million tonnes
of botanicals worked their way into products in 2025. That’s not wellness. That’s soothing at scale. But there is the opportunity, in ritual, we find patterns, in patterns we can earn loyalty.
This is the world brands must design for: one where clarity is worth more than innovation, and where “less but better” is not minimalism but self-preservation.
The long arc here, beyond 2026, is the slow erosion of optimisation culture. A decade from now, the winners will be the brands that relieved pressure, not the brands that applied it. But Agentism is going to do this for me, right> ?
Fiercely Unfiltered ,  Authenticity Becomes an Operating Condition
If “Comfort Zone” is the global softening, “Fiercely Unfiltered” is the sharpening. Nearly half of consumers want to be distinct from others. Two-thirds feel comfortable expressing their identity openly. And only
15%
still define beauty as “being accepted.” Acceptance has lost its value; comfort has taken its place. Go figure out your cohorts now.
This aligns with something I’ve written about repeatedly: the rebellion against the curated, the polished, the “strategised.” In
Clueless & Dope-Sick
, in
Seduction of Efficiency
, in
Grosse Pointe Blank
, you’ve argued that we live in a time when artifice collapses quickly because reality leaks through every crack. These are movies or TV shows and also aspects of my substack posting this year.
Euromonitor’s numbers confirm it. I am not mad. Read on.  Consumers are
demanding
authenticity. More than half now say they only buy from brands they fully trust. And they’re behaving accordingly: BNPL balances rising globally; livestream commerce growing because it feels like belonging, not retail; TikTok Shop converting not through funnels but through resonance.This is  a cultural correction. A revolt against perfection. Thank God, I don’t use spell check or take notes. Never have, never will, never will get that job as a result. For brand leaders planning beyond 2026, this is the existential question:
Can your brand afford to become more honest than it’s comfortable with?
Is it better to burn out, than fade away?.
Rewired Wellness ,  The Clinic Moves Into the Living Room
This is the most consequential shift in the entire report. Wellness is no longer scented candles and step counts. It is clinical. It is measurable. It is increasingly pharmaceutical. Aura, Whoop and countless others occupy this space well. Think of  your last few conferences even, the early morning founder jogs, the 0.0 beers and mocktails. The need for a game of Padel or Pickleball, just why?
Three in four
consumers now track some aspect of their health, and around
35%
say their current approach to wellbeing “isn’t working.” Wellbeing is needed as we have somehow meleded life and work into one fixed space and do not know other ways out of it.
That line alone should frighten every incumbent category leader, because it means consumers are
open to alternatives
. GLP-1 usage among people trying to lose weight rose from 6% to 9% in a single year. Dermocosmetics are growing at double-digit rates everywhere. More than
600
dermatologically tested products launched online in 12 months. Global spend on health goods will hit
USD 6.9 trillion
in 2026.Thisconvergence: beauty + health + nutrition + tech. The borders between categories are dissolving like sugar under hot water. But of course, you can have as much sugar as you want now because of GLP 1 - whatever happened to everything in moderation?
This is the beginning, not the middle, of the next decade’s commercial reordering.
The brand leaders who thrive past 2030 won’t be the ones with the best marketing, they’ll be the ones with: • scientific validation, • real-time data feedback loops, • clinical partnerships, • and product roadmaps that behave more like medical devices than FMCG items.
The Next Asian Wave ,  Cultural Gravity Rewrites Itself
Ccultural power has already shifted, and commerce is only now catching up. I was not as tuned into this as I should be, that crossover provides signals for arbitrage everywhere. What it does not mean is that we all need a metaverse presence to go with our WEB 3.0 thinkpiece or worse still our Christmas 2025 Roblox mash up. It means we need to be aware and able to action. Cliches are true. We see this play out on the AI playing field - the winners have already been here, slaying the little guy for years. Biding their time, hiding in the bushes ready to pounce. While many are taking about building new data centres to handle all this compute across North America, Sundar Pichai casually mentions, at every opportunity now how Googles data centre future will be orbiting us.
Two in three consumers say experiencing other cultures is important. More than 60% say international products are more available than ever. Asian-origin content dominates entertainment. And Chinese brands are reshaping global categories from beauty to EVs.
The real story, though, is structural: China’s exports are projected to reach
USD 4 trillion
in 2026. Its cross-border retail e-commerce is projected to hit
USD 139.5B
. And four of the world’s top five ecommerce retailers are now Chinese. TikTok Shop, SHEIN and Temu are not anomalies, they are heralds prophets for profits to drive some good business insider level material..
The next decade belongs to brands that understand: • speed is a strategy • culture is infrastructure • price-value equations can be rewritten overnight • and mobile-first isn’t a vertical, it’s the whole court
Brand leaders need to stop asking “How do we compete with Chinese platforms?” and start asking
“How do we compete in a world where consumers now expect this level of agility and cultural fluency?”
Why This Report Matters More Than Any Platform Roadmap
Euromonitor’s data is trustworthy because its methodology is transparent, global, longitudinal and verified. It is built from tens of thousands of respondents, nested sampling, on-the-ground analysts, and multi-market input. It is not speculation. It is measurement. It is behavioural truth at scale. And that’s why this report is helpful more for your long-term planning than any AI update or product release note.
Because the next decade will not be shaped by which companies build the best features. It will be shaped by:
• whether people feel overwhelmed; • whether they feel seen; • whether they trust brands with their bodies; • and whether they feel culture is speaking to them or past them.
In simple terms, those who listen better and act as a result.The companies that thrive beyond 2026 will be those that understand this:
Technology’s job is to follow behaviour.
Commerce’s job is to listen before it builds.
And brand leadership’s job is to set strategy at the speed of humanity, not the speed of hype.

excerpt: Shopify Editions 2025. It’s not what you said, it’s the way that you said it. Raw notes here, I have not styled them. I think this signals a real challenge for agencies and app providers. Where is the ability to earn revenue. It can be
_body:
Shopify Editions 2025. It’s not what you said, it’s the way that you said it. Raw notes here, I have not styled them.  I think this signals a real challenge for agencies and app providers. Where is the ability to earn revenue. It can be argued the billable hours model was terrible anyway, but if you are an agency owner, was it? Couple this with how Shopify said the commission fees are now going to be linked to long term performance. The days of the agency as we know it are coming to a close, more quickly than we know it. It is not to say merchants do not need support, but the role that agencies or SIs play is changing dramatically.
Also, what are Shopify saying about the org chart as we look 3 years ahead? In this model, it is smaller, and more rules based. AAll those years of accountancy based marketing is setting us up for rules based selling, if we want it. Rules don’t give us everything we want. Shopify Editions - Sidekick has been unreliable and inaccurate - part of its problem.
Rollouts and the ability to AB test means we have got to think about our role as traders or merchants. It means the idea of agentic is in the hands of the brand, not the consumer, yet. But it is priming itself for this. Range extensions and Shopify catalog point to a few things, 1 their partnership with Mirakl. How long before we see merchants selling via each other and earning out on the sale. Mirakl’s recent partnership has gone with a whimper rather than a roar. Combined with invoicing changes and inventory handling, this looks more like an ad exchange. Good merchants will know that this is a challenge to the way the categorise and cross sell.
Tis the season to collab. Comment from Amanda -
"You can instantly sell demand to your customers. Demand is changing. "
We are seeing a change in the way that we put product discovery together, the speed at which it occurs and the non linear relationship we now have. Retargeting budgets could take a bashing were this to be a successful scaling tool. Also paints a new light for the affiliate world. The best affiliate network may be your brands ability to build trust to share other experiences within your lifestyle portfolio.
The way the product is presented is not for enterprise level brands which massive catalogs. It is ideal for narrow range brand owners who have choices - do we extend our category reach, do we lean on the shoulders of others. In a day trading world, this is helpful, dynamically created products reduce the load on the site and remove your opportunity loss of not having the product. In a parallel universe, it forces us to think about the long term brand future. Example of a fast scaling single category FMCG brand, think Harry’s razors.
Your valuation will depend on many factors but one of those, is your ability to cross pollinate other categories and geographies. Removing this strategically will mean lower valuations. Hurrah, I hear you say. But this can, for the discerning among you talk to demand forecasting and product validation. Your role as a brand owner will be determining this. It also said you can manage the placement.
In kickstarter world, we saw , in our brand a 50% upsell ration in post sales cross selling. This is now being opened up to us. Huge new territories for us all. Weirdly, the successful kickstarter brands will relish this new world. Live AB testing and budget allocation. Cross pollination and designing instant store workflows for users. it is how Kickstarter has always behaved. IYKYK.
The commission payout challenge - who is paying, it looks like Shopify but redeploying that revenue to pay for your ads on your next campaign sounds like Shopify is trying to ringfence the experience. RMN much. Sidekick pulse will be interesting. The accuracy and reliability of sidekick today is less than brilliant, even by Shopify’s good enough standards. Pulse would want to do more than wake you up with some great ideas. It needs to at least let you sleep well knowing you trust the execution of said ideas. And what of disputes. I took action X expecting this outcome, but it didn’t happen, what then? Shopify support will not want to handle this. I expect agencies to be bullishly fired only to be hired back in. The chaos that will ensure for many SMBs cannot be understated.
Workflows too - always seem simple, made look simple. But writing and describing logic is still something best left to experts. Real experts. Workflows will get easier, because Sidekick says so, right? But I defined my own loyalty app - why can my customers not redeem their points, cash, rewards? Ask Jeeves.
Didn’t you use Simgym? tut tut .
The world of design and building is undoubtedly changing, not for the better in every case but maybe this is a good thing. For years we floundered on general conversion rates that don’t set the world on fire, but conversely Amazon have done sweet FA to their UX without huge damage. Function versus Form, function wins, just like sex panther.
A well observed point about agentic (not mine, but many other, better voices than mine) but a genuine opening for impactful change - opening up the MCP and designing for agentic means that not just product data needs updating, but policies can be rewritten or written for the first time. It means your reviews, your customer service queries not can be called on to deliver into the agentic display. Early wins will be those who adopt and refine here. Others will use MCP to change their product flow to make them more useful in early discover. Now all we need is customers to buy from their agents, easy right?
Tinker, haven’t Temu done this for a long time. Offline - HUb - stay connected always. Probably why nothing was said while latency dropped during cyber monday etc But this is useful, even just this is useful. Other interesting and useful points, Shop Pay BNPL coming to the UK and a Klarna expansion across the EU - give the consumer what they need so they can buy what they want. Next gen ready. Shopify capital expands much to the annoyance of some commentators, but the malaise of others.
For years, part of the strength of Shopify was their eco systems ability and willingness to spread their message. This output will leave many scratching their heads IMO. Where is our future and does Shopify really care. The people commentating are people like me, with little skin in the game. It used to be the ecosystem did the heavy lifting. Now they have real heavy lifting to do. Pinch of salt required as always and their will be the hurrah for everything crew.
Remember Alex Baldwin in Friends Phoebes boyfriend? Yeah, I forgot him too.
Parker, thanks for the memories.

title: To AI: The Cause of, and Solution to, All of Commerce’s Problems
