_body:
On this day in 1989 a seismic shift in culture and entertainment occurred, the Simpsons was born. The episode was titled Simpsons roasting on an open Fire and thankfully it was a Christmas episode. Now, purists will tell me about Tracy Ullman show, but this was the full episodic length show. 30 minutes long. Here we are 36 years later looking to Homer and the family for inspiration, direction and for a laugh.
The Simpsons has functioned as a funhouse mirror for modern life: exaggerating our politics, families, and institutions just enough that their absurdity snaps into focus, while accidentally feeling more prophetic the longer it runs. Sadly and ironically at times.  It helped invent a smarter, more cynical, more reference‑dense style of comedy that now underpins everything from Family Guy to contemporary prestige sitcoms. In case you didn’t notice, I reference it, ALOT.
Holding a mirror to us
From the start, Springfield was built as a microcosm of America: a town where environmental disasters, corrupt politicians, corporate greed, media sensationalism, and religious hypocrisy all sit a block apart from a fairly ordinary family. Episodes routinely tackled topics like pollution (“Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish”), consumerism (“Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy”), immigration (“Much Apu About Nothing”), and gay rights (“Homer’s Phobia”) long before they were default TV fare.
The show’s genius is that kids could laugh at slapstick while adults caught the jokes about Fox News, culture wars, and failing public institutions, training viewers to see politics and media with a skeptical eye. That tone helped normalize a more openly cynical, “of course the system is rigged” attitude that now feels baked into online culture and late‑night comedy.
The “predictions” phenomenon
The “Simpsons predicted it” meme works because the show has produced thousands of hyper‑specific gags about tech, politics, and culture over three decades; enough darts and some will hit the board. But some episodes are strikingly on‑the‑nose:
“Bart to the Future” (Season 11, 2000) casually mentions Donald Trump as a former U.S. president, years before his real‑world election.
“Lisa’s Wedding” (Season 6) imagines video calling on a hybrid phone‑screen device that looks uncannily like modern FaceTime.
“Lisa the Greek” (Season 3) correctly tracks multiple Super Bowl winners via re‑dubbed dialogue over several years, turning a character bit into a minor sports‑prediction legend.
“Marge in Chains” (Season 4) shows a flu‑like virus, panic buying, and an angry mob breaking open a crate of “killer bees,” later read as echoing Covid‑era shortages and murder‑hornet headlines.
Many more have followed since, but when you think of the job of the writers - “think of the most absurd outcome for this possibility”, this is where we end up.
And what looks like clairvoyance is mostly sharp satire plus a huge sample size, but it also underscores how often the show anticipated the logical endpoint of trends in politics, media, and technology.
It’s writers were not your average Motley crew.
Al Jean: Graduated from Harvard University with a bachelor’s degree in mathematics at age 16 and served as executive producer and head writer.
David S. Cohen (David X. Cohen): Earned a bachelor’s degree in physics from Harvard University and a master’s in computer science from UC Berkeley; he later co-created
Futurama
with Matt Groening.
Ken Keeler: Holds a bachelor’s and a PhD in applied mathematics from Harvard University, as well as a master’s in electrical engineering from Stanford.
Jeff Westbrook: Resigned from a senior research post as an associate professor at Yale University to write for the show. He has a PhD in computer science from Princeton University.
Bill Odenkirk: Earned a PhD in inorganic chemistry from the University of Chicago.
Matt Groening: The show’s creator, attended The Evergreen State College, where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in journalism and was the editor of the school newspaper.
Conan O’Brien: The former late-night host and a former writer for the show, graduated
magna cum laude
from Harvard University with a degree in history and literature
Its place in society
By the late 1990s, The Simpsons had gone from “bad role model” (banned T‑shirts, George H. W. Bush’s jab that families should be “more like the Waltons and less like the Simpsons”) to canonical Americana. It reshaped TV comedy with dense pop‑culture references, rapid‑fire gags, and emotional beats that treated animated characters as fully human, a template that shows like Futurama, South Park, and BoJack Horseman build on.
It also rewired everyday language: “D’oh!” entered dictionaries, and words like “cromulent” and “embiggen” escaped into real‑world usage, evidence of how deeply the show invaded the vernacular. After 30‑plus seasons, The Simpsons functions almost like a cultural operating system: a shared reference set people use to talk about politics, work, family, and the feeling that everything is a bit rigged and ridiculous.
Black Mirror Time - Simpsons Quotes:  where we are as a society
Below are quotes that double as social barometer, lines you can almost drop straight onto a Twitter/X feed or a political stump speech and they still land.
Homer Simpson
“Just because I don’t care doesn’t mean I don’t understand.”
“I’m not a bad guy! I work hard, and I love my kids. So why should I spend half my Sunday hearing about how I’m going to hell?”
“Alcohol: the cause of, and solution to, all of life’s problems.”
“If something’s hard to do, then it’s not worth doing.”
“Trying is the first step toward failure.”
Mayor Quimby
“I stand by my racial slur.”
“I’d like to remind everyone that I was elected by the narrowest of margins, and I can be replaced just as easily.”
“I propose that I use what’s left of the town treasury to move to a more prosperous town and run for mayor there. Once elected, I will send for the rest of you.”
“This time he’s the lesser of two evils.” (Campaign slogan.)
Moe Szyslak
“I’m better than dirt. Well, most kinds of dirt. Not that fancy store‑bought dirt. That stuff’s loaded with nutrients. I can’t compete with that.”
“Oh, loneliness and cheeseburgers are a dangerous mix.”
“I’ve done things I’m not proud of, and the things I am proud of are disgusting.”
“Good God! Homer, you know I support most any prejudice you can name, but your hero‑phobia sickens me.”
Taken together, those quotes and episodes sketch out the show’s core thesis: we are ridiculous, frequently venal, often lazy or corrupt, but also recognizably human and the systems around us are only as absurd as we let them be.
The Simpsons, to me is one of those moments of where a notable shift occurred. Today, Dec 17th 2025, we are in the midst of many more, one most notable being AI. Sadly, it is the misuse of the technology that is becoming the palace that energy goes and for all the wrong reasons. Imagine we realised the technology capabilities as a society and moved to harvest it for good. I am sure, at some point we will do this though. Right?
In ecommerce our job now is to live amidst all of this and make sense of it all in ways that are useful to our lifestyle and that pave the path to glory. Or at least for now survival. 2025 provided some things to note that are more shift that trend to me.
The Seven Allocation Shocks: How 2025 Rewired Where Ecommerce GMV Actually Went
There is a difference between a trend and a shift. I spoke about this before. In Sean Dowling’s economics class in September of 198, I was first introduced to the topic.
A shift in economics refers to a change in an entire curve (such as supply or demand) caused by an external factor other than the price of the good itself, leading to a new equilibrium. A trend, on the other hand, describes a long-term, underlying direction or general movement in economic data, such as a steady increase in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over a period of many years, often reflecting fundamental changes in the economy.
This year we experienced both, all at the same time. This, I realised, is the job. Operating on both of these curves, always and forever.
If you only looked at topline ecommerce numbers in 2025, you could convince yourself not much changed. Growth was… fine. Nothing like the 2020‑2021 sugar high, but not a catastrophe either. A sort of stubborn, grinding normality. Thank you discounting and BNPL (who we will hear from later).
But spend five minutes inside a P&L or a data warehouse and it’s obvious something else was going on.  GMV didn’t just “grow”. It rerouted. It slipped out of some hands and into others, often without anyone really noticing until the quarter was over and someone in finance started asking awkward questions.
What follows is my tour through the seven big stories that actually shaped where the money went this year:
Agentic AI stopped being a slide and started quietly routing demand.
Tariffs and the death of
de minimis
broke the ultra‑cheap China model.
Marketplaces pivoted into “local” to survive that shock.
BNPL’s regulatory hangover changed how carts were financed.
Retail media turned shelf space into an auction.
Cross‑border got risk‑priced; inventory got closer to home.
AI‑powered owned sites tried to fight back against marketplace gravity.
If you’re a brand, retailer, or marketplace operator, the question is no longer “is ecommerce growing?” but “who is the new traffic cop, and what are they optimizing for?”
Let’s get into it.
Agentic AI: When the Shopper Isn’t Really the Shopper Anymore
Somewhere around mid‑2025, shopping agents stopped being a demo and started showing up in real traffic logs.  Not as a big bang, not as “everyone now uses an AI concierge,” but as a steady rise of odd‑looking sessions: cleaner referral headers, fewer page views per session, higher intent, faster checkouts.
What changed? Three things.
Browsers and super‑apps quietly rolled out “do my shopping” flows: you tell the agent the brief and budget, and it brings back a shortlist, often with one‑click checkout.
The big consulting/strategy decks stopped calling this “a future scenario” and started treating agentic commerce as an actual, near‑term channel that brands needed to design for.
Consumers,  tired, time‑poor, and already delegating decisions to algorithms in other parts of life,  didn’t really resist. They just slid into it the way they slid into one‑click checkouts and saved cards.
The number that matters here isn’t adoption in some abstract “% of shoppers using AI” sense.  It’s the share of GMV that passes through an algorithmic intermediary that can compare you to everyone else in milliseconds and has no emotional attachment to your brand.
How that moved GMV
Agentic AI did two big things to GMV allocation this year:
It punished anyone whose catalog and data were a mess.  Agents don’t care about your brand story if they can’t read your size curves, ingredients, compatibility, shipping rules, or live price in a structured way. Retailers and brands with rich, standardized feeds and clean product data were picked more often because agents could actually evaluate them.
It rewarded whoever was set up to “win the query,” not “own the customer.”  If the agent’s job is to minimize hassle, maximize value, and reduce risk for the shopper, then GMV shifted toward players who were competitive on price, shipping, and availability in real time. That often meant big marketplaces, large multi‑brand retailers, and a handful of high‑signal DTCs with strong ratings and low friction.
Your old funnel thinking awareness, consideration, conversion doesn’t map neatly to a world where an AI agent compresses half your funnel into a single step. Why I feel this is noteworthy, all BFCM reports include their AI “take” - where ecommerce once resided, AI and agentic are now the residents.
How brands reacted
As you thought you should, move early gain an advantage - Arbitrage. The smart ones stopped treating this as “SEO, but with more buzzwords” and started doing three unglamorous things:
Fixing the pipes: product attributes, taxonomy, structured content, live pricing and availability feeds got board‑level attention. Not because it looks nice in the UX, but because agents literally won’t pick you if you don’t show up clean and comparable.
Negotiating with the new gatekeepers: from search engines to marketplaces to retail media networks, brands started asking “how does your agent rank options, and what do I have to do to be in the top three?”
Experimenting with “agent‑specific” offers: better bundles, dynamic discounts, or warranties surfaced only to certain intermediaries, to see how the ranking logic responded.
A few brands made the opposite call: opt out as much as possible, double down on first‑party relationships, and lean into categories where human preference and identity still dominate (fashion, beauty, hobbies). These behaviors are in direct contrast to brands being asked to fix data or develop SEO strategies instead of relying on paid media. Hmmm.
How consumers responded
Most people didn’t sit around saying, “today I will embrace agentic commerce.”  They just started using the AI button when it made their life easier.The pattern:
Agents for the boring stuff: replenishment, basic home goods, “I just need a decent cable that arrives tomorrow.”
Humans for the identity stuff: “I want a jacket that feels like me,” “I care about this brand’s ethics,” “I don’t trust a bot to choose my skincare.”
GMV followed that line: high‑frequency, low‑emotion spend quietly migrated toward whoever played best with the agents. The rest stayed messy, human, and up for grabs.
Tariffs, De Minimis, and the Great Cheap China Reset
In April and May, the other big story hit: the United States finally went after the tidal wave of cheap parcels coming in under the
de minimis
threshold. The Trump administration tore up the “sub‑$800 gets in duty‑free” rule and layered new tariffs on top, with some categories facing triple‑digit effective rates.
Temu, Shein, and the entire class of ultra‑low‑cost exporters were the obvious primary targets.  For a while, they’d effectively been riding a structural arbitrage: rock‑bottom manufacturing costs, direct entry into the U.S. postal stream, and no duties.
That model had limits, and 2025 found them.
How that moved GMV
Once tariffs and the end of de minimis started to bite, three things happened quickly:
Prices on the apps went up.  Headlines about “import charges,” “extra fees at checkout,” and “your order may incur additional costs” did exactly what you’d expect to conversion rates.
Marketing budgets pulled back.  When every parcel costs more to get into the U.S., the ROI on blasting performance ads at marginal customers falls. Chinese cross‑border players shifted spend away from hyper‑aggressive U.S. acquisition and toward Europe and other markets with looser rules.
GMV leaked back into domestic value formats.  Once the price delta between a Temu basic and a Walmart/Amazon private‑label basic narrowed, the “I’ll wait three weeks for it to arrive from who‑knows‑where” proposition made less sense for a meaningful chunk of shoppers. GMV drifted back to dollar stores, off‑price chains, and mainstream marketplaces where the trade‑off between price, trust, and speed looked better.
How brands and marketplaces responded
If you were a U.S. value retailer, this was a gift.  Suddenly, “cheap but slow” had to fight harder against “cheap enough and here tomorrow.”
U.S. retailers leaned harder into private label and “good enough” ranges, tightening value messaging and inventory depth in basic categories hit hardest by Chinese competition.
Amazon and large marketplaces quietly widened their own price ladders,  you could still find the ultra‑cheap stuff, but there was more emphasis on reasonably priced, Prime‑eligible lternatives.
On the other side of the Pacific, Chinese platforms moved fast:
More local warehousing, more U.S. 3PL partnerships, more SKUs pre‑cleared through customs.
A stronger push into “local seller” models where the inventory never crosses a border at all, just the customer relationship. (We’ll come back to that with Temu’s local seller play.
Make no bones about it either, the Chinese platforms have anticipated these moves and already stepped beyond these boundaries. Their models evolved and are now quietly back in the driving seat.
How consumers responded
The user behavior shift was subtle but important:
Heavy Temu/Shein users didn’t abandon them overnight, but they cut back the frivolous, experimental baskets,  the fifth novelty kitchen gadget, the “it’s only $3” impulse buys.
More of those low‑stakes purchases went back to Amazon, Walmart, and local discounters, where the price gap was smaller but the trust and delivery speed were higher.
The “ultra‑cheap everything” era didn’t end, but the free lunch got a lot more expensive. GMV rebalanced accordingly.
Temu, Local Sellers, and the Marketplace Pivot to “Here, Not There”
Chinese platforms do not f*ck about. Faced with tariffs and political pressure, Temu did something strategically smart: it stopped betting everything on cross‑border arbitrage and started acting more like a conventional marketplace in some markets.
The Local Seller Program,  launched late 2024 and scaled in 2025,  opened the doors to businesses outside China who could list on Temu and fulfill locally  The Shopify app that dropped this week is the most visible version of that: millions of Shopify merchants can now pipe their catalog into Temu, manage inventory and orders from one place, and reach Temu’s audience without shipping from Shenzhen.
How that moved GMV
This did two interesting things to GMV allocation:
It changed
what
GMV Temu was capturing.  Instead of 100% cross‑border cheap stuff, Temu’s mix tilted toward local inventory in 30+ markets, including the U.S., Canada, UK, Germany, Spain, and Australia. That means some GMV that might have happened on a brand’s own Shopify storefront,  or on another marketplace,  is now happening inside Temu’s app, but fulfilled from a warehouse down the road.
It softened the tariff blow without fully escaping it.  Local inventory isn’t tariff‑free forever (somebody still imported those goods), but once it’s in‑market and duties are paid, you can ship domestically at predictable cost. GMV gets re‑routed from “many parcels crossing customs individually” to “bulk shipments + local last mile.”
Underneath the political noise, this is just marketplaces evolving to match the new risk/reward equation of Cross‑border.Marketplaces, experience a quiet resurgence.
How brands responded
For Shopify merchants and SMB brands, Temu’s local seller rails look like any other incremental channel:
A place to chase new demand with relatively low integration friction.
A way to move surplus inventory or test price points without fully re‑architecting their own site.
Channel strategy suddenly matters again. If your SKUs are on Amazon, TikTok Shop, Temu, and your own site, the risk of price compression, gray‑market resellers, and brand dilution rises fast. Larger brands moved to stricter assortment segmentation, MAP enforcement, and packaging variants to keep some control over where GMV shows up and at what price.
How consumers responded
From the shopper’s perspective, Temu started to feel a bit different:
More recognizable brands in the feed.
Slightly faster and more reliable deliveries on some items.
That combination nudged some spend that might have gone to Amazon, Etsy, or even independent sites into the Temu ecosystem instead. The marketplace playbook repeats, just with a new cast. Since I started writing this Shopify have announced that the Temu native app exists now in their Shopify store, just like Klaviyo and eBay.
BNPL’s Regulatory Hangover and the Quiet Checkout Re‑Rank
While everyone was watching tariffs and AI, regulators were finally catching up with Buy Now, Pay Later. In the UK and Europe especially, 2025 was the year BNPL went from “light‑touch” to “you are now very much regulated credit.”
Consultations, draft rules, and implementation timelines crystallized around bringing BNPL into the same consumer‑protection orbit as traditional credit, with full FCA oversight kicking in from 2026.  Add in rising delinquencies and macro headwinds, and suddenly the “approve everyone, grow at any cost” era looked a lot riskier.
How that moved GMV
The impact on GMV was more about distribution than collapse:
Conversion at the margin dipped in some discretionary categories.  As providers tightened underwriting and pulled back the most aggressive “pay in 4” messaging, a slice of high‑ticket fashion, beauty, and electronics GMV that was floating on easy approvals just… didn’t happen, or happened at lower basket values.
GMV shifted toward “proper” credit and loyalty‑linked financing.  Merchants with co‑branded cards, 0% promos, or tightly integrated regulated financing became relatively more attractive for big‑ticket purchases, especially where BNPL approvals were no longer automatic.
In other words: the pie didn’t disappear, but the slices got re‑cut.
How brands responded
Retailers did three things in quick succession:
Rationalised their BNPL panels.  Instead of four providers jostling for real estate at checkout, many merchants now prefer one or two that play nicely with regulators and deliver sustainable economics.
Re‑balanced incentives.  Some pulled back on subsidizing BNPL promos and redirected that spend into price cuts, free shipping thresholds, or loyalty rewards that were easier to explain and defend.
Paid more attention to cohort behaviour.  When cheap credit is no longer a given, you need to understand which segments genuinely need BNPL to convert and which were just using it because it was there. The former get better‑designed journeys; the latter are nudged back toward debit or cards.
How consumers responded
For shoppers, it felt like a tightening of the tap rather than a total shut‑off:
Some got declined more often or found limits reduced.  Discretionary splurges became a bit less frictionless, which in turn pushed some GMV downmarket (cheaper alternatives) or out of the basket entirely
Others felt a bit safer.  With clearer disclosures, better complaints mechanisms, and the knowledge that a regulator was watching, mainstream consumers were more willing to use BNPL for bigger, considered purchases.
Again, GMV didn’t vanish; it walked to whichever merchants could offer financing that felt both safe and simple under the new rules. For context, in the US, credit card debt (consumers is about $1.23TN).
Retail Media: When Shelf Space Turned Fully Pay‑to‑Play
Retail media isn’t new. What
is
new in 2025 is how central it has become to the P&L and how unapologetically pay‑to‑play digital shelf space now is. Large retailers and marketplaces have effectively become ad platforms with logistics operations attached. Sponsored products, branded carousels, on‑site video, off‑site targeting using first‑party data,  all plugged into a measurement layer that claims to show precisely how ad spend translates into incremental GMV.
How that moved GMV
If you’re a shopper on a big marketplace, most of what you see is now, in some way, paid for:
GMV allocation inside those ecosystems tilted even more toward brands who could pay to win the auction for attention. Organic ranking still matters, but it is heavily shaped by sponsored demand.
Smaller brands,  or those that refused to play the game,  lost share of voice.  Many saw their organic placement erode under waves of paid placements from better‑funded competitors, pushing their GMV into niche platforms, direct channels, or obscurity.
In practical terms: within a given marketplace, the internal GMV pie was redistributed from “best match + relevance” to “best match + relevance + who’s paying today.”
How brands responded
The budget story here is straightforward:
Big brands moved serious money into retail media.  Not just test budgets; full reallocation from traditional digital and trade spend into closed‑loop, retailer‑owned inventory where they could see attributed sales and negotiate better terms.
Mid‑tier players tried to hack the efficiency side.  They leaned on better creative, smarter bidding (long‑tail keywords, defensive strategies), and joint business plans to secure programmatic visibility at lower cost.
Everyone started arguing about incrementality.  The central question: “How much of this GMV would I have got anyway?” The more retail media networks could prove incremental lift, the more money flowed in.
How consumers responded
From the outside, this mostly looks like “there are a lot more sponsored things everywhere,” but underneath:
Some shoppers started to push back, consciously or not.  Using filters, reviews, and,  increasingly,  AI agents to strip away sponsored clutter and search for “best value” or “most reliable” rather than blindly trusting the top row.
Others simply absorbed the new normal.  If everything is pay‑to‑play, the path of least resistance is to lean on aggregated ratings, social proof, or brand familiarity when choosing. GMV then consolidates around whoever can win both the auction and the trust game.
Retail media turned digital shelf space from a ranking problem into a budget allocation problem. GMV followed the money. And now it is getting physical, from OOHplacements, to instore and soon to be a Vizio TV in your home. As Colin Lewis might say, everything is an ad now.
Cross‑Border Re‑Priced, Inventory Moves Closer to Home
The journey to the holy grail, Cross Border Trade/. Tariffs were the loud part of 2025’s trade story, but beneath that, logistics and geopolitical risk kept reshaping how far products travel before they hit the customer. Even where duties didn’t spike, retailers and brands saw enough disruption over the past few years,  pandemics, port congestion, wars, weather,  to start asking whether the last dollar of cost savings from far‑flung supply chains was really worth it.
How that moved GMV
The practical effects on GMV looked like this:
Fewer ultra‑slow, ultra‑cheap shipping promises.  Retailers quietly de‑emphasised “it’ll be here in 25 days” options in favor of slightly higher‑priced but more reliable domestic or near‑shore fulfillment.
More conversion for those with resilient networks.  When everyone has been burned by “your order is delayed” emails, the merchants who can promise and deliver a 2–3 day window win GMV even if they’re not the absolute cheapest.
Near‑shoring to Mexico, Eastern Europe, or domestic production doesn’t eliminate risk, but it changes the balance between cost, control, and customer trust.
How brands responded
Operationally, this is where a lot of budgets went:
Re‑negotiating with suppliers and moving partial production closer to key markets.
Investing in better inventory visibility, so the promise on the product page matches reality in the warehouse.
Narratively, some brands turned this into part of the proposition:
“Made closer to home,” “shorter, more transparent supply chains,” and “we’re less likely to cancel on you” became subtle but powerful messages in categories where reliability and ethics matter.
How consumers responded
For shoppers, 2025 reinforced a lesson:
If a deal looks too good and too far away, something might go wrong.  Enough people experienced customs surprises, delays, or quality issues that a segment of customers simply opted for the boring, predictable option even if it cost a bit more.
GMV followed the reliable rails. The long‑tail cross‑border sellers still exist, but a meaningful slice of spend moved toward fewer, closer, more dependable nodes.
AI‑Powered Owned Sites vs Marketplace Gravity
The final story is about a fight that’s been going on for years: brand‑owned sites trying to hold onto direct relationships while marketplaces eat convenience and social platforms eat discovery. In 2025, brands finally got some better weapons.  AI‑driven on‑site search, conversational assistants, and personalisation engines went from bolt‑on chat widgets to core parts of the shopping experience. Do we ever really own customers? I am Scooby dubious.
How that moved GMV
Where this was done well, the impact was real:
Better conversion and higher average order values on first‑party sites.  Shoppers who might previously have bounced to Amazon for easier discovery could now ask the brand’s own assistant “show me something like the black one I bought last year, but lighter for summer,” and actually get a decent answer.
Shorter paths to purchase in complex categories.  For electronics, beauty, or B2B‑ish purchases, AI assistants that could decode jargon, explain trade‑offs, and remember context made first‑party sites less painful.
That didn’t break marketplace gravity, but it slowed the leak.
How brands responded
Strategically, brands split into two camps:
The “everywhere our customer is” crowd:  They accepted that a big chunk of incremental GMV would always come via marketplaces, social commerce, and agents, and invested in treating owned sites as relationship hubs rather than the only point of sale.
The “defensible direct” crowd:  They doubled down on exclusive products, member perks, service‑heavy experiences, and content that you could only really get by going direct,  using AI to scale the human bits rather than replace them.
Both camps invested in AI; they just framed success differently.
How consumers responded
Shoppers behaved much as you’d expect:
For low‑emotion buys, marketplaces still won on convenience: saved details, one cart, one app. GMV in these categories stayed highly concentrated.
For higher‑stakes or more personal buys, a growing segment was willing to engage with brand‑owned AI experiences,  especially when they actually solved problems instead of just mimicking a FAQ.
The result was a bifurcation of GMV: routine, replenishment, and commodity spend clustering around a handful of big ecosystems; considered, identity‑driven spend staying more distributed.
So What Do You Do With All This?
Taken together, these seven stories tell you less about “ecommerce growth” and more about “ecommerce power.”  Who has the power to steer demand? Who has the power to set terms? Who has the power to absorb shocks?You need to live amongst it.
In 2025, that power shifted in a few clear directions:
From human choice to algorithmic mediation (agents, retail media).
From cross‑border arbitrage to more localised, politically palatable models (tariffs, local sellers, near‑shoring).
From unregulated credit sugar highs to more sustainable financing rails (BNPL regulation).
If you’re a brand or retailer planning for 2026, the practical questions to ask off the back of this year are:
Are we legible and attractive to the agents that will increasingly front‑run demand?
Do we know which parts of our GMV depend on fragile arbitrage,  be it trade rules, advertising costs, or financing conditions?
Where are we consciously choosing to play in marketplaces, retail media, and local‑seller ecosystems,  and where are we drawing lines?
What do we offer on our own sites that is worth bypassing the convenience of the big platforms?
Because the headline for 2025 isn’t “ecommerce grew X%.”  It’s that GMV quietly re‑charted itself around new rules, new gatekeepers, and new constraints. If you’re still reading the old maps, you’ll spend next year wondering why your traffic looks fine but your checkout doesn’t.

title: The Ghost in the Machine: Goodbye MTV
excerpt: I. The 12:01 AM Prophecy On August 1, 1981, I was a six-month-old in County Kildare, Ireland, likely more concerned with the temperature of my bottle than the cultural temperature of the planet. But 3,000 miles away, at 12:01 AM, the world was being rewired.
_body:
I. The 12:01 AM Prophecy
On August 1, 1981, I was a six-month-old in County Kildare, Ireland, likely more concerned with the temperature of my bottle than the cultural temperature of the planet. But 3,000 miles away, at 12:01 AM, the world was being rewired. As the repurposed Apollo 11 footage flickered, a moon landing co-opted as a corporate identity, the "Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll" announcement wasn't just launching a channel. It was the start of the world we find ourselves trying to make head or tail of in 2026. MTV Music shut down for business, 44 years after bouldering onto our screens and changing the world in so many ways.
In my thesis,
The Cultivation of a New Generation
, I argued that MTV transcended brand to become a lifestyle. I looked at how increased doses of media led to the
narcotization of society
. We weren't just watching videos; we were being sedated by an aesthetic. We moved from the "gritty, analog 1970s" into a glossy, high-tech dream theory where the
image
of the product became the product.
Today, that narcotization is complete. We don’t just watch the world; we carry it in our palms, a black mirror that predicts our desires before we’ve even felt them. Video didn't kill the radio star; it just turned the star into an algorithm and the audience into a data point. Today, we are trying to determine which other part of our souls we hand over to our AI overlords, when in fact, they should, be paying us for this privilege.
The business history of MTV is a masterclass in
Value Capture
, and it provides the perfect, albeit haunting, blueprint for the SaaS companies and eCommerce consultants of 2026.
From a purely commercial perspective, MTV t was the world’s first successful
High-Margin Arbitrage Machine
.
1. The Ultimate Arbitrage: Content for Free
In 1981, the MTV founders pulled off a deal that would make a modern SaaS founder weep with envy. They convinced record labels to provide their "product" (music videos) for
free
.
The Business Logic:
They framed music videos as "promotional materials" the record labels paid to make them, and MTV provided the distribution.
The Result:
MTV had a nearly $0 cost of goods sold (COGS) for their primary programming. By 1984, they were the first profitable cable network in history, netting $11.9 million.
The Lesson for Today:
This is the "User-Generated Content" (UGC) model 20 years before its time. MTV didn't build the value; they built the
aggregator of value
.
2. The Viacom Deal: From Scrappy to Scale
In 1985/86, Warner sold MTV Networks to
Viacom
for roughly $513 million. Under the ruthless eye of Sumner Redstone, MTV became the crown jewel of a multi-billion dollar empire.
The "Network Effect":
Viacom used MTV as a battering ram to negotiate better carriage deals with cable operators. If an operator wanted Nickelodeon or VH1, they
had
to pay a premium for MTV.
The Financials:
By the late 1990s, MTV Networks was contributing over
20% of Viacom’s total revenue
(approx. $2.7 billion). Its cash flow margins were a staggering 40-41%. It was the "Cash Cow" that funded Viacom's acquisitions of Paramount Pictures and Blockbuster.
3. The VMAs: Monetizing the Lifestyle Moment
The
MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs)
, launched in 1984, were the business model’s "Peak Event."
The 360-Degree Monetization:
It wasn't just an awards show; it was an integrated marketing platform. By 2024, partnerships with brands like Pepsi, Spotify, and Samsung were no longer just "commercials", they were "integrated narratives." Brands became lifestyle and vice versa.
Integrated Commerce:
Pepsi wasn't just a sponsor; they had artists recording exclusive content in "Pepsi Studios" during the show. Samsung provided behind-the-scenes camera access that lived on social media for weeks. It was the birth of
Immersive Brand Storytelling
, a precursor to the "TikTok Shop" integration we see today.
4. The 2025/2026 Collapse: The Death of the Gatekeeper
As we speak, the era is ending. Paramount Global (the ghost of Viacom) is shutting down its iconic MTV music channels globally.
Why the model failed:
MTV was a
Gatekeeper
. In 1981, if you wanted to see Duran Duran, you
had
to go to MTV. In 2026, the "Distribution" is decentralized.
The Cautionary Tale:
Somewhere MTV  stopped being a "Curator" and became an "Efficiency Machine." They chased short-term reality TV ratings (Jersey Shore) and lost the "360-degree" soul of the music connection. Nike were on this path, but steadied the ship. Focus now on athletes again.
The Final Backdrop: 1981 vs. 2026
The Picture at the Beginning (August 1, 1981):
It’s 12:01 AM. A grainy moon landing gives way to the first video. The world is analog, beige, and centralized. There is one screen, one message, and one goal: "I Want My MTV." The technology is heavy, but the impact is profound because it is the only bridge to the future.
The Picture at the End (2026):
The world is hyper-saturated. We have the "Biome of AI" in our pockets. Every person is their own MTV, their own broadcaster, their own merchandiser. The technology is light, cheap, and ubiquitous but the impact is diluted.
We have traded the "360-degree lifestyle" for a
360-degree surveillance state of consumption
. The SaaS companies that followed the MTV blueprint (owning the platform but not the soul) are now facing their "1984" moment, irrelevance in the face of a decentralized world..
II. The Great Leveling: When Tech Becomes a Commodity
Ten years ago, the "Technology Question" was the primary hurdle. If you wanted to scale, you needed a "moat" made of proprietary code and expensive engineers. Today, that moat has evaporated. Blame Canada I say, or at least, those Canadians.
The
Empire of AI
has turned software into a commodity. Whether you are running on a legacy enterprise stack or a modular "headless" build, the capabilities are, by and large, identical. AI can write your product descriptions, optimize your PPC bidding, and generate your social creative in seconds. If everyone has a god-like intelligence at their disposal, then
having the tool is no longer an advantage.
The differentiator has shifted back to the human. Specifically, the
Operator
. But, if the Oracles are to be believed, this too, is temporary.
Think of the modern merchandiser as a
Day Trader of the Digital Shelf
. They are the unrelenting ones who realize that while AI can stimulate demand, only a human understands how to manage the friction of a soul-less interface. They thrive on the daily wins, the minute adjustments to conversion rate and the subtle shift in site experience. They know there is no "start" or "finish" to a digital store; there is only
doing
, always.
III. The CPG Invasion: Distribution as the Ultimate Truth
As we look at the senior leadership emerging in 2026, the faces aren't coming from Silicon Valley anymore. They are coming from the CPG world, the PepsiCos, the Unilevers, the giants of the physical shelf.
These leaders possess something the tech-first generation lacks:
Commercial Acumen
. They understand that in a world where everyone can make a product, the only thing that matters is
Distribution and Margin
. They know how to allow a network to make a profit periodically so the network stays healthy. They aren't distracted by the "SaaS-y" metrics of the last decade; they are focused on the "Ostrich Report" realities of the macro-economy. They know why others trust them to take their money.
IV. The SaaS Graveyard: The Death of MRR
Across the table from these CPG veterans sit the SaaS companies, and I fear for them. For fifteen years,
MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue)
was the holy grail. It was a metric of sustainability that justified astronomical valuations.
But in the age of AI, I don't believe MRR is sustainable. How can it be? If the cost of everything is moving to zero. What it billing days are billing minutes, or not to be billed at all. How useful is MRR when cash at bank rolls to zero too.
When the cost of building software trends toward zero, and a smart AI agent can replicate a platform's core utility for the price of a few API tokens, why would a merchant pay $50k a year for a seat? The SaaS companies are facing a structural reset. Success in 2026 isn't about "locking in" a customer; it's about providing
proven, measurable utility
that prevents the merchant's margin from being crushed.
If SaaS companies don't move from "Subscription" to "Success-based" or "Outcome-based" models, they are just "neoliberal slop" waiting for the next economic downturn to clear them away. And adding strategy will not work, every agency is doing this and offering it up. Shouldn’t you have been doing this all along - providing this type of stewardship. When this question arises, things will get even tougher.
V. The Convenience We Never Asked For
The political climate of 1981 was defined by the Cold War, a clear, binary struggle between two systems. Today, the struggle is internal. We are increasing credit to buy more stuff, fueled by an AI "convenience" that we didn't actually need. But what about the Smartphone I hear you say, we could do without that too. I just think of my 3 sons under 8 and how much better they would be without this life companion.
Does my life require an AI to decide which laundry detergent I buy? Clue:
None of it does.
We have traded our curiosity for convenience. We have allowed the "Industrial Production of Culture" (to quote my thesis) to become the "Algorithmic Production of Existence." We are embark on a journey where we buy more, feel less, and trust no one. Trust, is one of those timeless commodities like gold, that will continue to keep the metronome moving. I think now of all those kids I was mean to in school. In particular, the bullies ! You helped shape me but yeah, I was rude to you. I called you names, but let’s do business, after all time has passed. And according to the latest Ricky Gervais Netflix special cancel culture is dead,so we can live without recrimination again. But then there is that phone again, storying all that data, making us relive all the moments, the good and the goddamn awful. On repeat, forever. This, is to be amplified.
Community is the only antidote. Brands that thrive in 2026 are those with a leader who knows exactly why they exist, a person who isn't afraid to get on the "Struggle Bus" and show the world the messy, human reality of their product.
VI. The Abandoned Studio
As the 1981 MTV launch ended, it left a path open. It crossed cultural divides and created a global language of visual storytelling. But it didn't have the full tech capability to finish the job. We have that capability now, but we’ve used it to build walls.
We sit in the "Abandoned Studio" of the internet, surrounded by high-tech beige, watching the world operate in the palm of our hands. We are more connected than ever, yet more "narcotized" by the constant stream of media. But it did more than just that.
The concept of MTV 360 (often called 360-degree commissioning or glocalization) was the blueprint for what we now call a "content ecosystem." It was the first time a media company realized that a television screen was just one node in a larger nervous system.
In your thesis, you likely touched on how MTV "transcended brand to become a lifestyle." The 360 strategy was the mechanical implementation of that transcendence. It mandated that an idea (like
Jackass
or
The Real World
) must exist as a TV show, a website, a mobile alert, a ringtone, and a physical event.
If we look at the world today, there are several multi-billion dollar platforms and technologies that technically shouldn’t exist because they are simply the shrapnel of MTV’s original 360-degree explosion. They took a single limb of the MTV beast and turned it into a standalone empire.
1. TikTok: The "Short-Form" Shrapnel
MTV’s 360 strategy was built on the "snackable" nature of the music video, high-impact, visual-first storytelling that didn't require a long attention span.
The MTV DNA: The "Music Video" was the first viral loop.
The Reality: TikTok is essentially MTV’s
Total Request Live (TRL)
stripped of the human host and handed over to an AI. If MTV had successfully integrated its 360 strategy into the mobile era, TikTok wouldn't be a Chinese-owned sensation; it would be an MTV sub-feature.
2. Patreon & The Creator Economy
MTV’s 360 approach was the first to "monetize the fan" beyond the screen. They sold the lifestyle, the clothes, the attitude, the "unplugged" intimacy.
The MTV DNA:
MTV Unplugged
was the original "exclusive content" tier.
The Reality: The technology of Patreon exists because MTV failed to build a closed-loop financial system for its "lifestyle" followers. They created the "cultivation of a generation" but let the payment rails be built by others.
3. BeReal & The "Anti-Gloss" Movement
During research for my thesis, I stumbled on the "narcotization" of society through glossy media. MTV's 360 strategy eventually tried to pivot into "authenticity" through reality TV.
The MTV DNA:
The Real World
(1992) was the first attempt to show the "unvarnished" human.
The Reality: Platforms like BeReal or even the "Photo Dump" aesthetic on Instagram are reactions to the very narcissism MTV cultivated. These platforms exist to fix the psychological "friction" that MTV’s 360-degree perfection created in the youth psyche.
VI. The SaaS Mirage and the 360-Degree Ghost
When you look at the SaaS companies today, the ones providing the "360-degree marketing stacks", they are trying to sell us a ghost. They are selling the
capability
of MTV’s 360 strategy without the
soul
of the content.
They provide the "omnichannel" pipes (email, SMS, social, web), but the "practitioner" at the keyboard is often just a "narcotized" operator pushing buttons. We have reached a point where the Tech is Simple but the Connection is Broken.
We have 360-degree access to the consumer, but 0 degrees of actual trust.
VII. The Rise of the "Day Trader" Merchandiser
This is where you, the eCommerce operator, come in. In the MTV era, the "Video Jockey" (VJ) was the curator. Today, the Merchandiser is the VJ of the digital shelf.
You are the one managing the "friction" that the SaaS companies created by over-automating.
You are the one who knows that AI convenience is a clue to a deeper problem: we are automating the parts of life that actually make us feel something.
The "CPG world" leaders get this. They know that a 360 strategy isn't about being on every platform; it's about distribution of trust. They don't care if the tech is "beige" or "glossy"—they care if the product moves because a human wanted it, not because an algorithm tricked them into a "Buy Now" debt spiral.
VIII. The Final Frame: February 11, 1981, to Today
You were born in the transition. A cocky 6-month-old watching the gritty 70s become the neon 80s. You saw MTV attempt to bridge cultural divides and fail because they didn't have the tech.
Now, we have the tech. We have the "Empire of AI." We have the 360-degree visibility. And yet, we sit here on "The Struggle Bus," quietly pessimistic.
The world hasn't advanced; it has just accelerated. We are still looking for a leader who knows why they exist. We are still looking for a community that isn't a "narcotized" target audience. We are still looking for the "Rock and Roll" that MTV promised at 12:01 AM.
The technology question is easy. The human question? That’s the only one left worth answering.
Linger a moment more…… Where were you when.
The MTV Era: A Timeline of Major Events
August 1, 1981: The Launch
MTV goes on air at 12:01 AM. The first video is "Video Killed the Radio Star" by The Buggles.
December 2, 1983: "Thriller" Premieres
Michael Jackson’s 14-minute "Thriller" video changes music videos from promotional clips into a cinematic art form. It breaks the "color barrier" on the network and cements MTV as a cultural powerhouse.
September 14, 1984: The First VMAs
The inaugural Video Music Awards air. Madonna performs "Like a Virgin" in a wedding dress, crawling across the floor and creating the first of many VMA scandals.
July 13, 1985: Live Aid
MTV broadcasts the global benefit concert almost in its entirety, proving the network could handle massive, live global events and activism.
March 1987:
Headbangers Ball
Debuts
MTV dedicates a block to heavy metal, helping launch the "Hair Metal" era into the mainstream.
November 26, 1989:
MTV Unplugged
Premieres
The show strips away the synthesizers of the 80s for acoustic performances. Iconic sets by Nirvana, Eric Clapton, and Alice in Chains would later become legendary live albums.
January 1992:
The Real World
Launches
While not purely "music," this show marked the beginning of MTV's shift toward reality TV, which would eventually dominate the schedule.
September 1997:
TRL
(Total Request Live) Launches
Hosted by Carson Daly, this show becomes the epicenter of the late-90s teen pop explosion (Britney Spears, 'N Sync, Backstreet Boys).
September 2003: The VMA Kiss
Madonna, Britney Spears, and Christina Aguilera perform together, ending in a kiss that becomes one of the most talked-about moments in the history of the network.
February 2011: The End of "Music Television"
MTV officially drops "Music Television" from its logo, acknowledging its evolution into a general entertainment and reality lifestyle brand.

title: FUBAR - F*cked up Beyond All Recognition
pullQuotes: “Agenic Killed the Agency Stars” - sing it if you can, but it’s a lament, not a pop song.
excerpt: We all need to be better informed, and better users. It is claimed by many sources that 40% of all Enterprise software will be built on an AI layer by this year. Not bolted on, but driving it. We will not be led by AI
_body:
We all need to be better informed, and better users. It is claimed by many sources that 40% of all Enterprise software will be built on an AI layer by this year. Not bolted on, but driving it. We will not be led by AI in the way that we think about it, not really. The development of protocols, initiatives like the Open Order Exchange Network and other aspects have galvanised a steep 3 year transition curve into something way more fundamental. The Agentic Protocol for example is an evolution on Headless (and other aspects of architecture) but it opens up the possibility to think about commerce in new ways. How we discover and how we search and ultimately how we consumer -content, services and products. Maybe it is not a bad thing. To preface some of this thinking I reference Scot Wingo and his
RetailGentic
substack. This is one of the best ways to stay informed on such matters. But also to challenge my thinking. He is at pains to point out that at this stage Agentic does not mean an end to end full, process flow from thinking to post purchase cognitive loads, it is evolving. This is not a bad thing. Ecomm conversion rates have been relatively static for some time now.
eCommerce Conversion Rates - Dynamic Yield
eCommerce as a % of overall Retail - North America (FRED data)
2026 seems optimistic, and will depend on something new that is happening - how revenue is now being tracked for ecommerce. In recent earnings, all platforms reported on their AI contribution in terms of GMV take. Is this a recalibration or incremental or new? Probably a combo of all of the above. But AI led revenue is something we will have to sift through, for better or worse. The point of the graphs is to show a long held skepticism I have. Is the way we have delivered commerce or our expectations right? Or ambitious enough or really poor.Where ecommerce has been siloed for 2 decades, AI is becoming core. Just there, always and everywhere. Where ecommerce did not design education policy or shift requirements of government, AI is changing both of those aspects too. As I have putting this together for a few months, I got encouragement from
Kelly Goetsch
, a community leader who demonstrates empathy, vision and action. He is open and encouraging and cares about the betterment of the industry. He just gave me a nudge, not even suggesting I was right, but because he likes people thinking and questioning. A brilliant quality in a leader. For the record, he is only someone I met a handful of times and spoke to on a number of occasions, he wants or owes me nothing.Then last night as I was re reading this, a slack came into one of groups from my friend
Gireesh ⛁ ⛁ Sahukar
https://www.rediff.com/news/column/sree-sreenivasan-the-ai-financial-bubble-is-for-real/20260101.htm
- It is too interesting not to read. We are indeed in a hype cycle. It is fueled by the markets. Open capitalism is what we call it, but I do still think, underlying this is something different this is what I set out to do. They hype cycle may burst, but the layers are there to stay.
The AI Transition is Now Structural and Permanent
The Infrastructure Gestation (2023–2026)
For the past three years, much public discourse on artificial intelligence has been dominated by a “hype cycle” narrative. Rightly and in their large numbers critics point to the hallucinations of early chatbots and the high cost of training models as evidence of a bubble. Critics like Sree Sreenivasan rightly point to a ‘financial bubble’ at the top of the AI food chain, a cycle of overvaluation and unsustainable cash burn. However, as Sreenivasan himself admits, the technology is here to stay. We must distinguish between the
Financial Bubble
(the stock prices of model-builders) and the
Structural Bedrock
(the protocols like onX and the national compute grids). The bubble may burst, but the pipes remain. I think a certain, Mr Goetsch reccognizes this and his partners too. We are moving from the ‘Hype Era’ into the ‘Refinement Era,’ where the ability to orchestrate specialized agents is the only skill that matters.” The architects that get this will win early advantage and log term reliance too.   But from the vantage point of early 2026, it is clear that those three years were a
gestation period
. While the headlines focused on the software, the world was quietly building a new global utility.
The winners are not always immediate or obvious but they move in mysterious ways.
Donald Trump Junior - Board Roles. This is not out of judgement but I have watched enough movies to know to follow the money, start there is what Michael Lewis might advise.
We have started to move beyond the “Wild West” phase of AI experimentation and into a period of
Infrastructure Lock-in
. This will not be evident to everyone, nor will many care. I do. In my opinion, this transition is defined by three major structural pillars:
1. The Sunk Cost of Sovereignty
Since 2023, the scale of capital expenditure (CAPEX) has been staggering. The world’s largest hyperscalers have tripled their annual investment from roughly $150 billion to over
$500 billion in 2026
. This isn’t just “venture money” floating in the cloud. This has become a physical reality. It is expressed in 25-gigawatt data centers, thousands of miles of new fiber-optic cables, and specialized “AI Factories” that cost upwards of $50 billion per site. There are not enough of them, of course there aren’t but Google doesn’t care, or X, Space much?
On a national level, we have seen the rise of
Sovereign AI
. Governments in the UK, France, Japan, and the UAE have committed billions (such as the UK’s £2 billion Compute Roadmap) to build state-owned supercomputing reserves. As a citizen and a parent, I see this as the “Interstate Highway System” of our century. Once a nation invests this much in the physical “pipes” of intelligence, there is no political or economic path to retreat. AI is now a permanent layer of the national power grid.
2. From “Headless” to “Structural” E-commerce
In my professional world of e-commerce, the last three years saw the completion of the “Infrastructure Layer.” We spent a decade moving toward
Headless Commerce
, decoupling the storefront from the backend. But in 2026, we have taken the final step:
Structural AI Integration
.
AI is no longer a “plugin” on a Shopify store; it is the core database. The infrastructure now supports “Self-Healing” supply chains and “Anticipatory Shipping” as standard features. Large-scale investments have turned logistics from a reactive game of “where is my package?” into a predictive system where the infrastructure moves goods before the consumer even knows they want them. The “Lost 3 Years” were spent building the specialized nervous system that now runs global trade. eCommerce and Agentic are having their Buggles moment.
“Agenic Killed the Agency Stars” - sing it if you can, but it’s a lament, not a pop song.
This photo may be all the more telling in years to come. Free markets and decentralized control are helpful.
3. The Need for a Common Language: The Macro Alignment
As this massive infrastructure grew, we hit a wall: the systems couldn’t talk to each other. This is where macro-thinking caught up with the technology. The development of standards like the
Order Network eXchange (onX)
, pioneered by leaders like Kelly Goetsch form parts of  the missing pieces of the puzzle.
By creating a vendor-neutral, “common operational language” for commerce, onX has turned a collection of isolated AI experiments into a unified global network. It allows the massive compute power we’ve built to actually
execute
transactions across different platforms, warehouses, and shipping providers. We didn’t just build the engines (the models); in the last three years, we finally finished the tracks (the protocols) they run on. We also have agentic and payment protocols. The sands have shifted.
Dad of 3 now speaking.
As I look at these sunk costs, I realize that the world my children are entering is being “poured” right now. When billions are spent on physical infrastructure and global standards are codified into our trade systems, the technology becomes invisible, it becomes the floor we walk on. We can no longer debate
if
we should use AI; we must now focus on how to operate within a world where AI is the fundamental architecture of both our economy and our children’s future. Policies are being designed and written with the tech companies in mind. The language of policy does not read much like civil servant speak anymore. So much of what is being created is so very 1984 while all around us Animal Farm is being played out in real life.
Adoption pickles up. The Consumer Catalyst, The Year of the Agent (2025)
If the years leading up to 2025 were about building the “nerves and bone” of the system, 2025 was the year the system woke up. We will look back on last year as the definitive tipping point for consumer behavior. It was the year we stopped “using” AI as a tool and started “delegating” to it as an agent. And this makes me sad, to discover something is an innately human thing. It is not lost of me that discovery could be replaced. Convenience at every turn overruling the very human need for friction. Friction creates some of our best creative sparks in all walks of life, movies, books and music. This is what made the birth and death so symbolic to me in this context. Music was audible, then we added video, we had media making music a different expressive media for all involved. It created new industries, new skills and made us think how brands and art co exist. Today, the average American is consuming almost 7 hours of video content a day in some form. Integrated shopping seems to be part of this consumption process too, almost expected.
Adoption is real. Ask the nearly 1BN users of ChatGPT. They are informing a path forward despite themselves. Let’s look at some of those nuances that are changing our industry.
1. The Death of the Search Bar
For two decades, the “search bar” was the undisputed king of e-commerce. Success was measured by SEO, keywords, and how well a brand could “game” a results page. In 2025, that architecture began to crumble. With the rollout of systems like Amazon’s Rufus—which by late last year was handling nearly 40% of all platform queries the consumer experience shifted from “Search and Click” to “Intent and Delegate.” (yes, there is a stat for everything and this is an easy land grab turned PR story.)
As a professional in this space, I’ve watched our metrics transform. We are no longer optimizing for a human eye scrolling through a grid; we are optimizing for an AI agent that is scanning for “Contextual Relevance.” The consumer no longer wants to spend 20 minutes filtering for “size 10 waterproof hiking boots.” They tell their agent:
“I’m going to the Dolomites in October; find me the best-rated boots for damp limestone that will arrive by Thursday.”
The agent doesn’t present a list; it presents a solution. And by we, I say the platforms.
2. Behavioral Habituation: The New “Cognitive Prosthetic”
The adoption rate has been staggering, particularly among the younger demographic. By the end of 2025, roughly one-third of U.S. consumers expressed comfort in letting an AI agent complete a purchase on their behalf. For Gen Z, that number is even higher, nearing 45%.
This isn’t just a change in shopping; it is a change in cognition. We are witnessing a “Behavioral Habituation” where the AI assistant acts as a cognitive prosthetic. For the modern consumer, the friction of a traditional website the pop-ups, the login screens, the checkout flows now feels like a relic of the industrial age. Once a consumer experiences “Zero-Click Commerce,” where their agent negotiates a price and handles the logistics in the background, they never go back. The habit is locked in.
Images : RetailGentic
Or just read
Joe Keenan
3. The 24/7 Autonomous Marketplace
This shift has created a “Headless” marketplace that never sleeps. In 2025, we saw the rise of Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Commerce. On one side, the consumer’s agent knows the user’s budget, style, and urgency. On the other side, the merchant’s AI, powered by the “Infrastructure Layer” I mentioned earlier, is dynamically adjusting prices and inventory in real-time.
They “shake hands” in milliseconds. The transaction is done before the human even checks their notifications. This is the Catalyst Effect: the sheer speed and efficiency of agentic commerce have made traditional retail models obsolete. My kids will grow up in a world where the “middle-man” the search engine, the storefront, the manual comparison, has been abstracted away. It makes them hyper-efficient, but it also makes them dependent on a layer of technology that is largely invisible. I talked previously of passive commerce, the chasm has been crossed. We have crossed a behavioral Rubicon: we have traded the effort of “searching” for the convenience of “delegating,” and in doing so, we have made the AI agent a permanent fixture of the human experience.
The External Force, Regulation vs. Reality
Us EU folk are used to this. Intervention in our lives, as part of a common area, this has pros and cons. Many point to loss of sovereignty and national interest. For me, I like EU thinking. Having worked with so many colleagues over the years, the EU mentality offers pragmatism, proof before leaping and an alternative point of view. I loved the exposure to this and continue to place an enormous value on it.  So as we move through 2026, the second major structural pillar has arrived: the
External Force
. For the past few years, the tech industry operated in a state of “permissionless innovation,” but we have now entered the era of the
Enforcement Wall
. As a professional, I see this as the “regulatory concrete” that is being poured around the infrastructure mentioned earlier; as a father, I see it as a desperate, glacial attempt by the state to protect a public that wasn’t consulted in the first place. But we need it. The challenge is to stay up to pace, how this happens is not easy or clear.
1. The Enforcement Wall: August 2026
The most significant signal that AI is here to stay is the full enforcement of the
EU AI Act
, reaching its critical milestone in August 2026. This isn’t just “European red tape”; it is the
Brussels Effect
in action. Just as GDPR became the global standard for privacy, the EU AI Act is forcing every e-commerce platform,  from Seattle to Shenzhen, to redesign their systems to meet European standards of transparency and auditability.
In 2026, we are no longer debating ethics in the abstract. If an AI agent makes a purchase for a consumer, the infrastructure must now legally provide:
Proof of Authority:
A cryptographically signed mandate (leveraging protocols like Google’s AP2) proving the human actually authorized the agent to spend money.
The “Human Oversight” Kill-Switch:
Mandatory mechanisms that allow a human to intervene in high-risk automated decisions.
Algorithmic Transparency:
If a dynamic pricing engine raises the cost of an item, the platform must be able to prove—on demand—that it wasn’t based on “vulnerability markers” prohibited by law.
It will likely stifle investment, limit start ups and will develop something of an AI divide. We might win in the long term though. The brain drain and talent exodus from America will be one to watch. As funding diminishes in certain disciplines and other research stops altogether, the EU provides a haven from home for this brain power. The Guardian reported on this last year.
Application Surges:
In mid-2025, the
“Safe Place for Science”
program launched by
Aix-Marseille University
in France received more than
500 inquiries
and nearly
300 formal applications
within its first months. Applicants included senior researchers from elite institutions such as
NASA, Yale, Stanford, and Johns Hopkins
. A 2025 survey by the journal
Nature
found that
over 75% of U.S.-based scientists
(and nearly 80% of early-career researchers) were actively considering leaving the country, citing political interference and funding instability as primary drivers. Germany has set a goal to lure up to
1,000 top-tier researchers
by 2027, specifically targeting those affected by U.S. federal budget cuts. Similarly, the
European Research Council (ERC)
doubled its relocation allowance for third-country researchers moving to the EU. Slow said the tortoise.
The Pacing Problem: Glacial Policy vs. Exponential Tech
The central tension of 2026 is what scholars call the
“Pacing Problem.”
While technology moves at an exponential rate, government policy moves at a linear, glacial pace. By the time a law is drafted, debated, and enacted, the technology it aims to regulate has often been replaced by something entirely different.
This creates a
Consultation Void
. As a concerned dad, it’s frustrating to realize that the “public consultation” on AI happened after the technology was already in our children’s pockets. The government is essentially trying to “fence in” a forest that has already grown. Because they cannot keep up with the code, they have pivoted to
Procurement as Policy
, instead of passing laws, they are setting “Responsible AI” standards for any company that wants a government contract. This is a subtle but permanent way the state is “baking in” rules that the public never actually voted on.
The “Standardization” Savior: onX and the Macro-Bridge
This regulatory chaos is exactly why macro-thinking like
Kelly Goetsch’s Order Network eXchange (onX)
is so critical. Regulation thrives on standards, and onX provides the “common operational language” that regulators can actually audit.
By creating an open, vendor-neutral standard for order exchange, onX does more than just help AI agents talk to warehouses; it creates a
transparency layer
. It allows a regulator to look at a transaction and see exactly where the AI “handshake” happened, who authorized it, and how the fulfillment was triggered. It bridges the gap between the “wild” world of autonomous agents and the “controlled” world of government oversight.
The Educational Pivot. The Lady is not for Turning
Putting on my “concerned dad” and an e-commerce professional hats, this is part where I feel this all hits home. It looks beyond my work which may be beyond my paygrade, but c’est la vie.  In early 2026, we have reached a point of no return in our schools. The “Lost 3 Years” were spent in a panic of bans and firewalls, but the reality of 2026 is a total surrender to the fact that AI is now a core competency.
The educational policy changes we see today are not just “updates”; they are a fundamental re-wiring of what it means to be an educated human.
1. From “Banning” to “Critical AI Literacy”
In 2023, the response to AI was to block it on school Wi-Fi. In 2026, guided by the UNESCO and OECD AI Literacy Frameworks (AILit), the policy has shifted to mandatory integration. Schools have moved from teaching “how to write an essay” to “how to manage an intelligence.” How FUBAR is this?
The new curricula, rolled out in nations from France to the UK this year, are built on four pillars:
Engaging: Knowing when an AI is present.
Creating: Collaborating with models without losing the “human spark.”
Managing: Learning to delegate tasks to agents responsibly.
Designing: Understanding the probability and data science behind the machine.
Example of CHange: The Death of the Essay and the Rise of the “Log”
As an example of change. One of the most radical change for our children is the shift to Process-Based Assessment. Because an AI can generate a perfect 2,000-word history essay in seconds, the “product” has lost its value as a metric for learning.
National exam boards have moved to grading the AI Interaction Log. A student is no longer graded solely on their final thesis, but on:
The quality of the prompts they used to research.
Their ability to identify “hallucinations” or bias in the AI’s output.
Their documented critique of the AI’s first draft.
As a parent, I see this as a double-edged sword. My children are becoming master orchestrators, but I worry about the “Sunk Development Cost” of the human mind. Are they losing the ability to think deeply without a digital partner? The policy answer in 2026 is that it doesn’t matter the tool is permanent, so the skill must be the partnership itself. This insular way  of life is not healthy because it is not human.
Training the “Orchestrator Class”
This is where the educational shift meets the macro-commerce thinking of the Order Network eXchange (onX). We are no longer training kids to be “doers” of routine tasks—tasks that AI agents now handle in the onX ecosystem. We are training them to be the Architects and Auditors.
Just as Kelly Goetsch’s onX provides a standard for agents to talk to warehouses, our schools are trying to provide a “standard” for humans to talk to agents. We are teaching children to be the “Human-in-the-Loop” that the EU AI Act legally requires.
Finally, there is the financial reality. Governments have spent billions integrating AI-driven “Personalized Tutoring” to solve teacher shortages. These systems, like the ones recently mandated in several US states and EU member nations, are now the “operating system” of the classroom. To remove AI now would be to collapse the administrative and pedagogical backbone of the school system.
The Macro Bridge, Standardization, Agency, and the Path Forward
In 2026, the collision of massive infrastructure spending, agentic consumer habits, and rigid regulation has created a complex “new normal.” As a professional in the e-commerce trenches, I see the technical solution; as a dad, I see the existential challenge. The bridge between these two worlds, the macro-force that will determine if this ecosystem is a “walled garden” or an open utility, is the arrival of universal standards like the Order Network eXchange (onX). The Walled Garden is to be dominated by the small few and the moat is giving the ecosystem a chance to survive.
The Connective Tissue: Why onX Matters to the Macro-Story
We have spent the last three years building incredibly powerful “brains” (AI models) and “limbs” (global logistics). But until recently, they lacked a common nervous system. This is where the work of Kelly Goetsch and the Commerce Operations Foundation becomes the most important macro-development of our era.
The onX protocol, built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), is more than just a technical specification; it is a declaration of interoperability. In a world where government policy is often too slow to be relevant, onX provides a “private-sector constitution.”
For the Professional: onX allows our AI agents to “talk” to any warehouse, payment provider, or 3PL (Third-Party Logistics) without custom code. It turns the fragmented “Wild West” of 2023 into a plug-and-play grid.
For the Citizen: It provides a layer of Accountability. Because onX is an open standard, the “handshakes” between AI agents are transparent and auditable. It prevents the tech giants from creating “black boxes” where we can’t see how our money is being spent or our data is being moved.
Operating in the “Consultation Void”
In 2026, we have learned that we cannot wait for the state to protect us. The “public consultation” never happened because the technology moved too fast for the ballot box.
We are now living in a world of “Code as Law.” The real “policy” isn’t what is written in a legislative bill in Brussels or D.C.; it is what is written in the protocols like onX. If the code is open, we have freedom. If the code is proprietary, we have digital feudalism. As professionals, our responsibility is to “Demand the Standard”, to insist on open architectures that allow for competition and transparency.
Building for Resilience
As I watch my children prepare for a career in this “Agentic Era,” my concern as a father has shifted from
what
they know to
how
they navigate. The educational policy changes are just the beginning.
The “Tide is not going back,” and the sunk costs of this AI revolution are now the foundation of our civilization. We have built a world where our children will be “Orchestrators.” They will manage swarms of agents, negotiate through protocols like onX, and live within the guardrails of the EU AI Act.
Our path forward requires a dual-track strategy:
Professionally: We must champion the “Macro-Thinking” of open standards. We must move our businesses toward composable, agentic architectures that prioritize transparency over lock-in.
Personally: We must provide our children with the “Human Anchor.” In a world where AI can handle the “Order Exchange,” we must teach them the value of the Human Exchange—the things that cannot be standardized, automated, or regulated: character, intuition, and the courage to question the algorithm.
The Architecture of Intent
The last three years were a gestation period that ended in a permanent structural shift. In 2026, we are no longer “adopting” AI; we are inhabiting it. By aligning our commerce infrastructure with open standards like onX and our educational policies with critical agency, we can ensure that this new architecture serves us, rather than the other way around.
The infrastructure is buried deep, the agents are at our door, and the laws are being written in code. It is time to stop watching the tide and start steering the ship.

title: Life Moves Pretty Fast
excerpt: 2025 rewarded the decisive. Brands that picked their category, picked their channel mix, picked their efficiency floors, and then committed outgrew everyone else. The ones that hedged, tested endlessly, and waited for more data spent a year running on the spot while their CAC climbed
_body:
2025  rewarded the decisive. Brands that picked their category, picked their channel mix, picked their efficiency floors, and then
committed
outgrew everyone else. The ones that hedged, tested endlessly, and waited for more data spent a year running on the spot while their CAC climbed and their MER slid.
The market in 2026 will be the same:
be decisive, be clear, be bold, or watch someone else take the share you left on the table. This is all coming from a report according Northbeam.
2025: The Year That Punished Polite
Look, nobody wants to hear another “year in review.” But here’s the thing: if you ran a brand or retail operation in 2025 and you’re still standing, you probably didn’t do it by playing safe and hoping the vibes would sort themselves out. I’ve decided to bring some of this evidence crunching back. I stopped it last year as I didn’t think it always helpful. But, being brave requires evidence for those closer to Thomas than Peter.
Northbeam dropped their annual performance whitepaper this week and it basically confirms everything operators already felt in their bones:
growth came back, but the bill came with it.
Ad spend and revenue both rose across DTC brands, but MER (marketing efficiency ratio) slipped and first-time CAC climbed, meaning scale increasingly came at the cost of efficiency.
The market didn’t care how nice your brand story was. It cared whether you made a decision. And many people did not. Distraction and noise but we consume so much media now, this is hardly surprising.
The data doesn’t lie: 2025 rewarded conviction
Here’s the uncomfortable truth from the Northbeam report:
the brands that grew weren’t the ones who “tested into” everything.
They were the ones who picked a lane and ran. We talked about this last year too.
Brands spending over $50M/year ramped spend by ~20%+ and saw double-digit gains in total and first-time revenue.
Sub-$5M brands were hit hardest, with revenue declining YoY; this cohort focused on cash preservation and margin protection rather than aggressive growth.
Sophisticated operators “pulled ahead by using better measurement, creative, and channel strategy to lean into what worked, even when acquisition costs rose.”
In other words: the bold got bigger and the hesitant got squeezed.
There was no prize for waiting.
The “typical brand” trap
Northbeam makes a point of separating averages from medians in the report, and the gap is brutal. The average brand spent ~15% more on ads to drive similar revenue gains, with lower MER and higher first-time CAC signaling pay-to-grow dynamics. But the
median
brand? Modest gains in spend and revenue alongside a sharper drop in MER and higher CAC. Acceptable topline numbers, weak unit economics underneath.
Translation: most brands were running on the spot while telling themselves they were making progress.
If your 2025 performance looked “fine” on the headline numbers but you never interrogated your first-time MER or CAC, you were probably borrowing from the future without knowing it.
Industry reality: pick your battlefield
Not every category had the same fight. Northbeam broke down the 2025 performance by vertical and the story changes depending on where you operate.
Strong performers (beauty, fashion, home, sporting goods) turned incremental budget into real revenue, often with stable or improving MER. Slower performers (baby & kids, food & beverage, health & wellness) fought rising CAC and softer MER, showing that in tougher categories, selectivity on channels, offers, and timing matters more than simply adding spend.
The operator takeaway:
plan by category reality, not averages.
Your 2026 targets, caps, and channel mix should follow the path of your industry cohort, not the blended market headline.
The AI search thread nobody’s talking about
Here’s the part of the Northbeam report that will get zero LinkedIn engagement but matters more than anything else for the next 18 months.
AI-driven search started 2025 contributing less than 0.01% of all tracked visits. By December, it was 0.15% of total. Small? Sure. But that’s a 15x growth rate in 12 months for a channel that barely existed.
Within the AI/LLM visit mix (excluding Gemini), ChatGPT dominated at ~99% of visits, with Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, and Copilot splitting the remainder.
This isn’t a “plan for it now” moment. It’s a “watch it like a hawk and don’t be the last to notice when it tips” moment. If you’re still treating AI search as a footnote, you’re missing the new routeability layer that’s quietly inserting itself between intent and inventory.
