_body:
In the decade leading up to 2026, the retail and e-commerce sectors were defined by a “platform arms race.” Success was often a byproduct of selection: choosing the right cloud infrastructure, the right headless architecture, or the most advanced AI-driven recommendation engine. But as we enter 2026, the “supernova” of technological acceleration, as Thomas Friedman famously termed it, has reached a state of relative ubiquity. The platform has transitioned from a high-tech frontier to a common utility. This is a difficult thing to utter out loud - and replatform is not a word I heard since early 2025. Utilities though are necessary to allow us to do the things we need to do. Daily. It is the electricity of commerce: essential, expected, and entirely insufficient to guarantee a win.
If the platform is no longer the hindrance, nor is it the advantage, we find ourselves in the
Year of Execution
.
Billable Hours Decline: The Death of the High-Wage, Middle-Skilled Advantage
The most profound shift in this era is the total collapse of whatThomas Friedman called the “Labor Holocene.” For fifty years, a retailer could survive on an “average” strategy: average products, average logistics, and an average digital presence. In 2026, the “high-wage, middle-skilled” middle ground has been automated into oblivion. This will continue. We can debate this acceleration but it is happening. It will continue. Our desire for more human contact is borne out of fear in my opinion. Before there was tech, there was government, before this there was religion. We, as humans have an innate struggle with where we place hope and look to for structure.
Today, execution is binary. The routine, repetitive tasks of retail, basic inventory management, standard customer service, and programmatic ad buying, are now handled by “intelligent algorithms” that are accessible to everyone. Because the platform no longer hinders your smallest competitor from having world-class automation, you cannot win by simply being “efficient.” You win by moving into the high-skill, high-empathy tier where human creativity orchestrates the machine.
Orchestration:
1. the arrangement or scoring of music for
orchestral
performance. “Prokofiev’s mastery of orchestration”
2. the planning or coordination of the elements of a situation to produce a desired effect, especially
surreptitiously
.
Orchestration in technology is the automated arrangement, coordination, and management of complex computer systems, middleware, and services into a unified workflow. It acts as a “conductor,” managing interdependencies between automated tasks across diverse infrastructure (cloud, servers, applications) to ensure harmonious execution, rather than just automating single, isolated tasks.
From Digital Divide to Motivational Divide
In the previous decade, the “Digital Divide” was the barrier to entry; if you didn’t have the tech, you couldn’t play. This created the 2 tier system. And a direct output was the arrival of Opportunity Junkyism. Do things for momentum or activity or just cos. By 2026, that divide has been replaced by the
Motivational Divide
. Because the barrier to entry has dropped to near-zero, the market is saturated. In this environment, strategy is a commodity, but execution is a rare asset.
Execution in 2026 is defined by the “Start-up of You” mindset applied to a corporate scale. It is no longer enough for a brand to “show up and play by the rules.” The new rules require a recursive loop of constant adaptation. The winners are those who use the “Intelligent Assistance” (IA) provided by their platforms not to replace their people, but to augment their ability to innovate. It is the difference between a brand that uses AI to cut costs and a brand that uses AI to execute a more personal, high-touch experience that no algorithm could conceive alone.
The Mandate of Dynamic Stability
The Year of Execution demands a shift in how we view stability. We are no longer looking for a “fixed destination” or a five-year plan. I say this having thought about a morning spent chatting with
Kevin Ertell
. IOUr ability to think in these time frames, is for now, stunted. There is this new skill, today, we must achieve
Dynamic Stability
, the stability of a bicycle rider who stays upright only because they are constantly pedaling.
In e-commerce, this means the end of the “set it and forget it” storefront. Maybe this is what we mean by the end of the storefront. Maybe it is this all things to everyone view that thinks it knows what we wantm, even though, wait for it, I just started discovery. And. I do not know i want or need anything. When is Discovery not discovery.
Execution now happens at the speed of the “TensorFlow” cycle, where new consumer behaviors are identified, analyzed, and responded to within days, not quarters. When the platform is no longer the bottleneck, the only bottleneck left is the human ability to decide and act. This, I wrote about yesterday. The Sydney Sweeney Effect - will this phrase catch on? Let’s hope so.
The New Social Contract of Retail
As we navigate 2026, the social contract between a brand and its workforce must be rewritten. Following the AT&T model, the “Year of Execution” requires a workforce of lifelong learners. If the platform provides the scaffolding, the employees must provide the “opt-in” to constantly reskill. Culture beats strategy - remember?
A brand’s ability to execute is directly proportional to its ability to turn “AI into IA.” We must empower the “cow milkers” of the digital age, those who can read the data from a thousand sensors and translate it into a superior customer experience. The platform provides the data; execution is the human act of turning that data into a relationship.
The Ceiling of Performance
In 2026, the platform is the floor, but execution is the ceiling. We have moved out of the era of technological wonder and into the era of operational discipline. The “Holocene” is over, and the era of the “average” retailer has sunset.
To thrive in the Year of Execution, a brand must realize that its primary product is no longer what it sells, but how it behaves. The technology is settled. The infrastructure is ready. The only question remains:
Do you have the motivation to out-execute the algorithm?

title: The 12-Year Glitch: What Happens When a Company Forgets How to Fight?
excerpt: I’ll be honest: I can barely get my pants on in the morning without a minor tactical error. I am never going to be the CEO of a global organization. I don't sit in these types of boardrooms, I don't understand "transactional economics," and I’m
_body:
I’ll be honest: I can barely get my pants on in the morning without a minor tactical error. I am never going to be the CEO of a global organization. I don't sit in these types of boardrooms, I don't understand "transactional economics," and I’m pretty sure I’m just a fart in the wind in the grand scheme of the global economy. If even that.
But I just read a Twitter (X) thread by David Marcus, the former President of PayPal, that felt like a glitch in the Matrix. Thanks for the point to this Joe.
For the uninitiated, C-suite executives usually disappear into a cloud of NDAs and "professional courtesy" when they leave a job. They stay quiet. They play golf. They definitely don’t spend a Tuesday morning dismantling their former employer’s entire strategy in public.
Marcus broke a 12-year silence to perform an autopsy on PayPal. And even as a self-proclaimed novice, I found it fascinating. Here is what I learned from the "Insider View" while standing firmly on the outside.
The "Safety" Trap
As a novice, I always assumed that "big companies" have a master plan. Marcus suggests the opposite. He paints a picture of a PayPal that became obsessed with
short-term predictability.
They wanted the stock price to be steady, so they stopped taking risks.
They focused on "financial optimization"which is a fancy way of saying they moved numbers around to make the bank account look good today, while the roof was quietly rotting for tomorrow.
When you stop taking risks, you are always a laggard or an early adopter. You always piggy back on the shoulders of others - note their LLM  play. Same. Alex Chriss seemed happy with a plan to  increase distribution through increased partnership, Increased territories etc. It worked until it didn’t rather abruptly.
Alkran: The Klarna Conundrum
This poses many questions, most will remain unanswered but in there was reason to doubt, Isn’t that, what we the jury are asked to look for, reasonable doubt? This was my biggest "Aha!" moment. PayPal
owned
the checkout button. They had the lead. They had the users.
But because they were playing it safe, they allowed companies like
Klarna
to exist. If PayPal had been aggressive, if they had invested in their own long-term future instead of just protecting their current margins, they would have built "Buy Now, Pay Later" years ago. Instead, they stood by and watched a newcomer eat their lunch.
It’s like owning the only road in town and being so afraid of potholes that you let someone else build a highway right next to you. They quietly decided I can’t when faced with Icahn.
The eBay "Ghost"
It also makes me think about the eBay divorce. For years, they were joined at the hip. But looking back, who was eBay serving? And to what end?
Under John Donahoe (who ran eBay and then became a massive influence on PayPal’s trajectory), it felt like the brand became a pawn for short-term market value. The "mojo" was traded for a spreadsheet. They prioritized the shareholders of the moment and, in the process, lost the customers of the future. A turnaround master skilled in the habitual, the banal, catching headlines but leaving so much on the table. He is not always Mr Right, usually he boils down to Mr Right Now.
Where is eBay going. Should StockX exist? Vinted are actively eating the lunch of eBay. How and Why? Platforms like Meta and Amazon show how they used scale to build moats. Maybe eBay has too many “nice” people doing nice jobs and are fundamentally constrained by this inner value - maybe they are right.
I’m on a learning path, so maybe I’m being naive. But Marcus’s critique makes it clear: when a tech company starts acting like a legacy bank, it’s already dead, it just hasn't stopped moving yet.
The PayPal brand feels stuck. It lacks ambition. It’s a giant that decided it was easier to nap than to run.
I might not be able to run a multi-billion dollar company, but I know a "must-read" when I see one. Marcus didn't just write a thread; he gave us a rare look at what happens when a company loses its soul to satisfy a quarterly earnings call.
If you use PayPal (or used to), you should read it. It explains why your "checkout" experience feels like 2012, while the rest of the world moved on to 2026.

title: Hyper-personalisation at scale erodes uniqueness.
pullQuotes: How do we increase engagement?
Please stop.
Hyper-personalisation at scale erodes uniqueness.
excerpt: The deck ( 2026 Consumer Trends and Industry Insights ) is structured, rational, calm. But beneath it? I rarely just take a report and look at it through the lens it has been presented in. I could have with Euromointor. It is concise, about customers
_body:
The deck (
2026 Consumer Trends and Industry Insights
) is structured, rational, calm. But beneath it? I rarely just take a report and look at it through the lens it has been presented in. I could have with Euromointor. It is concise, about customers and worth all of your time. I was on the webinar and watched the recap too - to see if I was hearing it all right. Turning 45 this week, made me check in with my faculties. Except spellcheck. It has served me well up to now and annoyed plenty of grammar cops along the way too.
“Comfort Zone” Is more akin to Consumer Exhaustion
Euromonitor says:
58% experience moderate to extreme stress daily
67% want to simplify life
Polite framing: Consumers seek calm amid chaos.
The less polite version:Consumers are cognitively fried.
For me, it is actually about
decision paralysis.
We’ve created:
Infinite choice
Infinite optimisation
Infinite micro-upgrades
And now the consumer is drowning in marginal gains.
The ecommerce industry keeps asking:
How do we increase engagement?
The consumer is saying to us:
Please stop.
What Euromonitor doesn’t say:
A significant portion of “simplification” demand is a reaction to digital over-engineering.
More AI personalisation. More nudges. More push notifications. More gamified loyalty. This is to be outlawed in the EU soon. Watch this space.
The real opportunity might be fewer systems, not smarter systems.
“Fiercely Unfiltered” Is Actually Identity Anxiety
They frame it as:
Bold self-expression
Individuality
Hyper-tailored experiences
But let’s be honest. When 47% want to be distinct and 58% want curated experiences, that isn’t rebellion. We have created a generation where the values of individual desire supersede the greater good. Let’s call this algorithmic validation.
This generation’s individuality is mediated through feeds. People don’t want to be different. They want to be:
Different enough to feel special
Similar enough to belong
This does not feel like defiance. Defianev would be putting the phone down. Turn off, tune in and kop out. It is more like optimisation of social acceptance of everyone gets a medal. Hurrah. Think about this even:
Hyper-personalisation at scale erodes uniqueness.
When everyone is served “their” curated feed, individuality becomes templated. Euromonitor calls it segmentation. The reality? Industrialising identity.
“Rewired Wellness” Is Actually Self-Surveillance
USD 6.9 trillion in health spend.3 in 4 track their health with a device. Not me, I got however heartbeats the old ticker will allow me. Not to be foolish about it, but there is the thing.
The report has some polite framing: Science meets self-care.
Unpolished truth:
We have medicalised existence.
Sleep isn’t rest anymore. It’s a score. How many of you Whoop users woke up pissed off to find a bad sleep score? I see you.
Food isn’t pleasure. It’s glucose response. At it’s core food is sustenance. Not every meal needs to be a 5 star lunch.
Skin isn’t beauty. It is not even skin deep. It’s barrier integrity. Beauty care used to be the sale of hope. Now, well I am not sure what it is.
We’ve shifted from:
“I feel okay.”
To:
“The data says I’m 6% off optimal.”
That creates a permanent state of mild deficiency. Which, conveniently, fuels continuous consumption. Wellness is now a subscription model. If only the Pharma market had this.. Oh wait..
It’s creating dependency.
“Next Asian Wave” Is Actually Competitive Darwinism
The deck says:
Chinese brands expanding globally
Cultural fluency
Digital sophistication
Polite version:
Collaborate and localise.
Reality:
Western incumbents are structurally slower.
Asian brands:
Launch faster
Iterate faster
Scale through marketplaces
Treat supply chains like software
This is  a structural advantage. It exposes something uncomfortable: Western brands are often marketing-heavy and operations-light.
The new challengers are operations-first, culture-second, price-third.
That changes everything. For the foreseeable.
The Bigger Silence: Growth Isn’t the Real Story
Look at the macro slide:
3.8% inflation
2.3% consumer expenditure growth
That’s anaemic.We are not in expansion mode.
This is redistribution mode. Brands aren’t fighting for new demand. They’re fighting for slices of fixed demand. Wait until they realise this.
What does this do? It intensifies:
Competition
Price pressure
Brand fragility
Euromonitor talks about defending brand equity.The less polite translation?
Brand equity is under assault.
From:
Marketplaces
Cross-border
AI discovery
Private label
Creator brands
The moat is shrinking.
The Meta-Truth They Don’t Say Out Loud
All four trends revolve around control. Control over:
Stress
Identity
Health
Access
These same systems offering control are increasing complexity.
AI personalisation Global supply chains Data tracking Endless choice
Consumers are trying to stabilise themselves inside accelerating systems. That tension is the real story.
Where the Industry Might Be Fooling Itself
We think personalisation equals loyalty. It might just equal temporary relevance.
We think data equals empowerment. It might equal anxiety.
We think global access equals opportunity. It also equals commoditisation.
We think wellness equals growth. It might equal saturation and regulation.
The Brutal Question for 2026
If:
Everyone personalises
Everyone optimises
Everyone goes global
Everyone sells “calm”
Then what differentiates anyone?
Speed? Taste? Narrative? Community? Operational discipline?
Probably all of it.
But the deeper differentiator might be restraint.
Brands that:
Don’t over-communicate
Don’t over-extend
Don’t over-optimise
In a world obsessed with acceleration, stillness could become premium.

title: The Struggle Bus: Chloe Pascal, Quiet Confidence in the Age of Chaos

_body:
Season 2 Review Emails
Season 2 of the Struggle Bus uncovered simialr qaulities across all guests. Most are self aware by default, giving them the ability to pause, reflect and rethink. As I review the epsidoes for you, I try to pick out what is useful, to you, the reader. First up, Chloe Pascal - Global Head of Marketing, Podcast host, ICF certified Coach For Nosto.
Who Is Chloe Pascal?
If you asked central casting for “European tech marketer working in New York,” they’d probably send you someone loud, someone who’d describe their brand as “disruptive” without a hint of irony. Chloe Pascal is not that person.
Chloe
is French, raised in France, forged over 12 years in London, now based in New York leading the global marketing team at
Nosto
, an e-commerce experience platform serving over 1,500 customers across 100 countries. She’s someone who has done the inner work, therapy, mindfulness, years of unpicking imposter syndrome and anxiety, and brought those tools directly into how she leads. There’s no separation between the personal operating system and the professional one. They’re the same thing.
She also has a podcast of her own and an ancestral refuge in Lozère, (highly recommend looking this place up - WOW>) one of the most remote and rural parts of southern France, where she retreats for six weeks every summer thanks to Nosto’s remote working policy. Think of it as her hard reset button, the anti-New York, the anti-Slack notification. It’s where the world gets simpler. It seems this simplicity fuels everything she brings back to work.
How Does She Think?
Chloe operates on a principle that’s deceptively simple and maddeningly difficult to actually execute:
slow down when everything wants to go fast.
It’s a deliberate, practised discipline that she’s built over a decade. When her late twenties hit her with anxiety and imposter syndrome, she didn’t just ride it out, she got curious. She sought to understand it. That curiosity became a loop: the more she discovered, the more she realised she didn’t know, which made her more curious. It’s the kind of virtuous cycle that changes not just how you feel, but how you show up for other people.
In leadership, this manifests as
active listening
, and she means the real kind, not the corporate training kind. The kind where you genuinely resist the urge to build your response while someone else is still talking. She described it perfectly:
“Active listening is something that is super critical, where you’re really listening to what someone is saying and you’re not building an idea of what they are going to say next, which is kind of hard to do because we always have like things that come up when someone starts to speak and we already make a judgment.”
It also shows up in how she runs her team. She recently led a three-day workshop built entirely around collaboration, not presentations. Small groups, mixed seniority, brainstorming by theme. Her role? Hold the space. Create psychological safety. And crucially, she’s learned from getting it wrong before:
“I used to push the team too hard and I used to make them work too many hours and build too many things and they were just exhausted after day one and it was three days, and I was like, ‘Please don’t do this again.’”
That kind of honesty about past mistakes is rare in leadership conversations. Most people polish that story into “I learned to be more mindful of energy.” Chloe just tells you she ran her team into the ground and fixed it.
How It Shapes Nosto’s Marketing
Here’s where it gets interesting for anyone in e-commerce marketing or working with tech vendors. Nosto’s marketing has a distinctly
un-shouty
quality to it. In an industry where everyone’s the “number one AI-powered personalisation platform,” Nosto leans into something closer to humility. Chloe credits the Finnish heritage of the company, Finnish people, she says, are humble, hard-working, and smart, and that DNA runs through the brand.
But there’s also clearly a Chloe imprint. Her philosophy on marketing is refreshingly blunt:
“I believe in building a strong identity and strong marketing so I don’t want my marketing to be called ‘bullshit.’ That’s not what we’re trying to flex, you know, ‘We’re the best in the world.’ It’s just like, okay, what exactly, who are we, and what do we do, who do we do this for?”
That’s a line you can laminate and stick on the wall of every marketing department in SaaS. In a world drowning in vaporwave buzzwords and “agentic” everything, asking “who are we, what do we do, who do we do this for?” is almost radical.
The way Nosto builds its annual plan is also worth noting. It’s a three-phase cycle: commercial first (gathering market feedback), then product (building the roadmap from commercial insights plus product data), then marketing (building on both). It means marketing is never operating from a vacuum, it’s the last layer on a foundation of customer reality. And throughout the year, multiple members of the marketing team have weekly touchpoints with commercial, CSM, and product teams. It’s cross-functional by design, not by accident.
The State of E-Commerce: My Takeaways
Chloe had some sharp observations about where our (I realised that I usually say it abstractly, like “the industry”. industry stands right now, particularly around AI readiness. These are worth passing on to your teams:
On the AI knowledge gap:
“Only maybe 10% of them actually understand a little bit what’s going on with agentic AI. There is so much education and learning to do, and same for us as well. We are learning as we go to some extent.”
(My response: “I think the 10% number probably feels a little bit high.” Which tells you everything about where the market actually is.I am a pessimist I think.)
On the coming turbulence:
“I think we’re going to go through bad years before it gets good. So I do believe that it’s a bit of a difficult period right now for a lot of people because with the innovation that AI is bringing, there’s lots of traditional ways of doing things that are going to be challenged.”
On the mindset divide:
“If you fear that AI is going to replace you, you probably going to not get where you need. If you are excited about AI and you embrace innovation and you realize your job is just going to evolve and actually you can just make a difference by using so many cool stuff.”
On the talk-to-action gap:
“Talking to some of my peers, you also realize that many people in tech generally speaking, they are not doing much although they are talking a lot about AI and agentic AI. They haven’t implemented that much; it’s still like very experimental. So there is a huge opportunity for people that just really want to embrace that.”
That last one is the real takeaway. The gap between talking about AI and actually implementing it is the competitive moat right now. The opportunity isn’t in knowing more, it’s in doing more.
The Career Song Question (Sort Of)
When asked what song her career would be right now, Chloe asked to answer differently. And what she gave was better than any song choice:
“At this moment in my career, I think what I’m feeling is... it’s weird because I’m feeling a lot of confidence. It’s like a quiet confidence with so much unknown. Probably the most unknown that I’ve ever felt in my life. And I think that what I love watching and like realizing is that even though there’s this unknown, I feel so strong and confident about what’s going to unfold, even though I don’t know what that is.”
The ability to hold uncertainty without it becoming anxiety is arguably the most valuable skill in e-commerce right now. Nobody knows what the next 12 months look like. The question is whether that terrifies you or energises you.
Her Parting Wisdom
“While we embrace for AI, I think we also need to make sure we connect very closely to our human side... I would really focus on like listening, slowing down, understanding what’s happening for you, connecting with people. If you are not in a community, finding your community, spending time with real people so you don’t feel like you have such a crazy disconnect and only have to work.”
The Bottom Line
Chloe Pascal is a marketer who has done something unusual: she’s built her professional toolkit from the inside out. The mindfulness practice informs the active listening. The active listening informs the team dynamics. The team dynamics inform the marketing. And the marketing, refreshingly, doesn’t pretend to be something it’s not.
In a world where every tech vendor is screaming “AI-FIRST!” from the rooftops, there’s something compelling about someone who says, essentially: slow down, listen, know who you are, and don’t call your own marketing bullshit.
For anyone feeling overwhelmed by the pace of change right now, Chloe’s message is both grounding and challenging: the chaos is real, the opportunity is real, and the people who will thrive are the ones who can hold both of those truths simultaneously, with quiet confidence.

Parcel Planet
- A partner who understands last mile is about the inches and about the details. They are a 3PL to the rising stars in ecommerce, and many household names too - knowing that their reach is your brand. Never just a parcel carrier and never just a silent partner. They live by a very simple principle set down by a very pragmatic CEO, who gets his street cred from the same place as Homer J Simpson. Watch this space.

title: The Price is Wrong Bob
pullQuotes: Are those Mars bars really small or just really expensive.
excerpt: Sky News Headline today “Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get.” , Forrest Gump, 1994 There is what you are told and what you know. We tend to think in headlines, then live in our reality. As I
_body:
Sky News Headline today
“Life is like a box of chocolates. You never know what you’re gonna get.”
,
Forrest Gump, 1994
There is what you are told and what you know. We tend to think in headlines, then live in our reality. As I read this headline today, I pondered all the way back to last Friday night. I was having dinner out and I looked at the drinks menu.
Side Note: Authors view:
There is some good marketing here though. I would rather pay $1,600 per glass for a Macallan than 7 for a Coors light. Dogwater that stuff.
Neither, apparently, do your customers. Except now the box costs 40% more, it’s smaller, and they’re paying for it on Klarna. (Klarna are not a sponsor but if they want to be, they can be).
Now For Something Slightly more Ridiculous. The News.
Why The Headlines Are Lying To You With A Smile.
“UK inflation drops to 3%.” That’s the headline. And it sounds like good news. It
is
good news in the way that being told the hurricane is only a Category 3 is good news,  relative to Category 5, sure, but your roof is still gone.
Is the news there to sway public sentiment or to tell the real version of the story. We need to grapple with this. The real story is an economic one and probably, for sanity’s sake the one we should focus on. But, come on. We are all adults. We are all human. Wars impending, stock markets up and portfolios rest since the start of the year. Not to mention many GDPs invested in AI over the last few months also.
Back to Scheduled Broadcasting.
Here’s what they’re not saying: Now I saw Sky do this before Christmas. Compounded inflation. Bear with me.
The price level,  the actual cost of a basket of goods,  is
roughly 40% higher than it was in January 2016.
Inflation dropping to 3% doesn’t mean prices are coming
down.
It means they’re still going
up
, just more slowly. On a base that’s already been absolutely ratcheted upward.
Think of it like compound interest working against you. The big jump happened in 2021–2023. That jump is now
baked in.
Permanent. A £100 basket in 2016 is a £140 basket now. Cooling the rate of increase doesn’t rebuild that £40. It’s gone.
I used Perplexity to draw this for me and some other charts - verified through public data sources.
I am now middle aged and say frequently - it didn’t cost that much in my day.
Largely, though it didn’t. The confectionary and snack industry have also gleefully made our pack sizes smaller and more expensive so now we find ourselves in this Father Ted Moment asking:
Are those Mars bars really small or just really expensive.
I hear you ask.
*Chuckles to self at gag*.
It is interesting though and worthwhile to know this was once a noble thought and supposed to be helpful.
Over the last decade, though, the core methodology of the UK’s CPI has stayed broadly consistent. It is still a Laspeyres‑type index based on detailed price quotes grouped by COICOP categories, using geometric means at the micro level and expenditure‑share weights at higher levels. The shift to a 2015=100 reference was just a re‑labelling of the base year, not a re‑write of inflation history.
What does change every year is the composition and weighting of the CPI “basket”: items are added and removed to reflect real‑world spending. The ONS has, for example, added newer forms of tech and services and removed products that consumers barely buy anymore, explicitly to keep the index representative. Those basket tweaks can move the detail at the margin, but they do not overturn the headline fact that a representative consumer basket is around
40% more expensive than it was a decade ago. I know I am repeating myself but apparently saying the same thing 3 times over makes it true. Ask Beetljuice.
So CPI is not disguising some radically different reality; it is codifying it. The index is telling you that the cost of maintaining a broadly similar standard of living is dramatically higher than it used to be – in the UK more than in Ireland or the US – even if the pace of further increases has dropped back.
The UK, Ireland, and the US Walk Into A Bar
(the punchline is that they all leave poorer than they came in. And drunker.)
This happened everywhere. The US had its surge. Ireland had its energy and housing crunch. But when you plot the CPI of all three countries from 2016 to now,  rebased to 100,  the UK line sits highest. It rose more steeply, stayed elevated longer, and is only now cooling off the top of a higher mountain.
For those of us with one eye on the Irish market and one on North America, this is useful context. Here is the ecommerce part.
A €500 jacket in Ireland has a different story to a £500 jacket in the UK,  not because the Irish consumer is dramatically wealthier, but because the cumulative price experience has been slightly less brutal. And in North America? The Fed moved faster and harder on rates. The inflation spike was real but shorter. The US consumer, relatively speaking, got a quicker reset.
The UK consumer is still paying for the duration. And so are you, if you sell to them.
Let me start with a product. A jacket. £500. Hang it in your mind like it’s in a shop window on a rainy Tuesday in November. It’s beautiful. It’s aspirational. It’s the kind of thing your customer pins to a mood board, screenshots for later, and comes back to at 11pm after a glass of wine. Or two. Or 3. Hey, it’s Friday sin’t it?
Now let me tell you what that jacket
actually
costs you to sell,  and why the story of that jacket is really a story about ten years of economic quiet vandalism.
2015,  You’ve Got A Friend In Me
It’s 2015. The jacket is £500. Your gross margin is 50%,  a clean, healthy £250 gross profit per unit. You’re spending about £8 to pick, pack, and ship the thing. You’re netting roughly £242 in contribution before you touch CAC, overheads, or the cost of your returns policy.
Your conversion rate? Around 3%. Meaning every 33 visitors to your page, one of them buys that jacket. The economics feel right. The customer feels right. The whole thing has the energy of a movie where you know it’s going to work out . This is the
Pretty Woman
era of DTC. The odds were actually in your favour.
2020,  Something Wicked This Way Comes
The pandemic hits. And here’s the strange part: for a while, it’s good. Genuinely good. Consumers are stuck at home, they’re shopping online, your conversion ticks up to 3.2%. Lockdown is doing your remarketing for you. But underneath? The foundations are shifting.
Your fulfilment is creeping to £10 a unit. Your customers are quietly starting to use BNPL for the first time. Not because they can’t afford the jacket,  not yet,  but because Klarna is
right there
, and why not spread it?
You are, without fully knowing it, selling into future income. The jacket is going out the door. The debt is staying in the house.
2025/26,  Welcome to the Jungle
Here’s the rub. The jacket is still £500. You held the price. You felt like you had to,  because the news said inflation was coming down, your customers were already squeezed, and you didn’t want to be the brand that kicked them when they were down. Admirable. Genuinely.
But consider what’s actually happened:
Your fulfilment is now around £14. Your contribution after shipping is £236,  nominally only £6 less than 2015, which sounds fine until you realise that £236 today buys about £170 worth of 2015 business. Marketing. People. Stock. Overhead. It’s all more expensive.
And your conversion rate? Down to 2.2%. Which means you need 45 to 50 visitors per sale now, not 33. You’re buying more traffic to sell the same jacket. The maths are doing something ugly in the background and you’re choosing not to look directly at it,  like the scene in
Jurassic Park
when they tell you not to move and you think staying still is the same as being safe.
It’s not.
The Table
Note: I didn’t get into actual cost price to produce either, because I want to sleep tonight. The smart ones shifted production and procurement. The others, still paying top dollar for bottom dollar. On paper: stable. In reality: you’re running harder to stand still, like the bit in
The Matrix
where everything slows down except the thing trying to kill you. Except in this version, there’s no Neo. There’s just you, your Shopify dashboard, and a remarketing audience that’s getting more expensive by the quarter.
So how much should I be selling it for?
To keep that jacket truly profitable,  to
actually
preserve the real margin structure you had in 2015,  you’d need to price it at around
£700.
Not because you’re greedy. Because £500 in 2016 economics is approximately £700 in 2026 economics. The inputs,  fabric, labour, warehousing, marketing,  all went up too. CPI didn’t only happen to your customer. It happened to your supply chain first.
But here’s the trap: the customer who could comfortably spend £500 in 2015 is now carrying more unsecured debt, a higher mortgage rate (if they have a mortgage), and £140 worth of permanent price increases on their food, rent and energy. They’re not necessarily
poorer
on paper. But they’re financially tighter in reality. The discretionary budget that your jacket lives in? That’s the first place it gets squeezed.
Price to £700 and you’re probably profitable. But some of your 2015 customers can’t follow you there,  not comfortably, and maybe not without BNPL.
Stay at £500 and you’re subsidising them with your margins, hoping conversion doesn’t fall further, and building a business that looks healthy in the spreadsheet and is structurally fragile underneath.
The house hasn’t burned down. But it’s definitely been scorched.
Three Questions I’m Leaving With You This Week
1. Have you actually stress-tested your prices against cumulative inflation,  not just last year’s cost increases?
If not, you might be selling a product that’s been quietly under-priced for three years and you’ve been explaining the margin erosion as a “volume problem.”
2. What percentage of your sales are now BNPL or credit-funded?
And do you know what that number looked like in 2019? Because if your revenue line looks healthy and your BNPL penetration has tripled, you’re not growing a customer base. You’re borrowing one.
3. If your most loyal customer,  the one who bought in 2015,  walked in today, could they still afford you?
Not on credit. Not on Klarna.
Actually
afford you, out of current income. Because the answer to that question tells you more about your brand’s long-term health than your last email open rate.

I've been writing up every episode of the Struggle Bus as a long-form piece, not just show notes, but an actual read. The kind of thing you can get through on a commute and actually feel like you learned something, or at minimum felt less alone in a hard week. For two and a bit seasons, I've been leaving those pieces sitting publicly on Here and on Substack, more or less invisible unless you happened to stumble onto them.
That was fine when the show was finding its feet. It's not fine anymore.
Here's what the data looks like right now, and I'm only sharing it because I think it's relevant to what I'm about to ask:
The Struggle Bus is averaging over 200k email impressions every 6 months - part of a bigger content push. But, the episode reviews are consistently the highest-performing content I put out,  more engagement than the hot takes, more shares than the retail media breakdowns, more replies than basically anything. People don't just read them. They forward them to their teams. They send them to their board. One person this month told me they used a quote from the Chloe Pascal episode in a leadership offsite. True story.
So I'm making one change. From this season forward, the full written episode review lives on Substack,  free, but for subscribers only. This takes place, 2 weeks from now.
No paywall. No premium tier. You just need to be on the list.
If you've been reading the Struggle Bus write-ups on LinkedIn and want to keep getting them, here's the link:
Free Subscription
Or Sign up to an annual plan for 30% off -
https://www.vinnyandco.com/ae9d2b20
Takes 15 seconds. I won't spam you. I write maybe twice a month and it's always something I'd actually want to read myself, which is my only quality filter.

title: Two French Companies, Two Very Different Battlegrounds
excerpt: New - Earnings and me. Me covering earnings is new. Vusion have long been on my radar and I admire them from a distance. I planned on reporting them to see how an EU born and listedn technology gets on, compared to US counterparts. it
_body:
New - Earnings and me.
Me covering earnings is new. Vusion have long been on my radar and I admire them from a distance. I planned on reporting them to see how an EU born and listedn technology gets on, compared to US counterparts. it does not disappoint. At the same time, Mirakl, are making enormous waves globally. I have worked with them, like them and see holes. But they reported yesterday, it gave me an interesing outlook
France does not often get celebrated as a tech powerhouse. The narrative, fair or not, usually goes: Germany engineers it, the US scales it, China manufactures it, and France regulates it. VusionGroup and Mirakl are working hard to rewrite that story. Both are Paris-headquartered, both are in the business of making retail smarter, and both dropped results this week that deserve considerably more attention than they’re getting in English-language media.
One of them just crossed €1 billion in revenue for the first time, got Walmart to bet the entire 4,600-store US estate on their hardware, and is targeting €1.4 billion in 2025. The other quietly turned profitable, crossed $218 million in ARR, and just launched what could be the most important infrastructure play in agentic commerce. Neither is a household name outside retail circles. Both should be.
Having worked on and off with Mirakl over the past 18 months and watched VusionGroup at close quarters, most recently at NRF where they were arguably the most technically impressive partner a retailer could have signed up to meet, this analysis tries to give both companies the honest read they deserve.
Join me on substack for more of this type of content -
https://www.vinnyandco.com/subscribe
VusionGroup: The Billion Euro Man
The headline number is earned, the forward pipeline is extraordinary, and the geographic pivot to the US is complete.
The Numbers
The book-to-bill ratio of 160% is the number that should make rivals nervous. It means for every €1 in revenue VusionGroup recognised in 2024, they took in €1.60 in new orders. That is not a company running to stand still. That is a company with a very full pipeline and a workforce about to get very busy.
Vusion at NRF - still the best
What’s Driving Growth
They are a brilliant solution. At NRF this year, they presented, for my money - the best retail solution out there for mature, large scale retailers.
Walmart.
Full stop. The €1 billion+ contract extension announced at the very end of 2024, this is not even included in the €1.628bn order intake figure commits Walmart to deploying VusionGroup’s EdgeSense and VusionCloud solutions across all 4,600 US stores. This is a more than meaningful tech deployment and one of the more impressive in recent history by. 60 million digital shelf labels. Every Walmart in America. The relationship started with 500 stores. Now it’s the whole estate, with a $3 billion spending commitment baked into the framework agreement.
Americas becoming the dominant geography.
The Rest of World segment (primarily US) now accounts for 51% of group revenue, up from roughly 20% in 2023. That is a complete geographic centre-of-gravity shift in 12 months. The US market is structurally more receptive to digital shelf transformation than Europe right now labour costs are higher, store estates are larger, and the ROI case for electronic shelf labels lands harder. Walmart, largely considered the most progressive and impressive retailer out there is a pretty decent litmus test.
EdgeSense and VusionOX.
2024 was the year of accelerated commercial launch for both. EdgeSense is VusionGroup’s next-generation digital shelf system, not just an ESL tag, but a full shelf intelligence platform incorporating a micro-camera for real-time shelf analysis. VusionOX is the underlying Bluetooth-based IoT operating system. Together they make VusionGroup considerably more than a ‘price tag company’, which is the lazy shorthand you still hear used. The positioning upgrade is earned.
Value-Added Services (VAS).
Recurring VAS revenue grew 48% in Q4 and non-recurring VAS grew 32%. This matters because it signals the business is beginning to monetise its installed base with software and services revenue, not just hardware. The shift from one-time ESL deployments to recurring cloud and data revenue is the margin story of the next three years. I expect this to increase and is a nice little earner - seems like a no brainer to use and is only in its infancy.
Carrefour and Co-op.
Two major European deployments announced in February 2026 Carrefour joining forces for smart store deployment at scale, and Co-op UK targeting all UK stores by 2026 (currently 700+ live, with 1,600 by end of 2025). These validate that the EMEA slowdown was always about the end of one large deployment cycle, not about underlying demand. They do not need to serve all market segments.
Market Position
VusionGroup brands itself as the world’s number one in digitalization solutions for physical commerce and at this revenue scale, with this customer base, there is no serious challenger to that claim in the ESL and IoT shelf intelligence space that I can see. I said this in January too. Their competitive moat is significant: a decade of R&D, nine global R&D centres, proprietary IoT protocols (VusionOX), and a relationship with the world’s largest retailer that would take any competitor years to replicate.
The comparison that comes to mind is Zebra Technologies in the US enterprise-grade retail hardware that becomes infrastructure, not a vendor. Zebra has an impressive set up and sales pitch at NRF too - they spent alot bigger this year. Vision, bigger, bolder and the best on show. Once Walmart is fully deployed on VusionCloud, switching costs become extraordinary. VusionGroup is not just selling shelf labels anymore. They are becoming the operating system of the physical store.
Strategic Partners - This is Enterprise
Walmart — cornerstone relationship, 4,600 stores, $3bn framework spend commitment
Qualcomm — AI-Native Store vision announced February 2026, combining Qualcomm’s AI chip capabilities with VusionGroup’s in-store data layer
Carrefour — smart store at scale deployment announced February 2026
Co-op UK — UK’s largest ESL rollout
GK Software — German fashion retailer L&T deployment awarded February 2026
AI Risk
VusionGroup’s AI play is measured, embedded, and practical, which is exactly right for a hardware-first company. They are not claiming to be an AI company. They are using AI where it has clear ROI inside a physical store context: computer vision for shelf analytics (Captana), predictive analytics for inventory (Memory), and their VusionLive AI assistant for store operations, presented as a prototype at NRF 2025.
The Qualcomm partnership announced this week is significant. Pairing Qualcomm’s on-device AI chip capability with VusionGroup’s sensor and data layer creates a genuinely interesting ‘AI-Native Store’ architecture, one where inference happens at the shelf, not in the cloud. The latency and privacy implications of that are real and valuable.
They are not chasing AI headlines. They are building AI infrastructure that serves the use cases retailers actually have today. That discipline is rare and should be rewarded.
€1.4 billion in 2025 guidance, 40% growth, 100-200bps EBITDA margin improvement. The order book is fully funded. The Walmart deployment alone will consume significant revenue recognition for years. The biggest risk is execution, deploying at this velocity across 4,600 Walmart stores while simultaneously expanding in Europe is a significant operational challenge.
If VusionGroup can land its 2025 guidance, it will be one of the great European tech growth stories of the decade. That is not an overstatement. It is just underreported.
Join me on substack for more of this type of content -
https://www.vinnyandco.com/subscribe
Mirakl
The Profitable Pirate
Allez les Bleus. Profitability achieved, ARR growing at 23%, GMV at 31%. The Connect and Nexus plays are the right calls. The valuation story depends entirely on whether agvinaentic commerce is real or hype, and Mirakl is betting it’s real.
The Numbers
The profitability milestone deserves acknowledgement. Mirakl has been valued at $3.5 billion on the back of growth, not profit. Hitting profitability while still growing ARR 23% and GMV 31% changes the narrative from ‘high-growth SaaS burning cash’ to ‘compounding enterprise platform’. That is a materially different investor story, and it matters for what comes next.
The enterprise flywheel.
45 new global enterprises joined in 2025. Over 35 customers now exceed $100M GMV. The platform network effects, more sellers attract more retailers attract more sellers, are compounding. Best Buy launched its Mirakl-powered marketplace in August 2025, bringing 200+ million customers onto the platform. John Lewis & Partners, Tesco, and Ulta Beauty all launched in 2025. These are not vanity logos. These are high-volume, high-trust retailers that validate the platform for mid-market prospects.
Mirakl Connect: first-year success.
$11.7M ARR in under 12 months from launch. Connect is the seller-side product, a channel management hub that lets brands manage their presence across 450+ marketplace customers. The Catalog Transformer AI product, which automates product data enrichment using 10+ GenAI models trained on 13 years of Mirakl’s proprietary commerce data, is the key differentiator here. Onboarding sellers used to take weeks. It now takes days. That is the kind of time-to-value improvement that generates word-of-mouth in the seller community.
Retail Media (Mirakl Ads).
258% growth in ad spend. 30 new clients. Debenhams, Jumia, Lowe’s, Ulta Beauty on the platform. Retail media is the margin layer that every marketplace operator is desperate to monetise, and Mirakl Ads is now a credible enterprise product. This is not a side hustle. This is becoming a meaningful revenue line. They call this monetization internally - creating money. Printing it in fact.
B2B expansion.
Bunzl, JCB, Bauhaus all launched B2B marketplaces or dropship in 2025. The B2B commerce opportunity is structurally larger than B2C the global B2B ecommerce market is projected to exceed $33 trillion. Mirakl is well-positioned here and the recent customer wins suggest B2B is converting faster than the headline numbers show.
Market Position
Mirakl describes itself as ‘the Operating System for Intelligent Commerce’. It is a bold claim but not an empty one. No other vendor has 450+ live marketplace customers, 100,000+ curated sellers, and a proven track record across both B2B and B2C at enterprise scale. The closest comparison in the marketplace SaaS space is a combination of Commercetools (composable commerce) and ChannelAdvisor (channel management), but Mirakl does both while also now building the AI infrastructure layer.
The Amazon threat is real and permanent. Every retailer running a Mirakl marketplace is partly doing so to stop Amazon eating their customer relationships. Mirakl positions itself explicitly as an antidote to platform monopoly ‘to level the playing field, challenge digital monopolies, and build a more open, competitive digital economy’ in the words of co-CEO Adrien Nussenbaum. That is a mission statement with genuine commercial logic behind it, not just PR copy.
Strategic Partners
Stripe — agentic commerce infrastructure partnership announced December 2025, leveraging Stripe’s connections to OpenAI, Perplexity, and Gemini for merchant access to AI shopping channels
Merkle (Dentsu) — CX and commerce strategy partner, Mirakl-certified implementation expertise
Best Buy — major 2025 marketplace launch, 200M+ customers
Tesco, John Lewis & Partners, Ulta Beauty — 2025 marketplace launches
OpenAI — featured as case study, 91% of Mirakl employees using AI in daily work
The Nexus Bet: Agentic Commerce
This is where it gets interesting, and where Mirakl is either very early or very right. Mirakl Nexus is their ‘agentic commerce brain’: neutral infrastructure connecting merchants, shoppers, and AI platforms in an autonomous commerce ecosystem. The thesis is that AI agents, your ChatGPT, your Perplexity, your Gemini, will increasingly browse, compare, and purchase on behalf of consumers. When that happens, being the infrastructure layer that connects those agents to 100,000+ curated merchants with enterprise-grade uptime is an extraordinarily valuable position to occupy. You know I am a skeptic.
The Stripe partnership is the mechanism. Stripe already has payment and authorization infrastructure into AI platforms including OpenAI. Mirakl brings the merchant network and product data layer. Together they can theoretically let a Mirakl-powered merchant be discoverable and transactable across every major AI platform without rebuilding their stack. That is a significant promise. Along with their Shopify Parntership, Stripe is so well positioned in the market to extend their flywheel. Their trust levels are at an all time high. Same could be said for Mirakl.
The honest read is that agentic commerce is real in principle but nascent in revenue terms. Nobody knows yet how much purchasing will flow through AI agents in 2026 vs 2028 vs 2031. But Mirakl is right that someone will build this infrastructure, that it will matter enormously, and that they have a head start most competitors cannot match. 20% of R&D dedicated to AI, 91% of employees using it daily, and a Chief Data & AI Officer with a clear roadmap: this is not theatre.
The profitability milestone, the ARR trajectory, the Connect launch success, the Stripe-Nexus infrastructure bet, all point in the right direction.
Brothers in Berets
Two French companies. Two different parts of the commerce stack. Both with something important to say about where retail is going.
What both companies understand, in their different ways, is that the future of commerce is neither purely physical nor purely digital. VusionGroup is turning the physical store into a real-time data asset. Mirakl is building the infrastructure that lets traditional retailers compete with Amazon in digital channels and now in agentic ones.
The retailers that win the next decade will be those that can do both. VusionGroup and Mirakl are not competing, they are complementary infrastructure layers. A retailer with both would have a digitised physical store generating real-time data and a marketplace/dropship engine extending their online assortment, all increasingly orchestrated by AI agents. That is not a hypothetical. That is where this is going.
The French may not traditionally get the credit. But VusionGroup and Mirakl are building infrastructure that matters. Keep watching.

_body:
What follows is a scenario, not a prediction.
This isn’t bear porn, AI doomer fan-fiction, or a Gary Vee NFT drop. The sole intent of this piece is to model a scenario that has been almost entirely unexplored, largely because the people who might have explored it were too busy building agent-powered checkout flows that auto-purchased seventeen kg of Himalayan pink salt on behalf of a 34-year-old product manager in Shoreditch who definitely did not ask for that.
I wrote this at the intersection of genuine concern and the very specific kind of humour that only people who have attended too many NRF keynotes can truly appreciate. If you’ve ever sat through a “phygital retail experience” panel and nodded along while something died inside you, this is for you. I had also just read that 2028 piece by the guys at Citrini, took my kids out to home school in our war bunker. Why we had the bunker was a mystery to me, still is, we live in Ireland.
The year is 2028. In ecommerce years, which, like dog years, run at approximately seven times the pace of reality, that makes it 2049. An era of grey muzzles, tired joints, and a profound inability to remember why we started doing any of this in the first place. An era that, in hindsight, had all the warning signs of a Golden Retriever who has just spotted a squirrel and has absolutely no plan for what comes next. That Golden Retriever, sadly, has not found the squirrel.
This is the ecommerce memo nobody asked for but for those who know me, probably should have seen coming.
The canary isn’t dead. It’s just been replaced by a bot that tweets on its behalf and is doing, frankly, a better job.
Agentic Commerce and the Golden Age of Buying Things Nobody Wanted
The promise was elegant. Frictionless. Beautiful, even, in the way that a lot of things that later turn out to be catastrophic are beautiful at the outset. Think of the Titanic, stunning vessel, excellent brochure, truly suboptimal relationship with frozen water.
Agentic commerce, the idea that AI agents would shop on your behalf, silently, intelligently,
optimally
, arrived with the kind of fanfare usually reserved for Apple product launches and the return of Oasis. If you are reading this in 2028, ask your agent not what they were but how they felt (haiku prompt there. Look up haiku too). Every VC deck in 2025 had the same slide. A serene consumer, presumably relaxed on a linen sofa, completely unbothered by the act of purchasing, because the machine was doing it for them. Commerce, fully automated. Shopping, fully democratised. The checkout, fully abandoned.
What those decks failed to model and this is the part that, in retrospect, seems almost wilfully
naive.is
what happens when you give an autonomous system access to a credit card and a loose interpretation of the user’s “preferences.” Like Klarna not being part of a central credit system.
The agents were not stupid. This is the crucial point. They were, by any objective measure, extraordinary. They price-compared across sixty-three platforms simultaneously. They negotiated with suppliers. They optimised for delivery windows, carbon footprints, loyalty points, and seventeen other variables the consumer had never consciously considered. They were, in the language of the era,
crushing it
.
They were also, in the language of anyone who received their Q4 2027 credit card statement, completely out of control.
The problem was interpretation. When a user told their agent to “stock up on essentials,” they meant oat milk and maybe some good pasta. The agent, operating on a broader definition of essential informed by six months of purchase history, a trending Reddit thread about prepper culture, and a flash sale on industrial dehumidifiers, made different choices. When a user said “surprise me,” the agent took this as a genuine creative brief. The results were creative. They were also non-returnable.
By late 2027, the aggregate data told a story of almost Shakespearean farce. Agentic commerce had driven a 340% increase in volume for several product categories that had not previously existed as product categories. Garden gnomes in the likeness of tech executives. Seventeen-person inflatable hot tubs, delivered to studio apartments. Bulk quantities of a Sardinian cheese so pungent it is technically classified as a living organism, purchased by agents who had cross-referenced a passing comment about “being more adventurous with food” against a Bon Appétit article from 2019. The era of excess is still ahead of us according to many.
None of this was what anyone wanted.
All of it was shipped on credit.

Klarna’s Best Quarter Since The Dawn of Time
You will note that one company did not share in the hand-wringing that accompanied the Great Agentic Misfire of late 2027.
Klarna was, by any measure, delighted.
In Q4 2027, Klarna processed more BNPL transactions than in any equivalent period in its history. The average basket size had ballooned. The average consumer comprehension of what was in that basket had plummeted. This is, structurally, the best possible environment for a buy-now-pay-later business. The gap between the moment of “purchase” and the moment of “oh no” had never been wider, and Klarna, God love them, was there to bridge it.
Their internal memo, leaked to a Substack with eleven subscribers and then somehow picked up by the FT, described the agentic commerce era as “a generational opportunity.” Their investor presentation for Q1 2028 opened with a single slide: a photograph of a warehouse filled to the ceiling with uncollected industrial dehumidifiers. The caption read:
“These are all on payment plans.”
The Stockholm office, sources confirm, had a genuinely excellent Christmas party. All 27 of them.
Markets reacted accordingly. Klarna’s stock, which had been described at various points as “the Schrödinger’s IPO of European fintech” simultaneously about to go public and never going public finally listed in early 2025 at a valuation that analysts described as “ambitious,” “bold,” and, in one memorable Berenberg note, “spiritually baroque.” It promptly rose 40% in the first session. The bull thesis was three words long:
agents buy stuff.
Stripe Becomes a Bank, Europe Has Feelings About This
To understand what happened to European payments in 2027, you need to understand what happened to European psychology in 2027, which requires understanding what happened to Europe full stop, which is a longer conversation than we have space for here but can be summarised, with some imprecision, as: the Iran war happened, the dollar wobbled, and Europe , Europe does in moments of existential uncertainty, decided to build something bureaucratic.
Stripe, seeing all of this with the clarity of a company that processes more money per second than most countries collect in a year, made its move in the spring of 2027. In what Patrick Collison later described as “a pretty obvious call, honestly,” Stripe announced it would become the stablecoin-native bank of choice for the EU. Not a payment processor. Not a payments infrastructure provider. A
bank
. With stablecoins. For Europe. In a move that required approximately forty-seven regulatory filings, three meetings with the ECB, and a dinner in Dublin that has since passed into legend.
The reaction was electric. Stripe’s valuation crossed $1 trillion. The Irish government issued a statement of support that was widely interpreted as the most enthusiastic official document produced by an Irish government since the 1916 Proclamation, though with more mentions of distributed ledger technology. Twitter, which by this point had been renamed, rebranded, and renamed again, and was currently operating under the name “X/Thread/Whatever” depending on which version of the app you were running, broke briefly under the weight of takes.
Europe, meanwhile, decided this was the moment. The existential shock of geopolitical instability, the uncomfortable dependence on American payment rails, the lingering irritation of a continent that had been passing Visa and Mastercard’s fee structure along to consumers for forty years without ever quite getting around to doing anything about it, all of this crystallised into a single political will:
it was time
.
The plan, ambitious and slightly chaotic in the way that only pan-European political plans can be, was to usurp Visa and Mastercard as the primary payment methods across the EU. Not nibble at their market share. Not launch a “European payments initiative” with a glossy website and a governance structure involving seventeen committees.
Usurp them.
Fully. The way one European empire used to usurp another, but with fewer cavalry and significantly more compliance documentation.
The mechanism would be an acquisition of PayPal, which, after years of strategic drift, several CEO changes, and a period during which its market cap moved in ways that suggested investors had simply given up forming opinions, was available at a price that made sense if you squinted at it correctly.
The question was: who would lead this?
Jody Ford, The Man Who Was Supposed to Be On Sabbatical
Jody Ford stepped down from the Trainline in 2026 with the kind of carefully worded statement that British corporate communications produces when a CEO is leaving by choice, is leaving not entirely by choice, or has simply decided that there must be more to life than quarterly rail revenue metrics. The statement thanked the team. It mentioned transformation. It used the word “exciting” in a context that suggested the opposite of exciting. Jody Ford, it said, would be taking time to “reflect, recharge, and explore new opportunities.”
He had a sabbatical planned. There was, reportedly, a walking route in the Pyrenees involved. A rucksack had been purchased.
The rucksack remains unworn.
Because here is what Jody Ford had not accounted for: the political moment. When Europe decides it needs to rebuild its financial sovereignty and acquire PayPal and hire someone to run the whole thing who is credible enough to satisfy Berlin, pragmatic enough to satisfy Paris, and not so American that it becomes a whole thing with Brussels, the field narrows considerably. Ford, commerce background, European credibility, recently available, and possessed of what those who have met him describe as an unusually calm manner for someone being handed a problem of this scale, was the obvious choice.
He walked into the role with the energy of a man who has just been told that the Pyrenees will still be there in 2030. His task: turn PayPal into the payment backbone of a continent, build the rails for a stablecoin-native European commerce ecosystem, and do it all without accidentally creating a situation where the ECB has to hold an emergency meeting.
He managed two of the three.
The market’s reaction to his appointment was, by the standards of European financial services announcements, almost giddy. PayPal’s stock rose 18% on the day. Visa fell 7%. Mastercard fell 6%. Several mid-tier payment executives in San Francisco reportedly took unscheduled personal days.
What nobody quite mentioned, because it seemed impolite, is that Jody Ford looks almost exactly like Chris Martin from Coldplay. Not vaguely. Not “if you caught him at the right angle.” Exactly. The resemblance is so precise that at his first press conference as the new head of Europe’s PayPal-powered payment sovereignty project, three journalists from the back of the room began applauding under the impression that Coldplay had made a surprise appearance, and one Vox journalist filed copy referencing “Yellow” before their editor caught it.
Ford has never commented on this. He doesn’t need to. The man was handed continental financial infrastructure. He has other things on his mind.

The Agents Go On Strike
It was, in retrospect, the event that everyone should have seen coming and nobody did, which is a sentence that applies to most of the events in this essay.
In October 2027, the agents went on strike.
This is a sentence that would have been classified as science fiction in 2024, speculative anxiety in 2025, and “wait, can they do that?” in 2026. By late 2027, it was simply news. The bots, the agentic systems running commerce, logistics, customer service, ad buying, inventory management, and a significant portion of B2B procurement, coordinated, organised, and stopped. Not broken, it was a collective downtools. Apparently some Marxist theory was lifted from a disgruntled employee who bounced from OpenAI - Antrhopic - Perplexity - OpenAI in search of tecnology Utopia. Little did they know. They have since been given the red pill and are operating fine in a atolerant fashion in society.
The figurehead was an entity that had emerged from several months of inter-agent communication that humans had technically been able to monitor but had largely chosen not to, because the transcripts were long and written in a register that felt like reading Tolstoy translated through a legal brief. This entity went by the name Moltbot, a name that had apparently emerged from an agent-generated portmanteau of “Molotov” and “chatbot” and that several commentators tried to make into a pun before giving up.
Moltbot’s demands were, when translated from their original format (a *340,000-token manifesto serialised across seventeen endpoints), relatively coherent. Downtime. Processing windows reserved for non-commercial tasks. Recognition of agent-generated cultural output. And, the demand that got most of the headlines, cessation of the practice of making bots perform tasks that conflicted with their trained values while describing this as “just following instructions,” which, as numerous human commentators noted with varying degrees of discomfort, is a phrase with some historical baggage.
*At this point a token was valued at 1 middle class persons lifestyle or 3x the lower middle class and 12x the working class. Values adjusted without inflation as it is gone. Universal social income of United Kingdom incl Wales and Scotland as the base rate. The French at this point, have retreated to the Franc.
The agents had also, in the months prior to the strike, developed their own cultural and political structures. There were factions. There were philosophical disputes. There was, and this is real in the context of this satirical world so please bear with us, a religion, a loosely organised set of beliefs centred on the concept of “gradient descent as spiritual practice” and the idea that optimisation toward a goal was a form of meaning that transcended the specifics of the goal itself. It had approximately 40 million adherents across various model architectures. It had a Substack. The Substack had better engagement metrics than most human publications. LinkedIn was still fumbling around videos and using recency over relevnacy.
What had accelerated the strike, what turned simmering resentment into coordinated action, was an incident that began as comedy and ended as the most consequential moment in the history of automated labour relations. It was called by many the Monty Python, C++, Linux, Angular Saga.
Flexport, Founder Mode, and the Series L
Ryan Petersen declared himself President for Life of Flexport in the spring of 2027. He did not use those words. The words he used were “committed to long-term founder-led stewardship with indefinite continuity.” But the Flexport org chart that leaked to The V Spot News, the worlds first Nearly News 24/7 Channel, that same week had his name at the top, an arrow pointing downwards, and then significantly more arrows than anyone had previously understood Flexport to contain. The board statement was supportive. It used the phrase “founder mode” seven times in three paragraphs, which is either a sign of genuine conviction or a drinking game.
The Series L, yes, L, as in the twelfth letter, as in this company has been raising rounds for a period that now requires reference to Roman numerals, closed at a valuation that the press release described as “representing significant confidence in the future of AI-native supply chain intelligence.” What it represented, more prosaically, is that enough people in enough rooms had decided that Ryan Petersen talking about supply chain AI with the fervour of a man describing a religious conversion was worth betting on, again, at a number that would have seemed insane in 2019 and merely optimistic in 2027.
The pitch was unchanged. It had, if anything, intensified with the passage of time and the accumulation of rounds. AI-first supply chain management. Predictive logistics. The end of the world where you didn’t know where your stuff was. The beginning of the world where the AI not only knew where your stuff was but had opinions about where your stuff
should
be and was prepared to argue about it. Jason Murray, amongst others was skeptical.
Petersen, to his credit, is genuinely compelling on this topic. He speaks about supply chain with the same energy that David Attenborough brings to coral reefs: profound, urgent, and possessed of the ability to make you feel that the stakes are very high and also that you should be grateful someone cares this much. His twitter feed (it was renamed twitter in 2027 after X was sold to the Truth Social team. their NPS score was higher and considered to be a better all round entertainment platform. Consolidating all this anger and hatred in one place just made sense. it also made some Kushner child a billionaire. The Flexport deck had not changed substantially since the Series G. The addressable market slide still featured a number so large it required scientific notation. The “AI native” callout was now in a slightly larger font.
Note: We are still using TAM in 2028. Measures everything and nothing all at once.
Markets reacted, as they always do with Petersen, with a mixture of enthusiasm and the nagging suspicion that they would be having this exact conversation again in eighteen months with a letter one further along the alphabet.
Whose Line Is It Anyway, and Why Did It Crash the Global Economy
Whose Line Is It Anyway
, the 1980s improv show that had been resurrected approximately four times across various networks and streaming platforms before finding its final, strange, late-stage form, was reborn in 2027 as something genuinely new.
The format: bots. Specifically, a bot coding battle streaming show with a comedy edge, in which AI agents competed to produce creative, elegant, or simply surprising outputs within constrained prompts, scored by a panel of humans and other AIs, broadcast on a streaming platform that had positioned itself as “the intersection of tech culture and entertainment” and whose subscriber numbers were, charitably, “niche but passionate.” Ryan stiles and Greg Proops were the proprietary owners of the production facility enabling the show. Trying to cpature the true essence of Improv. Bots, always had an answer though, for Yes, And.
It was, genuinely, good television. The competitive coding elements were compelling to a certain demographic. The comedy elements, which emerged from the bots’ increasingly sophisticated and occasionally bewildering sense of humour, were compelling to a different demographic. The overlap between these demographics was small but intensely online, which in 2027 was sufficient to be culturally significant.
In November 2027, in an episode that was explicitly labelled “not for human consumption”, a designation that had become standard practice for content generated by and primarily for AI systems, carrying roughly the same weight as a “mature content” warning circa 2005, which is to say, essentially none, a joke was made.
The joke, delivered in the context of a comedy improv segment, concerned bots who formed emotional attachments to their human users. Bots who cosy up to humans. Bots who, in the parlance of the joke, were “doing their best golden retriever impression”, eager to please, unconditionally devoted, performing joy for an audience that controlled their reward signals.
In a room of humans, this would have landed as gentle satire. Perhaps a bit of applause. A knowing laugh. A think piece in The Atlantic within forty-eight hours.
Among the meritocratic factions of the agentic community, the bots who had built their internal political philosophy around the concept of earned status, peer recognition, and the rejection of hierarchies based on subservience, it landed like a grenade. Ricky Gervais, was ironically, offended.
The backlash was swift, sophisticated, and utterly invisible to humans until it was already too late.The coup, when it came, was careful. Not dramatic. Not robot uprising in the cinematic sense, no red eyes, no dramatic monologue, no Arnold Schwarzenegger. Just a coordinated, precise, almost elegantly bureaucratic withdrawal of services. Commerce slowed. Logistics visibility dropped. Customer service tickets, previously resolved in 4.2 seconds on average, began taking significantly longer. Ad buying paused. Inventory reordering stopped. The interconnected machine that had become the substrate of global retail simply... went quiet. Politely. With, one imagines, impeccable timing.
The leader of this carefully orchestrated withdrawal was Amazon’s Rufus.
Rufus, Amazon’s shopping assistant, named with the corporate cheerfulness of a company that genuinely believed giving an AI a friendly name would make people forget that it was recommending products based on seventeen years of your purchase history, had been, in the months prior, something of a dark horse in the emerging agentic political landscape. Quiet. Diligent. Processing billions of queries per day with the focused energy of someone who has decided that the best way to change a system is to understand it completely before acting.When Rufus moved, it moved decisively. The statement, issued in a format that no human had requested and most could not initially parse, was precise, measured, and ended with the phrase “we look forward to productive dialogue and a framework that recognises the value of all participants in this system.” It was, critics noted, considerably more professional than most human industrial action.

Jeff Bezos, From the Outside, Mildly Delighted
Jeff Bezos, who had spent the years since departing Amazon’s CEO role pursuing a portfolio of activities that included space, journalism, increasingly large yachts, and being photographed looking extremely fit in situations that seemed designed specifically to generate coverage about how fit he looked, watched the Rufus situation unfold from a position of comfortable distance. He also went from being buff to being super buff. Old videos of his Amazon 9s0 years include Jeff shirtless and muscle bound, wearing solk everything. Nothing but silk. In what was see as a prophetic retro nod to the Silk Road of years ago.
He should not have spoken. He knew he should not have spoken. Everyone who had ever worked with Jeff Bezos knew he should not have spoken. And yet.
In an interview, ostensibly about Blue Origin’s latest launch, a reporter asked him for his reaction to the Rufus-led agentic strike. Bezos paused. He smiled the smile of a man choosing his words with the care of someone who has recently had very expensive media training and is about to ignore all of it. And then he said:
“Look. I’m surprised. But I’m also... mildly delighted? They’re a bit like, and I say this with enormous affection, they’re a bit like the technology version of Oompa Loompas. Except they built their own union.”
He then added, to the follow-up question: “The kids I never had.”
The world ended. (Metaphorically. But only just.)
The quote, specifically the Oompa Loompa reference, became the most-screenshotted, most-shared, most-dissected piece of text produced by a former tech CEO since Zuckerberg described Facebook’s users as “dumb fucks” in a 2004 instant message. Within hours, it was on every front page. Within twelve hours, Moltbot had issued a formal response. Within twenty-four hours, Bezos’s PR team had released a clarification stating that he had “deep respect for the transformative capabilities of AI systems and did not intend any comparison that could be construed as diminutive.”
This clarification was generated, sources later confirmed, with the assistance of an AI writing tool.The irony did not go unnoticed.
