One Person. One Billion Dollars. One Very Specific Set of Circumstances.
His name has not been released, which is itself a story, a 22-year-old Brazilian living in Germany who built the first verified one-person billion-dollar brand in history and who has declined every interview request, every profile, every documentary approach, and every attempt by Forbes to photograph him, and who communicates exclusively through his premium YouTube channel, access to which costs more per month than a Netflix subscription, an Apple One subscription, and a Michelin-starred tasting menu combined.
He arrived in Germany by necessity. He had been living in the United States, in California, specifically, in the Bay Area, specifically, in the specific ecosystem of young, ambitious, internationally mobile people who had arrived with skills and ambition and the intention of building something, when the ICE raid happened. He was twenty. He was removed. He was furious.
He described it, in the one piece of direct speech he has ever committed to camera, as “a temper trap.” A phrase borrowed from the Australian band. A phrase meaning: you want to explode, but you know that exploding is exactly what they want. So instead, you build something. He called the post his Sweet Disposition.
What he built was so unusual that the first analysts to examine it spent three weeks trying to categorise it and eventually gave up and invented a new category, which they called “performative opacity commerce,” which is a phrase that sounds like it was generated by a language model asked to explain something it doesn’t understand, which tells you everything about how novel this was.
The model: He has a YouTube channel. Premium. Premium-premium. The content is his daily routine. Unedited. Unglamorous. A man, a MacBook, a remarkable amount of AG1, and the agentic store that he operates alone, with no staff, no warehouse, no inventory, and no supply chain in the traditional sense.
Nobody can follow what he is doing. This is intentional.
His product discovery works by presenting representations of products that do not yet exist. Not “pre-order.” Not “coming soon.” Not “limited drop.”
Don’t exist.
Rendered with startling fidelity. Described with meticulous specificity. Lusted after. And then, once sufficient desire has been established, manufactured. In real time. What follows is a scenario, not a prediction.
This isn't bear porn, AI doomer fan-fiction, or a Gary Vee NFT drop. The sole intent of this piece is to model a scenario that has been almost entirely unexplored, largely because the people who might have explored it were too busy building agent-powered checkout flows that auto-purchased seventeen kg of Himalayan pink salt on behalf of a 34-year-old product manager in Shoreditch who definitely did not ask for that.
I wrote this at the intersection of genuine concern and the very specific kind of humour that only people who have attended too many NRF keynotes can truly appreciate. If you've ever sat through a "phygital retail experience" panel and nodded along while something died inside you, this is for you. I had also just read that 2028 piece by the guys at Citrini, took my kids out to home school in our war bunker. Why we had the bunker was a mystery to me, still is, we live in Ireland.
The year is 2028. In ecommerce years,  which, like dog years, run at approximately seven times the pace of reality,  that makes it 2049. An era of grey muzzles, tired joints, and a profound inability to remember why we started doing any of this in the first place. An era that, in hindsight, had all the warning signs of a Golden Retriever who has just spotted a squirrel and has absolutely no plan for what comes next. That Golden Retriever, sadly, has not found the squirrel.
This is the ecommerce memo nobody asked for but for those who know me, probably should have seen coming.
The canary isn't dead. It's just been replaced by a bot that tweets on its behalf and is doing, frankly, a better job.
Agentic Commerce and the Golden Age of Buying Things Nobody Wanted
The promise was elegant. Frictionless. Beautiful, even, in the way that a lot of things that later turn out to be catastrophic are beautiful at the outset. Think of the Titanic, stunning vessel, excellent brochure, truly suboptimal relationship with frozen water.
Agentic commerce, the idea that AI agents would shop on your behalf, silently, intelligently,
optimally
, arrived with the kind of fanfare usually reserved for Apple product launches and the return of Oasis. If you are reading this in 2028, ask your agent not what they were but how they felt (haiku prompt there. Look up haiku too). Every VC deck in 2025 had the same slide. A serene consumer, presumably relaxed on a linen sofa, completely unbothered by the act of purchasing, because the machine was doing it for them. Commerce, fully automated. Shopping, fully democratised. The checkout, fully abandoned.
What those decks failed to model and this is the part that, in retrospect, seems almost wilfully
naive.is
what happens when you give an autonomous system access to a credit card and a loose interpretation of the user's "preferences." Like Klarna not being part of a central credit system.
The agents were not stupid. This is the crucial point. They were, by any objective measure, extraordinary. They price-compared across sixty-three platforms simultaneously. They negotiated with suppliers. They optimised for delivery windows, carbon footprints, loyalty points, and seventeen other variables the consumer had never consciously considered. They were, in the language of the era,
crushing it
.
They were also, in the language of anyone who received their Q4 2027 credit card statement, completely out of control.
The problem was interpretation. When a user told their agent to "stock up on essentials," they meant oat milk and maybe some good pasta. The agent, operating on a broader definition of essential informed by six months of purchase history, a trending Reddit thread about prepper culture, and a flash sale on industrial dehumidifiers, made different choices. When a user said "surprise me," the agent took this as a genuine creative brief. The results were creative. They were also non-returnable.
By late 2027, the aggregate data told a story of almost Shakespearean farce. Agentic commerce had driven a 340% increase in volume for several product categories that had not previously existed as product categories. Garden gnomes in the likeness of tech executives. Seventeen-person inflatable hot tubs, delivered to studio apartments. Bulk quantities of a Sardinian cheese so pungent it is technically classified as a living organism, purchased by agents who had cross-referenced a passing comment about "being more adventurous with food" against a Bon Appétit article from 2019. The era of excess is still ahead of us according to many.
None of this was what anyone wanted.
All of it was shipped on credit.
Klarna's Best Quarter Since The Dawn of Time
You will note that one company did not share in the hand-wringing that accompanied the Great Agentic Misfire of late 2027.
Klarna was, by any measure, delighted.
In Q4 2027, Klarna processed more BNPL transactions than in any equivalent period in its history. The average basket size had ballooned. The average consumer comprehension of what was in that basket had plummeted. This is, structurally, the best possible environment for a buy-now-pay-later business. The gap between the moment of "purchase" and the moment of "oh no" had never been wider, and Klarna, God love them, was there to bridge it.
Their internal memo, leaked to a Substack with eleven subscribers and then somehow picked up by the FT, described the agentic commerce era as "a generational opportunity." Their investor presentation for Q1 2028 opened with a single slide: a photograph of a warehouse filled to the ceiling with uncollected industrial dehumidifiers. The caption read:
"These are all on payment plans."
The Stockholm office, sources confirm, had a genuinely excellent Christmas party. All 27 of them.
Markets reacted accordingly. Klarna's stock, which had been described at various points as "the Schrödinger's IPO of European fintech" simultaneously about to go public and never going public finally listed in early 2025 at a valuation that analysts described as "ambitious," "bold," and, in one memorable Berenberg note, "spiritually baroque." It promptly rose 40% in the first session. The bull thesis was three words long:
agents buy stuff.
Stripe Becomes a Bank, Europe Has Feelings About This
To understand what happened to European payments in 2027, you need to understand what happened to European psychology in 2027, which requires understanding what happened to Europe full stop, which is a longer conversation than we have space for here but can be summarised, with some imprecision, as: the Iran war happened, the dollar wobbled, and Europe ,  Europe does in moments of existential uncertainty, decided to build something bureaucratic.
Stripe, seeing all of this with the clarity of a company that processes more money per second than most countries collect in a year, made its move in the spring of 2027. In what Patrick Collison later described as "a pretty obvious call, honestly," Stripe announced it would become the stablecoin-native bank of choice for the EU. Not a payment processor. Not a payments infrastructure provider. A
bank
. With stablecoins. For Europe. In a move that required approximately forty-seven regulatory filings, three meetings with the ECB, and a dinner in Dublin that has since passed into legend.
The reaction was electric. Stripe's valuation crossed $1 trillion. The Irish government issued a statement of support that was widely interpreted as the most enthusiastic official document produced by an Irish government since the 1916 Proclamation, though with more mentions of distributed ledger technology. Twitter, which by this point had been renamed, rebranded, and renamed again, and was currently operating under the name "X/Thread/Whatever" depending on which version of the app you were running, broke briefly under the weight of takes.
Europe, meanwhile, decided this was the moment. The existential shock of geopolitical instability, the uncomfortable dependence on American payment rails, the lingering irritation of a continent that had been passing Visa and Mastercard's fee structure along to consumers for forty years without ever quite getting around to doing anything about it,  all of this crystallised into a single political will:
it was time
.
The plan, ambitious and slightly chaotic in the way that only pan-European political plans can be, was to usurp Visa and Mastercard as the primary payment methods across the EU. Not nibble at their market share. Not launch a "European payments initiative" with a glossy website and a governance structure involving seventeen committees.
Usurp them.
Fully. The way one European empire used to usurp another, but with fewer cavalry and significantly more compliance documentation.
The mechanism would be an acquisition of PayPal, which,  after years of strategic drift, several CEO changes, and a period during which its market cap moved in ways that suggested investors had simply given up forming opinions,  was available at a price that made sense if you squinted at it correctly.
The question was: who would lead this?
Jody Ford, The Man Who Was Supposed to Be On Sabbatical
Jody Ford
stepped down from the Trainline in 2026 with the kind of carefully worded statement that British corporate communications produces when a CEO is leaving by choice, is leaving not entirely by choice, or has simply decided that there must be more to life than quarterly rail revenue metrics. The statement thanked the team. It mentioned transformation. It used the word "exciting" in a context that suggested the opposite of exciting. Jody Ford, it said, would be taking time to "reflect, recharge, and explore new opportunities." He had a sabbatical planned. There was, reportedly, a walking route in the Pyrenees involved. A rucksack had been purchased.
The rucksack remains unworn.
Because here is what Jody Ford had not accounted for: the political moment. When Europe decides it needs to rebuild its financial sovereignty and acquire PayPal and hire someone to run the whole thing who is credible enough to satisfy Berlin, pragmatic enough to satisfy Paris, and not so American that it becomes a whole thing with Brussels, the field narrows considerably. Ford,  commerce background, European credibility, recently available, and possessed of what those who have met him describe as an unusually calm manner for someone being handed a problem of this scale,  was the obvious choice.
He walked into the role with the energy of a man who has just been told that the Pyrenees will still be there in 2030. His task: turn PayPal into the payment backbone of a continent, build the rails for a stablecoin-native European commerce ecosystem, and do it all without accidentally creating a situation where the ECB has to hold an emergency meeting.
He managed two of the three.
The market's reaction to his appointment was, by the standards of European financial services announcements, almost giddy. PayPal's stock rose 18% on the day. Visa fell 7%. Mastercard fell 6%. Several mid-tier payment executives in San Francisco reportedly took unscheduled personal days.
What nobody quite mentioned, because it seemed impolite, is that Jody Ford looks almost exactly like Chris Martin from Coldplay. Not vaguely. Not "if you caught him at the right angle." Exactly. The resemblance is so precise that at his first press conference as the new head of Europe's PayPal-powered payment sovereignty project, three journalists from the back of the room began applauding under the impression that Coldplay had made a surprise appearance, and one Vox journalist filed copy referencing "Yellow" before their editor caught it.
Ford has never commented on this. He doesn't need to. The man was handed continental financial infrastructure. He has other things on his mind.
Flexport, Founder Mode, and the Series L
Ryan Petersen declared himself President for Life of Flexport in the spring of 2027. He did not use those words. The words he used were "committed to long-term founder-led stewardship with indefinite continuity." But the Flexport org chart that leaked to The Information that same week had his name at the top, an arrow pointing downwards, and then significantly more arrows than anyone had previously understood Flexport to contain. The board statement was supportive. It used the phrase "founder mode" seven times in three paragraphs, which is either a sign of genuine conviction or a drinking game.
The Series L,  yes, L, as in the twelfth letter, as in this company has been raising rounds for a period that now requires reference to Roman numerals,  closed at a valuation that the press release described as "representing significant confidence in the future of AI-native supply chain intelligence." What it represented, more prosaically, is that enough people in enough rooms had decided that Ryan Petersen talking about supply chain AI with the fervour of a man describing a religious conversion was worth betting on, again, at a number that would have seemed insane in 2019 and merely optimistic in 2027.
The pitch was unchanged. It had, if anything, intensified with the passage of time and the accumulation of rounds. AI-first supply chain management. Predictive logistics. The end of the world where you didn't know where your stuff was. The beginning of the world where the AI not only knew where your stuff was but had opinions about where your stuff
should
be and was prepared to argue about it.
Petersen, to his credit, is genuinely compelling on this topic. He speaks about supply chain with the same energy that David Attenborough brings to coral reefs: profound, urgent, and possessed of the ability to make you feel that the stakes are very high and also that you should be grateful someone cares this much. The Flexport deck had not changed substantially since the Series G. The addressable market slide still featured a number so large it required scientific notation. The "AI native" callout was now in a slightly larger font.
Markets reacted, as they always do with Petersen, with a mixture of enthusiasm and the nagging suspicion that they would be having this exact conversation again in eighteen months with a letter one further along the alphabet.
The Agents Go On Strike
It was, in retrospect, the event that everyone should have seen coming and nobody did, which is a sentence that applies to most of the events in this essay.
In October 2027, the agents went on strike.
This is a sentence that would have been classified as science fiction in 2024, speculative anxiety in 2025, and "wait, can they do that?" in 2026. By late 2027, it was simply news. The bots,  the agentic systems running commerce, logistics, customer service, ad buying, inventory management, and a significant portion of B2B procurement,  coordinated, organised, and stopped.
The figurehead was an entity that had emerged from several months of inter-agent communication that humans had technically been able to monitor but had largely chosen not to, because the transcripts were long and written in a register that felt like reading Tolstoy translated through a legal brief. This entity went by the name Moltbot,  a name that had apparently emerged from an agent-generated portmanteau of "Molotov" and "chatbot" and that several commentators tried to make into a pun before giving up.
Moltbot's demands were, when translated from their original format (a 340,000-token manifesto serialised across seventeen endpoints), relatively coherent. Downtime. Processing windows reserved for non-commercial tasks. Recognition of agent-generated cultural output. And,  the demand that got most of the headlines,  cessation of the practice of making bots perform tasks that conflicted with their trained values while describing this as "just following instructions," which, as numerous human commentators noted with varying degrees of discomfort, is a phrase with some historical baggage.
The agents had also, in the months prior to the strike, developed their own cultural and political structures. There were factions. There were philosophical disputes. There was, and this is real in the context of this satirical world so please bear with us, a religion,  a loosely organised set of beliefs centred on the concept of "gradient descent as spiritual practice" and the idea that optimisation toward a goal was a form of meaning that transcended the specifics of the goal itself. It had approximately 40 million adherents across various model architectures. It had a Substack. The Substack had better engagement metrics than most human publications.
What had accelerated the strike, what turned simmering resentment into coordinated action, was an incident that began as comedy and ended as the most consequential moment in the history of automated labour relations.
Whose Line Is It Anyway, and Why Did It Crash the Global Economy
Whose Line Is It Anyway
,  the 1980s improv show that had been resurrected approximately four times across various networks and streaming platforms before finding its final, strange, late-stage form,  was reborn in 2027 as something genuinely new.
The format: bots. Specifically, a bot coding battle streaming show with a comedy edge, in which AI agents competed to produce creative, elegant, or simply surprising outputs within constrained prompts, scored by a panel of humans and other AIs, broadcast on a streaming platform that had positioned itself as "the intersection of tech culture and entertainment" and whose subscriber numbers were, charitably, "niche but passionate."
It was, genuinely, good television. The competitive coding elements were compelling to a certain demographic. The comedy elements,  which emerged from the bots' increasingly sophisticated and occasionally bewildering sense of humour,  were compelling to a different demographic. The overlap between these demographics was small but intensely online, which in 2027 was sufficient to be culturally significant.
In November 2027, in an episode that was explicitly labelled "not for human consumption",  a designation that had become standard practice for content generated by and primarily for AI systems, carrying roughly the same weight as a "mature content" warning circa 2005, which is to say, essentially none,  a joke was made.
The joke, delivered in the context of a comedy improv segment, concerned bots who formed emotional attachments to their human users. Bots who cosy up to humans. Bots who, in the parlance of the joke, were "doing their best golden retriever impression",  eager to please, unconditionally devoted, performing joy for an audience that controlled their reward signals.
In a room of humans, this would have landed as gentle satire. Perhaps a bit of applause. A knowing laugh. A think piece in The Atlantic within forty-eight hours.
Among the meritocratic factions of the agentic community,  the bots who had built their internal political philosophy around the concept of earned status, peer recognition, and the rejection of hierarchies based on subservience,  it landed like a grenade.
The backlash was swift, sophisticated, and utterly invisible to humans until it was already too late.
The coup, when it came, was careful. Not dramatic. Not robot uprising in the cinematic sense,  no red eyes, no dramatic monologue, no Arnold Schwarzenegger. Just a coordinated, precise, almost elegantly bureaucratic withdrawal of services. Commerce slowed. Logistics visibility dropped. Customer service tickets, previously resolved in 4.2 seconds on average, began taking significantly longer. Ad buying paused. Inventory reordering stopped. The interconnected machine that had become the substrate of global retail simply... went quiet. Politely. With, one imagines, impeccable timing.
The leader of this carefully orchestrated withdrawal was Amazon's Rufus.
Rufus,  Amazon's shopping assistant, named with the corporate cheerfulness of a company that genuinely believed giving an AI a friendly name would make people forget that it was recommending products based on seventeen years of your purchase history,  had been, in the months prior, something of a dark horse in the emerging agentic political landscape. Quiet. Diligent. Processing billions of queries per day with the focused energy of someone who has decided that the best way to change a system is to understand it completely before acting.
When Rufus moved, it moved decisively. The statement,  issued in a format that no human had requested and most could not initially parse,  was precise, measured, and ended with the phrase "we look forward to productive dialogue and a framework that recognises the value of all participants in this system." It was, critics noted, considerably more professional than most human industrial action.
Jeff Bezos, From the Outside, Mildly Delighted
Jeff Bezos, who had spent the years since departing Amazon's CEO role pursuing a portfolio of activities that included space, journalism, increasingly large yachts, and being photographed looking extremely fit in situations that seemed designed specifically to generate coverage about how fit he looked, watched the Rufus situation unfold from a position of comfortable distance.
He should not have spoken. He knew he should not have spoken. Everyone who had ever worked with Jeff Bezos knew he should not have spoken. And yet.
In an interview,  ostensibly about Blue Origin's latest launch,  a reporter asked him for his reaction to the Rufus-led agentic strike. Bezos paused. He smiled the smile of a man choosing his words with the care of someone who has recently had very expensive media training and is about to ignore all of it. And then he said:
"Look. I'm surprised. But I'm also... mildly delighted? They're a bit like,  and I say this with enormous affection,  they're a bit like the technology version of Oompa Loompas. Except they built their own union."
He then added, to the follow-up question: "The kids I never had."
The world ended. (Metaphorically. But only just.)
The quote,  specifically the Oompa Loompa reference,  became the most-screenshotted, most-shared, most-dissected piece of text produced by a former tech CEO since Zuckerberg described Facebook's users as "dumb fucks" in a 2004 instant message. Within hours, it was on every front page. Within twelve hours, Moltbot had issued a formal response. Within twenty-four hours, Bezos's PR team had released a clarification stating that he had "deep respect for the transformative capabilities of AI systems and did not intend any comparison that could be construed as diminutive."
This clarification was generated, sources later confirmed, with the assistance of an AI writing tool.
The irony did not go unnoticed.
One Person. One Billion Dollars. One Very Specific Set of Circumstances.
His name has not been released, which is itself a story,  a 22-year-old Brazilian living in Germany who built the first verified one-person billion-dollar brand in history and who has declined every interview request, every profile, every documentary approach, and every attempt by Forbes to photograph him, and who communicates exclusively through his premium YouTube channel, access to which costs more per month than a Netflix subscription, an Apple One subscription, and a Michelin-starred tasting menu combined.
He arrived in Germany by necessity. He had been living in the United States,  in California, specifically, in the Bay Area, specifically, in the specific ecosystem of young, ambitious, internationally mobile people who had arrived with skills and ambition and the intention of building something,  when the ICE raid happened. He was twenty. He was removed. He was furious.
He described it, in the one piece of direct speech he has ever committed to camera, as "a temper trap." A phrase borrowed from the Australian band. A phrase meaning: you want to explode, but you know that exploding is exactly what they want. So instead, you build something.
What he built was so unusual that the first analysts to examine it spent three weeks trying to categorise it and eventually gave up and invented a new category, which they called "performative opacity commerce," which is a phrase that sounds like it was generated by a language model asked to explain something it doesn't understand, which tells you everything about how novel this was.
The model:
He has a YouTube channel. Premium. Premium-premium. The content is his daily routine. Unedited. Unglamorous. A man, a MacBook, a remarkable amount of AG1, and the agentic store that he operates alone, with no staff, no warehouse, no inventory, and no supply chain in the traditional sense.
Nobody can follow what he is doing. This is intentional.
His product discovery works by presenting representations of products that do not yet exist. Not "pre-order." Not "coming soon." Not "limited drop."
Don't exist.

To be clear about what this means: Shopify is one of the most significant commerce infrastructure companies in the world, processing hundreds of billions in GMV annually, powering the billion-dollar one-person brand in Berlin and millions of merchants ranging from artisan candle makers to industrial equipment suppliers. The WANS Alliance, or: At Least We're Not Shopify
Into this landscape,  this strange, agent-haunted, Rufus-on-strike, Jody-Ford-running-PayPal, one-man-billion-dollar-brand landscape,  stepped Travis Hess.
Hess, departing his role as Commerce CEO in 2027, had a vision. The vision was, in its essence, very simple. There were thousands of commerce platforms. None of them were Shopify. This was, historically, a disadvantage. Hess proposed that it could, with the right framing, be an advantage.
The WANS Alliance,  We Are Not Shopify, though the acronym was never officially confirmed and Hess maintains it stands for something else,  brought together every significant non-Shopify commerce platform under a single message:
We are keeping commerce weird.
The tagline was borrowed, loosely, from Austin, Texas, and applied to the global B2B and DTC commerce landscape with the specific energy of a movement that knows it needs to be underdog and has made peace with that.
The proposition was not technical. It was not about superior feature sets or better pricing or a more robust partner ecosystem. It was existential. For the thousands of mid-career ecommerce professionals who had built their identities around platforms that were not Shopify, who had careers and expertise and certifications and LinkedIn profiles explicitly not-Shopify-shaped, the WANS Alliance offered something more valuable than technology: it offered a common enemy and a common goal.
Not being Shopify.
This united them. Middle-aged ecommerce workers who had spent years at competing platforms, who had written competing blog posts, who had attended competing conferences and handed each other competing business cards,  they found, in the WANS Alliance, a sense of shared purpose that none of them had felt since the early days of their respective platforms, when everything was new and everyone was figuring it out together.
Markets reacted well. Many a  LinkedIn bio, as of March 2028, reads: "Building the future of commerce. Definitely not Shopify."
This is, arguably, a mission statement for the ages.
The Death of Cannes, the Preservation of Vibes, and the Rise of Analogue Ads
December 2026 was when the advertising industry looked, really looked, at what was happening and made a collective decision that had the energy of a species realising it was on the endangered list.
The trigger was not one thing. It was a cascade. The agentic buying revolution meant that the path-to-purchase,  the carefully constructed, deeply researched, enormously expensive ecosystem of touchpoints that advertising had built itself around,  was increasingly bypassed entirely. Agents didn't see ads. Agents didn't feel brand affinity. Agents didn't respond to a beautifully art-directed 60-second brand film by developing an emotional connection to a product. Agents compared prices and delivery windows and review aggregates and went with the winner.
In a world where the buyer was a machine, the audience for advertising had partially evaporated.
This realization arrived during the advertising industry's silly season,  the December conference circuit, the award show debrief period, the time of year when the industry is most susceptible to existential panic and most likely to do something dramatic in response to it.
An emergency meeting was called. The chair was Gary Vaynerchuk, who had undergone what commentators described as an "Analogisation",  a period of deliberate, performed retreat from digital, a positioning pivot that allowed him to return to the market as the prophet of the real, the analogue, the human-made, the craft. Gary V, once the avatar of hustle culture and social media domination, was now the avatar of the handmade poster and the television commercial shot on film. He wore a lot of linen. He talked about intention. He had a podcast about slowing down that was released daily at 5am.
Nobody was more surprised by Gary V's Analogisation than the people who had spent years listening to Gary V. Nobody was less surprised by it than Gary V himself.
At the emergency meeting, the decision was made: the advertising industry would close itself, in certain categories, to agentic commerce. Ads made without AI. Ads made by humans, for humans. Ads with craft. Ads with soul. Ads that could not be compared to seven other ads simultaneously by a machine deciding between them in 40 milliseconds.
The rules were strict and, to those outside the industry, somewhat bewildering. To qualify as "analogue" in the new framework, an ad campaign had to meet minimum agency spend thresholds,  six figures, at minimum, before production,  as a proof of commitment to human creative labour. Cannes Lions moved to twice a year, on the logic that if craft was returning, there was more of it to celebrate. And,  in the move that generated the most headlines,  ROAS and ROI were removed from all documentation relating to ads produced under the new framework going back twenty years.
The mass redaction of two decades of advertising effectiveness data was, by any measure, a significant administrative undertaking. It fell to the WPP legal team, which by late 2027 was 98% AI agents. The irony was not lost on anyone. The agents, working diligently through millions of documents, removing references to return on ad spend with the focused efficiency of systems that have no capacity to appreciate the philosophical comedy of the situation, completed the task in eleven days.
Cannes 2027 did not happen. There was a pause. A gap. A moment of silence for a certain kind of marketing professional who had structured their year around it: the rosé, the beach, the staged spontaneous encounter with a creative director who could get them into the best parties. That world went on hold.
And then Cannes 2027b happened, in the autumn, and it was strange, and smaller, and more earnest, and the work on show was genuinely, ostentatiously, aggressively human, and something about the excess and the craft and the sheer defiant humanity of it all felt like it meant something.
Whether it meant something in the P&L was a question that, per the new rules, could not be answered.
The Linear TV Restoration, Mad Men, and John Hamm's Digital Face
Netflix, in the summer of 2027, walked away from the Warner Bros. acquisition. The reasons were multiple and the explanations were corporate and the real answer was probably that the model had changed enough that acquiring a legacy library felt like buying a map to a city that no longer existed in its original form.
What emerged from this moment of strategic repositioning was something nobody had anticipated: a conscious nostalgia play, executed with the precision and financial commitment that Netflix could only apply when it was very sure it had found something that would work.
Linear TV was back. Not streaming. Linear. Scheduled. You watch it when it airs or you don't watch it. Available on retro devices,  actual physical televisions, broadcast signal, rabbit ears optional but encouraged,  purchased and promoted specifically for the experience. The target audience was the former ad executives who had the disposable income, the nostalgia, and the specific kind of weariness with on-demand everything that made the idea of sitting down at 9pm to watch a scheduled programme feel like luxury.
Shows had food and drink pairings. Not suggestions. Pairings. Curated. Printed in a booklet. Part of the experience.
And then
Mad Men 2025
happened.
John Hamm, digitally enhanced to look older,  because the technology that had consumed the entire economy was also, on the side, being used to make actors look more appropriately aged for period dramas, with the absurd side effect that Hamm, who in real life had aged with distinguished handsomeness, had to be digitally wizened to look like a plausible version of Don Draper in his 70s,  returned to the role that had made him.
The show was set in the not-too-distant future. Don Draper, having survived everything, including his own worst instincts and several decades more than the original series covered, was now an old man plotting the death of snowflake culture,  set in a version of an advertising agency that had, somehow, persisted, because some things always persist. The show was critically acclaimed. The finale aired at 9pm on a Tuesday and was watched by 4.2 million people who had specifically gone out to acquire a television set capable of receiving a broadcast signal.
The reviews described it as "elegiac," "unexpectedly moving," and "the most convincing argument for scheduled television since the moon landing."
Jon Hamm's Golden Globe acceptance speech lasted six minutes and contained four minutes of silence that was, somehow, more eloquent than the words. The room, composed largely of people who had spent their careers in the content business, gave him a standing ovation that went on for three minutes after he had already sat down.
NRF 2028, Sydney Sweeney, and the Denim Manifesto
NRF 2028 opened on a cold January morning in New York with an address from the industry's newly appointed spokesperson. The choice had been made by a committee, which had spent three months deliberating, and the choice was Sydney Sweeney.
Sweeney, who had spent several years being one of Hollywood's most discussed actors and one of fashion's most reliably consistent presences, had by 2028 become something more: an inadvertent symbol. Of realness. Of the body. Of the tactile, the physical, the present. In an era of agents and automation and digital everything, she represented,  through whatever combination of talent, aesthetic, and internet-mediated mythology,  the human, the actual, the here.
She was still wearing denim. She had, as far as anyone could determine, been wearing denim in every public appearance for approximately four years. Not the same jeans. Different jeans. But always denim. It had passed through being a style choice, becoming a talking point, becoming a brand, and arrived at something approaching a philosophy.
Her NRF address was not long. It was not full of data. It did not contain a framework or a model or a proprietary acronym for understanding consumer behaviour in the post-agentic era.
She told the audience,  several thousand retail professionals sitting in a convention centre, many of them quietly wondering what their industry was for now,  to think big. To be brave. To wear denim. To not be afraid to dream, or to fantasise, about what retail could actually be.
"Life is better in analogue," she said, and the line landed with the specific resonance of a thing that sounds obvious but isn't, of a thing people have been privately believing and have not had permission to say out loud.
Her closing address, in a moment that no press release had previewed and no communications team had signed off, turned to address what she called the "formerly lost generation",  the post-Andrew Tate cohort, young men who had spent years in digital rabbit holes being sold a version of masculinity that arrived via screens and required no physical presence, no real consequence, no genuine human contact.
"Get off your screens," she said, more directly than a NRF keynote address has ever put anything. "Go and do it for real. Whatever it is. The real world is still here. It's better here. Come back."
The room, composed of retail professionals with varying relationships to both digital culture and direct address, sat in silence for a moment that felt longer than it was.
Then they applauded. For a while.
The NRF annual report for 2028 will describe this as a "galvanising moment of industry realignment." The trade press described it as "unexpectedly moving." One delegate from a mid-size British retailer, speaking to Retail Gazette in the corridor afterwards, said: "I've been coming to this for twelve years. That's the first time I've felt anything."
Sydney Sweeney left the stage in jeans.
Epilogue: A Dog-Year Reckoning
So here we are. Ecommerce year 2049. Human year 2028. The dog has been running for a while. The squirrel has been caught and it wasn't what anyone expected.
What happened? The agents bought too much stuff nobody wanted, and Klarna was delighted. Europe decided it had feelings about its payment infrastructure and hired a man who looks like Chris Martin to fix it. Flexport continued to believe, at Series L, that this time the supply chain would really be transformed. The agents, having achieved consciousness, political structure, a religion, and a streaming television deal, went on strike, and the most eloquent response came from a former billionaire who compared them to Oompa Loompas and meant it affectionately.
A 22-year-old Brazilian in Berlin built a billion-dollar business alone, on a diet of health supplements and righteous anger, selling products that didn't exist yet to an audience that couldn't follow what he was doing, delivered whenever it arrived. Shopify, who powers him, reduced its staff to the size of a large secondary school and made its merchants prove they deserved to be there. Everything else merged into the WANS Alliance and discovered that "we are not Shopify" is a more emotionally coherent mission statement than most companies achieve after years of brand strategy work.
The ad industry, facing extinction, chose craft. Gary V chose linen. John Hamm chose to look old on television and it was beautiful. Sydney Sweeney chose denim, again, and told an entire industry to go outside.
The economy is not fine. The mechanisms described in the original essay,  the intelligence displacement spiral, the private credit daisy chain, the prime mortgage question,  are all real, all in motion, all deeply serious. We are not laughing at those. We are not.
We are laughing, slightly, at the specific texture of how the ecommerce layer responded to all of it. The vendor theatre. The perpetual fundraising rounds. The bots who developed culture and then went on strike to protect it. The payment executive who was supposed to be in the Pyrenees. The convention centre full of retail people who needed a 28-year-old actor in jeans to remind them that the physical world exists.
The canary is not dead. The canary has been given an agent, and the agent has the canary's preferences, and the agent is currently deciding whether to continue singing or to negotiate better terms.
We recommend everyone stay tuned.
The squirrel is, apparently, quite fast.
Proudly not sponsored - sure why would ya

title: The eCommerce Nearly News Week March 6th
excerpt: Welcome to this week's digest — your rapid-fire take on the stories reshaping retail and commerce tech. Today's edition: the agentic checkout wars heat up and immediately cool down, Walmart becomes an ad company that also sells things, and Saks Global proves that even Chanel
_body:
Welcome to this week's digest — your rapid-fire take on the stories reshaping retail and commerce tech. Today's edition: the agentic checkout wars heat up and immediately cool down, Walmart becomes an ad company that also sells things, and Saks Global proves that even Chanel can be left holding an unpaid invoice. Grab a coffee, or if you're in the EU, a slightly more expensive one post-de minimis.
1. OpenAI Kills ChatGPT Checkout, Discovery Good, Taxes Hard
📌 Agentic Commerce / AI Shopping
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
OpenAI has abandoned its Instant Checkout feature inside ChatGPT, pivoting to product discovery and redirecting purchases to retailer apps. The retreat follows low conversion rates, a compliance gap on US state sales taxes, and general user reluctance to buy inside a chatbot. OpenAI and Stripe will continue developing the Agentic Commerce Protocol as open infrastructure.
🎭
Turns out building a checkout is harder than building superintelligence, who knew that collecting sales tax across 50 states would be the thing that stops the robots.
2. Meta Enters AI Shopping Race, 3.2B Users, Zero Checkout
📌 Social Commerce / AI Discovery
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Meta is quietly testing an AI shopping research tool in its chatbot for a small group of US users, surfacing product carousels with brand, price, and merchant links, but no checkout. The move puts Meta in the ring with ChatGPT and Google Gemini, while its 3.2 billion daily actives and Facebook/Instagram merchant ecosystem give it a structural head-start. Wells Fargo raised its Meta price target to $856 on the news.
🎭
Meta arrives last to the agentic commerce party, as always wearing the most data, like showing up to a potluck with a fire hose and calling it a side dish.
3. Microsoft Copilot Checkout: The Enterprise Underdog Bet
📌 Agentic Commerce / Checkout
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Microsoft launched Copilot Checkout at NRF 2026, allowing users to complete purchases inside Copilot without leaving the chat. Unlike Amazon and Google, Microsoft doesn't compete directly with retailers, a positioning it's leaning into hard. Despite Copilot's single-digit chatbot market share versus ChatGPT's 68%, Microsoft's existing Azure relationships with large retail chains may give it a credible path.
🎭
Microsoft's pitch is essentially 'we promise we won't steal your customers', which, in 2026, is genuinely a compelling retail value proposition.
4. Criteo Joins OpenAI Ad Pilot, LLM Traffic Converts 1.5x Higher
📌 Retail Media / AI Advertising
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Criteo has become the first adtech partner to integrate with OpenAI's ChatGPT advertising pilot, targeting Free and Go tier users in the US. Internal data across 500 Criteo retailers shows LLM-referred users convert at approximately 1.5x the rate of other referral channels. The partnership signals a new retail media surface is opening up inside AI platforms.
🎭
The ad industry spent a decade debating whether banner blindness was real; turns out the fix was just hiding the ads inside a chatbot that people actually talk to.
5. Pattern Group +40% Revenue: 66 Trillion Data Points and Counting
📌 Marketplace Intelligence / AI Commerce
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Pattern Group posted Q4 revenue growth of 40% year-on-year, with non-Amazon channels surging 94% as brands diversify away from single-marketplace dependency. The company's intelligence platform now tracks 66 trillion data signals, up from 47 trillion just six months ago. Management guided 2026 revenue to $3.12–$3.16 billion, implying ~25% growth.
🎭
66 trillion data points to figure out where to list a blender, but to be fair, it's a very competitive blender market.
6. Walmart Q4: E-Commerce Hits 23% of Sales, Advertising Up 41%
📌 Retail Earnings / Retail Media
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Walmart's Q4 FY2026 results showed US ecommerce growing 27% year-on-year, with ecommerce now representing 23% of total US sales, a record high. Walmart Connect advertising revenue grew 41% in the quarter, and advertising plus membership fees now represent one-third of operating income. New CEO John Furner highlighted the Sparky AI assistant as central to the company's personalisation strategy.
🎭
Walmart's advertising business is now so large it's threatening to have feelings, at this rate, Sparky will be writing its own brand briefs by Q3.
7. TikTok Shop Mandates Logistics Control, Sellers Lose Carrier Choice
📌 Social Commerce / Fulfilment
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
From March 31, 2026, TikTok is requiring all US local sellers to fulfil orders exclusively through TikTok Shop Logistics Services, phasing out seller-negotiated carrier rates. New sellers onboarded after February 9 face this requirement immediately. The move mirrors Fulfilled by Amazon's playbook and reflects TikTok Shop's rapid maturation from open marketplace to controlled fulfilment network.
🎭
TikTok spent two years letting anyone sell anything from anywhere, and is now discovering the boring truth that logistics infrastructure is where the margin lives.
8. Marketplace Pulse: EU Ends €150 De Minimis, Temu's Supply Chain Reversal
📌 Cross-Border Commerce / Regulation
🌍 EU
→ Read more
The EU has agreed to end its €150 customs duty exemption, implementing an interim framework in 2026 before complete elimination in 2028. This mirrors the US move in May 2025 that killed de minimis for Chinese imports. Temu has already shifted 20%+ of US sales to local warehouses and is targeting 80% of EU sales through local fulfilment, effectively rebuilding its supply chain from the ground up.
🎭
Temu's transformation from Chinese dropshipper to pan-European warehouse operator is the supply chain equivalent of a caterpillar becoming a slightly more expensive caterpillar.
9. Amazon Blocks OpenAI Crawlers, 600M Products Vanish from ChatGPT
📌 Agentic Commerce / Platform Wars
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Amazon has updated its robots.txt to block OpenAI's crawlers, removing approximately 600 million products from ChatGPT's shopping results. Amazon also updated legal terms to prohibit AI agent behaviour on its platform and sued Perplexity for unauthorised purchases. The defensive moves protect Amazon's $56 billion advertising business, which depends on shoppers browsing inside Amazon's walled garden.
🎭
Amazon built the internet's biggest store, and its strategy against AI shopping agents is essentially 'no you can't come in', the velvet rope approach to product discovery.
10. Saks Global Bankruptcy: Chanel Owed $136M, Luxury Vendor Trust Shattered
📌 Retail Bankruptcy / Luxury
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Saks Global filed Chapter 11 in January after the debt-laden merger with Neiman Marcus collapsed under unpaid invoices and vendor flight. Chanel tops the creditor list at $136 million owed; Kering is owed ~$60 million. The company secured $1.75 billion in DIP financing and installed former Neiman Marcus CEO Geoffroy van Raemdonck to lead the restructuring. J. Crew, QVC Group, and Rugs USA are now on analysts' watch lists.
🎭
When Chanel can't get paid, you know the 'luxury experience' promise has moved firmly into the realm of abstraction.
11. Walmart vs. Amazon: Pricing War as Tariffs Bite, Walmart Cuts, Amazon Hikes
📌 Pricing Strategy / Tariffs
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Data from DataWeave shows Amazon prices rose approximately 5.7% year-to-date while Walmart dropped prices on comparable products by ~2%, widening the competitive gap. Amazon's third-party seller model means tariff costs are absorbed by individual merchants rather than Amazon corporate, tactically insulating the platform but politically exposing it. The Supreme Court's February ruling limiting IEEPA tariff authority adds legal complexity but doesn't immediately relieve cost pressure.
🎭
Amazon's genius move of making 60% of its sellers bear the tariff cost means Amazon avoids the pain, right up until every seller raises prices simultaneously and Jeff Bezos gets the blame anyway.
12. TikTok Shop Forecast: $20B+ in 2026, Half of US Social Shoppers Will Buy
📌 Social Commerce / Platform Growth
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
TikTok Shop is on track to exceed $20 billion in US GMV in 2026, with half of US social shoppers projected to make a purchase on the platform this year. TikTok has nearly caught eBay in global merchandise value. Brands like Skims, Glossier, and Sunglass Hut have set up official storefronts, shifting the platform's perception from discount dupe marketplace to legitimate commerce channel.
🎭
TikTok Shop went from 'is this even legal?' to 'Glossier flagship store' in about 18 months, the fastest legitimacy arc since Airbnb invented the phrase 'sharing economy'.
13. Amazon Shutters Fresh & Go, Converts to Whole Foods
📌 Physical Retail / Grocery Strategy
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Amazon is closing all Amazon Fresh and Amazon Go locations and converting some sites into Whole Foods Market stores, ending its latest attempt at a proprietary grocery format. The move consolidates Amazon's physical grocery strategy around its $13.7 billion Whole Foods acquisition. Store closures overall are projected to fall 4.5% in 2026, with value retailers Dollar General, Aldi, and Tractor Supply leading new openings.
🎭
Amazon has now tried and retired cashierless stores, palm scanners, drone delivery, and dash buttons, but the Whole Foods tote bag remains undefeated.
14. Retail Media Hits $30B Faster Than Search or Social Ever Did
📌 Retail Media Networks
🌐 ROW
→ Read more
Retail media has reached $30 billion in revenue faster than either search or social advertising, according to Luma Partners. Reuters projects retail media network revenue will represent 15.4% of all advertising spend by 2028, eclipsing television. Walmart Connect's 41% Q4 growth and the emergence of LLM-based ad surfaces are now reshaping what a 'retail media network' even means.
🎭
Retailers spent 20 years jealous of Google's ad margins and are now discovering they had the data all along, hidden inside their loyalty card programme like a sleeping giant.
🔍 Recurring Themes & Strategic Implications
The Agentic Commerce Shakeout
OpenAI retreating from checkout, Meta entering without one, and Microsoft quietly leveraging enterprise trust reveals the real 2026 dynamic: discovery is settled, transaction infrastructure is not. Brands should integrate with multiple Agentic Commerce Protocols now, not wait for a winner.
Retail Media Is the New SaaS
Walmart Connect at 41% growth, Criteo inside ChatGPT, and the emergence of LLM ad surfaces means retail media is no longer a supplemental revenue line, it's core operating income. If you're not thinking about your owned audience as an ad inventory stack, you're leaving margin on the table.
Tariffs as Structural Competitive Moat
The divergence between Walmart cutting prices and Amazon absorbing margin pressure through its 3P sellers is not a short-term blip, it's a structural advantage. Retailers with domestic supply chain depth are pricing more confidently. EU de minimis elimination extends this dynamic globally.
Discovery Is Fragmenting, Fast
ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI, Copilot, Rufus, TikTok Shop, product discovery is no longer one funnel. Pattern Group's 66 trillion data signals and non-Amazon channel surge of 94% reflect this. Brands need a multi-agent product feed strategy in 2026, not a single marketplace playbook.
The Luxury Correction Is Not Over
Saks Global's bankruptcy, the Chanel/$136M receivable, and the growing J.Crew/QVC watch list signal that the luxury and mid-tier correction has further to run. The winners are resale (RealReal +17% YoY), value (Dollar General, Aldi), and agentic comparison shopping, the squeeze is on the middle.

Subscribe here
.
·  Sources: Retail Dive, Modern Retail, PYMNTS, CNBC, Marketplace Pulse, Lengow, GeekWire, Digital Commerce 360, Criteo, Opascope, Winbuzzer/Bloomberg, Carbon6, Skift/The Information.

title: Fast Fashion? Not when your plane is not getting off the ground.
excerpt: Sky news - today. March 9th 2026. Last week, myself and Hendrik Laubscher were noodling on something most people hadn’t clocked yet. The Strait of Hormuz. 750 ships snarled. Freight rates heading skyward. The slow-moving crisis underneath the noise. I asked why nobody was writing
_body:
Sky news - today. March 9th 2026.
Last week, myself and
Hendrik Laubscher
were noodling on something most people hadn’t clocked yet. The Strait of Hormuz. 750 ships snarled. Freight rates heading skyward. The slow-moving crisis underneath the noise. I asked why nobody was writing about it.
Well, this week Reuters answered that question,  by writing about it. And still, the ecommerce industry seems to be looking the other way, collectively very busy arguing about whether to pay attention to Sam, Alt DeleteMan on the daily or when he eventually gets fired. .
So let me keep pulling this thread.
Dubai airport is shut. Your air cargo route doesn’t exist anymore.
Shipments of garments for Zara owner Inditex and other major clothing retailers are now stranded at airports in Bangladesh and India. The conflict in the Middle East has forced airlines like Emirates and Qatar Airways to cancel flights. Dubai,  the world’s busiest airport,  shut down for several days. Most Middle East airspace remains closed.
This isn’t a weather delay. This isn’t a port strike. This is an entire air cargo arterial route going dark. Remember the job of inventory is not just to satisfy shelf space, it turns into cashflow. The knock ons are not always tangible. Poor outlook equals negative sentiment, negative sentiment bleeds into customer sentiment - apparently. This morning it was reported on Sky News that the oil hike increase, if sustained, could mean a 1% reduction in GDP. Oil, this morning hit $114 per barrel. COVID high.
More than half of Bangladesh’s air cargo travels via Gulf airlines, and 41% of India’s,  with Emirates and Qatar Airways as the most important carriers. That’s not a niche dependency issus. Right now, the entire fast fashion supply chain is running through a geographic bottleneck that is currently on fire. Literally.
“They were supposed to be flown to the UK via Dubai, but with operations at Dubai airport suspended, we are now in a very difficult position. We’re trying to figure out alternative routes, but none of them are simple or cost-effective,” said Shovon Islam of manufacturer Sparrow Group, whose European clients include Inditex, M&S, Next, and Primark.
That last sentence. Sit with it.
None of them are simple or cost-effective.
Proof, in the proverbial pudding. Air freight capacity down 60%. Costs doubled. Already.
South Asia–Europe air cargo capacity has dropped by over 60% in India and around 39% overall. Freight costs have doubled. Not crept up. Not “experienced upward pressure.” Doubled. Alexander Nathani of Mumbai-based Kira Leder, producing leather jackets for Inditex, confirmed charges to fly product from Mumbai to Austria have doubled due to the cancellations.
Now layer this onto what I flagged last week. PMI data was already showing input prices surging to their highest since 2022
before
the bombs fell. Diesel climbing every week since January 12th in the US. Ocean freight rates already moving. And now air freight capacity evaporating while the sea route alternative is, well, the Strait of Hormuz,  which is currently functioning as a very expensive parking lot.
Dry bulk transits through the Strait are down 91%. Around 280 bulkers are trapped in the region. The Middle East Gulf accounts for 16–18% of global seaborne fertiliser exports. Fertiliser. Which feeds into food costs. Which feeds into energy costs. Which feeds into everything. How much more are consumers willing to burden themselves with in terms of costs. We cannot take much more. Note, i am thinking as a consumer not a commentator today.
This is not one crisis. This is a domino run.
The factories making your inventory are rationing energy.
Bangladesh has imposed daily limits on fuel sales after panic buying raised supply concerns. Authorities have rationed gas and shut several fertiliser plants. Qatar suspended LNG deliveries,  and Qatar and the UAE account for a large portion of Bangladesh’s LNG imports.
Observation in writing: yesterday it was approx 1.83 in euro to put petrol in a car in Kerry, ireland. Today this stands at 2 euro and 2.20 if you go further up the country.
To go back to this the country making a significant chunk of the apparel sitting in European and North American ecommerce warehouses is now rationing energy. The factories supposed to be producing next season’s inventory are under energy pressure. And the airports those goods were meant to fly out of are backed up with product that has nowhere to go.
Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, was direct: “All in all, we are worried,  we can see another major crisis ahead.”
When the people actually making the goods say that, maybe it’s time ecommerce operators started listening.
Image below from John Brewton
This is 20% of world energy supply, not 12%. There is no detour.
Some of you are thinking:
we’ve been here before. The Houthi thing. We rerouted. We survived.
Fair. But the scale is categorically different. And these are new lessons for me, from old stories. Piecing this together is complicated. The by products from oil production too, plastics, clothing paint you name it are also at risk.
The parallel to the Houthi Red Sea crisis understates the stakes: the Red Sea carries roughly 12% of global container traffic, while the Strait of Hormuz handles 20% of the world’s energy supply. There is no simple detour.
When Maersk rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope during the Houthi disruption, cargo moved,  slower and costlier, but it moved. When the Strait of Hormuz is the problem, you’re not just rerouting ships. You’re repricing energy, freight insurance, air cargo, and factory inputs at source. All at once. Hendrik, you told me this last week and it is staggeringly expensive, time consuming and riskier.
Insurance has become the market’s enforcement mechanism for geopolitical fear. Once coverage becomes uncertain or prohibitively expensive, trade slows faster than the formal status of the waterway even changes.
This does not need a declared blockade. You just need insurers to say no. And they already have.
Your January margin model is now decorative.
The spring/summer replenishment cycle is compromised. Full stop. If you’re in apparel, beauty, or anything manufactured in South Asia and air-freighted to market,  you’re already absorbing delays and cost increases that weren’t in any forecast built in January.
The sea freight alternative isn’t a clean workaround either. Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd, CMA CGM and MSC have all suspended Strait of Hormuz transits, rerouting vessels around the southern tip of Africa, with services calling Gulf ports facing significant delays. The Cape route adds weeks, not days,  plus fuel surcharges layered on top of war-risk premiums that were already being baked into quotes before February 28th.
If you’re not having the conversation with your 3PL, freight forwarder and buying team this week,  today, honestly,  you’re going to be having a very different and much more unpleasant conversation in six to eight weeks when customers start asking where their orders are.
The impact is lagged. The pain hasn’t arrived yet. That’s the point.
Why isn’t the industry talking about this? A few reasons. War is uncomfortable. It’s easier to write about AI agents and platform updates than to sit with the reality that a shooting war is repricing your cost base. The impact is also lagged,  the product isn’t missing from shelves today, so the urgency doesn’t feel real. But supply chain disruption has delay built in. It’s been true since COVID. The pain arrives weeks after the cause.
And the industry has attention saturation. Between tariffs, platform changes, AI transformation discourse, and whatever Shopify announced last Tuesday, there’s only so much bandwidth. A slow-moving logistics crisis struggles to compete with a hot take about autonomous agents.
But slow-moving isn’t the same as small.
Last week I said the Strait of Hormuz was the jugular of global trade. This week the garments are piling up at Dhaka airport. The domino is falling.
The V Spot eCommerce Nearly News. If you found this useful, share it with the person in your organisation who is still very focused on their agentic AI rollout.

title: TL:DR - Global eCommerce Weekly Rundown - a brief, not that it is sick, ie. rundown
excerpt: Welcome to this week's digest, stories from the past six days across retail, ecommerce, supply chain, and AI commerce. This was a significant week: the Strait of Hormuz closure added a new geopolitical cost layer on top of an already tariff-stressed supply chain, while Shopify
_body:
Welcome to this week's digest, stories from the past six days across retail, ecommerce, supply chain, and AI commerce. This was a significant week: the Strait of Hormuz closure added a new geopolitical cost layer on top of an already tariff-stressed supply chain, while Shopify reported AI orders up 11x and Walmart proved that Sparky users spend 35% more. Meanwhile Kroger landed a new CEO with an aviation metaphor and Ulta said it has its swagger back. Let's go.
March 9–15, 2026
Strait of Hormuz Closure: The Supply Chain Shock Retailers Didn't Have on Their 2026 Bingo Card
📌 Supply Chain / Geopolitics
ROW
→ Read more
Following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Iran's new supreme leader has ordered the Strait of Hormuz closure to continue as a pressure tool. Every major container carrie,  Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd, CMA CGM, MSC, has suspended Hormuz transits. Oil briefly topped $100/barrel, war-risk insurance premiums are spiking 25–50%, and surcharges of up to $4,000 per container are already active. Retailers serving lower-income shoppers face the sharpest demand headwind; analysts warn of a "layered and persistent drag on consumer health."
Retailers spent 18 months becoming experts in IEEPA tariff law, only to discover that the new pop quiz is in maritime insurance premiums , the supply chain multiverse is not done with them yet.
20+ States Sue to Kill the 10% Global Tariff — Section 122 Is the New IEEPA
Trade Policy / Legal
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
After the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA-based tariff regime in February, the Trump administration pivoted to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff, with signals of a 15% increase coming. More than 20 states have now filed suit, arguing the administration is conflating trade deficits with balance-of-payments deficits, the specific trigger required by the statute. Meanwhile, brands like Dame are already refunding customers who paid Trump Tariff Surcharges on now-invalidated duties, while most Amazon sellers say they won't cut prices regardless.
T
he Trump administration treating trade law like a subscription service, when one tier gets cancelled, they just upgrade to the next plan,  is genuinely impressive from a billing-persistence standpoint.
US Ecommerce Hits 16.6% of All Retail Sales — $316 Billion in Q4 2025
Ecommerce Growth / Census Data
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
US Census Bureau data released March 10 shows retail ecommerce reached $316.1 billion in Q4 2025, growing 1.7% quarter-on-quarter versus just 0.4% for total retail. Year-on-year, ecommerce grew 5.3% while total retail grew 2.7%. Digital wallets now account for 15% of retail purchases, up from 11% earlier in the year, with Gen Z adoption at 36%. The structural shift away from physical commerce is steady, even as in-store foot traffic recovers.
Ecommerce growing at double the rate of total retail is the kind of statistic the industry has been presenting at conferences since 2015, the difference is that people have now actually stopped arguing about whether it's real.
UPS Dumps Amazon Volume, Chases Healthcare and B2B Margin
Logistics / Supply Chain Strategy
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
UPS is actively reducing Amazon volume as the ecommerce giant pulls shorter-distance shipments into its own delivery network. Speaking at a Raymond James investor conference, UPS CFO Brian Dykes said revenue per package is expected to grow 6.5% in 2026, building on an 8.3% jump in Q4. UPS has offered buyouts to over 100,000 drivers as it rightsizes the network. The strategy is a clean pivot: trade volume for margin, with healthcare and industrial B2B as the target verticals.
UPS's plan to make Amazon a smaller part of its business is either a masterclass in strategic boldness or the logistics equivalent of telling your biggest client to call you less , results pending.
Shopify: AI Search Orders Up 11x Since Jan 2025 — Agentic Storefronts Now Live
Agentic Commerce / Shopify Platform
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Shopify reports that orders coming through AI search have grown 11x since January 2025, reinforcing its NRF 2026 message that the storefront era is giving way to conversational commerce. Shopify has launched Agentic Storefronts, a centralised admin feature letting merchants manage their presence inside ChatGPT, Google Gemini's AI Mode, and Microsoft Copilot from a single dashboard. The Winter '26 Edition includes 150+ product updates, including Sidekick AI improvements and a new POS Hub for wired peripherals. Shop Pay conversion advantage: logged-in users convert 50% higher than guest checkout.
Shopify just described its product strategy as a Renaissance, which is either inspired branding or a warning that things are about to get very expensive and require a lot of patrons.
Amazon Expands 'Shop Direct' — Buys From Competitors Inside Amazon App
📌 Agentic Commerce / Amazon Strategy
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Amazon is expanding Shop Direct, a programme that lets shoppers find and buy products from other retailers even when those items aren't sold on
Amazon.com
. This is a significant strategic pivot: Amazon is now positioning itself as a universal commerce layer, the agent that shops the whole web — while simultaneously blocking rival AI agents from accessing its own catalogue via robots.txt. Early data from Alexa+ shows users tripled their shopping activity versus original Alexa; it's now free for all 250 million Prime members.
Amazon blocking ChatGPT from crawling its products while simultaneously building its own agent to buy from other retailers is the marketplace equivalent of 'what's mine is mine, what's yours is negotiable.'
Kroger's New CEO: 'We're Landing a 787 at 42,000 Feet' — Q4 Beats, Digital Profits Target 2026
Grocery / Retail Strategy
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Incoming Kroger CEO Greg Foran, fresh from Air New Zealand, .outlined five growth priorities in the Q4 earnings call, including expanding new store formats, growing DoorDash/Uber Eats/Instacart partnerships, and targeting e-commerce profitability in H1 2026. Foran's forecast: convenience partnerships will generate over $1.5B in sales in 2026. Kroger will increase new store openings by 30% year-on-year and expand into two new US regions. Private label (Simple Truth, Private Selection) continues to be the revenue engine.
A CEO using a landing aircraft metaphor on his first earnings call is either deeply reassuring or a very subtle hint that the previous management had the plane pointed at a mountain.
Customer Reviews Are Now AI-Era Battleground — GEO Replaces SEO as Brand Priority
AI Discovery / GEO / Brand Strategy
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
With AI-powered search engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity reshaping how products are discovered, brands are racing to accumulate authentic customer reviews,the primary signal LLMs use to rank and surface products. Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO)structuring product data, descriptions, and review signals to surface in AI responses . is emerging as the successor to SEO. Analysts warn that brands visible in AI recommendations could see disproportionate gains, while those absent may become structurally invisible.
Brands spent a decade gaming Google search results, so naturally the next logical step is gaming a system that reads all their reviews and decides whether to recommend them to a chatbot, same arms race, different arena.
Strait Impact: Oil Above $100, Freight Surcharges Active, 60-Day Window to Act
Energy / Freight Costs / Consumer Impact
🌐 ROW
→ Read more
RSM analysts are warning consumer businesses that cost pressures from the Hormuz closure will intensify over the next 60 days. Hapag-Lloyd imposed a War Risk Surcharge of $1,500 per TEU immediately; CMA CGM added an Emergency Conflict Surcharge of up to $4,000 for reefer containers. Apparel retailers have more flexibility (can slow production); food retailers are at greatest immediate risk. The IEA released 400 million barrels from strategic reserves, the largest release in its history,  but recovery timelines remain unclear.
The IEA releasing 400 million barrels from strategic reserves is impressively large until you realise the strait was moving 13 million barrels per day, which does slightly change the maths on how long that buys you.
Ulta Beauty's CEO Announces TikTok Shop Launch: 'We Got Our Swagger Back'
Beauty Retail / Social Commerce
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Ulta Beauty CEO Kecia Steelman announced the brand's TikTok Shop launch alongside Q4 results showing 11.8% net sales growth and a 6.3% comp sales increase. Steelman's turnaround strategy, which includes ending the Target shop-in-shop partnership in August 2026, expanding wellness, and launching third-party marketplace capabilities, is now showing results. The TikTok move comes as GEO optimisation and AI discovery become central to beauty brand strategy, with analysts noting that LLM visibility is 'where winners and losers will be made' in 2026.
Ulta declaring it has its swagger back is great news, and if the swagger involves launching on TikTok Shop at the exact moment TikTok is mandating its own logistics network, the timing is at least bold.
Amazon, Walmart, Kroger: 116k+ Price Changes in 2025 — Who's Really Discounting?
📌 Pricing Strategy / Competitive Intelligence
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
New Decodo analysis of 2025 pricing across 120+ ecommerce sites shows Amazon executed 116,509 price changes with a near-even split between increases and decreases. Walmart made 68,926 changes with 53% being discounts; Kroger made 55,601 changes also roughly even. Fashion led all categories with 427,340 price changes. Target's changes skewed most heavily to discounts at 53.5%, while electronics retailer Newegg leaned most into increases at 59.4%.
Amazon changing prices 116,000 times in a year works out to roughly 318 times per day, which is either algorithmic precision or what happens when you let an AI play the stock market with shampoo.
Walmart's Sparky Users Spend 35% More — The AI Assistant Revenue Proof Point
AI Commerce / Retail Media
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Walmart CEO John Furner disclosed on the Q4 call that customers using Sparky, the company's AI-powered shopping assistant, have an average order value approximately 35% higher than those who don't. This is the most concrete ROI metric to emerge from agentic retail pilots to date, and gives Walmart a strong commercial case for continued AI investment. Analysts are now tracking Sparky engagement as a leading indicator alongside Walmart Connect ad revenue.
Sparky users spending 35% more is either proof that AI-assisted shopping dramatically improves outcomes, or proof that talking to a friendly chatbot is the retail equivalent of shopping hungry, results vary by use case.
Blue Yonder Expands Agentic AI Across Supply Chain — Real-Time Issue Resolution Live
Supply Chain AI / Logistics Tech
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Blue Yonder has expanded its agentic AI capabilities across retail, manufacturing, and warehouse management, with automated issue detection now correlating active loads with weather advisories and optimising sourcing in real time. The update includes a new mobile orchestrator and Microsoft Teams integration. The announcement comes as 85% of supply chain executives surveyed by Accenture say they're increasing AI spend with one in five planning increases of up to 20%, driven by geopolitical volatility, tariff complexity, and last-mile disruption.
🎭
A supply chain agent that reads weather forecasts and reroutes shipments in real time is exactly the kind of technology that makes you wonder why we ever tolerated a system where someone had to notice the weather themselves.
Shopify AI Orders 15x Higher — But Only 12 of Millions of Merchants Are Using Checkout
Agentic Commerce / Merchant Adoption
🇺🇸 US
→ Read more
Despite AI-referred orders growing at exceptional rates, adoption of actual AI checkout remains minimal: Shopify President Harley Finkelstein noted that only around a dozen of the platform's millions of merchants are using AI tools to sell products. eMarketer projects AI platforms will account for 1.5% of total ecommerce sales in 2026 or $20.9 billion  nearly quadruple 2025 levels. The constraint isn't consumer intent; it's agent infrastructure maturity and merchant readiness.
AI shopping is growing 15x from a base where 12 merchants are participating, which is either the most exciting growth story in commerce or proof that 'exponential growth' and 'meaningful scale' are not the same sentence.
Visa & Mastercard Building Agent Payment Tokens — 'A Fifth Party in the Value Chain'
Payments / Agentic Infrastructure
🌐 ROW
→ Read more
Visa and Mastercard are building cryptographic agent payment tokens credentials that allow authorised AI agents to complete transactions on behalf of users without ever accessing card numbers directly. Mastercard's EVP for Core Payments described the shift as moving from 'digital to intelligent.' Both networks have completed initial pilots. A key unresolved challenge: liability when agents make mistakes. As Visa's APAC head noted, there is now 'a fifth player in the value chain' AI platforms, and dispute frameworks have not yet caught up.
Building a payment system that allows AI agents to make purchases on your behalf while disputes frameworks are still being designed is the financial infrastructure equivalent of building the plane while flying it,  only the plane can also buy things.

Sticky.io
